note: Activity detail content. Titles, TAT, M/M and stage windows are NOT duplicated here — join on the id against docs/stage-template-v2.json.

purpose: Turn what customers and the market are asking for into one ranked, signed requirement set that the whole program is measured against.

Everything downstream is an answer to this list — the PPA targets, the cost model, the feasibility call, the architecture itself. Until it is baselined and signed, every one of those answers is provisional. A requirement that arrives in week 30 costs roughly a hundred times what it costs here, and the difference is paid in silicon.

steps.text: Anchor-customer interviews — two accounts, six sessions
Market and analyst input, segment sizing
Conflict resolution and MoSCoW prioritisation workshop
Traceability tagging to candidate KPIs and PPA targets

DEF-01.flowNote: Seven steps add up to 5.5 weeks of work inside a 4-week window — steps 3 and 6 run alongside the main sequence. That is why the activity TAT and the sum of its steps do not match, and why pulling either parallel step onto the critical path costs a further 1.5 weeks.
consumes: Field feedback and errata from the previous generation
produces: Requirement register — ID, owner, priority, acceptance measure

rel.text: Product requirements document (PRD). The register is the PRD's body — this activity is where the deliverable's content comes from, not merely a contributor to it.
Target specification — PPA and KPI table. Each ranked requirement becomes a KPI line that DEF-03 turns into a number. An untraced target is a target nobody asked for.
Product cost and margin model. Supplies the volume, segment and ASP assumptions the model is built on.
Feasibility report. DEF-07 tests this list against the candidate nodes — a feasibility study run against a different list proves nothing.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. The gate reads the sign-off sheet. An unsigned register is a No-Go condition, not a footnote.

risks: Requirements not signed off by all stakeholders. Sales agreeing verbally is not a signature, and the Go / No-Go gate reads signatures.
Late customer additions after baseline. With no change-control channel agreed at sign-off, the register keeps moving and nothing downstream can freeze.
Requirements written as solutions. "Use HBM3E" is an answer; "819 GB/s sustained" is a requirement. Solutions here remove the architect's options in ARCH-02.
No acceptance measure. A requirement that cannot be tested resurfaces at qualification, when the only remaining fix is a respin or a waiver.
One anchor account dominating the list. Requirements that fit a single customer and no segment turn a product into a bespoke part carrying a product's cost structure.

roles.d: Owns the register and the baseline
One per anchor account, through the interview window
Flags requirements the node cannot carry

entry: Program charter drafted and funded to study
exit: Every requirement has an owner, a priority and an acceptance measure
Conflicts resolved, or deferred with a named decision owner
Register baselined and signed by product, engineering and sales
DEF-01.dependsNote: Nothing upstream — this is the program's first activity. Its preconditions are the entry criteria above.
measuredBy: Requirements baselined against the expected count
Share carrying an acceptance measure
Change requests raised after baseline

purpose: The requirement register says what customers want. This says what the silicon has to do — the workloads it will actually run, and the KPI numbers derived from them.

A KPI with no workload behind it is a marketing number. ARCH-01 spends fourteen weeks simulating against whatever this activity hands over; if the traces are not representative of the deployed mix, the architecture is optimised for a workload nobody runs, and nothing in verification will catch it.

steps.text: Use-case shortlist drawn from the requirement register
Workload trace capture — LLM inference, vision, recommendation
Reference runs on the previous generation for a baseline
KPI derivation — TOPS, TOPS/W, tokens/s, time-to-first-token, batch scaling
Precision and quantisation policy — INT8, FP8, mixed
Sensitivity study — which KPI moves with which architectural knob
Workload suite packaging and handoff to architecture

DEF-02.flowNote: The main sequence fills the 5-week window exactly. Steps 3 and 5 ride alongside it — the reference runs need lab time rather than analyst time, and the precision policy can be settled while traces are still being captured.
consumes: Customer-supplied models and traces, where the NDA allows
Previous-generation silicon and its lab platform
Public model zoo and framework benchmarks
Deployment mix estimates from the segment sizing
produces: Workload suite — traces, models, and the harness to run them
KPI derivation worksheet, one row per requirement
Sensitivity table — KPI against architectural knob
Baseline measurements on the previous generation

rel.text: Target specification — PPA and KPI table. The KPI half of the deliverable is derived here; DEF-03 supplies the PPA half.
Product requirements document. The use-case list and the deployment mix are written back into the PRD as the context the requirements sit in.
Feasibility report. Feasibility is tested against these KPI numbers, not against the requirement prose.

risks: Traces that flatter the design. A workload suite assembled from what runs well on the previous generation will not find the case that breaks the new one.
Customer models unavailable under NDA. Substituting a public proxy is legitimate; not recording that a proxy was used is not.
Deployment mix guessed rather than sized. The architecture is tuned to the mix; a wrong mix misallocates silicon area that cannot be recovered later.
Precision policy left open. INT8 versus FP8 changes the datapath, the memory footprint and the KPI at once, and the decision gets more expensive every week it waits.
KPIs quoted without conditions. TOPS with no batch size, no sequence length and no precision is not a number anyone can design against.

roles.d: Owns the suite and the KPI derivation
Trace capture, reference runs, precision study
Takes the handoff and confirms it is modellable

entry: Requirement register at v0.9 or better
Lab access to the previous-generation platform
NDA coverage for any customer-supplied model
exit: Every KPI traces to a named workload and stated conditions
Workload suite runs end to end on the reference platform
Architecture has accepted the handoff as modellable
measuredBy: KPIs traceable to a workload
Workload suite runtime on the reference platform
Spread between the sensitivity study and the eventual ARCH-01 model

purpose: Convert the KPI set into the three numbers the design is actually held to — frequency, power envelope, die area — and allocate them so every block owner inherits a share rather than a slogan.

An unallocated target is not a target. "75 W board power" binds nobody until it is decomposed into a die budget, a per-domain budget and a per-block budget with an owner against each. That decomposition is what makes an overrun visible in week 20 instead of week 60.

steps.text: Frequency target from the KPI set and expected IPC
Power envelope decomposition — board, package, die, per-domain
Die area budget from the block list and the reuse inventory
Multi-Vt and operating voltage strategy, first pass
PPA sensitivity against the candidate nodes
Per-block allocation with a named owner against each budget
Target review with architecture and physical design

DEF-03.flowNote: Allocation is the step that matters and it sits late, because it cannot start until the block list is stable. Steps 4 and 5 run in parallel with the budget work — both are inputs to the review rather than to the budgets themselves.
consumes: Block list and reuse inventory from the architecture sketch
Thermal and board constraints from the requirement register
produces: Frequency target with the IPC assumption behind it
Power budget tree — board to per-domain

rel.text: Target specification — PPA and KPI table. The PPA half of the deliverable. DEF-02 supplies the KPI half; the two are published as one table.
Feasibility report. These are the numbers DEF-07 asks each candidate node to carry.
Product cost and margin model. The die area budget is the model's largest single input.

risks: Targets set from ambition rather than from the node. A frequency target the library cannot reach turns into an eighteen-month argument that ends in a respin or a reduced bin.
Power budget with no margin. A budget allocated to 100% at definition has nothing left for the ECO storm at physical design, when power always grows.
Area budget without the reuse inventory. Budgets set before knowing which blocks are reused assign area to work that will not happen and starve work that will.
Allocation without owners. An unowned budget is a budget nobody defends, and it is spent by whoever moves first.
Targets frozen before DEF-07 reports. Feasibility can only return a verdict against targets; setting them beyond reach makes the verdict meaningless.

roles.d: Owns the budget tree and the allocation
Frequency and IPC assumptions, block list
Reality-checks the frequency and area against the node
Arbitrates when blocks contest the same budget

entry: Block list stable enough to allocate against
At least two candidate nodes characterised by TECH-03
exit: Frequency, power and area targets each carry a stated assumption
Every block has an allocated budget and a named owner
Architecture and physical design have signed the review
measuredBy: Share of the die budget allocated to a named owner
Margin held back against each budget
Delta between these targets and the ARCH-06 allocation

purpose: Price the product before anyone commits to building it. Wafer, mask, package, test and yield fold into one model that says what the part costs at volume and whether the margin survives.

The cost model is also the veto. A design that meets every KPI and misses the cost ceiling is not a product, and the only cheap moment to discover that is here — while the die size is still an estimate rather than a floorplan.

steps.text: Die area estimate from the block list and the reuse inventory
Wafer cost and gross die per wafer, per node candidate
Defect density and yield model per node candidate
Package and substrate cost — interposer, substrate layers, HBM stacks
Test cost model — sort and final, with a test-time assumption
Sensitivity — the three assumptions the model is most exposed to

DEF-04.flowNote: The sensitivity step is not optional decoration. A 2.5D part's cost is dominated by yield, interposer supply and HBM price, and each of those is an assumption rather than a quote at this point in the program.
consumes: Wafer, mask and NRE quotations from TECH-04
Package architecture assumption from the requirement register
Volume forecast and ASP from the segment sizing
produces: Cost model workbook — wafer, package, test, yield
Gross die and yield curves per node candidate
Margin roll-up at the forecast volume
Sensitivity analysis on the three dominant assumptions
Cost ceiling statement for the design

rel.text: Product cost and margin model. This activity is the deliverable — the workbook and its assumptions are handed over intact, not summarised.
Feasibility report. A node that meets the PPA targets and breaks the cost ceiling is recorded as infeasible, and this model is what says so.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. The funding decision is a margin decision. A model that does not close is a No-Go condition.

risks: Yield assumed from a mature node. Defect density at a node in early ramp is not the number in the foundry's marketing chart, and the gap lands entirely in margin.
Package cost treated as a rounding error. On a 2.5D part with two HBM stacks the package can approach the die cost; modelling it as an adder hides the largest controllable line.
Test cost with no test time. Test cost is test time multiplied by tester rate; without a time assumption from DFT the line is decorative.
Single-point ASP. An ASP with no downside scenario turns the margin into a number nobody can be held to.
Die size estimate carried without a tolerance. An area estimate that later grows 15% moves gross die per wafer non-linearly, and the model reports it as a small change.

roles.d: Owns the model and its assumptions
Defect density and yield curves per node
Test time and tester rate assumptions

entry: Die area budget available from DEF-03
Wafer and mask quotations received from TECH-04
exit: Cost model closes at the forecast volume with stated margin
Every assumption is named, sourced and dated
Sensitivity identifies the three exposures and their range
measuredBy: Margin at forecast volume against the target
Share of model inputs backed by a quotation rather than an estimate
Cost delta carried by the sensitivity range

purpose: Fix the bandwidth the workloads need at each level of the hierarchy, and turn that into the interface count the package and the floorplan will have to carry.

Bandwidth is where a specification becomes physical. Two HBM stacks rather than one is not a line in a document; it is a larger interposer, a different substrate, a bigger power envelope and a different cost model. Deciding it here is cheap and deciding it at architecture is not.

steps.text: Bandwidth demand per workload, from the DEF-02 traces
Memory hierarchy sizing — on-die SRAM, HBM capacity and channels
Host interface sizing — PCIe / CXL generation and lane count
Die-to-die interface requirement, if a chiplet split is a candidate
Translation into a pin and bump budget
Requirement review with architecture and package

DEF-05.flowNote: Step 5 is the one that binds. Bandwidth stated in GB/s commits nobody; the same number stated as a bump count commits the floorplan, the package and the cost model at once.
consumes: Workload traces and KPI table from DEF-02
Requirement register — capacity and latency requirements
Interface standard revisions in flight (PCIe, CXL, UCIe)
produces: Bandwidth demand table, per workload and per hierarchy level
Memory configuration recommendation — capacity, stacks, channels
Review record with architecture and package

rel.text: Product requirements document. Bandwidth and capacity enter the PRD as requirements with numbers rather than as adjectives.
Target specification. The bandwidth figures become KPI lines, and the bump budget becomes an area constraint on the PPA half.

risks: Bandwidth sized on peak rather than sustained. Peak numbers size an interface nobody reaches and a cost nobody wanted.
Capacity and bandwidth conflated. HBM stack count is often set by capacity while the argument is conducted in GB/s; the two constraints do not move together.
Interface standard still in revision. Committing to a generation whose specification is not final transfers a standards-body schedule into the program's schedule.
Bump budget never derived. A bandwidth requirement that is not translated into bumps is discovered as a floorplan problem at PD-04, when the package is already ordered.
Chiplet option left open too long. A die-to-die interface is a large architectural commitment; deferring it past architecture freeze forces the conservative choice by default.

roles.d: Owns the hierarchy sizing and the bandwidth table
Sustained demand extraction from the traces
Confirms the bump budget is buildable

entry: Requirement register carries capacity and latency requirements
HBM and interface roadmaps available under NDA
exit: Bandwidth stated as sustained, per workload, with conditions
Memory configuration and interface count recommended with a reason
Bump budget accepted as buildable by package
measuredBy: Bandwidth headroom against sustained demand
Bump budget against the package's stated capability
Interface revisions still open at architecture freeze

purpose: Establish where the part lands against what will be shipping when it ships — not against what ships today.

A benchmark against the current generation is a comfortable exercise and a useless one. The program's silicon arrives thirty months out; the comparison that matters is against the parts that will be launching in that window, projected from public roadmaps and node cadence.

steps.text: Competitor set definition and launch-window mapping
Public benchmark, datasheet and disclosure collection
Normalisation to comparable metrics and conditions
Projection to our own launch window
Positioning statement and capability gap list

DEF-06.flowNote: Normalisation runs in parallel because it is slow, thankless and independent of collection — vendors quote TOPS at different precisions, batch sizes and power points, and none of the published numbers compare until they are restated.
consumes: Competitor datasheets, disclosures and conference material
Foundry node cadence and process roadmaps
produces: Normalised comparison table with stated conditions
Projection of the competitive field at our launch

rel.text: Product requirements document. The gap list becomes requirements — a gap nobody writes down is a gap nobody closes.
Product cost and margin model. Competitive positioning is what an ASP assumption is defended with.

risks: Benchmarking against today's field. The comparison that decides the product is against parts launching thirty months out, and those numbers have to be projected rather than read.
Vendor numbers taken at face value. TOPS quoted at a precision, batch size and power point chosen to flatter is not a comparable number until it is restated.
Gap list with no owner. A capability gap that does not become a requirement is an observation, and observations do not change silicon.
Positioning built on a single axis. A part positioned only on TOPS/W loses to one positioned on total cost of ownership, and the argument is not had until launch.
Competitor launch dates treated as fixed. A slip in the competitive field is as consequential as a slip in ours, and neither is knowable to a quarter.

roles.d: Owns the competitor set and the positioning
Turns the gap list into requirements

entry: Product concept defined well enough to name a competitor set
Access to analyst material and benchmark submissions
Launch-window assumption from the program schedule
exit: Every comparison is normalised to stated conditions
Field projected to our launch window, not read from today
Gap list handed to DEF-01 as candidate requirements
measuredBy: Competitors covered against the expected launch field
Share of comparisons normalised rather than quoted
Gaps converted into tracked requirements

purpose: Test the requirement set, the PPA targets and the cost model against real nodes and return a verdict: buildable as specified, buildable with named concessions, or not buildable.

Feasibility is the only activity in the stage whose output can be "no". Its value is entirely in being allowed to say so — a feasibility study run after the node is chosen and the budget is committed is a formality, and formalities do not stop programs that should be stopped.

steps.text: Candidate node shortlist agreed with TECH
PPA achievability per node — density, frequency, leakage
IP availability check per node, ahead of IPR
Package and thermal feasibility at the target power
Concession list — what must be given up, per node

DEF-07.flowNote: The concession list is the deliverable that gets used. A binary verdict tells the decision room nothing it can act on; a list saying "this node, at 200 MHz less, with the PHY bought rather than built" is a decision it can take.
consumes: Node characterisation and DTCO study from TECH-03
IP availability indications from vendors and internal inventory
produces: Feasibility verdict with a named recommendation

rel.text: Feasibility report. This activity is the deliverable. The verdict, the matrix and the concession list are published together — the verdict alone is not usable.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. A No-Go recommendation here is the only mechanism in the stage that stops the program, and it must reach the room unedited.

risks: Feasibility run after the node is already chosen. The study then documents a decision rather than informing one, and its independence is gone.
Optimism at the boundary. A target reachable "with aggressive closure" is a target reachable in a slide and not in a timing report.
IP availability taken from the vendor's roadmap. A block promised on the node and not yet ported is a schedule risk being recorded as an asset.
Thermal checked at typical rather than at the envelope. Feasibility at average power says nothing about the part at its rated envelope, which is the condition it is sold at.
No concession list. A bare yes or no gives the decision room no third option, and the third option is usually the right one.

roles.d: Owns the verdict and the concession list
Achievability per node against the DEF-03 targets
Availability and porting status per node
Feasibility at the rated power envelope
Carries the recommendation into the gate

entry: At least two nodes characterised by TECH-03
exit: Every target has an achievability finding per candidate node
Concessions named and costed, not described
Verdict recorded with a recommendation and a dissent record
measuredBy: Targets assessed against every candidate node
Concessions accepted at the gate against those raised
Findings later contradicted by ARCH-01 modelling

purpose: Turn the milestone profile into a dated plan for this program, and say what it takes in people — then set that against the people who actually exist.

A schedule that assumes a headcount curve the organisation cannot staff is not a plan; it is a forecast of a slip. The value of this activity is the comparison, not the Gantt chart: effort rolled up by stage and discipline, against the capacity on hand.

steps.text: Stage baseline adjustment for this program's scope
Effort roll-up by stage and by discipline
Headcount curve set against the organisation's real capacity
External lead-time overlay — substrate, probe card, IP, shuttle
Risk buffer placement and critical path identification

DEF-08.flowNote: The lead-time overlay runs in parallel and changes more dates than the internal plan does. A twenty-week probe card and a twenty-week substrate are ordered against dates this activity sets, and both sit outside the organisation's control once placed.
consumes: Effort figures per activity from the template
Organisation capacity and current program commitments
Supplier lead times — substrate, interposer, probe card, IP, shuttle
produces: Program schedule with dated stage boundaries and milestones
Effort roll-up by stage and discipline
Critical path and buffer placement record

rel.text: Program charter, staffing and budget plan. The schedule, the headcount curve and the effort roll-up are the charter's operative content.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. The gate approves a schedule and a headcount. An unresourced plan is a No-Go condition.

risks: Headcount curve nobody can staff. A peak of 200 engineers in a 120-engineer organisation is a slip already committed to, recorded as a plan.
Template baselines used unadjusted. The profile describes a typical program; a derivative or a first-of-node program is not typical, and the deltas belong in the plan.
Lead times discovered rather than planned. Probe card and substrate lead times run to twenty weeks; found late they move wafer-out, not the purchasing date.
Buffer at the end. A buffer placed after the last stage protects nothing; buffers belong in front of the gates that cannot move.

Critical path asserted rather than derived. On a 23-stage profile with parallel enablement workstreams the critical path is rarely the design spine, and assuming it is misdirects the attention that matters.

roles.d: Owns the schedule, the buffers and the critical path
Capacity, headcount curve and hiring plan
Confirm the effort roll-up for their stages
Supplier lead times and order-by dates

effort: Effort roll-up by stage and discipline
entry: Scope stable enough to adjust baselines against
exit: Schedule dated from a committed kickoff
Headcount curve reconciled against real capacity, gaps named
Critical path derived and buffers placed against the fixed gates
measuredBy: Peak headcount against available capacity
Buffer weeks held in front of fixed gates
Long-lead items with an order-by date on the plan

purpose: Assemble what the stage produced into the case the funding decision is made on, and put a named recommendation in front of the people who can say no.

This activity writes nothing new. Its work is selection and honesty: the feasibility verdict, the cost model and the resourced schedule carried into the room intact, with the downside scenario shown rather than described. A business case that only closes in the base case has not been reviewed.

steps.text: Financial model assembly — NRE, opex, revenue, breakeven
Risk register summary written for the decision room
Recommendation and the ask, stated as a number

DEF-09.flowNote: The decision meeting is a quarter of a week and the preparation is three weeks, which is the correct ratio. A gate that is argued in the room rather than before it is a gate whose outcome depends on who attends.
consumes: Cost and margin model from DEF-04
Feasibility verdict and concession list from DEF-07
Resourced schedule and headcount curve from DEF-08
Positioning and gap list from DEF-06
produces: Financial model — NRE, opex, revenue, breakeven
Scenario set with the downside made explicit
Risk summary for the decision room
Decision record with owners, conditions and dissent

rel.text: Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. This activity is the deliverable — the record, its conditions and its dissent, not the slides that preceded it.
Program charter, staffing and budget plan. The charter is only funded once this decision lands; the approved figure is written back into it.

risks: Base case only. A case that closes at forecast volume and is never shown at downside volume transfers the risk to whoever inherits the program.
Conditions accepted verbally. A Go granted "subject to" something nobody wrote down is a Go, and the condition is never revisited.
Dissent unrecorded. The objection nobody minuted is the objection that resurfaces at first silicon with nothing to point at.
Feasibility concessions edited on the way to the room. A concession list softened in the pack is the one failure mode that makes the whole stage worthless.
Decision owners unclear. A gate where nobody is identified as able to say no is a gate that cannot say no.

roles.d: Owns the pack, the ask and the record
Revenue, positioning and the market case
Chairs the decision and owns the outcome

exit: Case shown at base and downside, not base alone
Decision recorded with named owners, conditions and dissent
Approved budget written back into the program charter
measuredBy: Scenarios presented against those prepared
Conditions attached to the decision and their owners
Days from pack circulation to decision

purpose: Build the model the architecture is argued with. Every partitioning, sizing and interface decision in this stage is settled by simulation against the DEF-02 workload suite rather than by opinion.

Fourteen weeks and 28 M/M make this the largest activity in the stage by a wide margin, and that is the right shape. Being wrong in a model costs a re-run; being wrong in RTL costs a quarter; being wrong in silicon costs a respin. The model's credibility is the stage's credibility — the moment nobody trusts it, every decision reverts to seniority.

steps.text: Model scope and fidelity decision — analytical, trace-driven or cycle-approximate
Baseline model construction — compute, memory, interconnect
Design-space exploration sweeps — cluster count, SRAM capacity, HBM channels
Power model overlay and TOPS/W projection
Sensitivity analysis and a stated confidence interval
Model handoff and regression harness for later stages

ARCH-01.flowNote: Correlation sits early on purpose. A model that has never been checked against silicon produces numbers, not answers, and every sweep run before correlation has to be re-run afterwards.
consumes: Workload suite and KPI table from DEF-02
Previous-generation silicon and its measured performance
produces: Sensitivity analysis with a confidence statement

rel.text: Performance model and workload analysis report. The model, its correlation and its confidence statement are the deliverable — the report without the model is an assertion.
Architecture specification. Every quantitative claim in the specification traces back to a sweep in this model, or it does not belong in the specification.
Block partitioning and PPA budget table. The sweeps are what decide cluster count and SRAM capacity before ARCH-02 draws the boundaries.

risks: Model never correlated against silicon. An uncorrelated model has an unknown error bar, and every decision taken on it inherits that error silently.
Fidelity chosen for comfort. An analytical model that runs in seconds will answer the wrong question quickly; a cycle-accurate model that takes a week per sweep will answer nothing in time to matter.
Sweeps run on an unrepresentative workload. The model inherits whatever bias DEF-02 built into the suite, and amplifies it across every architectural decision.
Power model bolted on at the end. TOPS/W is a KPI; a performance model with no power overlay cannot answer the question the product is sold on.
No confidence statement. A projection quoted as a single number invites the organisation to plan against a precision the model does not have.

roles.d: Owns the model, its fidelity and its confidence statement
Model construction, sweeps and the regression harness

entry: Workload suite delivered and runnable from DEF-02
exit: Model correlated against silicon with a stated error band
Every architectural decision in the stage traced to a sweep
Regression harness handed over so later stages can re-run it
measuredBy: Correlation error against previous-generation silicon
Architectural decisions supported by a sweep
Model re-run turnaround once a parameter changes

purpose: Decide what sits on which die and where the block boundaries fall — including whether this is one die or several.

The monolithic-versus-chiplet call is the most expensive decision in the stage. It sets the package, the die-to-die interface, the test strategy, the yield model and the cost model at once, and after Architecture Freeze it is effectively irreversible: unwinding it means redoing the floorplan, the package design and the test hardware together.

steps.text: Block decomposition from the functional requirements
Reticle limit and die size feasibility check
Monolithic and chiplet options built as costed candidates
Yield and cost comparison per candidate, with the DEF-04 model
Partition boundary definition — what crosses, at what bandwidth

ARCH-02.flowNote: Boundary definition takes three of the eight weeks because it is the part that gets skipped. Deciding "two dies" is quick; deciding exactly which signals cross at what bandwidth and latency is the work that makes the decision real.
consumes: Cost and yield model from DEF-04
Reticle limit and node constraints from TECH-02
Package architecture options from the requirement register
produces: Partition boundary specification — signals, bandwidth, latency
Yield and cost comparison per candidate

rel.text: Block partitioning and PPA budget table. The partitioning half of the deliverable; ARCH-06 supplies the budget half against these blocks.
Architecture specification. The partition and its boundaries are the specification's structural spine — every other section is written against them.
Chip-level block diagram with pin and bump budget. ARCH-08 draws what this activity decides.

risks: Chiplet chosen for the roadmap rather than for this product. A die-to-die interface costs area, power and a test strategy; taking it on to be ready for the next program charges this one.
Boundaries drawn without bandwidth. A partition that names blocks but not the traffic between them is redrawn at PD-02 when the floorplan cannot carry it.
Reticle limit checked against the estimate, not the growth. Die area grows through implementation; a partition that fits at architecture and not at signoff is a partition that fails late.
Test implications deferred. Known-good-die coverage on a chiplet part is a DFT and test-hardware programme of its own, and it is priced after the decision is taken.
Decision recorded without the dissent. The objection nobody minuted resurfaces at first silicon with nothing to point at.

roles.d: Owns the partitioning decision and its record
Candidate comparison against the DEF-04 model

entry: First design-space results available from ARCH-01
Cost model usable for candidate comparison
Reticle and node constraints confirmed by TECH
exit: Partitioning decided and recorded with the alternatives it beat
Every boundary carries a bandwidth and latency budget
Test and yield implications priced, not deferred
measuredBy: Candidates evaluated against the one chosen
Boundaries carrying an agreed bandwidth budget
Partition changes raised after Architecture Freeze

purpose: Define how data moves and where it lives — dataflow, on-die SRAM capacity and organisation, HBM channel count — for each workload class the product serves.

An inference accelerator is a memory system with arithmetic attached. A hierarchy that does not match the reuse pattern of the workload shows up as a utilisation number nobody can lift afterwards: not by clock speed, not by more compute, and not by any amount of software.

steps.text: Dataflow selection per workload class — weight-stationary, output-stationary, hybrid
On-die SRAM capacity sizing against measured reuse distance
SRAM banking, port and bandwidth organisation
HBM channel count and address interleaving scheme
Hierarchy simulation against the ARCH-01 model

ARCH-03.flowNote: Sizing precedes simulation and simulation revises sizing — the two weeks in step 7 include at least one full turn back through step 2. A hierarchy accepted on its first simulation has almost certainly not been swept.
consumes: Workload traces and reuse analysis from DEF-02
produces: SRAM capacity, banking and port organisation
HBM channel count and interleaving scheme

rel.text: Architecture specification. The memory hierarchy chapter is authored here and lands in the specification whole; ARCH-09 assembles rather than rewrites it.
Block partitioning and PPA budget table. SRAM capacity is the largest single area line in the budget, and it is decided here.
Performance model and workload analysis report. The hierarchy sweeps are run in the ARCH-01 model and reported with it.

risks: SRAM sized on average reuse. Reuse distance has a tail; a capacity chosen at the median misses the workloads that define the product's worst case.
Banking decided after capacity. Capacity and bandwidth are separate constraints, and a bank organisation that cannot feed the compute wastes the area it took.
Memory compiler capability assumed. The instance the hierarchy needs may not exist on the node — PDK-05 is where that is found, and it is found after this decision unless someone asks early.
Dataflow chosen once for all workloads. A single dataflow optimised for one class starves another, and the deployment mix decides which mistake is cheaper.
Interleaving left to implementation. Address interleaving decides whether HBM channels are actually parallel; deferred, it becomes a bandwidth shortfall nobody predicted.

roles.d: Owns the hierarchy and its specification
Hierarchy sweeps in the ARCH-01 model

entry: Reuse analysis available from the DEF-02 traces
Memory compiler capability indicated by PDK-04
exit: Capacity and bandwidth justified by simulation, not by precedent
Dataflow chosen per workload class with the trade recorded
Memory instance requirements handed to PDK and AMS

Interfaces are where the program touches standards bodies and IP vendors, neither of which runs on the program's calendar. A generation selected before its specification is ratified imports someone else's schedule into this one, and the import is silent until the PHY is late.

Power intent is one of the few architectural artifacts consumed literally by tools. A domain boundary drawn here becomes isolation and level-shifter cells at SYN-06 and a verification obligation at DV-06. Drawn late, or drawn differently by two teams, it forces both to be redone.

risks: Domains drawn for elegance rather than for control. Every domain boundary costs isolation cells, level shifters and verification states; a domain that is never independently gated is pure overhead.
Crossing inventory incomplete. A clock crossing missing from the inventory is a crossing nobody constrains and nobody verifies, and it fails intermittently in silicon.
DVFS policy without measured operating points. Operating points chosen from the library rather than from silicon leave either performance or margin on the table.
UPF drafted after RTL starts. Power intent that arrives mid-RTL forces retrofitting into blocks already written, and the retrofit is never as clean as the design.
Reset sequencing left to bring-up. A reset order discovered in the lab is discovered on silicon that cannot be changed.

Allocation without acceptance. An unaccepted budget is defended by nobody and consumed by whoever moves first.

purpose: Define how the part boots trustworthily, protects its assets and identifies itself — secure boot chain, root of trust, key storage, fuse map and lifecycle states — and the debug lockdown that goes with them.

Security is architectural or it is absent. A root of trust cannot be retrofitted onto a design with no immutable boot path and no fuse plan. The tension worth naming early is that the debug access DFT and bring-up want is the same access an attacker wants, and only an architecture can resolve it.

Root of trust and key storage selection
Fuse map, chip identity and lifecycle state definition
Debug and test access lockdown policy, with DFT

ARCH-07.flowNote: Step 5 is a negotiation, not a decision taken alone. DFT-04 needs JTAG and trace access for silicon debug, and every path it opens is a path this activity has to close in production lifecycle states.
consumes: Security requirements from the requirement register
Block list and boot architecture from ARCH-02
eFuse and OTP capability from PDK-02
DFT access architecture intent from DFT-04
produces: Root of trust and key storage architecture
Fuse map and lifecycle state definition

rel.text: Architecture specification. The security chapter is authored here in full — boot chain, lifecycle states and lockdown policy — and lands in the specification whole.
Power / clock / reset architecture. Secure boot constrains the reset sequence: the root of trust must run before anything else is released from reset.

risks: Security started after the block list is fixed. A root of trust needs its own reset domain, its own ROM and its own fuse path; adding them later disturbs three architectures at once.
Debug access left open in production. The lifecycle state that locks JTAG is the one nobody tests, because testing it makes the part undebuggable.
Fuse map without a lifecycle model. Fuses are one-time; a map with no defined state transitions produces parts that cannot be returned to a testable state.
Key storage decided by IP availability. Choosing the root of trust because a block was available is choosing a threat model by accident.
No named security owner past architecture. Security decisions get eroded one waiver at a time through implementation unless someone owns them all the way to qualification.

Fuse map, chip identity, state transitions

The bump map is the first artifact the die and the package share, and the first hard constraint on bandwidth. An interface needing more bumps than the field can supply is an interface that has to shrink, and having that argument here costs a meeting. Having it at PD-04, with the substrate already ordered, costs the substrate.

Power delivery bumps underestimated. Too few power bumps is an IR-drop problem discovered at SIPI-04, when the bump map is already in the package design.

purpose: Write the document the rest of the program builds against, and run it through the review that ends in Architecture Freeze.

The specification is not a record of decisions already taken; writing it is what exposes the decisions nobody took. Every downstream stage reads this document, and every ambiguity left in it becomes an argument in RTL, a bug in verification, or a waiver at signoff. The consistency pass matters as much as the authoring.

Section authoring across the architecture team

Consistency pass skipped under schedule pressure. The same number appearing differently in two chapters is the defect that costs the most and is found the latest.
Downstream teams reviewing after freeze. A readiness review that happens after the gate cannot change anything, and becomes a complaint rather than a review.
Specification written as a narrative. Implementable specifications are tables, interfaces and constraints; prose is where ambiguity survives review.
Freeze treated as a date rather than a condition. A gate that passes because it was scheduled to teaches the organisation that gates do not mean anything.

The architecture specification says what each block does; this says how. Starting it inside the architecture stage rather than at RTL kickoff is what lets RTL-02 begin with something to write against instead of a paragraph — and it is the cheapest place to find out that two blocks disagree about the interface between them.

Interfaces written from one side. Each owner specifying their own side of a shared interface produces two consistent documents that disagree with each other.
Register map deferred to RTL. The register map is the software contract; defining it late means firmware development starts late and the two never converge.

Every other decision in this stage is conditional on this one, and so is most of the enablement band: IP availability, PDK maturity, library qualification and capacity all become node-specific the moment the short-list closes. The screen has to be quick and it has to be written down — a selection nobody can reconstruct is one that gets reopened at every setback.

A node name is not a specification. Two programs on the same node with different flavour sheets get different density, different leakage and different routing resource, and the difference is larger than most architectural decisions. This sheet is also what the foundry prices against, so it has to close before TECH-04 can finish.

Metal stack chosen without a congestion study. Too few routing layers is the defect that surfaces at PD-06, when the only remaining fix is a floorplan change.
Multi-Vt menu wider than the flow supports. Every extra Vt is a library to characterise, qualify and maintain; menus are chosen for leakage and paid for in methodology.

This is the technical evidence the selection stands on. Published node comparisons are made on somebody else's circuits at somebody else's operating point; a DTCO study run on representative structures is the only way to know whether the PPA targets survive the node, and it is what DEF-07 tests feasibility against.

Preliminary libraries treated as final. Early PDK models move, sometimes by more than the difference between the candidates, and a comparison made on 0.5 data can invert.
SRAM left out. On an accelerator the array is a large fraction of the die; a node comparison without a bitcell and Vmin study has skipped the dominant area and the dominant Vmin constraint.
Congestion never modelled. Density that cannot be routed is not density, and the routing resource question is decided by the metal stack chosen in TECH-02.
Results reported without margin. A target met exactly in a DTCO study will not be met in implementation, and reporting the number without the margin invites the wrong conclusion.

Capacity is not bought at tapeout; it is reserved a year before, against a date that will move. The commitment matters most in its escalation path: when the schedule slips or the market tightens, what the program has is whatever was written down, and a verbal understanding is worth exactly nothing at that moment.

Slot date against the DEF-08 tapeout date

purpose: Put the legal frame in place that everything technical depends on — NDA, design agreement, PDK and library licensing, the foundry IP frame, and liability terms — and execute it.

This is the longest activity in the stage at eight weeks and one of the smallest at 2 M/M, which is exactly the shape it should have: the elapsed time belongs to two legal departments and almost none of the work belongs to the program. It is on the critical path anyway, because production PDK access, memory compilers and foundry IP all sit behind the design agreement.

steps.text: NDA execution, to open technical discussion
Foundry IP licensing frame — memory compilers, IO, PHY
Execution and distribution to the teams that need it

TECH-06.flowNote: Step 1 is deliberately first and deliberately short. Nothing technical can be discussed before the NDA executes, so every week it takes is a week subtracted from TECH-03 — which is why the NDA is chased separately from the agreement it precedes.
consumes: Corporate legal templates and negotiation positions
IP requirements from ARCH-04 and IPR-01
produces: Distribution record — who is covered to access what

rel.text: Executed foundry design agreement (DA) and NDA. This activity is the deliverable, and until it executes the enablement band cannot legally start.
Capacity and tapeout slot commitment. Capacity is committed under the design agreement; the commitment has no standing without it.

risks: NDA treated as a formality and queued behind the agreement. Technical evaluation is blocked until it executes, and every week lost here is taken out of the DTCO study.
Foundry IP frame left out of scope. Memory compilers and IO libraries are licensed separately from the PDK; discovering that at PDK-04 stops library qualification.
Distribution not tracked. An executed agreement nobody circulated leaves engineers unable to download the PDK they are waiting for, and the delay looks technical.
Yield responsibility left ambiguous. Who owns a process excursion is a term, not a conversation to have after it happens.
Redline cycles unbudgeted. Two legal departments will take longer than either forecasts, and the program's plan should assume the longer number.

roles.d: Owns the agreements and the negotiation
Drives the redline cycles to closure
States what PDK and library access is needed

entry: Short-list narrow enough to engage legally
Corporate legal position and templates available
Compliance guidance for the candidate foundries
exit: NDA and design agreement executed, not merely agreed
PDK, library and foundry IP access all covered by scope
Access distributed to the teams that need it, and tracked
measuredBy: Weeks from engagement to executed NDA
Access requests blocked on missing scope
Redline cycles against those forecast

purpose: Establish where each candidate node actually is on its maturity curve — risk production timing, defect density trend, yield learning rate, capacity ramp — and turn that into a risk assessment the program plans against.

A node chosen at the right time is a node in volume production when the program taped out. A node chosen too early gives the program the foundry's learning curve as a yield problem, and the schedule to absorb it was never in the plan.

steps.text: Node maturity and risk-production timing review
Defect density trend and yield learning curve request
Foundry roadmap alignment against the program schedule
Capacity ramp profile at the node
Node risk assessment and mitigation options

TECH-07.flowNote: Step 2 asks for data the foundry treats as sensitive, and how much of it arrives is itself a signal. A foundry that will not share a defect density trend under NDA is telling the program something about the trend.
consumes: Foundry roadmap and node cadence under NDA
Defect density and yield learning data where available
Program schedule and tapeout date from DEF-08
DTCO findings as they emerge from TECH-03
produces: Defect density trend and yield learning curve
Roadmap alignment note against the program schedule
Node risk assessment with mitigation options

rel.text: Node risk assessment — maturity, defect density, yield learning curve. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what the yield assumption in the cost model should be built on.
Technology selection report. Maturity is a selection criterion in its own right, separate from the PPA the node can deliver.

risks: Marketing defect density used as a planning number. The published curve is a target; the yield the program gets is the curve at its own tapeout date, which is a different point.
Risk production date taken as the availability date. Risk production is when the node exists, not when it is ready for a large die at volume, and the gap can be two quarters.
Roadmap alignment checked once. Foundry roadmaps move; an alignment done at selection and never revisited is a stale assumption by tapeout.
No mitigation options developed. Identifying a maturity risk without a mitigation — a later slot, a shuttle, a conservative design rule set — leaves the program with a finding and no action.
Large-die yield inferred from small-die data. Defect density scales against area brutally, and a curve measured on small test die flatters a 600 mm² part.

roles.d: Owns the maturity and risk assessment
Defect density interpretation and area scaling
Turns the yield curve into a cost assumption

entry: NDA executed far enough to receive roadmap data
Program tapeout date estimated by DEF-08
exit: Yield curve stated at the program's own tapeout date, not in general
Every maturity risk carries at least one mitigation option
Assessment handed to DEF-04 as the model's yield input
measuredBy: Risks identified with a mitigation against those without
Yield assumption against the cost model's requirement
Roadmap revisions after selection

purpose: Decide, deliberately, whether the program accepts single-source risk — and if it does not, what dual-sourcing or migration readiness would cost in area, schedule and IP.

Most leading-edge programs end up single-source, and that is a defensible answer. What is not defensible is arriving there by default. This activity prices the alternative so that the acceptance is a decision with a number attached rather than a shrug.

steps.text: Second-source viability screen at the selected node class
Design rule and library delta analysis
Strategy recommendation — dual-source, migration-ready, or single-source accepted

TECH-08.flowNote: Migration readiness is a design-time choice, not a later option: it constrains which IP can be used and how aggressively design rules can be pushed. Deciding after RTL starts means the decision has already been made by everyone who chose an IP.
consumes: Selected node and flavour from TECH-01 and TECH-02
IP bill of materials direction from IPR-01
Design rule sets for alternative foundries
produces: Design rule and library delta analysis
Sourcing strategy recommendation and decision record

rel.text: Technology selection report and decision record. Single-source acceptance belongs in the selection record, priced, rather than being implied by its absence.
Node risk assessment. Supply concentration is a node risk, and its mitigation is either a second source or an accepted exposure.

risks: Single-source accepted by default. A decision nobody made is a decision nobody owns, and it surfaces during a supply disruption as a surprise.
Migration cost estimated without IP portability. Foundry-specific memory compilers, IO and PHY are the expensive part of a migration, and they are usually the part left out of the estimate.
Migration readiness assumed to be free. Designing to the intersection of two rule sets costs density and frequency on the node actually used.
Decision taken after IP selection. Once IPR-03 has committed to foundry-specific IP, migration readiness is no longer available at the price this study quotes.
Second source screened on capability alone. Capability without allocated capacity is not a second source; it is a phone number.

roles.d: Portability of the IP bill of materials
Design rule and library delta impact
Capacity and commercial viability of an alternative
Carries the accepted exposure into the risk register

entry: IP bill of materials direction available from IPR-01
Design rule sets accessible for at least one alternative
exit: Migration cost estimated with IP portability included
Recommendation recorded, including the option of accepting single source
Accepted exposure entered on the program risk register with an owner
measuredBy: Migration cost estimated against the exposure accepted
IP blocks assessed for portability
Whether the sourcing decision is recorded or implied

purpose: Open the backend supply chain early — OSAT capability and capacity, substrate and interposer suppliers, the foundry-to-OSAT logistics model, and who owns known-good die — so package design starts against real constraints.

On a 2.5D part the backend is not a downstream detail; it is a second supply chain with its own lead times, its own capacity constraints and its own qualification. Advanced packaging capacity in particular is allocated far ahead, and a program that starts asking at PKGD-10 is asking late.

steps.text: OSAT long-list against the package architecture assumption
Advanced packaging capability and capacity screen
Backend supply chain finding and handoff to package design

TECH-09.flowNote: Step 5 decides an argument before it happens. When a packaged unit fails, whether the die or the assembly is responsible is a contractual question, and settling it while nobody has lost money is far easier than settling it afterwards.
consumes: Package architecture assumption from the requirement register
Selected foundry and node from TECH-01
Volume and ramp profile from the business case
OSAT and substrate supplier capability data
Interposer technology options from the foundry
produces: Backend supply chain findings for package design

rel.text: Capacity and tapeout slot commitment. Front-end capacity without matching backend capacity delivers wafers that cannot be assembled.
Wafer, mask and NRE cost sheet. Interposer and assembly pricing is the backend half of the technology cost, and the cost model needs both.
Technology selection report. On a 2.5D part the choice of foundry constrains the interposer options, so backend capability belongs in the selection record.

risks: Advanced packaging capacity assumed available. CoWoS-class capacity is allocated quarters ahead and to a small number of customers; assuming access is the single most common backend planning error.
OSAT chosen after package design starts. Assembly process capability constrains the package design; choosing the OSAT afterwards means redesigning to fit.
Known-good-die responsibility left open. The first failed assembly lot is the wrong moment to discover that nobody agreed who owns the die.
Substrate lead time discovered rather than planned. Twenty-week substrate lead times set the order date, and the order date is derived from a wafer-out date nobody has committed yet.
Logistics model ignored. Wafers crossing borders between fab, sort and assembly carry customs, export control and transit time that the schedule rarely shows.

roles.d: Owns the OSAT and substrate engagement
States the capability the package will need

entry: Package architecture assumption stated in the requirement register
Foundry selected, so interposer options are known
exit: Advanced packaging capacity indicated, not assumed
Known-good-die responsibility model agreed in principle
Findings handed to PKGD before package architecture is chosen
measuredBy: Advanced packaging capacity indicated against the ramp requirement
Weeks between backend engagement and package architecture selection
Substrate lead time against the wafer-out date

purpose: Track what the foundry actually ships, version by version, and turn each release into a delta the program can act on — what changed, what it costs, and whether anything already done has to be redone.

A PDK is not a thing you receive; it is a sequence. Design starts on 0.5 because waiting for production would cost two quarters, and the 0.5-to-1.0 delta then arrives in the middle of physical design. Whether that delta is a two-week re-characterisation or a reopened timing signoff depends entirely on whether anyone was watching.

steps.text: Release calendar and version tracking framework
Gap list maintained against what the design actually needs
Library and deck re-qualification per version
Production PDK adoption and version freeze decision
Version freeze policy and exception handling
Readiness dashboard maintenance across the stage

PDK-01.flowNote: Step 8 runs for twenty of the thirty-four weeks and is the activity most likely to be dropped when the team is busy. It is also the only artifact that tells the program which of its assumptions have quietly expired.
consumes: Foundry PDK release calendar and notes
Selected node and flavour sheet from TECH-01 and TECH-02
Library and deck versions in use across the teams
Design status — what has been characterised against which version
produces: Delta impact analysis per version transition
Open gap list against the design's requirements
Re-qualification record per library and deck
Version freeze decision and exception log

rel.text: PDK readiness dashboard. This activity is the deliverable, and it is a living document rather than a report — its value is entirely in being current.
Qualified library list. Every version transition potentially invalidates a qualification, and this activity is what says which ones.
Golden environment release notes. The environment cannot be released against a version that has not been assessed and frozen.

risks: Design starts on a version the foundry calls preliminary and nobody re-checks. The gap between 0.5 and production has reopened timing signoff on more than one program.
Delta analysis done on the release notes alone. Foundry notes describe what changed; only re-running the design's own characterisation says what it costs here.
Teams on different versions. Synthesis on one library revision and physical design on another produces a mismatch that looks like a tool bug for weeks.
Freeze declared without an exception path. A hard freeze with no route for a critical fix gets broken quietly, which is worse than breaking it openly.
Dashboard maintained until the team gets busy. A stale readiness dashboard is more dangerous than none, because it is still trusted.

roles.d: Owns the dashboard, the deltas and the freeze decision
States what a delta costs in the flow

entry: Design agreement executed so PDK access is legal
Release calendar obtained from the foundry
exit: Every version transition assessed before adoption, not after
All teams on one recorded version, with exceptions logged
Production PDK adopted and frozen with an exception path defined
measuredBy: Days between a foundry release and its delta assessment
Teams on the recorded version against the total
Signoff reopened by a PDK change

purpose: Read the design rule manual as a constraint on this design rather than as a document — identify which restricted rules bite, dispose of every recommended rule, and get the exceptions requested early.

Restricted and recommended rules are where a node's real density lives. A design that adopts every recommended rule is safe and large; one that ignores them is dense and fails DFM. The disposition is a series of deliberate trades, and making them here is far cheaper than discovering them as violations at physical verification.

steps.text: DRM ingestion and change log against the previous node
Restricted rule identification and impact assessment
Recommended rule disposition — adopt, waive or defer
Density and spacing rule impact on the floorplan
Rule exception request preparation for the foundry
DRM review record and distribution to the design teams

PDK-02.flowNote: Exception requests in step 5 run in parallel because the foundry's response time is measured in weeks. Submitting them at the end of the review rather than as each one is identified adds a month to the answer.
consumes: Design rule manual for the selected node and flavour
Custom and analog design intent from AMS-01
produces: Rule change log against the previous node
Exception requests submitted to the foundry
DRM review record for the design teams

rel.text: PDK readiness dashboard. An outstanding exception request is a readiness gap, and it belongs on the dashboard with a date.
Internal reference flow and methodology guide. Rule dispositions become flow settings — what the tools are told to enforce and what they are told to allow.

risks: Recommended rules adopted wholesale. Safe, and it costs density the product was sized against; the trade should be made per rule, not once.
Restricted rules discovered at physical verification. A restricted rule that bites is a layout change, and finding it at SO-02 means finding it after routing closed.
Exception requests batched to the end. Foundry turnaround runs to weeks per request; batching them converts a parallel wait into a serial one.
Analog rules read only by the digital team. Pushed-rule and analog-specific sections matter to AMS-07, and they are the sections a digital-led review skips.
Disposition never distributed. A decision the layout engineers never saw is a decision that does not exist.

roles.d: Owns the disposition and the review record
Floorplan and routing impact of each rule

entry: DRM released for the selected node and flavour
Exception request process agreed with the foundry
exit: Every recommended rule dispositioned with a reason, not defaulted
Exception requests submitted, with expected response dates
Disposition distributed to digital and custom teams alike
measuredBy: Recommended rules dispositioned against those in the DRM
Exception requests answered before physical design starts
Rule violations at signoff traceable to a missed disposition

purpose: Choose the standard cell libraries the design will be built from and qualify them rather than assume them — track height, Vt menu, multi-bit flops, and the timing models every downstream tool will trust.

Library selection is a PPA decision disguised as a procurement one. Track height sets density and drive strength; the Vt menu sets leakage; multi-bit flops set clock power. And a timing model that is wrong at one corner produces a design that closes in the tool and fails in silicon, which is the failure mode nobody catches until bring-up.

steps.text: Track height and library family selection
Multi-Vt menu qualification against the flavour sheet
Multi-bit flop and special cell evaluation
Timing model quality check across corners
Physical view and abstract consistency check
Library re-characterisation where the foundry data is thin

PDK-03.flowNote: Step 4 is the step that earns the activity. Foundry timing models are qualified by the foundry against the foundry's test cases; checking them at this design's corners and slew ranges is what catches the model error before it becomes a silicon failure.
consumes: PDK release under tracking from PDK-01
PPA targets and clock power budget from ARCH-06
Foundry library release notes and characterisation data
produces: Library family and track height selection record
Qualified Vt menu with leakage projections
Timing model quality report across corners

rel.text: Qualified library list with .lib / LEF / GDS views. The standard cell half of the deliverable; PDK-04 adds memory and PDK-07 adds IO.
PDK readiness dashboard. An unqualified library is a readiness gap that blocks synthesis, and it shows on the dashboard as one.
Signoff corner definition. The corners a library is characterised at bound the corners signoff can be run at.

risks: Timing models trusted without a quality check. A model error at one corner produces a design that closes in the tool and fails on silicon — the most expensive class of library defect.
Track height chosen from the previous program. Density and drive strength trade differently at each node; inheriting the choice inherits an answer to a question nobody asked here.
Vt menu wider than the flow can maintain. Every Vt is a characterisation, a qualification and a maintenance burden across every version transition.
Multi-bit flops evaluated after synthesis starts. Clock power is largely decided by flop banking, and retrofitting it means re-running synthesis and re-closing timing.
LEF and GDS inconsistency. An abstract that disagrees with the layout produces DRC violations at the very end, after routing has been built on the abstract.

roles.d: Owns the selection, the qualification and the freeze
Vt menu and multi-bit flop implications
Track height, abstracts and routing resource
Release data, known issues and fixes

entry: Library release available under the design agreement
PPA and clock power budget available from ARCH-06
exit: Timing models checked at this design's corners, not only the foundry's
Vt menu frozen with a maintenance owner per corner
Abstract and layout views confirmed consistent
measuredBy: Corners with a validated timing model
Library defects found downstream against those found here
Vt menu size against the flow's maintenance capacity

purpose: Get the memory compiler licensed, evaluate what it can actually produce, and generate the instances the design asked for — with every view a downstream tool needs.

On an inference accelerator the memory array is a large fraction of the die, and the compiler decides most of it. What the compiler can generate is a hard boundary on the architecture: a configuration outside its range is not a compiler setting, it is a custom design programme in AMS-05 costing four months.

steps.text: Memory requirement collection from the hierarchy definition
Compiler capability screen against the requirement list
Instance generation across the required configurations
Compiler view completeness check — .lib, LEF, GDS, CDL, models

PDK-04.flowNote: Step 3 is the one with a schedule consequence. A capability gap found here opens the PDK-06 decision with fifteen weeks of runway; found at instance generation, it opens the same decision with three.
consumes: Memory hierarchy and capacity requirements from ARCH-03
PDK version under tracking from PDK-01
BISR and repair architecture intent from DFT-03
produces: Compiler capability screen and gap list

rel.text: Qualified library list. The memory half of the deliverable — instances with every view a downstream tool consumes.
Memory PPA gap analysis and custom-instance decision record. The capability screen is where the gap first appears; PDK-05 quantifies it.
PDK readiness dashboard. Compiler access and instance availability are tracked readiness items in their own right.

risks: Compiler licence assumed to be covered by the PDK agreement. Memory compilers are licensed separately, and discovering that here stops the activity for weeks.
Capability screened after generation starts. The gap is the same size either way; what differs is how much runway the custom path has.
Views generated but never checked. A missing or inconsistent view surfaces at PD-02 when the macro cannot be placed, and the compiler run has to be repeated.
Redundancy chosen without DFT. Repair schemes have to match the BISR architecture in DFT-03, and a mismatch is found at pattern generation.
Instance count explosion. Generating every configuration a block owner asks for produces a library nobody can characterise or maintain; consolidation is cheaper here than later.

roles.d: Owns compiler access, generation and the instance library
Compiler capability, known issues and updates

entry: PDK version stable enough to generate against
exit: Every required configuration either generated or recorded as a gap
All views present and checked, not merely produced
Redundancy scheme aligned with the DFT architecture
measuredBy: Configurations generated against those requested
Views complete against the tool requirement list
Instance count against what the flow can maintain

purpose: Measure what the generated instances actually deliver — density, Vmin, access time, leakage — and set it against the budget each block was allocated.

This is the activity that decides whether the custom memory path opens. The compiler produces an instance that meets the specification; the question here is whether it meets the budget, and the answer is frequently no by a margin large enough to matter but small enough to be argued about.

steps.text: Block memory budget extraction from ARCH-06
Area efficiency against the block budget

PDK-05.flowNote: The gap analysis is quantified rather than described on purpose. "The compiler misses the budget" starts an argument; "the L2 array misses its density budget by 14%, which is 3.1 mm² of die" starts a decision.
consumes: Vmin and operating voltage requirements from ARCH-05
Access time requirements from the hierarchy specification
produces: Vmin and access time characterisation results

rel.text: Memory PPA gap analysis and custom-instance decision record. The gap analysis half — PDK-06 adds the decision that follows from it.
Qualified library list. An instance that fails characterisation does not belong on the qualified list, whatever the compiler says.

risks: Density measured on the datasheet rather than the instance. Compiler datasheets quote best-case configurations; the instance the design needs is rarely one of them.
Vmin characterised at nominal only. Vmin is a distribution, and the number that matters is at the corner and the sigma the product is sold at.
Gap described rather than quantified. A shortfall without a number in square millimetres cannot be traded against schedule in PDK-06.
Measurement late enough to remove the option. Characterisation completing after the AMS window has closed makes the custom path unavailable regardless of the gap.
Access time measured without the wire load. An instance that meets access time standalone and misses it in place has not been characterised usefully.

roles.d: Owns the measurements and the gap analysis
Confirm the budget and accept or contest the gap

entry: Instances generated and released by PDK-04
exit: Every instance measured against its block's budget
Gaps quantified in area, power and Vmin, not described
Results delivered with enough runway for PDK-06 to act
measuredBy: Instances characterised against those released
Gap quantified in die area
Weeks of runway left for the custom decision

purpose: Decide what to do about the memory shortfall — push rules, build a custom array, or change the architecture — and hand the chosen scope to AMS with a schedule attached.

This is a gate, not a study. The compiler instance missed the budget; the options each cost something different and one of them has to be taken. Deferring the decision does not preserve the options — the custom array path needs its full window in AMS-05 through AMS-10, and every week of deferral removes one from the end.

steps.text: Shortfall review against the block budgets
Option definition — pushed rules, custom array, or architecture change
Schedule impact assessment against the AMS window
Foundry appetite for pushed rules and the approval path
Cost and risk comparison of the options
Decision and scope handoff to AMS

PDK-06.flowNote: Step 4 runs in parallel and can veto an option outright. A pushed-rule array the foundry will not approve is not an option, and finding that after the decision is taken costs the whole custom window.
consumes: AMS capacity and window from the program schedule
Foundry pushed-rule policy and approval process
Cost impact of the die area at stake from DEF-04
produces: Option definition with cost, schedule and risk per path
Schedule impact assessment against the AMS window
Decision record with the alternatives rejected

rel.text: Memory PPA gap analysis and custom-instance decision record. The decision half of the deliverable, and the record downstream stages will point at.
PDK readiness dashboard. An undecided memory gap is the most consequential open item the dashboard can carry — it holds both library closure and the AMS plan.

risks: Decision deferred to preserve options. Deferral removes the custom option rather than preserving it, because the window is fixed at the far end by physical design.
Pushed rules chosen without foundry commitment. Approval is a process with its own duration, and an unapproved pushed-rule array is a layout nobody can tape out.
Architecture change dismissed too quickly. Reducing the array is sometimes cheaper than building it; the option deserves the same costing as the other two.
Scope handed to AMS without a schedule. A custom instance request with no date is a request that competes with the SerDes for the same engineers and loses.
Decision taken without the block owner. The owner who accepted the budget in ARCH-06 is the one who has to accept the concession here.

roles.d: Owns the decision and its record
Arbitrates when the option is an architecture change

entry: AMS window and capacity known from the program plan
exit: Decision taken and recorded with the rejected options priced
Foundry approval path confirmed if pushed rules are chosen
Scope handed to AMS with a date, not only a requirement
measuredBy: Weeks from gap quantification to decision
Options costed against options considered
AMS window remaining at handoff

purpose: Qualify the IO, ESD and latch-up collateral — the library that sits at the die edge and decides whether the part survives handling, and whether its interfaces meet their electrical specifications.

IO qualification is unglamorous and it is where parts die. An ESD strategy chosen late constrains the pad ring after the bump map is fixed; a latch-up rule missed produces a part that fails qualification for reasons no functional test would ever find.

steps.text: IO requirement collection from the interface and bump plans
IO library selection against the interface list
Latch-up rule review and guard ring strategy
IO timing and signal integrity model quality check

PDK-07.flowNote: The ESD strategy in step 3 has to precede pad ring layout, which in turn precedes the bump map freeze in ARCH-08. Late ESD is a pad ring change, and a pad ring change is a bump map change.
consumes: Bump and pad ring plan from ARCH-08
Foundry IO library and ESD rule set
Latch-up and reliability requirements from the qualification plan
produces: ESD strategy and clamp selection record
IO timing and SI model quality report

rel.text: Qualified library list. The IO and ESD half of the deliverable — the cells at the die edge, qualified rather than assumed.
Signoff corner definition. ESD and latch-up verification conditions are part of what signoff has to run, and they are defined here.

risks: ESD strategy chosen after the pad ring. Clamp placement and rail topology constrain the ring; retrofitting means redoing the ring and the bump map with it.
IO models unchecked. IO timing models feed both STA and the channel simulation in SIPI-07; an error propagates into two signoffs at once.
Latch-up rules read as a formality. Guard ring strategy affects area at the die edge, and a late change competes with the interfaces for the same space.
Package and board ESD requirements ignored. The part's ESD rating is a system property; qualifying only the die produces a rating the system cannot use.
Library selected per interface with no consolidation. Several IO families in one ring multiplies the qualification and the pad ring complexity for little gain.

roles.d: Owns the selection and the qualification record
IO model quality for channel and timing use

entry: Pad ring and bump plan drafted in ARCH-08
Foundry IO library and ESD rules released
exit: ESD strategy fixed before the pad ring is committed
IO models validated for both timing and channel use
Latch-up strategy reviewed against the qualification plan
measuredBy: IO families in the ring against those qualified
Model errors found downstream
ESD rating achieved against the system requirement

purpose: Decide which tool at which version each flow step runs on, qualify that combination on the node, and freeze it — so that a result from one team means the same thing as a result from another.

Tool versions are a correctness question, not an IT one. A node this advanced needs certified versions for extraction, timing and physical verification, and mixing versions across teams produces disagreements that consume weeks before anyone suspects the tools rather than the design.

steps.text: Tool and version matrix definition per flow step
Physical verification and EM/IR tool qualification
Interoperability and database version check across tools
Version freeze and upgrade exception policy
Tool matrix publication to every team

PDK-08.flowNote: Step 6 catches what per-tool qualification cannot. Each tool can be certified on the node and still disagree with the next one about a database format or a parasitic convention, and only a cross-tool check finds it.
consumes: Selected node and flavour from TECH
Vendor certification matrices for the node
Existing internal tool estate and licences
produces: Tool and version matrix per flow step
Version freeze and upgrade exception policy

rel.text: EDA tool and version matrix (qualified and frozen). This activity is the deliverable, and the freeze is the part that matters.
Internal reference flow and methodology guide. The flow is written against specific tool versions; the guide and the matrix are read together.
Compute and license capacity plan. Which tools and how many concurrent seats is what the licence plan is built from.

risks: Teams on different versions. Two teams with different STA versions will disagree about timing, and the disagreement is diagnosed as a design problem for weeks first.
Certification status assumed. Vendor node certification lags node release; an uncertified version produces results the foundry will not accept at signoff.
Interoperability never checked. Per-tool qualification passes and the handoff between them fails, usually on parasitic or database conventions.
Freeze with no upgrade path. A critical tool fix will arrive mid-program, and a policy that has no route to accept it will be broken informally.
Matrix published once. A matrix nobody re-reads after month three is a matrix that describes an estate nobody is running.

roles.d: Owns the matrix, the qualification and the freeze

exit: Every flow step has a qualified, named tool version
Cross-tool interoperability checked, not assumed
Freeze published with an exception route for critical fixes
measuredBy: Flow steps with a qualified version against the total
Cross-tool defects found here against those found downstream
Version exceptions granted against the policy

purpose: Take the foundry's reference flow, adapt it into a methodology this design can actually run, and prove it on a representative block before the whole team depends on it.

A reference flow is a starting point written for a generic design. This one has hierarchical partitions, hard macros, multiple power domains and a memory subsystem the reference never contemplated. The pilot in the last step is what turns an adapted flow into a trusted one.

steps.text: Gap analysis against internal methodology and design needs
Signoff flow adaptation and deck integration
Low-power flow integration against the UPF intent
