Flow pilot on a representative block

PDK-09.flowNote: Three of the ten weeks are the pilot, and it is the step under most pressure to be skipped. A flow that has never been run end to end on a real block is a flow whose first user is doing the debugging on the critical path.
consumes: Rule and extraction decks from PDK-10
produces: Adapted synthesis, P&R and signoff flows
Pilot results on a representative block

rel.text: Internal reference flow and methodology guide. This activity is the deliverable, and the pilot is what makes it credible.
Golden environment release notes. The environment in PDK-13 packages this flow; the two are released together.
PDK readiness dashboard. Flow readiness is tracked alongside library and deck readiness — a design cannot start on any one of them alone.

risks: Pilot skipped under schedule pressure. The flow's first real user then debugs it while on the critical path, which is the most expensive place to do it.
Reference flow adopted rather than adapted. A generic flow on a hierarchical design with hard macros produces results nobody can close.
Low-power flow bolted on late. UPF handling touches synthesis, placement and verification; adding it after the flow is built means rebuilding it.
Methodology deck written after the flow changes. A guide that lags the scripts teaches the wrong flow to every engineer who joins.
Pilot block unrepresentative. A small clean block pilots nothing; the pilot has to include a macro, a domain crossing and real congestion.

roles.d: Owns the flow, the deck and the pilot
Runs the pilot on a real block
Reference flow support and known issues

entry: Decks under version control from PDK-10
exit: Flow run end to end on a representative block, not a toy one
Methodology deck matches the scripts as released
Hierarchical and block flows both defined, not only the top
measuredBy: Pilot blocks run end to end
Flow defects found in the pilot against those found in production use
Deck and script version agreement

purpose: Put every rule deck, extraction file and verification runset under version control, validate them on known-good structures, and make deck changes a notified event rather than a surprise.

Decks are the quiet dependency. A DRC runset revision that arrives without notice changes what passes verification, and if two teams are running different revisions the disagreement looks like a layout problem. Version control here is what makes a signoff result reproducible six months later.

steps.text: Version control and release process definition
QRC tech file and extraction deck validation
DRC and LVS deck validation on known-good structures
Deck change notification and impact process
Continuous deck version tracking across the stage

PDK-10.flowNote: Validation on known-good structures in step 4 is what makes a deck trustworthy. A runset that has never been tested against a layout with a known answer will report both false positives and, far worse, false negatives.
consumes: Foundry rule decks, runsets and tech files
Known-good test structures from previous programs

rel.text: Internal reference flow and methodology guide. A flow is only reproducible if the decks it calls are versioned; the guide names the versions.
Golden environment release notes. The environment pins deck versions, and this activity is what makes pinning possible.
PDK readiness dashboard. Deck currency and validation status are readiness items on the dashboard.

risks: Decks used from a shared directory. An unversioned deck makes every result unreproducible, and the problem is invisible until two results disagree.
Extraction deck unvalidated. Parasitic extraction errors move timing by amounts that look like design problems, and they are found after weeks of closure work.
Deck updates applied silently. A runset revision mid-closure changes what passes, and nobody can explain why yesterday's clean run is dirty today.
No known-good structures. Without a layout whose answer is known, deck validation is an assertion.
Tracking stops when the stage ends. Decks keep moving through signoff; a process that stops at PDK 1.0 leaves the most critical period unmanaged.

roles.d: Owns deck version control and the release process
QRC tech file and parasitic deck validation
Change notification against the version tracking
Deck releases, fixes and known issues

entry: Foundry decks released under the design agreement
PDK version tracking established by PDK-01
exit: Every deck versioned and pinned, none used from a shared path
Extraction and verification decks validated against known answers
Change notification process running, with a log
measuredBy: Decks under version control against the inventory
Deck-induced result changes explained on the first day
Reproducibility of a signoff run six months later

purpose: Agree with the foundry exactly which corners and derates signoff will be run at — PVT combinations, modes, and the OCV, AOCV or POCV methodology — and write it down before anyone closes timing against it.

A corner set is a contract. Sign off at corners the foundry does not recognise and the foundry will not accept the result; sign off at more corners than necessary and every closure iteration costs runtime and licence capacity the program has not budgeted for.

steps.text: Corner and mode enumeration from the operating conditions
OCV, AOCV or POCV derate methodology selection
Foundry alignment on the corner set and derates
Corner count against runtime and licence cost

PDK-11.flowNote: Step 6 exists because corner count multiplies. Nine corners across three modes is twenty-seven signoff runs per iteration, and the compute plan in PDK-12 is sized against whatever number this activity settles on.
consumes: Operating conditions and DVFS points from ARCH-05
IO and ESD conditions from PDK-07
Foundry signoff requirements and recommended derates
produces: PVT corner set, agreed with the foundry
Corner count impact on runtime and licences

rel.text: Signoff corner definition agreed with foundry. This activity is the deliverable, and "agreed" is the operative word — an internal corner set has no standing.
Compute and license capacity plan. Corner count multiplied by modes is the single largest driver of signoff compute demand.

risks: Corner set agreed after closure starts. Adding a corner mid-closure invalidates the work done, and the addition usually comes from the foundry.
Derate methodology chosen for margin. OCV is conservative and expensive in area and power; POCV is tighter and demands better data. Choosing without the data is choosing margin blindly.
Corner count unbounded. Every corner is a full signoff run per iteration; a set nobody trimmed becomes a schedule problem at SO-02.
Modes forgotten. Corners multiply by modes, and a mode discovered late — a test mode, a low-power mode — multiplies the whole set.
Library corners narrower than the signoff set. Signing off at a corner the library was never characterised at is signing off against extrapolation.

roles.d: Owns the corner set and the derate methodology
Corner and mode enumeration, runtime implications
Confirms characterisation covers the proposed corners
Agreement on corners and recommended derates

entry: Operating conditions and DVFS points defined by ARCH-05
Library characterisation corners known from PDK-03
exit: Corner set agreed with the foundry in writing
Every signoff corner covered by library characterisation
Runtime and licence impact quantified and accepted
measuredBy: Corners agreed against corners later added
Signoff runs per closure iteration
Corners covered by library characterisation

purpose: Model what the program will actually need in compute, EDA licences and storage across its peak, and procure it against a lead time rather than discovering it during timing closure.

Compute is a schedule input disguised as an IT line item. Timing closure at PD-09 runs multi-corner across a 600 mm² die; if the farm or the licence pool caps concurrency, every iteration takes longer and the closure burn-down flattens for reasons nobody attributes to infrastructure.

steps.text: Compute demand model per stage and per flow step
EDA licence demand model against peak concurrency
Farm capacity plan against procurement lead time
Licence negotiation support and pooling strategy

PDK-12.flowNote: The demand model is built per flow step rather than per team because that is how contention actually happens: three teams running the same tool at the same point in the schedule contend for one licence pool, whatever the org chart says.
consumes: Flow step definitions and runtimes from PDK-09
Corner and mode count from PDK-11
Program schedule and stage overlap from DEF-08
produces: Compute demand model per stage and flow step
EDA licence demand model at peak concurrency
Farm capacity plan with procurement dates

rel.text: Compute and license capacity plan. This activity is the deliverable, and its value is that it is dated against lead times.
EDA tool and version matrix. Which tools are pooled and at what seat count is decided against the matrix.

risks: Demand modelled per team rather than per flow step. Contention happens when several teams hit the same tool at the same time, which an org-chart model cannot see.
Peak sized to the average. Signoff and closure peaks are several times the steady state, and a farm sized to the average flattens the burn-down exactly when it matters.
Licences procured without lead time. Additional seats are a commercial negotiation with a duration; needing them next week is needing them next quarter.
Storage forgotten. Multi-corner signoff databases are large, and a farm that runs out of storage stops as hard as one that runs out of cores.
Plan never reviewed against actual usage. A capacity plan is a forecast; without a comparison to actuals nobody learns that it was wrong until closure.

roles.d: Owns the demand model and the capacity plan
Runtime and concurrency data per flow step

entry: Flow steps and runtimes known from PDK-09
Corner and mode count settled by PDK-11
exit: Peak demand modelled per flow step, not per team
Procurement dated against lead time, not against need date
Plan published with a review cadence against actual usage
measuredBy: Peak concurrency modelled against peak observed
Licence denials during closure
Procurement lead time against the need date

purpose: Package everything this stage produced into one environment every team runs from — tools, decks, libraries, scripts — prove it with a regression, and release it with known issues stated.

Enablement only becomes real when it is a single thing an engineer can load. Until then the program has a qualified library here, a validated deck there and a flow in someone's home directory, and every new engineer assembles a slightly different version of the design environment.

steps.text: Environment scope definition — tools, decks, libraries, scripts
Regression run on the reference block
Result comparison against the pilot baseline

PDK-13.flowNote: Step 5 is what makes the release trustworthy. If the golden environment produces different results from the PDK-09 pilot on the same block, something in the packaging changed the answer, and finding that after release means everyone's results are suspect.
consumes: Qualified libraries from PDK-03, PDK-04 and PDK-07
Adapted flow and methodology deck from PDK-09
produces: Regression results against the pilot baseline

rel.text: Golden environment release notes. This activity is the deliverable — the environment itself, with what is in it and what is known to be wrong with it.
PDK readiness dashboard. The dashboard closes when the environment releases; until then every readiness item is still individually tracked.
Internal reference flow and methodology guide. The guide describes the flow; this environment is the flow, packaged and versioned.

risks: Environment released without a regression. An untested package is a package whose first regression is run by whoever is closest to a deadline.
Results differ from the pilot and the difference is not chased. A packaging change that moves results silently invalidates the pilot's credibility and everything built on it.
Known issues omitted. An environment released as clean produces bug reports for problems the team already knew about, and the reports go to the wrong place.
No onboarding. A golden environment nobody was shown how to use is a directory people copy from and modify, which is where divergence starts.
Released and then not maintained. Decks and PDK versions keep moving; an environment frozen at release drifts away from what signoff will require.

roles.d: Owns the environment, its release and its maintenance
Confirms the environment is usable for real work

entry: Decks validated and under version control
exit: Regression reproduces the pilot baseline, or the difference is explained
Known issues published with the release, not after it
Teams onboarded onto the environment rather than copying it
measuredBy: Regression deviation from the pilot baseline
Teams on the golden environment against those running private copies
Known issues published against those later reported as new

purpose: Decompose the product into the IP it actually needs — every block, with its specification, its interfaces and the requirement it traces back to — and publish it as a bill of materials the program can be held to.

An IP-BOM derived from the last program's list is the most common way to arrive at the wrong one. What this product needs follows from its requirements and its architecture, and the blocks that differ from last time are exactly the ones with the longest lead times.

steps.text: Requirement-to-IP decomposition against the requirement register
Block-level IP identification from the architecture sketch
Foundry IP identification — memory compilers, IO, standard cells
Per-IP specification stub — function, performance, interfaces
Bill of materials assembly and traceability check

IPR-01.flowNote: Step 6's traceability check is what separates a list from a bill of materials. An IP that traces to no requirement is an IP nobody needs; a requirement that traces to no IP is a gap nobody has staffed.
consumes: Architecture sketch and block list direction from ARCH-02
Previous-program IP list as a starting reference
Foundry IP catalogue for the selected node
produces: IP bill of materials, block by block

rel.text: IP bill of materials with make / buy / reuse decision per block. The bill half of the deliverable; IPR-03 adds the decision against each line.
IP readiness report. Readiness is assessed per line of this bill, so the bill's completeness bounds the report's.

risks: Bill inherited from the previous program. The blocks that differ are the ones with the longest lead times, and inheriting the list hides exactly those.
Foundry IP omitted. Memory compilers, IO and standard cells are IP with licences and lead times, and a bill that lists only third-party blocks understates the procurement.
Specification stubs too thin to evaluate against. A vendor cannot be assessed against "a PCIe PHY"; the stub has to carry performance, interface and process detail.
Traceability skipped. Without it, blocks appear because someone assumed them and requirements go unserved because nobody noticed.
Bill frozen before architecture settles. A bill written before ARCH-02 partitions will miss the die-to-die interface entirely if the part turns out to be a chiplet.

roles.d: Owns the bill of materials and its traceability
Confirms the block list and its interfaces
Carries the bill into procurement planning

entry: Requirement register available at v0.9 from DEF-01
Architecture direction known well enough to name blocks
exit: Every IP traces to a requirement, and every requirement to an IP or a gap
Foundry IP included alongside third-party and internal blocks
Specification stubs detailed enough to evaluate a vendor against
measuredBy: IP lines traceable to a requirement
Requirements with no IP against them
Bill changes after the architecture freeze

purpose: Audit what the organisation already owns and can actually reuse on this node — not what it owns in general, which is a different and much longer list.

Reuse is where the schedule is won, and it is also where optimism concentrates. A block proven on the previous node is not available on this one until it has been ported, re-characterised and re-verified, and that work is a project with a duration. The audit's job is to separate genuine reuse from hopeful reuse.

steps.text: Internal IP inventory against the bill of materials
Node availability check per internal block
Collateral completeness audit — views, testbenches, documentation
Maintenance and ownership status per block
Reuse classification — direct, port required, or rebuild

IPR-02.flowNote: Step 4 asks who still maintains each block, and the answer is often nobody. An unmaintained block is technically reusable and practically a rebuild, because the first bug found has no owner.
consumes: IP bill of materials from IPR-01
Node and flavour selection from TECH
produces: Internal IP inventory mapped to the bill

rel.text: IP bill of materials. Reuse classification is one of the three answers the make / buy / reuse column can take, and it is decided here.
IP readiness report. An internal block on the wrong node is exactly as unready as an external one, and belongs in the same report.

risks: Reuse claimed on the previous node. Availability is node-specific; a block not yet ported is a porting project, not a reuse.
Collateral assumed complete. Missing multi-corner .lib files or an absent testbench turns reuse into re-characterisation and re-verification.
Unmaintained blocks counted as reuse. A block with no owner has no one to fix its first bug, and the fix lands on the integration team.
Audit run on the catalogue rather than the repository. Catalogues describe intent; repositories contain what actually exists.
Silicon history ignored. A block that shipped with an erratum is reusable with that erratum, and the erratum belongs in the audit.

roles.d: Owns the audit and the reuse classification
Ownership and maintenance status per block
Errata and known issues from previous silicon

entry: Bill of materials available from IPR-01
Node selected so availability can be assessed
exit: Every internal block classified as direct reuse, port, or rebuild
Collateral gaps listed per block, not assumed away
Blocks with no maintainer flagged as such
measuredBy: Blocks classified as direct reuse against those later ported
Collateral gaps found here against those found at integration
Blocks with a named maintainer

purpose: Take each line of the bill and decide, with a reason, whether it is made, bought or reused — and record what the rejected options would have cost.

Make/buy is a schedule decision more than a cost one. Building a PHY internally is cheaper on paper and costs nine months in AMS-03; buying it costs a licence and a vendor dependency. Neither is wrong, and the program only gets to argue about it once.

steps.text: Decision criteria definition — cost, schedule, differentiation, risk
Differentiation screen — which blocks are the product's own value
Internal capacity check against the make candidates
Cost and schedule comparison per line
Decision per line and record of rejected options

IPR-03.flowNote: Step 3 is the check that changes answers. A make decision assumes engineers who are also assigned to the custom SRAM and the PLL; capacity, not capability, is what usually decides.
consumes: IP bill of materials from IPR-01
AMS capacity and schedule from the program plan
produces: Make / buy / reuse decision per line
Rejected option record with cost and schedule
Internal capacity commitment for make decisions

rel.text: IP bill of materials with make / buy / reuse decision per block. The decision half of the deliverable, with the rejected options priced rather than forgotten.
IP risk register. Every buy decision creates a vendor dependency and every make decision creates a capacity dependency; both belong on the register.

risks: Make decided on capability rather than capacity. The team can build it; whether it can build it alongside everything else it is already committed to is the real question.
Differentiating IP bought. Buying the block that is the product's actual advantage buys a product the competitor can buy too.
Commodity IP built. Building a standard interface consumes analog engineers who are the program's scarcest resource, for no differentiation.
Foundry-specific IP chosen without reference to sourcing strategy. It forecloses the migration option TECH-08 was pricing, and usually after that study concludes.
Decisions recorded without the alternatives. Every setback reopens a decision whose reasoning nobody can reconstruct.

roles.d: Owns the decisions and their record
Differentiation screen — what is the product's own value

entry: Bill of materials complete from IPR-01
AMS capacity known from the program plan
exit: Every line decided with a criterion attached, not by default
Make decisions backed by a named capacity commitment
Rejected options priced and recorded
measuredBy: Lines decided against lines in the bill
Make decisions with a capacity commitment behind them
Decisions reopened after IP Plan Freeze

purpose: Run a real evaluation of the vendors behind every buy decision — technical capability, deliverable quality, support model and track record — rather than choosing from a datasheet.

A PHY vendor is a nine-month dependency. What matters is less the block's peak specification than whether the deliverables arrive complete, whether the support engineer answers, and whether the last three customers taped out on schedule. None of that is on the datasheet.

steps.text: Technical evaluation against the specification stubs
Reference customer checks and tapeout track record
Support model and escalation path assessment

IPR-04.flowNote: Step 4 is the step most often skipped and the one that predicts the outcome best. A vendor's last three customers know whether the deliverables arrived complete and on time, and they will usually say.
consumes: Node and process option from TECH-02
produces: Vendor evaluation matrix and selection record

rel.text: Vendor evaluation matrix and selection record. This activity is the deliverable, and the matrix is what a later dispute is settled against.
Executed licences and POs. Selection precedes negotiation; IPR-07 contracts with whoever this activity chose.
IP readiness report. Vendor track record is part of an IP's maturity rating, not separate from it.

risks: Evaluation from the datasheet. Peak specifications are marketing; deliverable completeness and support responsiveness are what the integration actually depends on.
Reference checks skipped. The vendor's previous customers know what the program is about to find out, and asking costs an hour.
Single vendor evaluated. An evaluation with one candidate is a justification, and the commercial position that follows is weak.
Support model unexamined. A block with no named support engineer becomes the integration team's problem the first time it misbehaves.
Node-specific capability assumed from a different node. A PHY proven at the previous node is not the same product; IPR-05 is where that is confirmed.

roles.d: Owns the evaluation and the selection

entry: Specification stubs detailed enough to evaluate against
NDAs in place with candidate vendors
exit: At least two candidates evaluated per significant line
Reference customers contacted for the critical blocks
Selection recorded against the matrix, with support model assessed
measuredBy: Candidates evaluated per line
Reference checks completed on critical blocks
Vendor changes after selection

purpose: Establish, for each bought and reused block, whether it has actually run in silicon on this node and this process option — and if not, what it would take to get it there.

"Silicon-proven" is the most abused phrase in IP procurement. It can mean proven on a different node, on a different process option, at a different speed grade, or in a test chip that was never characterised. This activity replaces the phrase with a fact, and the fact is what the integration schedule should be built on.

steps.text: Proven-status definition — what the program will accept as evidence
Evidence request per block — test chip, production part, characterisation data
Node and process option match verification
Speed grade and operating condition match check
Errata and known-issue review per block

IPR-05.flowNote: Step 1 is not bureaucracy. Without an agreed evidence standard, every vendor's claim is accepted at its own definition, and the readiness report becomes a collection of adjectives.
consumes: Node and process option from TECH-02
Vendor silicon evidence and characterisation data
Errata from previous programs and vendor disclosures
produces: Silicon evidence per block, with node and option match
Speed grade and condition match findings
Maturity level per block and a gap list

rel.text: IP readiness report — silicon-proven status and maturity level per IP. This activity is the deliverable, and it is the one that replaces a claim with a fact.
IP risk register. Every block below the maturity bar is a risk with a name, an owner and a mitigation.
IP delivery schedule. An unproven block needs a hardening window, and the window has to be in the schedule.

risks: Vendor claim accepted at the vendor's definition. Without an evidence standard, "silicon-proven" means whatever is most convenient.
Node matched, process option not. The same node with a different flavour sheet is a different library, different rules and often a different PHY.
Errata not requested. Every silicon-proven block has errata; a block presented with none has either not been characterised or is not being fully disclosed.
Assessment done after the licence is signed. The finding has no commercial consequence once the PO is placed, and the leverage is gone.
Speed grade ignored. A PHY proven at a lower rate on the same node is an engineering project, not a proven block.

roles.d: Owns the evidence standard and the readiness report
PHY and analog block evidence interpretation
Errata review and characterisation data reading
Uses findings as negotiating position before signature

entry: Node and process option fixed by TECH-02
Vendor NDAs allow access to characterisation data
exit: Every block carries a maturity level backed by evidence, not by claim
Node and process option match verified per block
Findings available before licences are signed in IPR-07
measuredBy: Blocks with evidence against blocks with a claim
Node and option mismatches found
Errata disclosed against errata found later

purpose: Define exactly what a complete IP delivery contains — every view, model, testbench and document — and get that list agreed before it becomes a contractual obligation.

Most IP delivery disputes are not about whether the block works; they are about whether a delivery counted as a delivery. A block that arrives without multi-corner timing views or without its verification collateral has arrived in a form the program cannot integrate, and the argument that follows is unwinnable if the checklist was never agreed.

steps.text: Deliverable checklist definition per IP class
View and model requirements against the tool matrix
Documentation, errata and integration guide requirements
Acceptance criteria and incoming inspection procedure
Checklist publication and handoff to procurement

IPR-06.flowNote: Step 5 turns the checklist into something enforceable. A list of expected files is a wish; an acceptance procedure that says what is checked, by whom, and what happens when it fails is a term.
consumes: Tool matrix and view requirements from PDK-08
produces: Acceptance criteria and incoming inspection procedure

rel.text: IP deliverable acceptance checklist. This activity is the deliverable, and its value is entirely in being agreed before the PO rather than after the delivery.
Executed licences and POs. The checklist becomes a contractual schedule, which is the only form in which it is enforceable.

risks: Checklist agreed after the PO. Once the commercial terms are closed, a missing view is a favour rather than an obligation.
Views specified without the tool matrix. A .lib set that does not cover the signoff corners in PDK-11 is incomplete in a way nobody notices until closure.
Verification collateral omitted. A block delivered without its testbench has to be verified from scratch, and that effort was never in the DV plan.
No incoming inspection. Deliverables accepted without a check are found incomplete weeks later, when the vendor's engineer has moved on.
One checklist for all IP classes. A memory compiler, a PHY and a controller have genuinely different deliverable sets, and a single list serves none of them.

roles.d: Owns the checklist and the acceptance procedure
View and model requirements against the tools
Collateral requirements and what DV will need
Makes the checklist a contractual schedule
Agree the list is deliverable as written

entry: Signoff corner intent known from PDK-11
exit: Checklist agreed with each vendor before the PO is placed
Acceptance procedure names who checks what, and when
Views cover the signoff corners the program will actually run
measuredBy: Vendors with an agreed checklist before PO
Deliveries rejected at incoming inspection
Missing views discovered after acceptance

purpose: Turn selections into executed licences and purchase orders with committed delivery dates, including the deliverable checklist as a contractual schedule.

Twelve weeks for 5 M/M — this is the stage's longest activity and among its smallest in effort, because the elapsed time belongs to two legal departments and a procurement process. It is on the critical path regardless: nothing arrives until it executes, and RTL-03 has integration windows that assume it did.

steps.text: Commercial terms definition per IP line
Licence model negotiation — per-use, per-project, royalty
Delivery date commitment and milestone schedule
Deliverable checklist attached as a contractual schedule
Liability, indemnity and IP warranty terms

IPR-07.flowNote: Step 3 is the one the program cares about and the one commercial negotiation treats as secondary. A licence with excellent terms and no committed delivery date has bought a block that arrives when the vendor is ready.
consumes: Readiness findings from IPR-05 as negotiating position
Integration window requirements from the program schedule
produces: Distribution record of what has been licensed to whom

rel.text: Executed licences and POs with committed delivery dates. This activity is the deliverable, and the committed date is the part the schedule depends on.
IP delivery schedule. Committed dates are what IPR-09 aligns against the integration windows.
IP deliverable acceptance checklist. The checklist only has force once it is attached to an executed agreement.

risks: Licence executed without a committed delivery date. The block then arrives when the vendor is ready, and the integration window absorbs the difference.
Readiness findings not used in negotiation. A block that is not proven on the node is a commercial position; signing before IPR-05 reports discards it.
Checklist not attached. An agreed checklist outside the contract is an understanding, and understandings do not survive a disputed delivery.
Redline duration underestimated. Two legal departments take longer than either forecasts, and the program's plan should assume the longer figure.
Support terms omitted. A block with no support commitment becomes unsupported precisely when integration needs help.

roles.d: Owns the negotiation, the POs and the terms
Technical terms and the deliverable schedule
Licence model, royalty exposure and budget

exit: Every licence carries a committed delivery date, not an intention
Deliverable checklist attached as a contractual schedule
Access distributed and tracked to the teams that need it
measuredBy: Licences with a committed delivery date
Weeks from selection to execution
Deliveries received against the committed date

purpose: For every block that is not proven on this node, scope the work that gets it there — porting, hardening, re-characterisation, re-verification — and put it in the schedule as a project with an owner.

Unproven IP does not become proven by being licensed. Someone ports it, re-characterises it at the program's corners and re-verifies it, and that someone is either the vendor on a schedule the program does not control, or the program's own engineers who are already committed elsewhere.

steps.text: Unproven block list from the readiness report
Porting scope per block — layout, characterisation, verification
Vendor versus internal execution decision per block
Effort and duration estimate per block
Dependency mapping against the integration windows
Hardening plan with owners and dates

IPR-08.flowNote: Step 3 decides who absorbs the risk. Vendor-executed hardening is on a schedule the program cannot influence; internally executed hardening competes with AMS-03 for the same analog engineers. Both are real answers and neither is free.
consumes: Readiness report and gap list from IPR-05
AMS capacity from the program plan
Integration window requirements from RTL and PD
produces: Unproven block list with porting scope
Execution decision per block — vendor or internal
Hardening plan with owners and dates

rel.text: IP readiness report. A block's maturity level is only actionable alongside the plan that raises it, and this activity supplies the plan.
IP delivery schedule. A hardening window is part of the delivery date, and omitting it produces a schedule that cannot hold.

risks: Hardening treated as vendor overhead. It is a project with a duration; leaving it off the plan means the block arrives on a date nobody derived.
Internal execution assumed available. The engineers who would port a PHY are the engineers building the PLL and the custom array, and they cannot do all three.
Re-verification omitted from scope. Porting changes the block; the verification collateral has to be re-run, and that effort belongs in the DV plan.
Characterisation corners not matched to the program's. A block re-characterised at the vendor's corners still cannot be signed off at the program's.
Plan without dates. A hardening plan with owners and no dates does not integrate with the program schedule and is therefore not tracked.

roles.d: Internal capacity and analog porting scope
Dates, owners and integration window alignment

entry: AMS capacity known from the program plan
Integration windows known from RTL and PD planning
exit: Every unproven block has a scoped plan with an owner and a date
Internal execution decisions backed by a capacity commitment
Re-verification scope included, not assumed
measuredBy: Unproven blocks with a dated plan
Internal hardening committed against AMS capacity
Hardening completed against plan

purpose: Line up every IP delivery date against the window that actually needs it — RTL integration, synthesis, floorplan — and surface the mismatches while they can still be fixed.

An IP schedule is only meaningful against the design schedule. A PHY delivered in week 40 is early for RTL and late for the floorplan, because PD-02 needs the abstract long before RTL-03 needs the model. Alignment means matching each deliverable to the window that consumes it, not the block to a date.

steps.text: Integration window extraction — what each stage needs and when
Committed delivery date collection per block and per deliverable
Deliverable-level alignment — abstracts before models before collateral
Schedule integration into the program plan

IPR-09.flowNote: Step 3 is where the useful detail lives. Vendors quote one date for a block; the design needs the LEF abstract for floorplan months before it needs the multi-corner .lib for signoff, and asking for the abstract early is often free.
consumes: RTL integration windows from the program schedule
Floorplan and macro placement needs from PD planning
produces: Integration window map per consuming stage
IP schedule folded into the program plan

rel.text: IP delivery schedule folded into the program plan. This activity is the deliverable, and "folded in" is the operative part — a separate IP schedule is one nobody tracks.
IP risk register. Every mismatch that cannot be closed becomes a tracked risk with a mitigation.

risks: Block-level dates instead of deliverable-level. One date per block hides that the abstract is needed months before the model, and the earlier need is the binding one.
IP schedule maintained separately. A schedule outside the program plan is not reviewed at program reviews and drifts unnoticed.
Mismatches recorded without escalation. A known gap with no owner and no escalation is a gap that is discovered again at integration.
Hardening overlay omitted. Delivery dates for unproven blocks are meaningless without the porting window that follows them.
Floorplan needs underestimated. Physical design needs abstracts and blockages very early; planning against RTL's needs alone produces a late floorplan.

roles.d: Owns the alignment and the escalation list

entry: Integration windows known from the program schedule
exit: Alignment done per deliverable, not per block
Every mismatch has an owner and an escalation path
IP schedule visible inside the program plan, not beside it
measuredBy: Deliverables aligned to a consuming window
Mismatches closed against those raised
IP deliveries late against the window that needed them

purpose: Rate every IP line for maturity and supply risk, and decide where a contingency is worth having — a second source, an internal fallback, or an accepted exposure with a trigger.

Some risk here is unavoidable and pretending otherwise is what makes it dangerous. The point is not to eliminate single-vendor dependencies but to know which ones would stop the program, and to have decided in advance what would be done about each.

steps.text: Risk rating per IP line — maturity, vendor, schedule, supply
Critical dependency identification — which failures stop the program
Contingency decision and trigger definition per critical block

IPR-10.flowNote: Step 5 defines triggers, not intentions. "We would build it internally if the vendor slipped" is worthless without the date at which that decision has to be taken to still be executable.
consumes: Readiness report and maturity levels from IPR-05
Delivery schedule and mismatches from IPR-09
produces: Contingency plan with triggers and decision dates

rel.text: IP risk register and contingency plan. This activity is the deliverable, and the triggers are what make it a plan rather than a list.
IP readiness report. Maturity and risk are read together — a mature block from a fragile vendor is not a low-risk line.

risks: Register without triggers. A contingency with no decision date cannot be executed, because by the time the need is obvious the option has expired.
Every line rated as critical. A register where everything is critical directs attention nowhere; the point is to identify the few that stop the program.
Second source assessed on capability alone. An alternative vendor without a licence, an evaluation and a delivery date is not a contingency.
Internal fallback assumed. A fallback that depends on engineers already committed to the critical path is not a fallback.
Register written and not reviewed. IP risk changes as deliveries land; a register reviewed once at IP Plan Freeze is stale by RTL integration.

roles.d: Owns the register and the contingency plan
Confirms which failures actually stop the program

exit: Critical dependencies identified and separated from the rest
Every critical block has a contingency with a trigger date
Register has a review cadence, not just an author
measuredBy: Critical dependencies with a triggered contingency
Register reviews held against those planned
Contingencies executed against those defined

purpose: Turn each custom block from a name on the make list into a specification with budgets — jitter, BER, PSRR, area, power — that a circuit designer can start against and a reviewer can hold them to.

Analog specifications are budgets before they are targets. Total jitter is divided between the PLL, the distribution network and the PHY; each owner gets a share, and a share nobody allocated becomes an argument at integration when the eye closes and no one can say whose fault it is.

steps.text: Custom block list confirmation from the make decisions
System-level budget decomposition — jitter, noise, BER
Area and power allocation per block

AMS-01.flowNote: Step 2 is the one that prevents the integration argument. A jitter budget divided explicitly between PLL, distribution and PHY gives each owner a number; an unallocated total gives each owner a reason to believe the problem is somewhere else.
consumes: Power and clock architecture from ARCH-05
produces: Per-block specifications with jitter, BER, PSRR and area budgets
Area and power allocation per block

rel.text: AMS IP specifications and design review packages. This activity is the deliverable — the specifications every other AMS activity is executed and reviewed against.
Integration guide. The specification is what the integration guide's limitations are stated relative to.

risks: Budgets stated as totals rather than allocations. An unallocated jitter budget produces three designers each assuming the others left them room.
Specifications written without the PHY vendor. Where a PHY is bought, its jitter tolerance bounds what the PLL must deliver, and the two have to be written together.
Area allocated before the architecture is understood. Analog area is set by matching, isolation and routing, and an allocation made from a digital estimate is not usable.
PSRR requirements omitted. Supply sensitivity is what turns a working block into a failing one once the digital neighbours switch, and it is rarely specified up front.
No owner acceptance. A specification the designer has not accepted is one they will design around rather than to.

roles.d: Owns the budgets and the specification set

entry: Custom memory scope handed over by PDK-06
Interface and clock architecture defined by ARCH-04 and ARCH-05
exit: Every system budget decomposed into per-block allocations
Each specification accepted by its named owner
Area and power allocations reconciled against ARCH-06
measuredBy: Blocks with an accepted specification
System budgets fully allocated
Specification changes after design start

purpose: Design the clock generation the whole chip runs on — PLLs, their loop dynamics, their supply immunity and their jitter — and close them across process, voltage and temperature.

A PLL is small, slow to build and impossible to work around. Twenty-six weeks for a block of a few hundred microns square looks disproportionate until the first silicon that will not lock over temperature, at which point the entire program is waiting on a circuit nobody can patch.

steps.text: Architecture selection — integer, fractional, ring or LC
Loop dynamics and phase noise budget
VCO design and tuning range definition
Charge pump, loop filter and divider design
Lock detection, calibration and startup sequencing
Layout with matching, shielding and isolation
Clock distribution interface definition with physical design

AMS-02.flowNote: Step 8 is where the schedule risk lives. Post-layout jitter is routinely worse than pre-layout by more than the margin, and the fix is a layout change that takes the six weeks of step 7 again.
consumes: Jitter and PSRR budgets from AMS-01
Clock architecture and DVFS points from ARCH-05
Reference clock specification from the system requirements
Node device models and PDK from PDK-01
Supply and rail topology from ARCH-05
produces: PLL architecture selection and loop design

rel.text: AMS IP specifications and design review packages. The PLL review package is the largest single item in the set.
Characterisation reports across PVT and Monte Carlo. Jitter across PVT is the headline number in the report.
Hard macro GDS with abstract views. The PLL is one of the macros AMS-15 abstracts and hands to physical design.

risks: Post-layout jitter worse than budget. The commonest analog schedule failure, and the fix is a layout iteration measured in weeks, not days.
PSRR ignored until integration. A PLL that meets jitter on a clean supply and fails beside switching digital logic has met a specification nobody can use.
Tuning range too narrow across corners. A VCO that cannot cover the DVFS range at the slow corner is a DVFS policy that has to be reduced in silicon.
Lock time and startup unspecified. Boot sequencing depends on lock time, and discovering it at bring-up delays every subsequent test.
One PLL designed for several very different uses. Sharing one design across HBM, SerDes and core clocking usually means it is optimal for none.

roles.d: Owns the architecture, the loop and the closure

entry: Jitter and PSRR budgets accepted in AMS-01
Clock architecture and DVFS points fixed by ARCH-05
Device models available from the tracked PDK
exit: Jitter closed post-layout across PVT, not pre-layout
Lock time and startup sequence characterised and documented
Macro released with views and a behavioural model
measuredBy: Post-layout jitter against budget
Tuning range coverage at the slow corner
Layout iterations after first post-layout simulation

purpose: Deliver the high-speed interfaces — PCIe or CXL, die-to-die, HBM PHY — either designed from scratch or hardened from a vendor's deliverable onto this node and this flavour sheet.

At thirty-four weeks and sixty man-months this is the largest single activity in the entire template, and it is the one most likely to decide the tapeout date. Even a bought PHY is not free: hardening, integration, and closing its analog margins on this process option is a project, and the vendor's schedule for it is not the program's.

steps.text: PHY strategy per interface — build, buy hardened, or buy soft
Vendor deliverable ingestion and gap assessment
TX and RX front-end design or adaptation
HBM PHY integration and training sequence
Layout, matching and lane pitch closure
Post-layout BER and eye closure across PVT
Compliance simulation against the interface specification

AMS-03.flowNote: Step 7 is eight weeks of layout because lane pitch is a floorplan constraint as much as a circuit one — the PHY has to fit the bump pitch ARCH-08 defined, and a pitch mismatch found here forces a change at the die edge.
consumes: Interface selections and revisions from ARCH-04
Vendor deliverables and licences from IPR-07
Bump pitch and PHY placement from ARCH-08
produces: TX/RX front-end and clock recovery designs
Post-layout BER and eye results across PVT
Released PHY macros with integration support

rel.text: Characterisation reports across PVT and Monte Carlo. The PHY's eye and BER characterisation is the report's most consequential section.
Hard macro GDS with abstract views. The PHY macros are the largest and most constrained of the set.
Integration guide with known limitations and errata. PHY limitations — training corner cases, unsupported modes — are what integration most needs stated.

risks: Bought PHY assumed to need no work. Hardening, integration and margin closure on this flavour sheet is a multi-quarter project regardless of who designed the circuit.
Lane pitch incompatible with the bump map. Discovered at layout, it forces a change at the die edge where there is least room to make one.
Compliance simulated late. A PHY that closes its own eye and fails the interface specification's compliance mask has to be reworked with no schedule left.
Channel budget not shared with SI. The PHY closes against an assumed channel; if SIPI-07 extracts a worse one, the margin was never real.
Vendor support model untested until integration. The first hard question is when a support relationship is discovered to be a ticketing system.

roles.d: Owns the strategy, the design and the closure
TX/RX front end and clock recovery

entry: Vendor licences executed where PHYs are bought
Bump pitch and PHY placement known from ARCH-08
exit: BER and eye closed post-layout across PVT at the specified channel
Compliance simulated against the interface specification, not only internally
Macros released with a stated limitation list
measuredBy: Eye margin against the compliance mask
Lane pitch against the bump map constraint
Weeks of vendor-side schedule the program cannot influence

purpose: Build the power management cells everything else depends on — LDOs, bandgap references, bias generation — quietly and correctly, because every other block's specification assumes them.

These blocks are small, unglamorous and load-bearing. A bandgap that drifts moves every analog threshold on the die; an LDO with insufficient PSRR at the switching frequency turns the PLL's careful jitter budget into noise. They are specified against by everyone and reviewed by almost nobody.

steps.text: Supply topology and regulation requirement per domain
Bandgap reference design and trim strategy
LDO design — load range, stability, PSRR
Layout with matching and supply isolation
Post-layout stability and PSRR verification across PVT
Trim and calibration procedure definition for test

AMS-04.flowNote: Step 8 is easy to leave until later and expensive to. A trim procedure that test engineering only sees at TEST-05 becomes a test-time cost, and a bandgap with no defined trim is a part with a distribution nobody can tighten.
consumes: Supply and rail topology from ARCH-05
Load profiles from the digital power estimate
Node device models and precision element availability
Test and trim capability from TEST-01
produces: Bandgap reference design with trim strategy
LDO designs with stability and PSRR results
Trim and calibration procedure for production test

rel.text: Characterisation reports across PVT and Monte Carlo. Bandgap drift and LDO PSRR across corners belong in the same report as the PLL and PHY results.
Hard macro GDS with abstract views. Power management cells are delivered as macros like any other analog block.
Reliability report. LDO pass devices and bandgaps carry EM and aging exposure that belongs in the reliability assessment.

risks: PSRR specified at DC. The frequency that matters is where the digital load switches, and a regulator flat at DC can be transparent at that frequency.
Stability verified only at nominal load. LDO compensation has to hold across the full load range including the transitions, which is where it usually does not.
Bandgap trim undefined. An untrimmed reference has a distribution wide enough to move every analog threshold, and there is no way to tighten it in production.
Brown-out and startup behaviour unspecified. The part's behaviour at supply ramp is discovered at bring-up, on silicon that cannot be changed.
Reviewed by nobody. Blocks everyone assumes and nobody reviews are the ones that fail in a way that looks like someone else's problem.

roles.d: EM and aging on pass devices

entry: PSRR and load requirements available from AMS-01
exit: PSRR verified at the digital switching frequency, not only at DC
Stability held across the full load range post-layout
Trim procedure agreed with test engineering
measuredBy: PSRR at the switching frequency against requirement
Load range over which stability is proven
Reference distribution before and after trim

purpose: Architect the custom SRAM instance the compiler could not deliver — bitcell choice, array organisation, sense amplifier topology and replica timing — against the density and Vmin the block budget demands.

This activity exists only because PDK-06 opened it. That decision came with a quantified gap and a fixed window, and the architecture chosen here determines whether the rest of the custom memory chain can close inside it. A conservative architecture will not recover the density; an aggressive one may not close Vmin.

steps.text: Scope confirmation against the PDK-06 decision and gap
Bitcell selection — foundry cell, pushed rules, or custom
Array organisation — banking, segmentation, aspect ratio
Sense amplifier topology and offset budget
Replica timing and self-timed path design
Peripheral circuit architecture — decoders, drivers, IO
Density projection against the block budget

AMS-05.flowNote: Step 7 closes the loop with PDK-05. If the projected density still misses the budget, the answer is to reopen the architecture now rather than to discover it after sixteen weeks of layout in AMS-07.
consumes: Custom instance decision and gap from PDK-06
Density and Vmin measurements from PDK-05
Foundry bitcell options and pushed-rule policy
produces: Sense amplifier topology and offset budget

rel.text: Custom SRAM instance specification with Vmin and sigma-yield report. The specification half of the deliverable; AMS-08 supplies the yield half.
AMS IP specifications and design review packages. The array's architecture review is one of the stage's formal gates.

risks: Architecture that does not recover the gap. A conservative organisation produces a custom array with the compiler's density and none of the compiler's maintenance advantages.
Bitcell pushed beyond foundry appetite. A cell the foundry will not approve is a layout that cannot tape out, and the approval path runs through PDK-06.
Sense amplifier offset budget optimistic. Offset drives Vmin more than any other single choice, and an optimistic budget is discovered in AMS-08 when it is far too late to change topology.
Replica timing not proven across corners. Self-timed paths that track at nominal and diverge at the corner produce read failures that look random.
Architecture frozen without the density projection. Freezing before step 7 means committing sixteen weeks of layout to an organisation that may not close the gap.

roles.d: Owns the array architecture and its freeze

entry: Custom instance decision taken by PDK-06 with a quantified gap
exit: Projected density closes the gap the decision was taken on
Bitcell choice within the foundry's stated approval appetite
Architecture frozen with an offset and Vmin budget attached
measuredBy: Projected density against the PDK-05 gap
Offset budget against what the topology can deliver
Architecture reopened after freeze

purpose: Design the assist circuits that buy Vmin — wordline boost, negative bitline, VDD collapse — and decide how much of each the array actually needs.

Assist is what makes an aggressive array workable, and it is not free: each technique costs area, power and complexity, and some of them interact badly. The design question is not which assist is best but which combination reaches the Vmin target at the least cost, verified statistically rather than at nominal.

steps.text: Vmin gap analysis against the AMS-05 architecture
Assist technique selection and interaction study
Vmin verification with assist enabled, across corners

AMS-06.flowNote: Steps 3 and 4 run in parallel and step 2 decides whether both are needed. Write assist and read assist pull in opposite directions on the cell, and enabling both without studying the interaction can leave Vmin worse than either alone.
consumes: Array architecture and Vmin budget from AMS-05
Vmin requirements from ARCH-05 operating points
Node assist circuit precedents from the foundry
Power budget for the array from ARCH-06
produces: Vmin gap analysis with assist requirement
Assist technique selection and interaction findings
Wordline boost, negative bitline and collapse circuits
Vmin verification results with assist enabled

rel.text: Custom SRAM instance specification with Vmin and sigma-yield report. The Vmin the instance is specified at is the Vmin with assist enabled, and this activity produces it.
Characterisation reports. Assist-enabled Vmin across corners is one of the report's core tables.

risks: Assist techniques combined without an interaction study. Read and write assist push the cell in opposite directions; enabling both blindly can make Vmin worse.
Assist verified at nominal. Vmin is a statistical quantity; verification at nominal proves nothing about the tail that decides yield.
Boost levels beyond reliability limits. Wordline boost stresses the cell, and a level chosen for Vmin alone shortens life in a way AMS-14 will find late.
Assist timing not calibrated. Fixed assist timing that works at one corner and misfires at another produces intermittent failures indistinguishable from a marginal cell.
Area cost of assist unbudgeted. Assist circuits sit in the periphery and can consume the density the custom array was built to recover.

roles.d: Owns the assist circuits and their verification
Cell response to assist and reliability limits
Area and power cost against the recovered density

entry: Vmin target set from the operating points in ARCH-05
exit: Vmin target met statistically, not at nominal
Assist interactions studied rather than assumed
Boost levels within the reliability limits AMS-14 will check
measuredBy: Vmin with assist against the target
Area cost of assist against the recovered density
Assist-related failures found in silicon

purpose: Lay out the custom array at pushed rules, and get the foundry to approve it — because a layout the foundry will not sign is a layout that cannot tape out.

Sixteen weeks of layout is what the density recovery actually costs. Pushed rules are the mechanism, and they carry an approval process with its own duration and its own possibility of refusal. Running layout and approval in sequence would not fit the window, so they run together, which means designing against rules that are not yet certain.

steps.text: Pushed-rule set proposal and foundry pre-alignment
Bitcell array layout at pushed rules

AMS-07.flowNote: Step 5 runs in parallel out of necessity rather than choice. Waiting for approval before laying out would not fit the window, so the array is laid out against rules that may still be refused — which is why step 1's pre-alignment matters more than its two weeks suggest.
consumes: Pushed-rule policy and approval path from PDK-06
Design rule manual and exceptions from PDK-02
Density target from the block budget
produces: DRC, LVS and antenna clean layout

rel.text: Per-macro DRC / LVS clean signoff, pushed rules approved by foundry. This activity is the deliverable, and the approval is the half that cannot be produced internally.
Custom SRAM instance specification. The achieved density is a layout result, and it is what the specification finally states.

risks: Foundry refuses a pushed rule after layout is built on it. The mitigation is pre-alignment in step 1, and it is the single most valuable two weeks in the activity.
Density target missed despite the pushed rules. The array then costs sixteen weeks and delivers the compiler's density, which is the worst available outcome.
Approval iterations underestimated. Each foundry round trip runs to weeks, and the five-week allowance assumes no more than two.
Fill and density compliance left to the end. Fill interacts with the array's matching and can undo careful layout if applied late.
Layout frozen before extraction is proven. An array that extracts badly has to be re-laid out, and the extraction handoff is where that is found.

roles.d: Owns the layout and the density result

entry: Foundry pushed-rule approval path agreed in PDK-06
exit: Every pushed rule approved by the foundry in writing
Achieved density meets the target the decision was taken on
Layout DRC, LVS and antenna clean, and extractable
measuredBy: Pushed rules approved against those proposed
Achieved density against the target
Foundry approval iterations against the allowance

purpose: Prove the array works at the tail of the distribution rather than at nominal — sigma-Vmin, bitcell variation, sense amplifier offset — using importance sampling because brute-force Monte Carlo cannot reach six sigma.

A memory array of this size fails at the tail by definition: with hundreds of millions of cells, the six-sigma cell is not a hypothetical, it is present in every part. Nominal simulation says nothing about it, and the yield the cost model assumed depends entirely on where that tail sits.

steps.text: Statistical methodology selection — importance sampling, scaled sigma
Bitcell variation model validation against silicon data
Sigma-Vmin analysis for read, write and retention
Array-level yield projection with redundancy applied

AMS-08.flowNote: Step 2 is the step that makes the rest meaningful. A variation model that has not been validated against silicon produces a six-sigma number with an unknown error, and the number is then used to justify a yield assumption in the cost model.
consumes: Assist circuits and Vmin results from AMS-06
Foundry variation models and silicon data
produces: Sigma-Vmin results for read, write and retention

rel.text: Custom SRAM instance specification with Vmin and sigma-yield report. The yield half of the deliverable, and the half the cost model depends on.
Characterisation reports across PVT and Monte Carlo. The statistical results sit alongside the corner results, and the two say different things.

risks: Brute-force Monte Carlo used at the tail. Reaching six sigma by direct sampling is computationally impossible; a run that terminates has not reached the tail it claims.
Variation model unvalidated. The six-sigma answer inherits the model's error, and nobody knows its size.
Redundancy assumed to cover the tail. Repair fixes a bounded number of failing bits; a distribution problem produces more than the repair scheme can absorb.
Retention overlooked. Read and write Vmin get the attention; retention failures at low voltage and high temperature are found in qualification.
Result reported without the methodology. A sigma number quoted without stating how it was obtained cannot be compared or challenged.

roles.d: Owns the methodology and the sigma results
Interprets results back into circuit changes
Array yield projection and cost model input

entry: Array architecture and assist circuits complete
Foundry variation models and silicon data accessible
exit: Sigma targets met for read, write and retention
Variation model validated against silicon, not assumed
Yield projection handed to the cost model with its methodology
measuredBy: Sigma achieved against target for each failure mode
Variation model error against silicon
Array yield projection against the cost model assumption

purpose: Build redundancy and repair into the array and make it match the BISR architecture DFT is designing — spare rows and columns, fuse allocation, repair algorithm, and the interface between them.

Redundancy is worth several points of yield and only if the two halves agree. The array provides spares and a repair interface; DFT-03 provides the BIST engine and the repair analysis. A mismatch between them is found at pattern generation, when both are effectively frozen.

steps.text: Redundancy scheme selection — row, column, or both
Spare allocation against the projected defect distribution
Repair interface definition with the BISR architecture
Redundancy verification and yield contribution analysis

AMS-09.flowNote: Steps 3 and 5 are joint work with DFT-03 rather than handoffs. Both sides can specify a repair scheme that is internally consistent and mutually incompatible, and only writing them together prevents it.
consumes: Fuse map and lifecycle model from ARCH-07
Yield target from the cost model
produces: Repair interface specification, agreed with DFT

rel.text: Custom SRAM instance specification. Repairable and unrepairable yield are different numbers, and the specification has to state which it quotes.
Integration guide. The repair interface is one of the integration points most likely to be misunderstood, and it belongs in the guide.

risks: Repair interface specified independently by both sides. Two consistent specifications that disagree with each other, discovered at ATPG when both are frozen.
Spare allocation not matched to the defect distribution. Row spares against a column-clustered defect mode repair nothing.
Fuse capacity insufficient. Repair data has to be stored; an allocation made without counting the worst-case repair set produces parts that cannot be repaired.
Redundancy credited twice. Yield projections that apply repair in both the array analysis and the product model double-count the benefit.
Repair algorithm assumed rather than agreed. The BIST engine implements one algorithm; the array assumes another, and the mismatch is silent until silicon.

roles.d: Owns the redundancy scheme and the array side
BISR architecture and the repair algorithm
Area cost of spares against yield gain

entry: BISR architecture intent available from DFT-03
exit: Repair interface written jointly with DFT, not in parallel
Spare allocation matched to the projected defect modes
Fuse capacity sized against the worst-case repair set
measuredBy: Repair interface mismatches found at pattern generation
Yield gain from repair against projection
Fuse capacity against worst-case repair need

purpose: Generate the views the custom array needs to behave like a compiler instance — timing, power, physical, functional — characterised across the same corners, so nothing downstream has to treat it as a special case.

A custom array that cannot be dropped into the flow like a compiler macro has not finished. Synthesis, place-and-route, timing signoff and verification all expect a standard view set; anything missing becomes a manual exception that has to be remembered at every iteration by everyone.

steps.text: View requirement definition against the tool matrix
Timing characterisation across the signoff corners
Physical abstract, blockage and pin view generation
Compiler-equivalence check against a reference instance

AMS-10.flowNote: Step 6 is the test that matters. Dropping the custom instance into the flow in place of a compiler instance and confirming the tools behave identically is what proves the view set is complete — reading the file list does not.
consumes: Vmin and assist results from AMS-06
produces: Timing views across the signoff corners

rel.text: Custom memory views characterised to compiler equivalence. This activity is the deliverable, and equivalence is the standard it is measured against.
Hard macro GDS with abstract views. The custom array is delivered into the macro set on the same terms as the analog blocks.

risks: Characterised at fewer corners than signoff runs. A missing corner turns into an extrapolation at SO-02, which the foundry will not accept.
Equivalence assumed from the file list. A complete-looking view set can still behave differently in the tools, and only a substitution test finds it.
Behavioural model diverging from the circuit. Verification passes against a model that does not match the array, and the mismatch reaches silicon.
Abstract blockages wrong. Over-blocking wastes routing resource; under-blocking produces shorts found at SO-02.
Views released before the layout freezes. Characterising against a layout that then changes means doing the whole activity twice.

roles.d: Owns the view set and its characterisation
Corner coverage against the signoff set

entry: Layout frozen and extractable from AMS-07
Tool view requirements known from PDK-08
exit: Characterised at every corner signoff will run
Equivalence proven by substitution, not by inspection
Views released only after the layout freeze
measuredBy: Corners characterised against signoff corners
Equivalence test results against a reference instance
View defects found downstream

purpose: Run the schematic-level design and pre-layout simulation that every analog block passes through — the common engineering discipline underneath the PLL, the PHY, the regulators and the array periphery.

This is the shared substrate rather than a block: topology exploration, device sizing, pre-layout corner simulation and the design reviews that gate a block into layout. Separating it makes the schedule honest — a block that has not passed pre-layout review is not ready for the sixteen weeks of layout that follow.

steps.text: Design environment and testbench framework setup
Device sizing and operating point definition
Pre-layout Monte Carlo and mismatch analysis
Testbench and regression suite per block
Pre-layout design review and layout entry gate

AMS-11.flowNote: Step 7 is a gate rather than a meeting. Layout is the longest and least reversible part of an analog block, and letting a schematic that has not closed at the corners enter layout guarantees that the corner failure is found after the layout is built.
consumes: Node device models from the tracked PDK
Design environment and simulator versions from PDK-08
Reliability rules and limits from the DRM
produces: Pre-layout corner and Monte Carlo results

rel.text: AMS IP specifications and design review packages. The pre-layout review package is the formal record that a block was fit to enter layout.
Characterisation reports. Pre-layout corner results are the baseline post-layout results are compared against.

risks: Blocks entering layout without passing the gate. Sixteen weeks of layout on a schematic that fails at the corner is the most expensive way to discover a topology problem.
Corner simulation run at typical mismatch. Mismatch dominates analog corner behaviour, and a corner run without it is a nominal run in disguise.
Testbenches written per block by different people. Inconsistent testbenches make results incomparable across blocks and unusable as a regression.
Device models used from an unfrozen PDK. Analog is far more model-sensitive than digital, and a model update mid-design can invalidate the sizing.
No regression suite. Every subsequent change is then verified by hand, and the coverage of that verification degrades under schedule pressure.

Confirms designs meet their allocated budgets
Model version control for analog design

exit: Every block passes a pre-layout gate before entering layout
Corner simulation includes mismatch, not only process corners
Regression suite exists per block and runs automatically

Corner failures found pre-layout against post-layout
Regression coverage per block

purpose: Lay out every analog and custom block to DRC, LVS and antenna clean, with the matching, shielding and fill discipline analog requires — and get the layouts extractable.

Eighteen weeks is the largest single block of time in the stage after the PHY, and it is largely irreducible. Analog layout is where matching, isolation and parasitic control are actually implemented, and none of it can be automated or parallelised the way digital place-and-route can.

steps.text: Floorplan and pin placement per macro
Supply and bias routing with EM compliance
Fill and density compliance without disturbing matching

AMS-12.flowNote: Step 5 is where careful layout is most often undone. Fill applied without regard to matching structures changes the parasitics the whole design was tuned against, and the effect is only seen in post-layout simulation.
consumes: PLL, PHY and regulator designs from AMS-02 to AMS-04
Design rules and exceptions from PDK-02
Macro placement intent from ARCH-08 and PD-01
Golden environment and decks from PDK-13
produces: DRC, LVS and antenna clean layouts

rel.text: Per-macro DRC / LVS clean signoff. Every analog macro's physical signoff, alongside the pushed-rule approvals from AMS-07.
Hard macro GDS with abstract views. The layout is the GDS half of every macro delivery.

risks: Fill applied late and without care. It disturbs the parasitics the design was tuned against, and the damage appears only in post-layout results.
Matching implemented by intent rather than by construction. Common-centroid and dummy structures are a layout discipline; describing them in a review is not implementing them.
EM checked only at signoff. Analog supply routing carries high current density in small geometries, and an EM failure found at SO-03 is a layout rebuild.
Pin placement not agreed with physical design. A macro whose pins face the wrong way costs routing resource at the top level for the life of the design.
Layout frozen without an extraction check. A macro that extracts slowly or badly stalls every post-layout simulation that follows.

Design rules and exceptions available from PDK-02
Macro placement intent known from ARCH-08
exit: Every macro DRC, LVS and antenna clean
Fill applied without disturbing matching structures
Pin placement agreed with physical design before freeze

Post-layout degradation against pre-layout results
EM violations found at signoff

purpose: Simulate every block with its layout parasitics extracted, across process, voltage and temperature and across the Monte Carlo distribution — and close whatever the layout took away.

Post-layout is where analog designs are actually judged. Parasitics reduce bandwidth, add mismatch, degrade PSRR and move every margin in the wrong direction. The gap between pre- and post-layout is the real measure of layout quality, and closing it is what the sixteen weeks are for.

steps.text: Extraction flow setup and parasitic model selection
Monte Carlo and mismatch analysis post-layout

AMS-13.flowNote: Step 6 is planned iteration rather than contingency. Analog blocks essentially always need at least one layout turn after post-layout simulation, and a schedule with no allowance for it is a schedule that will slip on the first block.
consumes: Frozen layouts and extraction from AMS-12
Block specifications and budgets from AMS-01
produces: Extraction flow and parasitic model selection
Post-layout functional and corner results per block

rel.text: Characterisation reports across PVT and Monte Carlo. This activity is the deliverable — the numbers every downstream consumer of these macros relies on.
AMS IP specifications and design review packages. Post-layout results are what each block's final review is held against.

risks: No layout iteration in the plan. At least one turn per block is normal; a schedule with none slips on the first block and never recovers.
Corner closure on a subset of blocks. The block skipped for time is the one that fails in silicon, and it is usually skipped because it looked simple.
Parasitic model too coarse. A model that misses coupling produces post-layout results that are optimistic in exactly the cases that matter.
Degradation not analysed. Knowing a block passed post-layout is less useful than knowing how much margin the layout consumed, which is what predicts the next block.
Monte Carlo run at reduced sample count. Cutting samples to save runtime narrows the distribution and flatters the tail.

roles.d: Flow setup and parasitic model selection
Corner and Monte Carlo data assembly
Schedules iterations and arbitrates margin trades

entry: Layouts frozen and extractable from AMS-12
exit: Every block closed post-layout at every signoff corner
Degradation from pre-layout quantified per block
Characterisation data complete enough to release the macros
measuredBy: Blocks closed post-layout at all corners
Margin lost from pre- to post-layout
Layout iterations per block against the allowance

purpose: Check every analog macro for the failure modes that appear over time rather than at test — electromigration, IR, aging, ESD and latch-up — because none of them show up in a functional simulation.

Analog blocks carry high current densities in small geometries and run continuously for the product's life. A design that passes every corner and fails EM has passed everything the design flow checks and none of what qualification will.

steps.text: Electromigration analysis on supply and signal routing
Aging and lifetime simulation at the rated conditions
ESD path verification through the macro

AMS-14.flowNote: Step 4 is the one that needs the product's actual mission profile. Aging simulated at nominal conditions for a nominal lifetime says nothing about a part that runs at the top of its DVFS range continuously, which is exactly how an accelerator is used.
consumes: Post-layout results and parasitics from AMS-13
Reliability rules from PDK-02 and the DRM
Mission profile and lifetime requirements from the qualification plan
produces: EM analysis results on supply and signal routing
ESD path verification and latch-up review

rel.text: Reliability report — EM/IR, ESD, latch-up, aging. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what qualification will be checked against.
Integration guide. Reliability limits — maximum current, boost duty cycle, operating conditions — are integration constraints and belong in the guide.

risks: Aging simulated at nominal conditions. An accelerator runs near its limit continuously; a nominal mission profile understates the stress by a wide margin.
EM checked on supplies only. High-speed signal routing in a PHY carries current densities that matter, and signal EM is routinely omitted.
ESD path assumed from the strategy. The strategy defines the intent; only tracing the path through the actual layout confirms it exists.
Assist boost stress not fed back. The boost levels AMS-06 chose for Vmin have an aging cost, and the two activities have to reconcile.
Waivers granted without a lifetime calculation. A reliability waiver without a quantified life impact is a decision nobody can defend at qualification.

roles.d: Owns the analysis and the report
Interpret findings back into design changes
Implement routing and guard structure fixes

entry: Mission profile and lifetime requirements defined
exit: Aging simulated against the product's real mission profile
EM checked on signal routing as well as supplies
Every waiver carries a quantified lifetime impact
measuredBy: Macros passing EM and aging at rated conditions
Waivers with a quantified lifetime impact
Reliability findings at qualification traceable to a missed check

purpose: Wrap every finished block into a hard macro physical design can place and verification can simulate — GDS, abstract, timing views, netlist, power intent and a behavioural model.

This is the handoff the whole stage exists to make. The macro set has to arrive before PD-02 places it, and the abstracts specifically have to arrive well before the models do, because floorplan needs the shape long before signoff needs the timing.

steps.text: View requirement confirmation with physical design and verification
GDS finalisation and macro boundary definition
Abstract generation — blockages, pins, routing layers
Timing view generation from characterisation data
CDL netlist and UPF power intent generation
Integration verification on a trial placement

AMS-15.flowNote: Step 7 is worth the two weeks. Placing every macro in a trial floorplan and running the flow over it finds abstract errors, pin conflicts and missing views before the whole physical design team is depending on them.
consumes: View and tool requirements from PDK-08 and PD-01
produces: Physical abstracts with blockages and pins
CDL netlists and UPF power intent

rel.text: Hard macro GDS with abstract views. This activity is the deliverable, and it is the stage's milestone — AMS Macro Handoff.
Custom memory views characterised to compiler equivalence. The custom array joins the macro set here on the same terms as the analog blocks.
Characterisation reports. The views are generated from the characterisation data and have to stay consistent with it.

risks: Abstracts delivered with the models. Floorplan needs the shape months before signoff needs the timing; a single delivery date serves the later need and misses the earlier one.
Trial placement skipped. Abstract and pin errors are then found by the physical design team, at the point where the whole floorplan depends on them.
