Views inconsistent with the characterisation. A timing view generated from stale data produces a design closed against numbers the silicon does not have.
Macro released without version control. Two teams on different macro revisions produce a mismatch that is diagnosed as a tool problem.
Power intent omitted. A macro with no UPF view breaks low-power verification and forces a manual exception at every run.

roles.d: Owns the macro set and its release

entry: View requirements confirmed with PD and DV
exit: Abstracts released ahead of models, on the schedule PD needs
Trial placement run and clean before general release
Every macro version-controlled and its views mutually consistent
measuredBy: Macros released against the PD need date
Abstract and view defects found at trial placement
Macro revisions issued after release

purpose: Keep the analog and digital halves talking — co-simulation, integration support and the errata that come out of it — through the whole period when the macros are being integrated.

Analog blocks fail at their boundaries: a reset that arrives before a rail is stable, a calibration sequence nobody scheduled, a control interface each side interpreted differently. Co-simulation is where those are found, and the integration guide is where they stop being rediscovered.

steps.text: Behavioural model correlation against circuit simulation
Integration support to RTL and physical design
Errata capture and integration guide authoring
Bring-up support material and debug hooks

AMS-16.flowNote: Step 5 runs across the whole window and is the reason this activity is marked continuous. Integration questions do not arrive in a block; they arrive one at a time for four months, and the engineer who can answer them has to still be assigned.
consumes: Startup and sequencing requirements from ARCH-05
produces: Boundary and control interface verification results
Errata list and bring-up debug material

rel.text: Integration guide with known limitations and errata. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what stops the same integration question being asked four times.
AMS IP specifications and design review packages. Where co-simulation contradicts a specification, the specification is what gets corrected.

risks: Behavioural models never correlated. Digital verification then passes against a model that does not match the circuit, and the mismatch reaches silicon undetected.
Boundary conditions unverified. Reset ordering, rail sequencing and enable timing are where analog blocks actually fail, and none of them are internal to the block.
Support engineer unassigned. Integration questions arrive for months; without a named engineer they are answered by guesswork or not at all.
Errata captured in email. A limitation known to one integrator and nobody else is rediscovered by every other integrator in turn.
Calibration sequence not co-simulated. A calibration that works in the circuit and is never exercised from the digital side is first tried at bring-up.

roles.d: Bring-up debug hooks and support material

entry: RTL integration environment available from RTL-03
exit: Every behavioural model correlated against circuit simulation
Boundary and sequencing verified, not assumed
Integration guide published and maintained, not held in email
measuredBy: Models correlated against those released
Integration questions answered within a working day
Errata found at bring-up that co-simulation could have caught

purpose: Decide what the test chip is for — which specific risks it retires — and select the structures that will actually answer those questions rather than the ones that are easy to include.

A test chip with no objective becomes a collection of everything anyone wanted to try, and it answers nothing in time to matter. The discipline is subtractive: name the two or three uncertainties that would change a production decision, and carry only what measures them.

steps.text: Objective definition — which production decisions this chip informs
Schedule feasibility — does the answer arrive before the decision
Cost and area budget for the shuttle die

TC-01.flowNote: Step 3 can cancel the activity, and should be allowed to. A test chip whose results land after the production design has committed is an expense with no decision attached, and finding that out in week three is far better than in week forty.
consumes: AMS block risk list from AMS-01
produces: Test chip specification and risk coverage matrix

rel.text: Test chip specification and risk coverage matrix. This activity is the deliverable, and the matrix is what every later result is reported against.
Design guidance and margin decisions. The guidance can only address risks this activity chose to carry — everything else stays unmeasured.

risks: Scope grows until the shuttle is missed. Every team has something worth measuring, and a chip that carries all of them misses the slot that made it useful.
Results arrive after the decision. A test chip is only worth its cost if the answer lands while the production design can still act on it.
Structures chosen for measurability rather than for risk. Ring oscillators are easy and tell you about the node; the risk is usually in a specific circuit nobody has built before.
No decision rule attached to a result. Measuring something without agreeing in advance what each outcome would change produces data and no decisions.
Area budget set after structure selection. Shuttle die area is expensive and fixed; selecting first and budgeting second guarantees a painful subtraction later.

roles.d: Owns the objective, the scope and the coverage matrix
Confirms which risks would change a production decision
Analog risk items and the structures that measure them
Schedule feasibility against the production decision dates
PCM and process monitor structure selection

entry: Node risk assessment available from TECH-07
IP and memory gaps known from IPR-05 and PDK-06
Production design schedule dated by DEF-08
exit: Every carried structure traces to a named risk and a decision rule
Schedule feasibility confirmed against the decision dates
Area and cost budget fixed before structures are finalised
measuredBy: Structures traceable to a risk item
Risks covered against risks identified
Shuttle die area against budget

purpose: Design and integrate the vehicle itself — the IP under test, its access wrappers, the process monitors and the measurement structures — as a small chip that has to work first time.

A test chip gets one shuttle. There is no bring-up iteration and no respin, so the access paths, the monitors and the pad ring have to be right on submission. That makes it a small design with an unusually high verification burden relative to its size.

steps.text: Device-under-test wrapper and access path design
Ring oscillator and process monitor array
Pad ring and ESD for the shuttle die
Verification of access paths and measurement modes

TC-02.flowNote: Step 8 gets two and a half weeks for a chip that is mostly structures, because an access path that does not work makes the structure behind it unmeasurable. Every mode has to be exercised in simulation, since there is no second chance in silicon.
consumes: Test chip specification and coverage matrix from TC-01
IP-under-test deliverables from AMS and IPR
Process monitor structure definitions from the foundry
Shuttle die area and pad count limits from TC-03
produces: Ring oscillator and process monitor arrays
Access path and measurement mode verification results

rel.text: Test chip GDS and shuttle submission record. The design half — TC-04 turns it into a submittable database.
Test chip specification and risk coverage matrix. Where a structure cannot be built as specified, the matrix is what gets updated.

risks: Access paths unverified. A structure that cannot be reached is a structure that was not measured, and the failure is only discovered in the lab.
Pad count exceeded. Shuttle die have few pads; a measurement scheme needing more forces multiplexing that has to be designed and verified.
IP under test modified for the vehicle. A block wrapped or altered to fit the test chip is no longer the block the production design will use.
Monitors placed without regard to position. Process variation across the die is part of what is being measured, and monitors clustered in one corner cannot see it.
No redundancy in critical structures. A single instance of the structure that matters most means one defect loses the answer entirely.

roles.d: Owns the integration and the access architecture
Process monitor and PCM structure design
Access path and measurement mode verification
Pad ring, area and structure placement

entry: Specification and coverage matrix from TC-01
IP-under-test available in a form that can be instantiated
Shuttle die area and pad limits known
exit: Every structure reachable through a verified access path
Monitors distributed to see across-die variation
Pad budget met without unverified multiplexing
measuredBy: Structures with a verified access path
Measurement modes exercised in simulation
Pad count against the shuttle limit

purpose: Book the shuttle slot and work backwards from its submission date — because the shuttle calendar is fixed, and missing a slot costs a quarter rather than a week.

One man-month across four weeks: almost all of this is scheduling and paperwork. Its importance is out of proportion to its effort, because the submission date it fixes is what every other test chip activity is planned against.

steps.text: Shuttle calendar review and slot options
Foundry or broker engagement and pricing
Slot booking against the production decision dates
Data format and submission requirement collection
Submission schedule and checklist working backwards from the slot

TC-03.flowNote: Step 5 is the useful output. A shuttle slot is a date on which a compliant database must exist; scheduling backwards from it is what tells TC-04 when physical verification actually has to finish.
consumes: Test chip objective and schedule feasibility from TC-01
Shuttle calendars from the foundry or broker
Capacity and pricing terms from TECH-05

rel.text: Test chip GDS and shuttle submission record. The booking and its requirements are half the submission record; the database is the other half.

risks: Slot booked without checking the production decision date. An available slot that returns silicon too late buys nothing.
Submission requirements collected late. Shuttle submissions have their own format and layer rules, and discovering them near the date forces rushed rework.
Backward schedule not enforced. A submission date that is not translated into a physical verification deadline gets missed by exactly the amount by which signoff runs long.
No contingency slot identified. A missed shuttle costs a quarter, and knowing the next available date in advance changes how the schedule is managed.
Cost approved after booking. Shuttle die area is charged by area and layer count; booking before the budget is agreed produces an invoice nobody planned.

roles.d: Owns the slot booking and the backward schedule
Confirms the slot serves the objective
Confirms the backward schedule is achievable

entry: Objective and schedule feasibility confirmed by TC-01
Budget authority for the shuttle cost
exit: Slot confirmed in writing with a submission date
Submission requirements collected and understood
Backward schedule agreed with physical design
measuredBy: Weeks between slot booking and submission
Submission date against the production decision date
Contingency slot identified

purpose: Implement the test chip physically and sign it off to shuttle submission standard — the same DRC, LVS and antenna closure a production die needs, on a fraction of the schedule.

The vehicle is small and the standard is not reduced. A shuttle rejects a non-compliant database, and the rejection costs the slot. What compresses the schedule is that timing closure is easy here; what does not compress is physical verification, which has to be as clean as production.

steps.text: Power delivery network for measurement accuracy
Timing closure on access and control paths
Fill, seal ring and shuttle frame compliance

TC-04.flowNote: Step 3 exists because a test chip measures small signals. A power delivery network adequate for function but noisy in the measurement bands turns a characterisation result into an argument about the vehicle rather than the device.
consumes: Test chip netlist and structures from TC-02
Submission requirements and date from TC-03
PDK, libraries and decks from PDK-13
Shuttle frame and seal ring rules from the foundry

rel.text: Test chip GDS and shuttle submission record. This activity is the deliverable, and the submission record is what proves the slot was met.
Test chip silicon and characterisation report. Measurement quality is determined here — a noisy vehicle produces uncertain results.

risks: Submission rejected on frame or format compliance. Shuttle frames have their own rules, and a rejection costs the slot rather than a re-run.
PDN adequate for function and inadequate for measurement. The results then carry vehicle noise that cannot be separated from device behaviour.
Physical verification compressed because the chip is small. Size does not reduce the standard, and a DRC violation is as fatal here as on a production die.
Structures placed without regard to the measurement plan. Placement affects what across-die variation can be seen, and it is decided here rather than in the lab.
No margin against the submission date. Everything before this activity can slip and this one cannot, so its schedule needs the buffer.

roles.d: DRC, LVS, antenna and frame compliance

entry: Netlist and structures complete from TC-02
Submission date and format requirements from TC-03
exit: Database clean against production physical verification standards
Shuttle frame and format compliance confirmed before submission
Submission made on the booked date
measuredBy: Submission accepted at first attempt
Days of margin against the submission date
Measurement-band noise on the PDN

purpose: Wait, visibly — mask, fabricate, dice and deliver — while keeping the program informed about a schedule it has almost no ability to influence.

Sixteen weeks and four man-months. The work here is tracking and logistics rather than engineering, and the value is that the rest of the program knows what date to plan against. A shuttle lot moves for reasons that have nothing to do with this program, and being told late is the avoidable part.

steps.text: E-test and PCM data review as it becomes available

TC-05.flowNote: Step 5 matters more than its 1.5 weeks suggest. PCM and e-test data arrives before packaged parts do, and it answers some of the process questions the chip was built for weeks earlier than the lab can.
produces: WIP status reporting against the program schedule

rel.text: Test chip silicon and characterisation report. The silicon itself, plus the PCM data that arrives with it.

risks: Shuttle lot slips and the program hears late. The slip cannot be prevented; the surprise can, and the surprise is what damages downstream plans.
Packaging not arranged in advance. Diced die with no package and no socket cannot be measured, and arranging it after delivery adds weeks.
PCM data ignored until parts arrive. Some process questions are answered by e-test alone, weeks earlier and at no additional cost.
Insufficient parts requested. Shuttle quantities are small; a characterisation plan needing more parts than were ordered cannot be run.
Logistics and customs not planned. Cross-border shipment of engineering samples carries paperwork that stops parts at a border for weeks.

roles.d: Confirms part quantities against the characterisation plan

entry: GDS submitted and accepted by the shuttle
Packaging and socket requirements defined by TC-06
exit: Parts delivered in the quantity the characterisation plan needs
PCM and e-test data reviewed before parts arrive
Schedule communicated at every status change, not only at delivery
measuredBy: Delivery date against the forecast at submission
Parts delivered against parts planned
Days between a lot status change and the program hearing about it

purpose: Have the board, sockets, instruments and automation ready before the parts arrive, so that characterisation starts on the day of delivery rather than six weeks later.

This is the small-scale version of the same mistake the production program makes with EVB. Parts arriving into a lab with no board is a delay that consumes the schedule advantage the test chip was supposed to buy, and it is entirely avoidable by starting during fabrication.

steps.text: Measurement requirement definition from the coverage matrix
Board design — supplies, bias, measurement paths
Socket or probe card selection and lead time
Measurement automation and data capture scripting

TC-06.flowNote: Step 3 has a lead time that can exceed the whole activity. Sockets for an unusual package are made to order, and a socket ordered when the parts ship arrives after they do.
consumes: Coverage matrix and measurement plan from TC-01
Pad assignment and access modes from TC-02
Package and die dimensions from TC-05
produces: Test chip board design and assembled boards

rel.text: Test chip silicon and characterisation report. The measurement quality the report can claim is bounded by the board and the automation built here.

risks: Board started when parts ship. The lab then waits, and the schedule advantage the test chip existed to buy is spent waiting for a PCB.
Socket lead time discovered late. Custom sockets are made to order and can take longer than the board itself.
Measurement automation deferred. Manual measurement of a full characterisation matrix is slow enough to consume the window and inconsistent enough to weaken the data.
Board noise floor above the signal of interest. A board adequate for function cannot measure a low-jitter clock or a small offset, and the limitation is found with the parts in hand.
Instruments not reserved. A shared high-end instrument booked by another program stops characterisation as effectively as a missing board.

roles.d: Owns the measurement setup and automation
Test chip board design and bring-up
Confirms the setup covers the matrix

entry: Coverage matrix and measurement plan available from TC-01
exit: Board bring-up complete before parts are delivered
Sockets in hand, not on order
Automation able to run the matrix without manual steps
measuredBy: Days between part delivery and first measurement
Board noise floor against the smallest signal of interest
Matrix points automated against total

purpose: Measure the silicon and correlate it against the models the production design is being built on — which is the only reason the chip exists.

Characterisation without correlation produces a data set. Correlation produces a statement of the form "the model is optimistic by 8% on this parameter at this corner", and that statement is what TC-08 converts into margin decisions the production design can act on.

steps.text: Incoming inspection and basic functionality check
Ring oscillator frequency and leakage measurement

TC-07.flowNote: This window overlaps the tail of fabrication because the stage as templated does not allow a clean sequence — PCM and e-test data are worked first, and device characterisation follows once packaged parts arrive. It is worth noting that the stage's forty weeks are tight for its own chain.
consumes: Packaged parts and PCM data from TC-05
produces: Functional and characterisation results per structure
Variability analysis across wafer and lot

rel.text: Test chip silicon and characterisation report. The measurement half of the deliverable.
Silicon-to-model correlation report. The half that makes the measurements actionable — a delta against what was predicted, per parameter and corner.

risks: Characterisation without correlation. A data set with no comparison to prediction cannot change a design decision, and changing decisions was the point.
Sample size too small for variability. Across-wafer and lot-to-lot variation is often the question, and a handful of parts cannot answer it.
Measurement uncertainty larger than the effect. A correlation claim that sits inside the measurement error is not a finding.
Outliers discarded. The parts that behave unexpectedly are usually the informative ones, and discarding them removes the tail the yield model depends on.
Results delivered too late for TC-08. Correlation completed after the production design has committed is a report nobody can act on.

roles.d: Owns the measurements and the data quality
PCM extraction and process parameter analysis

exit: Every measured parameter compared against its prediction
Measurement uncertainty stated alongside each correlation claim
Results delivered with time for TC-08 to act
measuredBy: Parameters correlated against parameters measured
Measurement uncertainty against effect size
Parts characterised against the sample size the plan required

purpose: Convert correlation findings into changes the production design actually makes — corrected models, revised margins, methodology updates — and track that they were adopted.

This is where a test chip earns or wastes its cost. A correlation report that circulates and changes nothing has bought an expensive confirmation of what everyone assumed. The output has to be specific: this model corrected by this factor, this margin increased by this amount, owned by this person, adopted by this date.

steps.text: Correlation gap analysis — where model and silicon disagree
Design rule and methodology update proposals
Margin decisions for the production design

TC-08.flowNote: Step 6 is the one that distinguishes a useful test chip from an expensive one. Publishing guidance is easy; tracking that physical design actually changed its margin and that the model was actually re-characterised is what turns the finding into a change.
consumes: Production design status and open margins
Model and library data from PDK-03
Production design change control process from RTL-10
produces: Model correction requests and re-characterisation scope
Margin decisions for the production design

rel.text: Design guidance and margin decisions for the production chip. This activity is the deliverable, and adoption tracking is what makes it more than a report.
Silicon-to-model correlation report. The gap analysis is published with the correlation, so the finding and its consequence stay together.

risks: Guidance published and not adopted. The most common way a test chip wastes its cost: everyone reads the report and nobody changes a margin.
Findings arrive after the design has committed. A margin decision for a block that has already closed is a decision that cannot be taken.
Model corrections requested but not scheduled. Re-characterisation is work; a correction with no owner and no date does not happen.
Only bad news acted on. Where silicon is better than the model, the margin released is real and usually left on the table.
Guidance stated as observation. "Leakage is higher than modelled" is not actionable; "increase the leakage budget for the compute cluster by 12%" is.

roles.d: Owns the guidance and its adoption tracking
Margin decisions against the production budgets
Change requests through the ECO board

entry: Production design status known well enough to act on
Change control process available from RTL-10
exit: Every finding converted into a specific, owned action
Margin released where silicon beat the model, not only tightened where it did not
Adoption tracked to completion, not just published
measuredBy: Findings converted into owned actions
Actions adopted against actions raised
Margin released where silicon outperformed the model

purpose: Complete the microarchitecture specification for every block — pipeline, interfaces, control, register map — to the level of detail an implementer can write code against without inventing anything.

ARCH-10 started these inside architecture; this finishes them. The distinction matters: a block whose specification is still being written while its RTL is being written produces code that documents itself, and the specification then follows the code instead of leading it.

steps.text: Specification completion plan and block-owner assignment
Pipeline and datapath detail per block
Block interface and protocol detail against the NoC
Verification hook and observability requirements with DV
Specification review and implementation entry gate

RTL-01.flowNote: Step 5 is the section most often left thin and the one verification spends the most time on. Corner-case behaviour that the specification does not define is behaviour the implementer chooses and the verification engineer has no basis to check.
consumes: Architecture specification and block chapters from ARCH-09
PPA budgets per block from ARCH-06
produces: Interface and protocol detail per block

rel.text: Block and top-level RTL release. The specification is what the release is checked against; without it, review has nothing to compare code to.
RTL Freeze package. A block whose specification was never completed cannot be declared frozen against anything.

risks: Specification written alongside the code. The document then records what was built rather than defining it, and verification loses its independent reference.
Corner cases left undefined. The implementer decides, verification cannot check, and the disagreement surfaces at chip-level integration.
Interfaces specified from one side. Two blocks each documenting their own view of a shared protocol produces two consistent documents that disagree.
Entry gate skipped for schedule. Coding against an incomplete specification is faster for two weeks and slower for two months.
Observability requirements added later. Debug and coverage hooks designed in cost little; retrofitted they cost timing and an RTL change under control.

roles.d: Owns the entry gate and specification quality
Resolves conflicts against the architecture specification

exit: Every block passes an entry gate before implementation starts
Corner-case behaviour defined, not left to the implementer
Shared interfaces agreed by both sides
measuredBy: Blocks passing the entry gate before coding starts
Specification changes raised during implementation
Corner cases defined against those found in verification

purpose: Write the synthesisable logic for every block, to a coding standard that survives lint, CDC, synthesis and gate-level simulation without rework.

At 180 man-months this is the largest single activity in the entire template — nearly 5% of the program's effort in one line. It is also the one most exposed to specification churn: every change upstream lands here, multiplied by the number of blocks that inherit it.

steps.text: Coding standard, directory structure and naming conventions
Bug fix and refinement against block verification
Block-level PPA refinement against trial synthesis

RTL-02.flowNote: Step 6 is seven weeks of fixing rather than writing, and it is the honest half of RTL. First-pass code is written in step 2; what makes it correct is the loop against block-level verification, and shortening that loop is where schedule pressure does the most damage.
consumes: Coding and lint standards from the methodology
produces: Block release tags with known issues

rel.text: Block and top-level RTL release, tagged. The block half of the deliverable; RTL-04 assembles the top.
Lint / CDC / RDC clean reports. Clean reports are a property of the code, and the coding standard set here largely determines them.

risks: Specification churn arriving mid-implementation. Every upstream change lands here multiplied by the blocks affected, which is why RTL-10 exists.
Coding standard imposed after code exists. Retrofitting a standard across 180 man-months of code is a project nobody schedules and everyone half-does.
Assertions treated as verification's job. Assertions written by the implementer capture intent; written by someone else they capture observed behaviour.
Blocks declared complete without verification feedback. First-pass code is not correct code, and a block frozen before its verification loop closes freezes its bugs.
Configurability added everywhere. Parameterisation nobody uses multiplies the verification space at no benefit, and the cost lands on DV-03.

roles.d: Implement, review and refine their blocks
Coding standard, review discipline and freeze

entry: Block specifications passed the RTL-01 entry gate
Coding standard and build environment available
Block-level verification environment starting up in DV-02
exit: Every block reviewed against its specification, not only linted
Blocks frozen only after their verification loop has closed
Releases tagged with known issues listed
measuredBy: Blocks frozen against blocks planned
Bugs found per block after freeze
Specification changes absorbed during implementation

purpose: Bring every third-party, foundry and internal IP into the design — wrappers, glue, configuration and version control — and prove each one behaves as its documentation claims.

IP integration fails at the boundary rather than in the block. A PHY that meets its specification and a controller that meets its specification can still disagree about reset ordering, and the disagreement is found here or it is found in the lab.

steps.text: IP receipt, incoming inspection against the acceptance checklist
Configuration, tie-off and parameter setting per IP
Boundary and reset sequencing verification per IP
AMS macro integration with behavioural models
IP version manifest and update handling
Integration report and issue escalation to vendors

RTL-03.flowNote: Step 1 is the acceptance check IPR-06 defined, and it is the last point at which an incomplete delivery is the vendor's problem. Accepting a delivery without inspecting it transfers the missing views to the integration team.
consumes: IP deliveries against the schedule from IPR-09
AMS macros and models from AMS-15 and AMS-16
Integration requirements from the architecture specification
produces: Boundary and reset sequencing verification results
Integration report and vendor issue log

rel.text: IP integration report and version manifest. This activity is the deliverable, and the manifest is what makes an IP-related bug traceable to a version.
Block and top-level RTL release. Integrated IP is part of the release, and its versions are part of the tag.

risks: Deliveries accepted without inspection. Missing views and collateral then become the integration team's problem rather than the vendor's.
Boundary behaviour assumed from documentation. Reset ordering, enable timing and calibration sequences are where IP integration actually fails.
Version manifest not maintained. An IP bug that cannot be traced to a version cannot be reported usefully or fixed reproducibly.
IP updates absorbed silently. A vendor drop applied without impact assessment can change behaviour verification has already signed off.
Late IP compressing integration. The integration window is fixed at its far end by RTL-04; a late delivery does not move it, it shortens it.

roles.d: Owns integration, inspection and the manifest
Vendor escalation on delivery and quality issues

entry: IP delivery schedule aligned by IPR-09
exit: Every delivery inspected against its checklist on receipt
Boundary and reset behaviour verified, not assumed from documentation
Version manifest complete and maintained through updates
measuredBy: Deliveries inspected on receipt
Boundary defects found here against those found at chip level
IP issues traceable to a manifest version

purpose: Assemble the blocks and the IP into one top-level design that elaborates, connects and boots — the first point at which the chip exists as a single object.

Chip-level integration is where every optimistic assumption made in isolation meets every other one. Connectivity, clock and reset distribution, address maps and configuration all become concrete here, and the defects found are the ones no block-level test could have seen.

steps.text: Address map and configuration space assembly
Chip-level smoke tests and first boot
Integration issue closure and top release

RTL-04.flowNote: Step 7 — the first chip-level boot in simulation — is the moment the design becomes real. It is also slow, because the first boot exercises paths that no block test touched, and each failure takes a full-chip simulation to reproduce.
consumes: Power and clock intent from RTL-05
produces: Assembled address map and configuration space

rel.text: Block and top-level RTL release, tagged. The top half of the deliverable — the object every downstream stage actually consumes.
RTL Freeze package. Freeze is declared on the top-level release, so its state is what the package describes.

risks: Connectivity checked by inspection. A chip this size has too many connections to review; automated connectivity checking is the only reliable method.
Integration started before blocks are stable. Integrating moving blocks produces defects that are re-found every time a block updates.
Address map assembled from block documentation. Generated maps agree with the code; hand-assembled maps agree with the documentation, which is a different thing.
First boot deferred. The boot path exercises reset, clocking, configuration and the fabric together, and delaying it delays every defect that only appears in combination.
Clock and reset distribution treated as a wiring task. It carries the crossing inventory from ARCH-05 and the CDC obligations that follow from it.

roles.d: Owns the top level and its release
Chip-level smoke tests and first boot
Boot path and configuration space expectations

entry: Blocks stable enough to integrate from RTL-02
IP integrated and boundary-verified in RTL-03
exit: Connectivity verified automatically, not by inspection
Chip boots in simulation before freeze is contemplated
Top-level release tagged with its full IP manifest
measuredBy: Connectivity defects found by checking against by simulation
Weeks from first integration to first successful boot
Blocks integrated against blocks released

purpose: Implement the clock, reset and power intent the architecture defined — domain boundaries, isolation, retention, crossing synchronisers — and produce a UPF file the tools accept.

Power intent is where architecture becomes an obligation on every downstream tool. Synthesis inserts isolation cells from it, verification checks against it, and physical design implements it. An intent file that is wrong or incomplete propagates the same error into all three.

steps.text: Domain boundary implementation against the ARCH-05 definition
Isolation, level shifter and retention strategy implementation
UPF authoring and tool acceptance check
Intent review with synthesis, verification and physical design

RTL-05.flowNote: Step 5 includes a tool acceptance check because UPF that reads correctly to a human and fails to elaborate in synthesis is common. The file has to be exercised in the actual flow, not reviewed as a document.
consumes: Power and clock architecture from ARCH-05
Block list and hierarchy from RTL-01
Library low-power cell availability from PDK-03
produces: Isolation, level shifter and retention implementation

rel.text: UPF power intent file. This activity is the deliverable, and "tool-accepted" is the standard rather than "reviewed".
Lint / CDC / RDC clean reports. The synchroniser implementation is what CDC closure in RTL-06 is checking.

risks: UPF written as a document. Intent that has never been elaborated in synthesis is intent whose errors are found by the first person who runs the flow.
Crossings implemented without reference to the inventory. A synchroniser strategy chosen per crossing by each designer produces inconsistency CDC will flag hundreds of times.
Retention strategy decided late. Retention cells cost area and change the physical implementation; adding them after floorplan is expensive.
Reset sequencing implemented from the block view. Reset order is a chip-level property, and blocks each releasing in their own order produces a boot that works in simulation and not in silicon.
Intent reviewed only by its author. Synthesis, verification and physical design each consume it differently, and each has to confirm it works for them.

roles.d: Owns domains, intent and the UPF file
Confirms the intent elaborates and infers correctly

entry: Power and clock architecture fixed by ARCH-05
exit: UPF elaborates in synthesis, not only reviews well
Every crossing on the inventory has an implemented synchroniser
Intent accepted by synthesis, verification and physical design
measuredBy: UPF elaboration errors at first synthesis run
Crossings implemented against the inventory
Intent revisions after RTL freeze

purpose: Drive lint, clock domain crossing and reset domain crossing to closure — every violation either fixed or waived with a reason someone signed.

These checks find the class of defect that simulation cannot: a crossing without a synchroniser works in every simulation and fails intermittently in silicon. The discipline is in the waivers — an unexamined waiver list is where the surviving bugs live.

steps.text: Lint, CDC and RDC methodology and rule set definition
Chip-level CDC closure against the crossing inventory
RDC closure and reset domain analysis

RTL-06.flowNote: Step 4 is chip-level rather than block-level because most real crossings are between blocks. Block-level CDC finds the easy ones; the crossing that fails in silicon is usually one neither block owner considered theirs.
consumes: Block and top RTL from RTL-02 and RTL-04
Lint and CDC tool setup from PDK-08
produces: Lint, CDC and RDC rule sets
Waiver list with dispositions and signatures
Closure regression in the CI flow

rel.text: Lint / CDC / RDC clean reports with waiver list. This activity is the deliverable, and the waiver list is the part that needs review rather than filing.
RTL Freeze package. Freeze with open CDC violations is freezing a class of defect that will not appear until silicon.

risks: Waivers accumulated rather than reviewed. A waiver list nobody re-reads is where the surviving crossings hide, and they are the hardest silicon bugs to diagnose.
CDC run only at block level. The crossings that matter are usually between blocks, and neither owner runs the check that would find them.
Closure not regressed. Clean at one release and dirty at the next, with nobody noticing until the freeze package is assembled.
Rule set weakened to reduce noise. Turning off the rule that produces the most violations is the fastest way to a clean report and the slowest way to a working chip.
Crossing inventory not reconciled. Crossings found by the tool but absent from ARCH-05's inventory mean the architecture and the implementation disagree.

roles.d: Owns lint, CDC and RDC closure
Block-level closure of their own violations

entry: Blocks stable enough to lint meaningfully
Tools set up and qualified by PDK-08
exit: Every violation fixed or waived with a signed reason
Chip-level CDC clean, not only block-level
Closure regressed in CI so it stays clean
measuredBy: Waivers reviewed against waivers granted
Crossings found at chip level that block level missed
Closure regression failures after first clean

purpose: Define the register map — the software contract — and generate the RTL, headers and documentation from one source so they cannot disagree.

The register map is where hardware and firmware meet, and it is the interface most often maintained in three places. Generating the RTL, the C headers and the documentation from a single description is what makes them consistent; hand-maintaining them is what produces a driver that writes to the wrong offset.

steps.text: Register description language and tooling selection
Access policy, reset value and side-effect specification
Generation flow — RTL, headers, documentation, UVM model

RTL-07.flowNote: Step 6 is a review by the people who will use the map rather than the people who wrote it. A register set that is natural to the hardware and awkward to drive is a set the driver will work around, and the workaround becomes the real interface.
consumes: Security and lifecycle access rules from ARCH-07
produces: Generated RTL, headers, documentation and UVM model

rel.text: Register map / RDL and generated headers. This activity is the deliverable, generated from one source rather than maintained in several.
Block and top-level RTL release. Generated register RTL is part of every block, so the map's release cadence is tied to the RTL's.

risks: Map maintained in more than one place. RTL, headers and documentation drift apart, and the driver eventually writes to an offset that moved.
Software reviews the map after freeze. An awkward interface then gets worked around in the driver, and the workaround becomes the contract nobody documented.
Side effects undocumented. A read that clears a status bit is a behaviour firmware has to know about, and discovering it in the lab costs days per instance.
Security access rules omitted. Registers that should be locked in production lifecycle states are locked late or not at all.
Reset values unspecified. Registers whose reset value is whatever the implementer chose produce a boot sequence that depends on undocumented behaviour.

roles.d: Owns the description source and the generation flow
Define their block's registers and side effects
Reviews the map from the driver's perspective

entry: Address map intent from the architecture specification
exit: RTL, headers and documentation generated from one source
Map reviewed by firmware before it is frozen
Side effects and reset values specified for every register
measuredBy: Artifacts generated against artifacts hand-maintained
Register changes after software review
Side effects documented against those found in bring-up

purpose: Run trial synthesis continuously against the evolving RTL and feed timing, area and power back to block owners while the code can still change cheaply.

RTL that has never been synthesised is RTL whose PPA is unknown. A block that misses its area budget by 30% is a redesign if found at SYN-02 and an afternoon if found here, and the difference is only whether anyone was running synthesis during implementation.

steps.text: Trial synthesis flow and constraint bootstrap
Per-block trial synthesis and QoR baseline
Area and budget tracking against ARCH-06
Power and clock gating effectiveness feedback
Recurring trial synthesis cadence and reporting

RTL-08.flowNote: Step 7 is the activity's real shape — a weekly cadence rather than a one-off study. A single trial synthesis is a snapshot; a weekly one is a feedback loop, and only the loop changes how blocks are written.
produces: Timing, area and power feedback reports

rel.text: Block and top-level RTL release. A block released without a trial synthesis result has an unknown PPA, and the release quality reflects that.
RTL Freeze package. The package states where each block sits against its budget, and this activity is where that number comes from.

risks: Trial synthesis run once. A snapshot tells a block owner where they were; only a cadence tells them whether they are improving.
Feedback delivered without constraints. Timing results against bootstrap constraints that do not resemble the real ones send block owners chasing paths that do not matter.
Area overrun tolerated because it is early. Blocks rarely shrink after implementation, and an overrun accepted at trial synthesis is an overrun accepted permanently.
Congestion ignored. Routability problems are cheaper to fix in RTL structure than in placement, and the early indication is the only chance to do so.
Results not tied to the budget. QoR reported in absolute terms rather than against ARCH-06 tells nobody whether the block is acceptable.

roles.d: Owns the trial flow and the reporting cadence
Act on the feedback in their RTL
Budget tracking and escalation on overruns
Enforces that feedback is acted on

entry: Library and environment available from PDK-13
exit: Every block has a current QoR result against its budget
Feedback delivered on a cadence, not on request
Overruns escalated rather than noted
measuredBy: Blocks with a current QoR result
Area against budget at RTL freeze
Weeks between a block change and its next QoR number

purpose: Run the build, regression and release machinery the whole stage depends on — continuous integration, nightly regressions, tagged releases and a reproducible environment.

This is infrastructure, and its value shows only in its absence. Without a nightly build, a break introduced on Tuesday is found on Friday by whoever needed the design; without release tagging, a bug cannot be reproduced against the version that had it.

steps.text: Build system and dependency management setup
Release tagging and version manifest process
Compute and licence capacity management for regressions
Continuous operation and maintenance across the stage

RTL-09.flowNote: Twenty-two of the thirty weeks are step 7, which is maintenance rather than construction. A CI system that is not maintained degrades into one everyone ignores, and an ignored red build is worse than no build at all.
consumes: RTL source from RTL-02, RTL-03 and RTL-04
Compute and licence capacity from PDK-12

rel.text: Integration testbench and build system. This activity is the deliverable, and its measure is that every release is reproducible from a tag.
Block and top-level RTL release. Releases are produced and tagged by this machinery; without it a release is a directory copy.

risks: Red builds tolerated. Once a broken build is normal, the signal is gone and every subsequent break is invisible.
Regression runtime exceeding the night. A nightly that takes thirty hours is not nightly, and the feedback loop silently doubles.
Releases produced by hand. An untagged release cannot be reproduced, and an IP bug found against it cannot be reported precisely.
Capacity not managed. Regressions competing with verification for the same licences slow both, usually at the point in the schedule where both matter most.
Triage unowned. Failures nobody is assigned to investigate accumulate until the regression result is meaningless.
exit: Every release reproducible from a tag
Nightly regression completing within the night
Failures triaged within a working day, with an owner
measuredBy: Days the build stays red
Nightly regression runtime
Releases reproducible from their tag

purpose: Control what changes and when — specification change requests, ECO board decisions and the freeze itself — so the design converges rather than oscillates.

Every stage downstream assumes RTL stops moving at some point. Change control is how that point is created: not by refusing changes, but by making each one visible, costed and decided by people who can see what it affects. The freeze is this activity's output, and its credibility is the whole program's.

steps.text: Change control process and ECO board definition
Change request intake and impact assessment workflow
ECO board operation and decision records
Change tracking against blocks, verification and synthesis
Freeze criteria definition and readiness tracking
Freeze declaration and post-freeze exception policy

RTL-10.flowNote: Step 3 runs for twenty weeks and is a standing meeting rather than a task. Its discipline is impact assessment: a change that looks like an afternoon in one block can invalidate a month of verification, and the board exists so that cost is visible before the change is approved.
consumes: Change requests from every source — architecture, verification, synthesis, IP
Trial synthesis and PPA status from RTL-08
Lint and CDC closure status from RTL-06
Freeze criteria from the program plan
produces: Change control process and ECO board charter
Change request log with impact assessments

rel.text: RTL Freeze package. This activity is the deliverable — the freeze, its criteria, its exceptions and the change history behind it.
Block and top-level RTL release. After freeze, a release is only produced through an approved exception.

risks: Freeze declared by date rather than by criteria. A gate that passes because it was scheduled teaches everyone that gates mean nothing.
Impact assessment skipped for small changes. The cost of a change is rarely in the block that changes; it is in the verification that has to be re-run.
Post-freeze exceptions ungoverned. Changes will be needed after freeze; without a policy they happen informally and nobody knows what the design contains.
Board without downstream representation. Verification and synthesis are the ones who pay for most changes, and a board without them approves costs it cannot see.
Change log not reconciled with the release. A freeze package that does not match what was actually built is a package nobody can rely on.

roles.d: Chairs the ECO board and owns the freeze
Impact assessment on the design side

entry: Process agreed and board membership named
Change intake path published to every team
Freeze criteria defined in the program plan
exit: Freeze declared against criteria, not against a date
Every change carries an impact assessment before approval
Post-freeze exception policy published and used
measuredBy: Changes with an impact assessment before approval
Freeze criteria met at declaration
Post-freeze exceptions against the policy

purpose: Write the plan that says what will be verified, how, and how anyone will know it is done — feature by feature, with a coverage model behind each claim.

Verification is the largest line of effort in the program, and without a plan it is 650 man-months of activity with no definition of completion. The coverage model is what turns "we tested it" into a measurable statement, and the features nobody writes into the plan are the features nobody verifies.

steps.text: Feature extraction from the architecture and block specifications
Verification strategy per feature — simulation, formal, emulation
Coverage model definition — functional, code, assertion
Closure criteria and sign-off definition per block
Verification plan review with design and architecture

DV-01.flowNote: Step 6 is a review by the people who wrote the specification, and its purpose is to find features the plan missed. Verification reviewing its own plan confirms it is coherent; architecture reviewing it confirms it is complete, and incompleteness is the failure mode that matters.
consumes: IP verification collateral requirements from IPR-06
produces: Feature list extracted from the specifications
Coverage model — functional, code and assertion
Closure criteria per block and at chip level

rel.text: Verification plan (vPlan) and coverage model. This activity is the deliverable, and the coverage model is what every later closure claim is measured against.
DV closure signoff package. Closure is defined here; a signoff against criteria written later is a signoff against a moving target.

risks: Plan written from the RTL rather than the specification. It then verifies what was built rather than what was specified, and the two differ exactly where the bugs are.
Coverage model that measures activity rather than intent. Code coverage says lines were executed; functional coverage says features were exercised, and only the second answers the question.
Closure criteria left vague. "High coverage" is not a criterion anyone can sign, and it becomes whatever the schedule allows.
Architecture not in the review. The features the plan missed are exactly the ones only the specification's author would notice.
Resource model omitted. A plan that needs more compute or more engineers than exist is a plan whose closure date is fiction.

roles.d: Owns the plan, the coverage model and the criteria
Confirms feature completeness against the specification
Confirms the plan is verifiable as the design is built

entry: Compute capacity model available from PDK-12
exit: Every specified feature has a verification strategy and a coverage point
Closure criteria written and agreed before verification starts
Plan reviewed by architecture and design, not only by verification
measuredBy: Features with a coverage point against features specified
Closure criteria signed before verification starts
Features added to the plan after it was reviewed

purpose: Build the verification environment — UVM agents, scoreboards, sequences, VIP integration — that every test in the program will run inside.

The environment is infrastructure with a long lead time and no visible output until it works. Sixty man-months buys agents for every interface, scoreboards that actually check, and reusable sequences. Testbench bring-up running late is the single most common reason verification starts late, and it starts late invisibly.

steps.text: Register model integration from the RDL source
Environment bring-up on the first block

DV-02.flowNote: Step 4 is where verification quality is decided. A scoreboard that compares against a reference model finds bugs; one that only checks protocol legality confirms the design does something rather than the right thing.
consumes: Block and interface specifications from RTL-01

rel.text: UVM testbenches and integrated VIP. This activity is the deliverable — the environment every subsequent verification activity runs inside.
Verification plan and coverage model. Coverage is collected by the environment, so what it can measure bounds what the plan can claim.

risks: Bring-up slower than planned and invisible. Environment work has no test-pass metric, so slippage is not visible until testing should have started.
Scoreboards that check protocol rather than function. A legal transaction carrying wrong data passes, and the bug survives to chip level.
No reuse strategy. Every block building its own environment multiplies effort and makes results incomparable across blocks.
Register model hand-written. A model that diverges from the RDL source produces tests that pass against the wrong offsets.
VIP licences short. Verification concurrency is capped by VIP seats, and the cap is discovered when regressions start queuing.

roles.d: Owns the environment architecture and reuse

entry: Interface specifications stable enough to build agents against
exit: Environment running on a real block, not on a stub
Scoreboards checking against reference models
Environment documented and reused rather than rebuilt per block
measuredBy: Blocks running in the shared environment against total
Bugs found by scoreboards against by manual inspection
Environment bring-up against plan

purpose: Verify every block against its specification with constrained-random and directed testing, and drive each one to its coverage closure criteria.

Two hundred man-months — the largest activity in the template — spread across thirty weeks and every block in the design. This is where most bugs are found and most verification time is spent, and its efficiency is set almost entirely by decisions taken in DV-01 and DV-02.

steps.text: Per-block testbench instantiation from the shared environment
Directed test development for specified behaviour
Coverage analysis and hole closure per block
Debug and bug reporting loop with block owners

DV-03.flowNote: Step 7 runs in parallel across the whole window because debugging is continuous rather than a phase. It is also where the largest single share of the effort goes — finding a bug is usually quicker than proving what caused it.
consumes: Coverage model and closure criteria from DV-01
produces: Coverage analysis and hole closure records

rel.text: UVM testbenches and integrated VIP. Per-block testbenches extend the shared environment and are delivered with it.
Regression and coverage dashboards. Block coverage is the largest contributor to the dashboards DV-10 maintains.
DV closure signoff package. Block sign-off is the substance of chip-level closure; the package aggregates it.

risks: Coverage closed by adding coverage points rather than tests. Redefining the model to match what was tested produces a closure number that measures nothing.
Constrained-random left unconstrained. Random stimulus without well-designed constraints spends compute exploring illegal or uninteresting space.
Corner cases skipped because the specification is silent. The gap belongs back in RTL-01, not quietly into the untested set.
Debug loop bottlenecked on block owners. Verification finds faster than design fixes, and the queue is where the schedule quietly goes.
Blocks signed off against different standards. Without enforced criteria from DV-01, each block closes to whatever its owner considered enough.

roles.d: Own their block's testing and closure

entry: Coverage model and criteria set by DV-01
exit: Every block closed against the DV-01 criteria, not its own
Coverage holes closed by tests, not by model changes
Sign-off records complete per block
measuredBy: Blocks closed against plan
Coverage achieved against the model
Bug find and fix rates over time

purpose: Verify the chip as one system running realistic scenarios — boot, configuration, traffic, power transitions, error recovery — rather than as a collection of verified blocks.

Blocks that each pass in isolation routinely fail together. Chip-level verification is where arbitration, ordering, deadlock, reset sequencing and end-to-end data integrity are actually tested, and none of those are visible from inside a block.

steps.text: End-to-end data path and integrity testing
Interconnect stress, arbitration and deadlock testing
Power state transition and DVFS scenario testing
Error injection and recovery at system level
Realistic workload scenarios from the DEF-02 suite

DV-04.flowNote: Step 7 uses the same workloads DEF-02 assembled and ARCH-01 modelled. Running them in simulation is slow and worth it: it is the only place the design, the model and the product's actual intent are compared against each other before silicon.

rel.text: DV closure signoff package. Chip-level closure is the part of the package that speaks to whether the system works, rather than the parts.
Regression and coverage dashboards. Chip-level scenarios are the slowest and most informative regressions on the dashboard.

risks: Started too late because blocks are not ready. Chip-level defects take longest to find and fix, and compressing the window pushes them into silicon.
Scenarios written by verification alone. Realistic use comes from the workload suite and from software; invented scenarios test what verification imagined.
Deadlock and arbitration untested. These fail only under contention, which random block-level stimulus does not create.
Power transitions verified functionally only. Retention, isolation and sequencing across a real power state change are where low-power designs actually fail.
Simulation too slow to run meaningful scenarios. If a boot takes a day, the scenario set shrinks to what fits, and emulation in DV-08 is the answer.
exit: Realistic workload scenarios run, not only synthetic ones
Deadlock and arbitration tested under contention
Chip-level coverage closed against the DV-01 model
measuredBy: Scenarios run against scenarios planned
Chip-level bugs found against block-level
Simulation throughput on the boot scenario

purpose: Use formal proof where simulation is weak — connectivity, control logic, arbiters, security properties, register access — and prove exhaustively what testing can only sample.

Formal answers a different question. Simulation shows that the cases tried worked; a proof shows that no case exists that does not. For arbiters, protocol state machines and security isolation, the space is too large to sample and the failure modes are exactly the ones random stimulus misses.

steps.text: Target selection — where formal beats simulation
Connectivity and structural proof at chip level
Proof closure, bounded results and reporting

DV-05.flowNote: Step 6 is what separates a proof from a false claim. A property that passes because assumptions excluded the failing case has proved nothing, and reviewing assumptions is the only way to know which of the two happened.
consumes: Verification plan target selection from DV-01
produces: Assumption list and proof closure report

rel.text: Formal proof reports with assumption list. This activity is the deliverable, and the assumption list is what makes the proofs auditable.
DV closure signoff package. Formally proved properties are a different kind of evidence from coverage, and the package should distinguish them.

risks: Over-constrained proofs. Assumptions that exclude the failing case produce a green result and no information, and only assumption review catches it.
Formal applied where simulation is better. Datapath and workload behaviour are poor formal targets; applying it there consumes specialist time for little return.
Bounded results reported as proofs. A property proved to depth twenty is not proved; the bound has to be stated with the result.
Properties written from the RTL. A property derived from the implementation proves the implementation matches itself.
Security properties omitted. Isolation and access control are exactly the properties simulation samples poorly and formal proves well.

roles.d: Owns target selection and proof quality
Integrates formal results into closure evidence

entry: Block RTL stable enough to prove against
exit: Every proof reported with its assumptions and its bound
Assumptions reviewed for over-constraint, not just listed
Security properties proved rather than sampled
measuredBy: Properties fully proved against bounded
Assumptions reviewed against assumptions made
Bugs found by formal that simulation had missed

purpose: Verify the design against its power intent — isolation, retention, level shifting, power sequencing — because none of it is visible in a normal functional simulation.

A design that passes every functional test can still corrupt state on a power-down, drive an isolated domain, or fail to retain what it needed. Low-power verification simulates the domains actually powering down, and it is the only place these failures appear before silicon.
DV-06.flowNote: Step 4 is the one that finds real bugs. Retention verification requires actually powering a domain down in simulation and checking what survives; a design that has never been simulated through a power cycle has never been tested for the failure mode.
consumes: Power management controller RTL from RTL-05
produces: Isolation and level shifter verification results

rel.text: Low-power verification report. This activity is the deliverable, and it is the only evidence that the power architecture works as intended.
Regression and coverage dashboards. Power-aware regressions belong in the same dashboard as functional ones, not in a side report.

risks: Only static checking performed. Structural UPF checks find missing cells; only simulation finds a design that corrupts state when the domain actually goes down.
Retention verified for the intended state only. What is not retained matters as much as what is, and a design that retains too little fails on resume.
Power sequences tested in isolation. The failure is usually a power transition during traffic, not a clean idle transition.
Power-aware simulation excluded from regression. It is slow, so it gets run once; a later RTL change then breaks it silently.
UPF used for verification differing from synthesis. Two versions of the intent means verifying one design and building another.

roles.d: Confirms the verified states match the architecture

entry: UPF available and tool-accepted from RTL-05
exit: Domains simulated powering down, not only statically checked
Retention verified for both what is kept and what is not
Power-aware tests running in the regular regression
measuredBy: Power states simulated against states defined
Retention defects found pre-silicon
Power-aware tests in the nightly regression

purpose: Verify the boundary between the analog macros and the digital design — control interfaces, calibration sequences, startup ordering — with the analog represented by models correlated to its circuits.

Analog blocks fail where they meet digital. A PLL that locks perfectly and a controller that sequences perfectly can still disagree about when lock is valid. Co-simulation is where those disagreements appear, and the alternative is finding them at bring-up with an oscilloscope.

steps.text: Model fidelity review against AMS characterisation

DV-07.flowNote: Step 2 decides whether any of this is meaningful. Verification against a behavioural model that does not match the circuit proves the digital side works with a fiction, and the correlation in AMS-16 is what makes the model a proxy rather than a guess.
consumes: Startup and sequencing requirements from ARCH-05

rel.text: UVM testbenches and integrated VIP. The co-simulation environment extends the shared testbench rather than standing beside it.
DV closure signoff package. Mixed-signal boundary closure is a distinct claim in the package, because it rests on models rather than on RTL alone.

risks: Models never correlated. Digital passes against a fiction, and the mismatch reaches silicon as a bring-up failure nobody predicted.
Calibration sequences untested from the digital side. A calibration that works when the analog engineer drives it manually is first exercised by firmware at bring-up.
Ready and lock signalling assumed. When a lock signal becomes valid is a contract; each side assuming a different answer produces intermittent boot failures.
Degraded modes unverified. What the digital side does when a PLL fails to lock is behaviour that only matters in the field, where it matters a great deal.
Co-simulation too slow to regress. Run once and never again, it cannot catch a later change on either side.

roles.d: Calibration sequences as software will drive them

exit: Every model correlated against its circuit before being relied on
Calibration sequences exercised from the digital side
Degraded and fault behaviour verified, not assumed
measuredBy: Models correlated against models used
Boundary defects found here against at bring-up
Calibration sequences verified against those implemented

purpose: Stand up emulation and FPGA prototyping — partitioning, capacity, speed, debug — so that scenarios too long for simulation can actually be run.

A boot that takes a day in simulation takes minutes in emulation, and workload scenarios that are impossible in one are routine in the other. Emulation is also the platform firmware development runs on, which makes its availability date a dependency for a team outside this stage entirely.

steps.text: Memory and interface modelling on the platform
Bring-up and first boot on emulation
Platform handover to firmware and validation

DV-08.flowNote: Step 8 makes this activity a dependency for people outside verification. Firmware cannot start on real workloads until the platform runs, and the handover date belongs in the program schedule rather than in the verification plan alone.
consumes: Emulator or FPGA capacity and licences
Memory and interface models for the platform
Debug requirements from validation and firmware

rel.text: Emulation platform and system test suite. This activity is the deliverable, and it serves firmware and validation as much as verification.
Regression and coverage dashboards. Emulation regressions cover scenarios simulation cannot reach, and belong in the same view.

risks: Partitioning consuming more time than expected. Splitting a large design across emulator capacity is difficult and iterative, and it is routinely underestimated.
Capacity contended with another program. Emulator capacity is expensive and shared; a program without a booked allocation runs when the other one is not.
Debug visibility inadequate. A platform that runs fast and cannot be probed produces failures that cannot be diagnosed.
Handover date not in the program schedule. Firmware plans against it, and treating it as an internal verification milestone means nobody outside knows when it slips.
Models diverging from the design. Memory and interface models built for the platform can drift from the RTL, and results then reflect the model.

roles.d: Owns the platform, partitioning and bring-up
Visibility and trace on the platform

exit: Design boots on the platform at usable speed
Debug visibility sufficient to diagnose a failure
Platform handed over to firmware on a scheduled date
measuredBy: Emulation speed against target
Weeks from RTL availability to first platform boot
Scenarios run on emulation that simulation could not

purpose: Check that the design actually delivers the performance the architecture promised — bandwidth, latency, utilisation — against the same workloads ARCH-01 modelled.

Functional correctness and performance are separate questions, and passing every test says nothing about the second. A design that computes correctly at 60% of modelled throughput is a product that misses its headline KPI, and finding that in silicon leaves no options.

steps.text: Performance measurement infrastructure in the testbench
Workload execution on emulation and simulation
Bandwidth and utilisation measurement against the model
Correlation against the ARCH-01 performance model

DV-09.flowNote: Step 6 closes a loop opened at architecture. Where the RTL and the model disagree, one of them is wrong — and finding out which is what tells the program whether it has a design problem or a modelling problem.
consumes: Performance model and predictions from ARCH-01

rel.text: DV closure signoff package. Performance evidence is part of tapeout readiness — functional closure alone does not say the product meets its KPIs.
Emulation platform and system test suite. The performance workloads become part of the standing suite the platform runs.

risks: Performance treated as a bring-up activity. Discovered in silicon, a throughput shortfall has no remaining fix except software and marketing.
Measured only on synthetic traffic. Synthetic patterns exercise the interconnect; real workloads exercise the design, and only the second predicts the product.
Model and RTL disagreement left unresolved. Whichever is wrong, not knowing which means every downstream projection is unreliable.
Bottlenecks found without root cause. Knowing throughput is low is not actionable; knowing which queue saturates is.
No time left to act. Findings that arrive after RTL freeze can only be documented, not fixed.

roles.d: Decides between design change and model correction

entry: Performance model predictions available from ARCH-01
exit: Real workloads measured, not only synthetic traffic
Every model disagreement resolved as design or model error
Findings delivered with time to act on them
measuredBy: Measured throughput against modelled
Bottlenecks with an identified root cause
Weeks between findings and RTL freeze

purpose: Keep the regressions running and the coverage moving toward closure — triage failures, manage capacity, publish where every block stands, and close the holes that remain.

Coverage closure is not a phase at the end; it is a curve that either bends or does not. This activity owns the curve: which holes are real, which tests would close them, and whether the regression is stable enough for the numbers to mean anything.

steps.text: Coverage hole analysis and test targeting

DV-10.flowNote: Step 6 is unglamorous and load-bearing. A regression with intermittent failures trains everyone to ignore red results, and once that habit forms the regression has stopped being a signal.
consumes: Coverage model and criteria from DV-01
Test suites from DV-03 through DV-09
Regression capacity from PDK-12 and RTL-09
Build and CI infrastructure from RTL-09
produces: Hole analysis and targeted test list

rel.text: Regression and coverage dashboards. This activity is the deliverable, and its value is that the numbers are current and trusted.
DV closure signoff package. Closure is assembled here from the evidence every other DV activity produced.

risks: Flaky regressions tolerated. Once red results are routinely ignored, the regression has stopped providing information and nobody notices when it matters.
Coverage merged without stability. Numbers from an unstable regression are noise presented as a trend.
Holes closed by waiving rather than testing. A hole waived without analysis is untested behaviour recorded as covered.
Capacity insufficient at peak. Regression queues at the point of closure directly extend the closure date.
Closure signed with the curve still climbing. Coverage still rising at sign-off means the plan's completion criteria were not what stopped the work.

roles.d: Triage and close their own failures

entry: Test suites producing coverage from DV-03
exit: Regression stable enough that a red result is believed
Every hole analysed before it is closed or waived
Coverage curve flat at sign-off, not still climbing
measuredBy: Regression flake rate
Coverage against the model at sign-off
Holes analysed against holes waived

purpose: Simulate the gate-level netlist, first functionally and then with real timing, to catch what RTL simulation structurally cannot — X-propagation, reset behaviour, timing-dependent failures and synthesis or DFT-induced differences.

RTL simulation is optimistic about X and blind to timing. Gate-level simulation is slow, painful and the last check before the design becomes masks — it is also where scan insertion, clock gating and synthesis transformations are proved not to have changed behaviour.
DV-11.flowNote: Step 3 finds the class of bug RTL simulation is structurally incapable of seeing. RTL X-optimism hides uninitialised state; at gate level the X propagates, and a design that boots in RTL can fail to come out of reset in gates.
produces: Scan and DFT mode simulation results

rel.text: Gate-level simulation report. This activity is the deliverable, and it is a tapeout checklist item rather than an optional confirmation.
DV closure signoff package. Gate-level results close the gap between what was verified and what will be manufactured.

risks: Skipped because it is slow. The failures it finds — X propagation, reset, timing-dependent behaviour — have no other pre-silicon detector.
Run only in functional mode. Scan and test modes are how the part is tested at ATE, and a scan mode that does not work makes the part untestable.
Started after netlist churn has settled. Waiting for a stable netlist means starting too late; running early on an imperfect netlist finds environment problems while there is time.
X failures suppressed rather than fixed. Forcing initial values to make the simulation run hides exactly the uninitialised state the check exists to find.
Timing simulation on a subset of corners. Timing-dependent failures appear at specific corners, and the corner skipped is the one that fails.

roles.d: Owns the runs and the closure

entry: SDF available from PD-09 for timing runs
exit: X-propagation issues fixed rather than suppressed
Scan and test modes simulated, not only functional
Timing simulation run at the corners that matter
measuredBy: Modes simulated against modes the part will use
X failures fixed against suppressed
Gate-level defects found that RTL simulation could not

purpose: Run the bug disposition board — triage every defect, decide what gets fixed, and make the risk of what does not explicit and owned.

Every program reaches tapeout with open bugs. The question is whether they were assessed and accepted or simply ran out of time, and the difference is entirely this activity. Its output at the end is the errata list bring-up will work against and the risk statement the Go / No-Go decision reads.

steps.text: Bug tracking, severity and triage process definition
Bug rate and closure trend analysis
Open bug list and risk statement for tapeout

DV-12.flowNote: Step 6 is the loop that improves the process rather than the design. Asking why a bug found in week 34 was not found in week 12 usually points at a missing coverage point or an untested mode, and fixing that finds the next one earlier.
consumes: Coverage and closure status from DV-10
Tapeout criteria from the program plan
produces: Bug rate and closure trend analysis
Open bug list and risk statement

rel.text: DV closure signoff package. The open bug list and its risk statement are the part of the package the Go / No-Go decision actually reads.
Regression and coverage dashboards. Bug find and closure rates sit alongside coverage as the two curves that say whether verification is converging.

risks: Bugs deferred without risk assessment. An unassessed open bug at tapeout is a risk nobody quantified being accepted by nobody in particular.
Severity assigned by the finder. Consistent severity requires a board; without one, the same defect is critical in one block and minor in another.
Bug rate still rising at closure. A find rate that has not turned over means the design has more defects than have been found, whatever the coverage says.
No escape analysis. The process that let a bug survive to week 34 will let the next one survive too.
Errata list assembled after tapeout. Bring-up needs the known-issue list on day one, and assembling it later means debugging problems that were already known.

roles.d: Severity and product impact of deferred defects
Turns deferred bugs into bring-up watch items

effort: Open bug list and risk statement
entry: Bug tracking system and severity scheme agreed
Tapeout criteria defined in the program plan
exit: Every deferred bug carries an assessed, owned risk
Bug find rate turned over before closure is recommended
Errata list ready for bring-up on day one
measuredBy: Deferred bugs with a risk assessment
Bug find rate trend at closure
Escapes analysed against escapes found

purpose: Decide how the chip will be tested before it is built to be testable — scan style, compression ratio, hierarchical partitioning, and the test modes the design will support.

Every one of these choices constrains the design rather than following it. Compression ratio decides pattern volume and therefore test cost; hierarchical DFT decides whether a block can be tested independently; and both have to be settled before SYN-01 writes constraints against them.

steps.text: Test strategy definition — what is tested where and how
Hierarchical DFT partitioning against the design hierarchy
Test mode definition and mode control

DFT-01.flowNote: Step 3 is a cost decision disguised as an architecture one. Compression ratio sets pattern volume, pattern volume sets tester memory and test time, and test time is a per-unit cost for the life of the product.
consumes: Design hierarchy and partitioning from ARCH-02
Coverage and test-time targets from DFT-02
Memory list and BISR intent from ARCH-03

rel.text: DFT architecture specification and coverage plan. This activity is the deliverable, and everything else in the stage is executed against it.
DFT signoff entry for the tapeout checklist. An architecture that was never fixed cannot be signed off against.

risks: Architecture decided after synthesis starts. Scan insertion and constraints depend on it; deciding late means re-running both.
Compression ratio chosen without the test cost model. Ratio trades pattern volume against silicon area, and only TEST-09's cost model says which side to favour.
Hierarchical DFT ignored on a large die. Flat scan on a design this size produces pattern volumes and runtimes that become their own schedule problem.
Test modes defined without the security architecture. Every test mode is an access path, and ARCH-07 has to lock the ones that should not exist in production.
