Architecture written and not reviewed by test engineering. A scheme that is elegant in design and unrunnable on the chosen ATE is discovered at TEST-08.

roles.d: Owns the architecture and its specification

entry: Coverage and test-time targets agreed in DFT-02
Test platform direction available from TEST-02
exit: Architecture fixed before synthesis writes constraints against it
Compression ratio chosen against a test cost model
Specification reviewed by test and product engineering
measuredBy: Architecture decisions taken before synthesis starts
Compression ratio against pattern volume budget
Architecture changes after freeze

purpose: Agree the coverage and test-time targets with the people who pay for them — product engineering, who own quality, and test engineering, who own the tester seconds.

Coverage and test time pull against each other, and neither belongs to DFT alone. A defect-per-million target sets required coverage; a cost-per-unit target sets allowable test time; and the architecture in DFT-01 is chosen to sit between them. Negotiating this first is what makes the architecture decidable.

steps.text: Quality target translation — DPPM to required coverage
Test time budget from the product cost model
Fault model selection — stuck-at, transition, cell-aware
Coverage target per fault model and per block class

DFT-02.flowNote: Step 3 has a large downstream cost. Cell-aware patterns catch defects the other models miss and multiply pattern count doing it, so the decision belongs here with the cost model in the room rather than at DFT-07 when the patterns are being generated.
consumes: Quality and DPPM targets from the product requirements
produces: Coverage target derived from the DPPM requirement

rel.text: DFT architecture specification and coverage plan. The coverage plan half — the numbers DFT-01's architecture is chosen to reach.
ATPG pattern sets with coverage report. The report is measured against the targets set here, not against what the tool happened to reach.

risks: Coverage target set by convention. "99% stuck-at" carried from the last program may be far from what this product's DPPM requirement needs.
Test time budget not derived from cost. A test time nobody costed becomes whatever the patterns need, and the per-unit cost is discovered at production.
Fault model chosen at pattern generation. Adding cell-aware late multiplies pattern volume against a tester memory budget already fixed.
Targets agreed without product engineering. The organisation that owns field quality has to own the coverage number, or it will be renegotiated when patterns run long.
No per-block differentiation. Memory-dominated blocks and control logic need different approaches, and a single flat target over-tests one and under-tests the other.

roles.d: Owns the target negotiation and record
Test time, tester memory and cost
Defect density and fault model relevance
Records the agreement and its cost implication

entry: Test cost budget from the DEF-04 model
exit: Coverage target derived from DPPM, not inherited
Test time budget traced to a per-unit cost
Targets signed by product and test engineering
measuredBy: Coverage target against DPPM requirement
Test time budget against the cost model
Targets renegotiated during pattern generation

purpose: Architect memory test and repair — MBIST engines, BIRA analysis, BISR repair and the fuse path — for a design where memory is most of the die.

On an accelerator the arrays dominate both area and defect exposure, and they cannot be tested by scan. MBIST is how they are tested and repair is how the yield is recovered; both have to be designed jointly with AMS-09, because the array provides the spares and this activity provides the engine that uses them.

steps.text: Memory inventory and test requirement per instance
BISR and fuse path integration with ARCH-07
Repair interface agreement with the memory designers

DFT-03.flowNote: Step 6 is the joint decision with AMS-09. Both sides can specify an internally consistent repair scheme that the other cannot implement, and writing the interface together is the only reliable way to avoid it.
consumes: Memory instances from PDK-04 and AMS-10
Fuse map and lifecycle from ARCH-07
Repair yield expectations from the yield model

rel.text: MBIST / BISR insertion and test collateral. This activity is the deliverable, including the repair collateral test engineering will run.
DFT architecture specification. Memory test is a large part of the overall architecture, not a separate subject.

risks: Repair interface specified separately from the array. Two consistent specifications that disagree, found at pattern generation when both are frozen.
Algorithms chosen without the failure modes. March algorithms differ in what they catch; a default choice misses the defect modes this array actually exhibits.
Fuse capacity insufficient. Repair data has to be stored, and an allocation made without counting the worst-case repair set produces unrepairable parts.
MBIST runtime unbudgeted. Memory test on an array-dominated die can dominate test time, and it is often costed after the architecture is fixed.
Repair not verified end to end. A repair path proven in pieces and never exercised from failure through analysis to fuse blow fails at production test.

roles.d: Owns MBIST, BIRA and BISR architecture
MBIST runtime and repair flow at ATE

entry: Redundancy scheme from AMS-09 in progress
Fuse map and lifecycle model from ARCH-07
exit: Repair interface written jointly with the memory designers
Repair path verified end to end, not in pieces
MBIST runtime inside the test time budget
measuredBy: MBIST runtime against the test time budget
Repair interface mismatches at pattern generation
Repair yield recovered against projection

purpose: Design the access network — boundary scan, IJTAG, TAP controller and the debug paths — that every test, every repair and every silicon debug session runs through.

The TAP is the door into the chip. It is used at wafer sort, at package test, during bring-up and in the field, and it is also the door ARCH-07 needs to lock in production. Designing it is a negotiation between access and security rather than a purely technical exercise.

steps.text: Access architecture — TAP, IJTAG network topology
IJTAG instrument network and description files
Debug and trace access path definition
Security lockdown integration per lifecycle state
Access network verification and description file generation

DFT-04.flowNote: Step 5 is where the negotiation with ARCH-07 lands. Every path this activity opens for debug is a path security has to close in production lifecycle states, and the lock has to be testable without making the part permanently undebuggable.
consumes: Debug requirements from validation and BU-09
produces: Instrument network with ICL and PDL descriptions

rel.text: JTAG / IJTAG description files (BSDL, ICL, PDL). This activity is the deliverable, and these files are what board test and ATE consume.
DFT architecture specification. The access network is how every other DFT feature is reached.

risks: Debug access designed out for security. A part that cannot be debugged in the field is a part whose first field failure has no diagnostic path.
Lockdown untested. The lifecycle transition that locks the TAP is the one nobody exercises, because exercising it makes the part undebuggable.
Description files generated late. BSDL and ICL are consumed by board test and ATE; generating them near tapeout leaves no time to validate them.
Access network verified only in functional mode. The network exists to work when the design does not, and that is the mode that needs proving.
Pin budget for debug not reserved. Trace ports need pins, and a bump map fixed without them means debug through a narrow channel.

roles.d: Owns the TAP, the network and the description files
Debug and trace requirements for bring-up
Pin and routing budget for the network

entry: Security lockdown policy defined by ARCH-07
Pin and bump budget known from ARCH-08
exit: Lockdown transitions tested, not only implemented
Description files generated and validated before tapeout
Debug access preserved for the lifecycle states that need it
measuredBy: Lifecycle lockdown transitions tested
Description files validated before tapeout
Debug access available in the states validation needs

purpose: Design the on-chip clock controllers that generate at-speed test clocks — because transition-fault testing needs clock pulses the tester cannot supply at frequency.

Stuck-at testing runs slowly and catches static defects. The defects that matter for a high-frequency part are timing-related, and catching them needs launch-capture pulses at functional speed. The tester cannot produce them, so the chip has to produce them for itself.

steps.text: At-speed test requirement per clock domain

DFT-05.flowNote: Step 4 is the difficult part. Single-domain at-speed test is well understood; testing paths that cross domains at speed requires the domains to have a defined phase relationship in test mode, which is a constraint on the clocking architecture rather than on DFT.
consumes: Clock architecture and domains from ARCH-05
Test platform clocking capability from TEST-02
Transition fault coverage targets from DFT-02

rel.text: DFT architecture specification. At-speed clocking is what makes transition-fault coverage achievable, so it belongs in the architecture.
ATPG pattern sets with coverage report. Transition patterns cannot be generated for domains the OCC cannot clock at speed.

risks: At-speed test not supported on every domain. Coverage then has a hole exactly where the fastest logic is, which is where transition defects concentrate.
Cross-domain paths untested at speed. These are among the most timing-marginal paths in the design and the hardest to cover.
OCC interaction with the PLL unverified. A controller that cannot get a clean clock from the PLL in test mode produces patterns that fail on good silicon.
Power during at-speed test ignored. Scan shift followed by at-speed capture creates switching activity far above functional, and the IR drop can cause failures on good parts.
OCC inserted late. It sits in the clock path, so adding it after clock tree synthesis means redoing the tree.

roles.d: Domain phase relationships in test mode
PLL behaviour and interface in test mode
Clock tree impact of OCC insertion

entry: Clock architecture and domains fixed by ARCH-05
PLL test-mode behaviour known from AMS-02
exit: At-speed clocking available on every domain that needs coverage
Cross-domain at-speed strategy defined and verified
OCC inserted before clock tree synthesis, not after
measuredBy: Domains with at-speed capability against domains needing it
Cross-domain paths covered at speed
Test-mode IR drop against the functional case

purpose: Insert the scan chains, compression and test logic into the design during synthesis, and drive DFT design-rule checking to clean.

This is where the architecture becomes logic. DFT DRC violations — uncontrollable clocks, unresettable flops, blocked scan paths — reduce coverage silently, and each one is a set of faults ATPG will never be able to target.

steps.text: Test point insertion for coverage improvement
DFT DRC analysis and violation closure

DFT-06.flowNote: Step 5 is the substance. Every DFT DRC violation is a region of logic ATPG cannot control or observe, and the coverage loss is silent — the tool simply reports a lower number without saying which violation caused it.

rel.text: DFT DRC clean report. This activity is the deliverable, and clean means every violation fixed or explicitly accepted with its coverage cost.
ATPG pattern sets with coverage report. Coverage achievable at DFT-07 is bounded by how clean this activity got.

risks: DRC violations accepted without measuring their coverage cost. Each one silently removes faults from the targetable set, and the total is invisible until ATPG reports a low number.
Test points inserted without area budget. They improve coverage and cost area and timing, and adding them late competes with closure.
Chain balance ignored. Unbalanced chains set shift time by the longest one, and shift time is most of the test time.
Insertion done once and not re-run. Netlist changes after insertion leave chains stale, and the mismatch appears at pattern validation.
Chain integrity unverified. A broken chain makes everything behind it untestable, and finding that at ATE rather than in simulation costs a silicon turn.

roles.d: Fix DRC violations in their logic
Accepts violations with their coverage cost

exit: Every DRC violation fixed or accepted with a measured coverage cost
Chains balanced against the shift time budget
Chain integrity verified in simulation before ATPG
measuredBy: DRC violations closed against accepted
Coverage cost of accepted violations
Chain length imbalance against budget

purpose: Generate the ATPG patterns — stuck-at, transition and cell-aware — and drive coverage to the targets DFT-02 agreed, inside the pattern volume the tester can hold.

Two constraints pull against each other here: coverage has to reach the quality target and pattern volume has to fit tester memory and test time. Every technique that raises one raises the other, and closing both is the work.

steps.text: ATPG setup, constraints and test mode configuration
Stuck-at pattern generation and coverage analysis
Untestable fault analysis and coverage justification
Coverage closure against the DFT-02 targets

DFT-07.flowNote: Step 5 is what makes a coverage number honest. Faults reported as untestable are either genuinely untestable — tied off, redundant — or untestable because of a DRC violation, and only analysis distinguishes a real limit from a fixable one.
consumes: Coverage targets and fault models from DFT-02
Test time and memory budget from TEST-09
OCC and at-speed setup from DFT-05
produces: Stuck-at, transition and cell-aware pattern sets

rel.text: ATPG pattern sets with coverage report. This activity is the deliverable, and the coverage report is what the quality target is measured against.
DFT signoff entry for the tapeout checklist. Coverage against target is one of the checklist's quantitative entries.

risks: Coverage target missed and accepted late. The remedies — test points, DRC fixes, architecture changes — all need an RTL or netlist change, and none are available near tapeout.
Pattern volume exceeding tester memory. Patterns that do not fit have to be split across loads, which multiplies test time and cost.
Untestable faults accepted without analysis. A fixable DRC violation reported as an untestable fault is coverage given away.
Cell-aware added late. It multiplies pattern count against a budget already set, forcing a choice between coverage and test time with no room to negotiate.
Patterns generated on a netlist that then changes. Any netlist change after generation invalidates the set, and regeneration takes weeks.

roles.d: Owns pattern generation and coverage closure
Untestable fault analysis and coverage decisions
Pattern volume, memory and test time
Accepts final coverage against the quality target

entry: Scan-inserted netlist available and DRC clean from DFT-06
Tester memory and test time budget known from TEST-09
exit: Coverage meets the DFT-02 targets per fault model
Pattern volume inside tester memory without splitting
Untestable faults analysed rather than accepted
measuredBy: Coverage achieved against target per fault model
Pattern volume against tester memory
Untestable faults analysed against accepted

purpose: Prove the patterns actually run — simulate them against the netlist with timing, convert them to tester format, and hand ATE a set that works.

A pattern set that passes in ATPG and fails in gate-level simulation is a pattern set that would have failed on silicon. This activity is the last place a pattern problem is cheap, and it is also where the format conversion for the tester is proved rather than assumed.

steps.text: Zero-delay pattern validation by gate-level simulation
Tester format and timing set validation
Pattern release and DFT tapeout sign-off

DFT-08.flowNote: Step 3 catches what zero-delay cannot: patterns that violate timing at the capture edge. On an at-speed pattern set this is not a formality — a launch-capture sequence that closes in ATPG and fails in timing simulation would have produced yield loss on good die.
consumes: Gate-level netlist and SDF from PD-09
Timing sets and tester capability from TEST-02

rel.text: Pattern validation (GLS) report and ATE-ready pattern files. This activity is the deliverable — patterns proved to run rather than assumed to.
DFT signoff entry for the tapeout checklist. DFT signs the checklist on validated patterns, not on generated ones.

risks: Validation skipped for schedule. A pattern failure then appears at ATE bring-up, where the diagnosis competes with everything else happening at first silicon.
Only zero-delay simulation run. Timing-related pattern failures are exactly what at-speed patterns are meant to detect, and they are invisible without SDF.
Format conversion assumed. STIL and WGL translation has tool-specific quirks, and a set that converts cleanly can still time incorrectly on the tester.
Regeneration cost underestimated. A pattern failure requiring regeneration puts the whole set back through DFT-07, which takes weeks not days.
Timing sets not validated against the actual tester. A pattern that assumes an edge placement the ATE cannot produce fails on hardware for a reason no simulation shows.

roles.d: Format conversion and tester timing sets

entry: Netlist and SDF available from PD-09
exit: Patterns validated with timing, not only zero-delay
Format conversion validated against the actual tester capability
DFT tapeout checklist entry signed on validated patterns

purpose: Work with physical design on whether the scan chains and compression network can actually be routed — and fix the plan before routing rather than after.

Compression networks connect every chain to a shared decompressor and compactor, which produces long routes across the die competing with functional signals for the same resource. A compression ratio that is optimal on paper and unroutable in practice is discovered at PD-06, when the remedies are expensive.

steps.text: Chain routing feasibility analysis with the floorplan
Compression network topology against physical partitioning
Physical DFT plan agreement with physical design

DFT-09.flowNote: Step 3 is where the two disciplines usually collide. DFT wants chains ordered for balance and diagnosis; physical design wants them ordered for routing. Reordering after placement is the standard compromise, and agreeing it here avoids arguing about it during closure.
consumes: DFT architecture and compression from DFT-01
Floorplan and partitioning from PD-01 and PD-02
Routing resource from the metal stack in TECH-02
produces: Compression topology aligned to physical partitions

rel.text: DFT architecture specification. An architecture that cannot be routed is not an architecture, and this is where that is established.
DFT DRC clean report. Physical feasibility findings often send work back into insertion, so the two are closed together.

risks: Compression ratio unroutable. A ratio chosen for pattern volume alone produces a network that consumes routing resource the functional design needs.
Chain reordering breaking diagnosis. Physical reordering improves routing and can destroy the chain-to-block mapping diagnosis depends on.
Test clock distribution treated as functional. Scan shift clocks reach every flop and have their own skew and power requirements.
Feasibility assessed after routing starts. The findings then arrive when the only remaining remedy is to reduce coverage.
Hierarchical partition boundaries ignored. Chains crossing physical partitions carry a routing and timing cost that a logical view does not show.
entry: DFT architecture and compression defined by DFT-01
Scan insertion in progress in DFT-06
exit: Compression network confirmed routable at the chosen ratio
Chain reordering strategy preserves diagnosis capability
Physical DFT plan agreed before detailed routing starts

purpose: Build the fuse and identity infrastructure — eFuse arrays, chip ID, repair storage, lifecycle state — that repair, traceability and security all depend on.

Fuses are written once and read forever. They store memory repair, trim values, chip identity and lifecycle state, and every one of those consumers has its own requirements. Getting the capacity or the read path wrong produces parts that cannot be repaired, identified or secured.

steps.text: Fuse consumer inventory — repair, trim, ID, lifecycle, security
eFuse array integration and programming path
Fuse read, shadow register and distribution design

DFT-10.flowNote: Step 2 is the step that fails silently. Every consumer asks for a modest allocation, the total is set once, and the worst-case repair set — which is a distribution rather than an average — exceeds it on the parts that most needed repairing.
consumes: Repair storage requirement from DFT-03 and AMS-09
Lifecycle and security states from ARCH-07
produces: eFuse array integration and programming path

rel.text: MBIST / BISR insertion and test collateral. Repair is only useful if the repair data can be stored and read back, which this activity provides.
JTAG / IJTAG description files. Fuse programming and readback run through the access network, and the instrument descriptions cover them.

risks: Capacity sized to the average repair need. Repair need is a distribution, and the parts needing most repair are exactly the ones the allocation fails.
Programming path untested. Fuses are one-time; a programming path that does not work correctly produces parts that are permanently wrong.
Fuse read timing in the boot path unconsidered. Repair and trim values have to be distributed before the logic that uses them is released from reset.
Traceability scheme designed late. Chip identity is needed for yield analysis and field returns, and retrofitting it means parts that cannot be traced.
Lifecycle encoding without a test path. A lifecycle transition that cannot be exercised in test is a transition whose correctness is unknown until the field.

Lifecycle transitions exercisable in test

purpose: Design the observability the lab will need — trace, triggers, internal visibility, design-for-debug — because at bring-up the only view into the chip is the one designed in months earlier.

Silicon debug is constrained entirely by what was built. A failure that cannot be observed cannot be diagnosed, and the difference between a two-day debug and a two-month one is usually whether someone put a trigger and a trace port where it was needed.

steps.text: Debug requirement collection from validation and design
Internal state snapshot and scan dump capability

DFT-11.flowNote: Step 5 is the cheapest debug capability available. Scan chains already reach every flop; adding the ability to halt and dump their contents turns the test infrastructure into a full internal state view for almost no extra area.

Pin and bump budget from ARCH-08

rel.text: JTAG / IJTAG description files. Debug instruments are part of the access network and are described alongside it.
DFT architecture specification. Design-for-debug is part of the DFT architecture rather than a separate concern.

risks: Debug traded away for area. The saving is small and the cost is paid at bring-up, in weeks, by a different team.
Requirements collected from design rather than validation. The people who will debug the silicon know what they need to see; the people who built it usually assume it works.
Trace bandwidth inadequate. A trace port too narrow to capture the event of interest produces a debug capability that cannot answer the question.
Debug infrastructure unverified. It is used first when the chip is misbehaving, which is the worst moment to discover the debug path is broken.
No documentation. A capability the lab does not know exists is a capability that was not built.

Trace bandwidth sufficient for the events validation named
Capabilities documented for the people who will use them

purpose: Write the constraints the whole implementation is optimised and signed off against — clocks, generated clocks, IO timing, exceptions, test modes — and validate them rather than assume them.

Constraints are the specification synthesis and physical design actually read. A missing clock definition produces a design optimised for a path nobody cares about; a wrong false path produces one that closes in the tool and fails in silicon. Every hour spent validating them here saves days at PD-09.

steps.text: Mode and corner enumeration against the operating conditions
Clock and generated clock definition across the design
Exception, false path and multicycle specification

SYN-01.flowNote: Step 6 is not review, it is tooling. Constraint quality checkers find unconstrained paths, conflicting exceptions and clocks that reach nothing, and they find them in minutes — which is why every drop should be re-checked rather than checked once.
consumes: Clock architecture and DVFS points from ARCH-05
Corner and mode definition from PDK-11

rel.text: Validated SDC constraint set per mode and corner. This activity is the deliverable, and "validated" is what distinguishes it from a file of assertions.
Synthesis QoR report per drop. QoR is only meaningful against constraints; an unconstrained path reports as passing.

risks: Unconstrained paths reported as clean. A path with no constraint is a path the tool ignores, and it appears in the report as no violation at all.
Exceptions written to close timing. A false path added because the path would not close is a silicon failure being converted into a green report.
Constraints diverging between synthesis and signoff. Two constraint sets means optimising against one and being judged against the other.
Test mode constraints written late. Scan shift and at-speed modes have their own timing, and a design closed only in functional mode fails at ATE.
IO constraints assumed from the interface specification. Actual budgets come from the package and channel analysis in SIPI-07, not from the protocol document.

roles.d: Owns the SDC set and its validation
Constraint consistency between synthesis and signoff

Every exception justified by a design reason, not by a violation

Constraint differences between synthesis and signoff

purpose: Map the RTL onto the qualified library and optimise it for the PPA budget — Vt mix, multi-bit banking, useful skew, datapath structure.

Technology mapping is where architecture becomes gates and where most of the achievable PPA is decided. The same RTL mapped two ways can differ by 20% in area and a hundred millivolts in achievable frequency, and the difference is entirely in how this activity is configured.

steps.text: Multi-bit banking and useful skew configuration

SYN-02.flowNote: Step 5 is where area is won without cost. Most of a design is not on the critical path, and recovering area and leakage there is free performance-wise — but it only happens if someone configures the flow to do it rather than optimising everything for speed.

rel.text: Synthesis QoR report per drop. This activity produces the QoR the report describes, drop after drop.
N1 and N2 netlist drops. Each drop is this activity's output at a point in time, with whatever optimisation was enabled.

risks: Everything optimised for speed. Area and leakage on non-critical paths are given away for performance nobody asked for, and the die grows.
Multi-bit banking configured late. Clock power depends heavily on it, and adding it after closure means re-timing the design.
Useful skew used to hide a timing problem. It buys real margin and also makes the clock tree harder to build; using it to rescue a path that should be restructured moves the problem to PD-07.
Library subset used without knowing it. Synthesis using only part of the Vt menu produces avoidable leakage, and nobody notices because the design closes.
QoR compared drop to drop without normalising. A netlist with more RTL in it is not directly comparable to the last one, and the trend becomes noise.

roles.d: Vt menu and special cell usage
RTL restructuring where synthesis cannot close

entry: Libraries qualified and frozen by PDK-03
exit: Area recovered on non-critical paths, not only speed optimised
Vt menu used across its range, not defaulted
QoR reported normalised so drops are comparable
measuredBy: Area and leakage against the ARCH-06 budget
Clock power against the multi-bit projection
QoR trend across drops

purpose: Release the N0 flow-flush netlist — functionally incomplete, structurally representative — so physical design can build and debug its flow against a real database months before the design is ready.

N0 exists to be wrong in the right way. It has the right hierarchy, the right macros and roughly the right size, and it does not need to work. Its entire purpose is to let PD-01 find its flow problems on a throwaway netlist rather than on the one the schedule depends on.

steps.text: N0 scope definition — what must be representative, what may be stubbed
Black-box and stub strategy for incomplete blocks

SYN-03.flowNote: Step 1 is the whole activity. N0 has to be representative in the dimensions PD's flow cares about — hierarchy, macro count, instance count, pin count — and can be arbitrarily wrong in everything else. Getting that distinction right is what makes it cheap.
consumes: RTL in whatever state exists from RTL-02
Macro list and abstracts from AMS-15
produces: N0 scope definition and stub strategy
Released N0 netlist with a stated limitation list

rel.text: N0 flow-flush netlist for PD flow setup. This activity is the deliverable, and its value is entirely in arriving early rather than in being correct.
Physical design handoff package per drop. N0 is the first handoff, and it sets the format every later one follows.

risks: N0 delayed until it is good. The point is to be early; a correct N0 delivered late has become N1 and left PD's flow undebugged.
Not representative in the dimensions that matter. A netlist with a tenth of the instances exercises none of the runtime and capacity problems PD needs to find.
Limitations not stated. Physical design chasing timing on a stubbed netlist wastes a week before someone explains it was never going to close.
Stub strategy that changes the hierarchy. A hierarchy that differs from the real one means the flow is set up for a structure that will not arrive.
Treated as a milestone rather than a tool. N0 is scaffolding; celebrating it as progress distracts from the fact that no real design has been synthesised.

PD flow setup ready to receive a netlist
exit: Representative in hierarchy, instance count and macro content
Limitations stated explicitly with the release
Delivered on the date PD's flow setup needs it, not when it is good
measuredBy: Days from PD flow setup start to N0 availability
Representativeness against the dimensions PD named
Flow problems found on N0 against on N1

purpose: Synthesise with the floorplan in the loop — physical-aware mapping, congestion feedback, placement-driven restructuring — so the netlist that reaches physical design is already routable.

Logic synthesis without physical information optimises for a wire model that does not exist. On a large die the difference between estimated and actual wire delay is large enough to invalidate the optimisation, and the correction happens either here or as weeks of congestion work at PD-06.

steps.text: Physical-aware flow setup with the floorplan
Macro and blockage awareness in placement
Congestion feedback loop with physical design

SYN-04.flowNote: Step 6 answers whether the added runtime is worth it. Physical-aware synthesis is slower; comparing its QoR against the wire-load-model result is what justifies the cost, and occasionally shows the floorplan is the problem rather than the logic.
consumes: Macro placement and blockages from PD-02

rel.text: Synthesis QoR report per drop. Physical-aware results are the ones that predict what physical design will actually achieve.
Physical design handoff package per drop. A netlist synthesised against the floorplan is a materially better handoff than one synthesised against a wire model.

risks: Floorplan too immature to synthesise against. Physical-aware synthesis against a floorplan that then changes produces optimisation for a layout that never exists.
Congestion feedback one-directional. Synthesis restructures and physical design re-places; without both, each optimises against the other's stale result.
Runtime cost not justified. Physical-aware flows are slow, and without the QoR comparison nobody knows whether the extra hours bought anything.
Restructuring breaking hierarchy. Aggressive cross-boundary optimisation improves QoR and makes the netlist harder to close hierarchically and harder to equivalence-check.
Blockages not modelled. Macros and their keep-out regions dominate placement on this die, and synthesis blind to them produces logic that cannot be placed where it assumed.

roles.d: Runtime and capacity for physical-aware runs

entry: Floorplan available and stable from PD-02
exit: Netlist synthesised against a floorplan PD is actually using
Congestion feedback flowing in both directions
Runtime cost justified by a measured QoR improvement
measuredBy: QoR improvement against non-physical synthesis

purpose: Release the N1 drop — the first netlist meant to be closed — against PD's feedback from its flow setup, and establish the QoR baseline every later drop is measured against.

N0 proved the flow ran. N1 is where the design's actual QoR first becomes visible: real timing, real area, real congestion. The number it establishes is the one PD-05 will work from and the one everyone will argue about for the next three months.

steps.text: RTL drop intake and delta review against N0
QoR delta analysis against the N0 baseline
Issue list for the next drop
Release and handoff to physical design

SYN-05.flowNote: Step 5 is what makes the drop cadence a process rather than a sequence of releases. Each drop should hand forward a named list of what it could not fix and why, so the next one starts from a position rather than from scratch.
consumes: PD flow setup feedback from PD-01

rel.text: N1 and N2 netlist drops with QoR delta reports. The first of the two quality drops, with the baseline it establishes.
Synthesis QoR report per drop. N1 sets the baseline the QoR trend is measured from.

risks: N1 released before RTL is worth synthesising. A drop taken from unstable RTL produces a baseline that means nothing and a PD turn that chases moving targets.
QoR delta not analysed. Knowing the numbers without knowing what changed them leaves the next drop guessing about what to fix.
Issue list not carried forward. N2 then rediscovers the same problems, and the drop cadence loses its cumulative benefit.
PD feedback arriving after the drop. Feedback from flow setup has to reach synthesis before N1 is run, not after it is released.
Baseline set on a partial design. A QoR baseline missing significant blocks flatters the trend and hides the growth that follows.

Feedback into the drop and acceptance out of it
Confirms RTL readiness for the drop

PD flow setup complete and feedback available from PD-01
exit: QoR baseline established against a substantially complete design
Delta against N0 explained, not only reported
Issue list handed forward to N2

purpose: Reduce power where it is actually spent — clock gating, operand isolation, Vt mix — driven by real switching activity rather than by defaults.

Power optimisation without activity data is guesswork. Clock gating inserted everywhere costs area and saves little; inserted where the data says the logic is idle it saves a meaningful fraction of dynamic power. The activity data comes from verification, which makes this a cross-stage dependency more than a synthesis setting.

steps.text: Power analysis baseline and hot-spot identification
Clock gating insertion and efficiency analysis
Activity-driven optimisation with real switching data
Power QoR and comparison against the budget

SYN-06.flowNote: Step 5 is what separates power optimisation from power decoration. Switching activity from the DV-04 workload simulations tells the tool which logic is actually idle; without it, gating is inserted by structural heuristic and saves a fraction of what it could.
consumes: Switching activity from DV-04 workload simulations
produces: Power analysis baseline and hot spots
Clock gating insertion and efficiency report

rel.text: Synthesis QoR report per drop. Power is one of the three QoR axes, and the only one that needs external activity data to measure honestly.
Power intent implementation report. Dynamic power optimisation sits alongside the UPF implementation from SYN-07 in the same report.

risks: Optimisation driven by default activity. Uniform switching assumptions produce gating where it saves nothing and none where it would.
Clock gating efficiency unmeasured. Gates inserted without measuring how often they actually gate cost area and leakage for no benefit.
Vt mix skewed to low-Vt for timing. Leakage grows non-linearly, and a design closed on low-Vt everywhere blows its static power budget.
Power measured at the wrong operating point. The number that matters is at the DVFS point the product runs at, not at nominal.
Optimisation deferred to the final turn. Power changes timing; a design closed on timing and then power-optimised has to be re-closed.

roles.d: Vt menu usage and leakage characterisation

exit: Optimisation driven by real activity data, not defaults
Clock gating efficiency measured, not assumed
Power reported at the operating point the product uses
measuredBy: Dynamic power against budget
Clock gating efficiency
Leakage against the Vt mix projection

purpose: Implement the power intent in the netlist — isolation cells, level shifters, retention flops, always-on paths — from the UPF, and prove the netlist and the intent still agree.

UPF describes what should happen; synthesis is where it becomes cells. An isolation cell missing at a domain boundary is a design that corrupts data on power-down, and it is invisible in any functional check that does not model power. The consistency check between netlist and intent is the only reliable detector.

steps.text: UPF ingestion and elaboration in the synthesis flow
Isolation and level shifter inference and insertion

SYN-07.flowNote: Step 5 runs in parallel and is the one that must not be skipped. The netlist and the UPF are two descriptions of the same intent, and any divergence between them propagates into physical design and verification as a defect nobody can attribute.
produces: Elaborated UPF in the synthesis flow
Inserted isolation and level shifter cells
Retention cell insertion and control logic

rel.text: Power intent implementation report. This activity is the deliverable — what was inferred, what was inserted, and where intent and netlist agree.
Formal equivalence clean report per drop. Low-power cells complicate equivalence checking, and the two activities have to agree on how they are handled.

risks: Isolation inferred but not verified. A missing cell at one boundary corrupts state on power-down and appears in no functional test.
Retention cells inserted without physical planning. They have a different footprint and power connectivity, and adding them late disturbs the floorplan.
Always-on paths not identified. Logic that must survive a domain shutting down and is not marked always-on is powered down with it.
UPF and netlist diverging. Two descriptions of the same intent, and downstream tools reading different ones.
Level shifters omitted between voltage domains. The design functions in simulation and fails at the voltage extremes in silicon.

roles.d: Owns intent implementation in the netlist

entry: UPF available and tool-accepted from RTL-05
exit: Every domain boundary has verified isolation
UPF and netlist consistent, checked rather than assumed
Retention and always-on requirements handed to physical design

purpose: Release the N2 drop with everything enabled — full optimisation, power, low-power intent, physical awareness — and state honestly how much closure risk remains.

N2 is the last drop before the FFN and the last chance to change anything structurally. Its QoR is the best prediction available of what the final turn will achieve, and the closure risk statement it carries is what tells the program whether the tapeout date is credible.

steps.text: RTL and ECO intake since N1
Full synthesis with all optimisations enabled
Release with a closure risk statement

SYN-08.flowNote: Step 6 is the honest part. A drop released with "timing is converging" tells nobody anything; one released with "forty paths in two blocks remain, all in the compute cluster, requiring a restructure or a frequency concession" gives the program a decision.
consumes: RTL updates and ECOs since N1
Turn 1 results and feedback from PD-05

rel.text: N1 and N2 netlist drops with QoR delta reports. The second quality drop, and the last structurally changeable one.
Synthesis QoR report per drop. The N2 QoR is the best available prediction of what the final turn will reach.

risks: Closure risk understated. An optimistic risk statement at N2 removes the program's last opportunity to take a frequency or feature concession while it is still cheap.
Late RTL changes absorbed without assessment. A functional change arriving between N1 and N2 can invalidate the turn-1 closure work entirely.
All optimisations enabled for the first time at N2. Enabling power, low-power and physical awareness together for the first time produces a QoR nobody can attribute.
Turn-1 feedback not incorporated. N2 then repeats N1's physical problems, and turn 2 spends its time on the same issues.
Treated as the final netlist. N2 is not the FFN, and freezing behaviour around it removes the RTL freeze discipline that SYN-09 depends on.

Consumes the risk statement for schedule decisions

Late changes assessed before inclusion

purpose: Release the FFN — the final full netlist — against frozen RTL, with constraints frozen and equivalence proved, and declare that nothing functional changes after it.

The FFN is a commitment more than a deliverable. Everything after it is physical: PD-13 closes on this netlist and SO-02 signs off on what PD produces. A functional change after the FFN restarts both, which is why the freeze around it has to be real.

steps.text: RTL freeze confirmation and final intake
Final equivalence and UPF consistency verification
FFN release and functional freeze declaration

SYN-09.flowNote: Step 1 is a confirmation rather than a formality. If RTL-10 has not actually declared freeze, the FFN is a snapshot of a moving design, and the final turn in PD-13 will be closing against something that changes underneath it.
consumes: Optimisation configuration from SYN-06 and SYN-07
N2 results and closure risk from SYN-08
produces: Final equivalence and UPF consistency results
Handoff package for the final turn
FFN release with functional freeze declaration

rel.text: FFN — final full netlist, release-tagged. This activity is the deliverable, and the milestone the stage ends on.
Validated SDC constraint set. Constraints freeze with the FFN — closing against moving constraints is closing against nothing.
Physical design handoff package per drop. The final handoff, and the one PD-13 closes against.

risks: FFN released against RTL that is not actually frozen. The final turn then closes against a moving netlist, and every change restarts it.
Constraints still changing after the FFN. A design closed against one constraint set and signed off against another has not been signed off.
Equivalence not proved on the final netlist. The last synthesis run is the one most likely to contain a transformation error, and the least likely to be checked under schedule pressure.
Functional freeze declared and not enforced. Post-FFN functional ECOs are sometimes unavoidable and must be exceptional, visible and costed.
Handoff package incomplete. The final turn needs constraints, UPF, DFT collateral and abstracts together; a missing item stops closure at its start.

Accepts the handoff for the final turn

Equivalence methodology proven across earlier drops
exit: Equivalence proved on the actual FFN, not on a proxy
Constraints frozen with the netlist
Functional freeze declared and its exception process published

Handoff completeness at the final turn's start

purpose: Prove that every netlist still means what the RTL meant — formal equivalence per drop, including through DFT insertion, clock gating and low-power transformations.

Synthesis rewrites the design, and the tools that do it are not infallible. Equivalence checking is the only evidence that the netlist implements the RTL that verification actually verified; without it, a transformation error is discovered in silicon as behaviour nobody can trace to a bug.

steps.text: Black-box and constraint handling for incomplete drops
DFT and clock gating equivalence handling
Continuous checking across the drop sequence

SYN-10.flowNote: Step 5 is where most of the difficulty lives. Scan insertion and clock gating change the netlist in ways that are correct and not structurally equivalent, and setting up the checker to accept those and reject everything else is the skilled part of the activity.
consumes: UPF and low-power implementation from SYN-07
produces: Block and chip-level equivalence results per drop
DFT and clock gating handling configuration

rel.text: Formal equivalence clean report per drop. This activity is the deliverable, and "per drop" is what makes it a control rather than a final check.
FFN — final full netlist. An FFN that has not been proved equivalent is a netlist nobody can claim was verified.

risks: Equivalence run only on the final netlist. A transformation error introduced at N1 is then found at the FFN, when the debug competes with tapeout.
Non-equivalences waived to make progress. Each waiver is a place where the netlist may not implement the verified RTL, and they accumulate quietly.
DFT transformations not modelled. The checker reports thousands of differences and everyone stops reading the report.
Black-box handling too permissive. Boxing out a block to get a clean result excludes exactly the logic that was not checked.
Debug capacity underestimated. A single real non-equivalence on a design this size can take a week to localise, and there is rarely a week available.

exit: Every drop checked, not only the final one
Non-equivalences resolved rather than waived

purpose: Report timing, area and power against the budget after every drop, and escalate when a block is diverging rather than when it has already blown its allocation.

QoR reported in absolute terms tells nobody anything. Reported against the ARCH-06 allocation and trended across drops, it says which blocks are converging, which are not, and how much of the gap is still recoverable — which is the only version a program manager can act on.

steps.text: Trend analysis across the drop sequence

SYN-11.flowNote: Step 5 is the part that predicts. A block 10% over budget and improving is a different problem from one 5% over and flat, and only a trend across drops distinguishes them.
produces: Per-drop timing, area and power reports

rel.text: Synthesis QoR report per drop against PPA targets. This activity is the deliverable, and "against targets" is what makes it usable.
N1 and N2 netlist drops with QoR delta reports. The delta report accompanying each drop comes from here.

risks: QoR reported in absolute terms. Numbers with no budget reference cannot be acted on, and everyone forms their own opinion of whether they are acceptable.
No escalation rule. Divergence noticed and not escalated becomes a surprise at the final turn, when there is nothing left to do about it.
Reports not normalised across drops. More RTL in a later drop makes the trend meaningless unless the comparison accounts for it.
Power reported at nominal only. The number that matters is at the product's operating point, and reporting at nominal understates it consistently.
Reporting stopping between drops. The interesting question is whether a block is improving, and that needs data between releases as well as at them.

The handoff is where two teams either share a picture of the design or maintain two. Six man-months across the stage buys a structured package and a joint review per drop, and it prevents the pattern where physical design spends a week discovering what synthesis already knew.

purpose: Decide where everything physically goes — partitions, macros, block boundaries, pins, utilisation — and freeze it, because everything downstream is built on it.

The floorplan is the most consequential and least reversible decision in the stage. Macro placement sets routing congestion, block boundaries set what can be closed independently, and pin placement sets the top-level routing burden. A floorplan changed at turn 2 invalidates the clock trees, the power grid and the routing built on it.

steps.text: Partition definition against the design hierarchy
Standard cell area planning and utilisation targets

PD-02.flowNote: Step 2 is where a memory-dominated die is won or lost. Hundreds of macro instances have to be placed so their access paths are short, their power can be delivered and the logic between them can be routed — and moving one late moves everything around it.

Macro abstracts from AMS-15 and PDK-04

Turn 1 and Turn 2 databases. Every turn is placed and routed inside this floorplan; changing it invalidates the turns.

risks: Macro placement not congestion-aware. Macros placed for access and not for the logic between them produce routing congestion that cannot be fixed at PD-08.
Floorplan changed after turn 1. Clock trees, power grid and routing are all built on it, and all of them are invalidated.
Utilisation set too high. A dense floorplan closes area and cannot be routed or timing-closed, and the discovery comes after weeks of work.
Pin placement ignoring top-level routing. Block pins facing the wrong way make top-level routing expensive for the whole rest of the program.
Partitions that do not match the design hierarchy. Closing blocks that cut across logical boundaries makes timing budgets and equivalence checking harder for no gain.

purpose: Build the power delivery network — grid topology, straps, switches, decap — and prove by early IR analysis that it can actually feed the die at its power envelope.

The PDN is built early because everything routes around it. Grid density trades directly against routing resource: too sparse and IR drop eats timing margin, too dense and there is nothing left to route with. Getting it wrong is discovered at SO-04, when the fix is a metal change across the whole die.

steps.text: PDN topology and grid definition per domain
Power switch and always-on region planning

PD-03.flowNote: Step 4 has to happen while the grid can still change. Static IR on a placed design with real power numbers tells you whether the grid works; running it after routing means any fix competes with a routed design for the same metal.

MCMM timing closure reports. IR drop consumes timing margin, so the PDN's quality shows up in closure.

risks: Grid density traded against routing without analysis. Both constraints are real, and choosing by feel produces either IR problems or congestion.
IR analysed only statically. Dynamic IR under real switching is worse, and SIPI-04 with the package model is worse again.
Decap placed where there is room. Decoupling works where the current is drawn, not where the floorplan left space.
Power switches planned late. They need area, always-on routing and their own control, and retrofitting them disturbs the floorplan.
PDN frozen before power numbers are real. A grid designed against estimates and fed a design that draws more is a grid that fails at signoff.

purpose: Turn the architecture's bump budget into an actual bump map and RDL, iterating with package design until both sides can build what the other needs.

The bump map is the contract between the die and the package, and it is negotiated rather than declared. Signal escape on the package constrains bump position; power delivery constrains bump count; and the die's floorplan constrains where either can go. All three have to close at once.

steps.text: Bump map ingestion from the architecture budget
Signal escape planning with the substrate
Bump map freeze and interface file release

PD-04.flowNote: Step 6 is a hard date rather than a milestone. PKGD-11 freezes package design against this map, and the substrate order that follows has a twenty-week lead time — a late bump map moves wafer-out by moving the substrate.
consumes: Bump budget and map intent from ARCH-08
Floorplan and IO ring from PD-02
produces: Bump map with signal and power assignment
Frozen bump map and package interface files

rel.text: Bump map, RDL and package interface files. This activity is the deliverable, and it is consumed directly by package design.
Floorplan and PDN specification. Bump position constrains where power can be delivered, so the two documents have to agree.

risks: Bump map frozen late. Package design and the substrate order both wait on it, and the substrate lead time makes the delay a wafer-out delay.
Escape routing not checked on the package side. A map that is optimal on the die and unroutable on the substrate has to be redone.
Power bump count reduced to fit signals. The signals that fit are then fed by a PDN that cannot deliver, and SIPI-04 finds it.
RDL treated as free. Redistribution has its own rules and resistance, and a plan that ignores them produces IR and EM problems in the RDL itself.
Co-design conducted by file exchange. Two teams iterating asynchronously on the same interface converge slowly or not at all.

roles.d: Owns the map and the interface files
Power bump count and rail assignment

entry: Floorplan and IO ring available from PD-02
exit: Bump map frozen on the date package design needs it
Escape routing confirmed feasible on the substrate
Power bump count sufficient for the delivery requirement

purpose: Run the first real turn on the N1 netlist — place, build clocks, route — and establish the QoR baseline that says how far the design is from closing.

Turn 1 is the first honest measurement of the design's physical difficulty. Everything before it was estimate; this produces real congestion, real timing and real power on a real floorplan, and the gap it reveals is what the next two turns exist to close.

steps.text: Timing analysis and first ECO round
Power analysis on the placed and routed design
QoR baseline and feedback to synthesis

PD-05.flowNote: Step 8 is what makes turn 1 worth its cost. The turn's purpose is not to close — it will not — but to produce a measured baseline and a specific list of what synthesis and RTL must change before turn 2.
consumes: N1 netlist and handoff package from SYN-05 and SYN-12
produces: Feedback list to synthesis and RTL

rel.text: Turn 1 and Turn 2 databases with QoR delta reports. The first turn, and the baseline the second is measured against.
MCMM timing closure reports. The violation burn-down starts here, with turn 1's numbers as its origin.

risks: Turn 1 expected to close. It will not, and treating the gap as a crisis rather than as data produces panic instead of a plan.
Feedback not specific. "Congestion is high" changes nothing; "the compute cluster is over 90% utilisation in three regions and needs restructuring" changes the next drop.
Turn run on an incomplete netlist. A baseline missing blocks understates the difficulty and misleads the closure plan.
Congestion mitigated locally. Fixing congestion by rip-up and reroute hides a structural problem that only synthesis or floorplan can solve.
Clock tree built before the floorplan is stable. A CTS on a floorplan that then changes is work thrown away.

roles.d: Owns the turn and its QoR baseline
Receives and acts on the feedback

exit: QoR baseline measured on a substantially complete netlist
Feedback to synthesis specific enough to act on
Congestion characterised as structural or local
measuredBy: QoR gap at turn 1 against budget

purpose: Run the second turn on N2 and converge — congestion, timing and power — then quantify honestly how much closure risk remains for the final turn.

Turn 2 is where the design either starts converging or reveals that it will not. Its output is a number: how many violations remain, in which blocks, and whether the trend from turn 1 projects to closure. That number is what the program uses to decide whether the tapeout date holds.

steps.text: N2 intake and delta assessment against turn 1
Closure risk quantification for the final turn

PD-06.flowNote: Step 3 is joint work with SYN-04 rather than a physical design task. Congestion that survives placement optimisation is structural, and the only remedies are logic restructuring or a floorplan change — both of which belong to someone else.
consumes: N2 netlist and handoff from SYN-08 and SYN-12
Turn 1 database and QoR from PD-05

rel.text: Turn 1 and Turn 2 databases with QoR delta reports. The second turn, and the last one before the netlist is frozen.
MCMM timing closure reports. The burn-down trend across turns is what predicts whether the final turn closes.

risks: Closure risk understated at turn 2. This is the last point at which a frequency or feature concession is cheap, and an optimistic number removes the option.
Congestion fixed locally rather than structurally. Rip-up and reroute buys a turn and leaves the problem for the final one, when there is no time.
Turn 2 not compared against turn 1. The absolute number matters less than the trend, and only the delta says whether the design is converging.
Power convergence deferred. Power fixes change timing; leaving them to the final turn means re-closing timing after every one.
Late RTL changes absorbed into turn 2. A functional change mid-turn invalidates the comparison the turn exists to produce.

roles.d: Owns the turn and the closure risk statement
Consumes the risk quantification for the tapeout decision

entry: Turn 1 QoR baseline available from PD-05
Congestion feedback loop running with SYN-04
exit: Convergence trend measured against turn 1, not only reported
Structural congestion addressed structurally
Closure risk stated with paths, blocks and options
measuredBy: Violation count trend from turn 1
Congestion resolved structurally against locally
Closure risk at turn 2 against final-turn outcome

purpose: Build and refine the clock trees across turns — skew, insertion delay, jitter budget, power — for a design with dozens of domains and crossings between them.

Clock tree synthesis is rebuilt every turn and improved each time. Skew directly buys or costs timing margin; insertion delay costs power and OCV; and cross-domain paths need a defined phase relationship that only a deliberately built tree provides. It is one of the few areas where a good result is worth several percent of frequency.
PD-07.flowNote: Step 6 is the hardest part and the one that pays. Useful skew moves margin from paths that have it to paths that need it, and cross-domain handling decides whether those paths can be closed at all — but both make the tree harder to build and harder to verify.

rel.text: MCMM timing closure reports. Clock skew and insertion delay are inputs to every timing number in the report.
Turn 1 and Turn 2 databases. Each turn contains its own clock tree, rebuilt and improved.

risks: Clock power ignored. The clock network is a large fraction of dynamic power on a design this size, and a tree optimised only for skew is expensive to run.
Useful skew applied without a plan. It buys margin and complicates every subsequent ECO, because moving one path's timing moves its neighbours'.
Cross-domain phase relationship undefined. Paths between domains cannot be closed reliably, and the failure appears as intermittent silicon behaviour.
Insertion delay allowed to grow. Deep trees increase OCV derate and jitter accumulation, consuming the margin the skew balancing bought.
Tree quality not checked. Clock DRC violations — transition, capacitance, pulse width — degrade the tree in ways timing analysis reports as margin loss without explaining.

roles.d: Owns CTS, skew and tree quality

entry: Placement available from the current turn
exit: Clock power inside the ARCH-06 budget
Cross-domain relationships defined and closed
Clock DRC clean, not only timing-clean
measuredBy: Clock skew and insertion delay per domain
Clock power against budget
Clock DRC violations at each turn

purpose: Route the design and drive it to DRC clean — global, detailed, antenna, via optimisation — across every turn, on a die where routing resource is the scarcest commodity.

Routing is where the floorplan, the synthesis and the power grid are all judged. Sixteen weeks and forty man-months buys convergence on a design where congestion is structural rather than local, and where every metal layer is contested between signals, clocks and the power grid.
PD-08.flowNote: Step 6 takes four weeks because DRC convergence on an advanced node is iterative and asymptotic. The last few hundred violations take as long as the first hundred thousand, and they are the ones that need manual attention.
consumes: Placement and clock trees from PD-05, PD-06 and PD-07
Metal stack and routing rules from TECH-02 and PDK-02

rel.text: Interim physical DRC / LVS clean. This activity is the deliverable at each turn, and clean here is what makes SO-03 tractable.
Final-turn routed database on the FFN. The final route is this activity's last execution.

risks: Congestion treated as a routing problem. Structural congestion cannot be routed around, and rip-up cycles spent on it consume time without converging.
Antenna violations left late. Fixes need diodes or layer jumps, both of which need space that a fully routed design does not have.
DRC convergence assumed linear. The last violations are the hardest, and planning as if the rate is constant produces a schedule that misses.
Manufacturability ignored until signoff. DFM-clean routing is cheaper to produce than to retrofit, and SO-08 finds what was not.
Layer plan not respecting the PDN. Signals and the power grid contend for the same upper layers, and a plan that ignores the grid produces conflicts everywhere.

roles.d: Owns routing strategy and DRC convergence
Global, detailed routing and violation fixing

entry: Placement and clock trees available for the turn
Metal stack and routing rules available from PDK-02
exit: DRC clean at each turn, not only at the final one
Congestion resolved structurally where it is structural
Manufacturability addressed during routing, not after
measuredBy: DRC violations remaining per turn
Rip-up cycles spent on structural congestion
Antenna violations at first detailed route

purpose: Close timing across every corner and every mode — setup, hold, cross-corner, cross-mode — and drive the violation burn-down that decides the tapeout date.

Twenty-two weeks and sixty man-months, the largest activity in the stage. Multi-corner multi-mode closure on a large die is a long grind of analysis, ECO and re-analysis, and its burn-down curve is the single best predictor the program has of whether it will tape out on time.

steps.text: Timing setup and MMMC scenario definition
Signoff timing correlation with the SO flow

PD-09.flowNote: Step 7 prevents the worst surprise available. A design closed in the implementation tool and re-analysed in the signoff tool will show differences; discovering their size early lets the team close with the right margin rather than re-closing after SO-02 reports.
consumes: Placed and routed databases from each turn
Corner and derate definition from PDK-11

rel.text: MCMM timing closure reports with violation burn-down across turns. This activity is the deliverable, and the burn-down is the program's best schedule predictor.
Final-turn routed database. A database is only handed to signoff when this activity says it is closed.

risks: Closing at some corners and deferring others. The deferred corner is the one that fails, and it fails when there is no time to fix it.
Implementation and signoff timing diverging. A design closed in one tool and judged in another can be weeks from closure without anyone knowing.
Hold fixed after setup. Hold fixes add buffers that change setup, and doing them sequentially means iterating both.
Burn-down not tracked. Without a trend nobody can distinguish a design that is converging slowly from one that is not converging at all.
ECO volume exceeding what the database can absorb. Thousands of ECOs degrade the physical result, and at some point a re-run is cheaper than another ECO round.

roles.d: Owns closure, burn-down and the tapeout prediction
Uses the burn-down for schedule decisions

entry: Routed database available from the current turn
Corner and derate definition final from PDK-11
Signoff flow available for correlation from SO-01
exit: Closed at every corner and mode, not a subset
Implementation and signoff timing correlated within a stated tolerance
Burn-down trend projecting closure before the tapeout date
measuredBy: Violations remaining per corner and mode
Implementation-to-signoff timing correlation
Burn-down rate against the tapeout date

purpose: Fix what the routing did to the electricals — crosstalk, noise, electromigration, dynamic IR — before signoff has to reject the design for them.

Signal and power integrity problems are created by routing and found by analysis. Crosstalk between adjacent nets, EM in high-current wires and dynamic IR under real switching are all consequences of physical decisions, and fixing them means changing routing that was closed for timing.

steps.text: Crosstalk fixing — spacing, shielding, buffer sizing
Dynamic IR iteration with the PDN
SI and PI iteration and closure

PD-10.flowNote: Step 6 is an iteration rather than a step, because every fix perturbs something else. Widening a wire for EM changes its coupling; adding shielding consumes routing resource; and both change timing, which sends the design back to PD-09.
consumes: Switching activity from SYN-06 and DV-04
produces: Dynamic IR results and PDN adjustments

rel.text: Interim physical DRC / LVS clean. SI and EM fixes are routing changes, so they close together with DRC.
MCMM timing closure reports. Crosstalk-induced delay is part of timing, and SI fixes change timing in both directions.

risks: SI analysed after timing closes. Crosstalk delay is timing, and closing without it means closing against numbers that will move.
EM checked only on power. High-toggle signal nets on advanced nodes carry EM exposure too, and they are usually the ones nobody checks.
Dynamic IR analysed with uniform activity. Real switching is bursty and localised, and uniform assumptions understate the worst case badly.
Fixes applied without re-timing. Shielding and spacing change delay, and a fix that breaks timing has moved the problem rather than solved it.
Package effects excluded. Die-only dynamic IR is optimistic; SIPI-04 with package inductance is the number signoff will use.

roles.d: Owns crosstalk, noise, EM and IR analysis
Apply spacing, shielding and width fixes

entry: Signoff SI/PI methodology agreed with SO-05
exit: Crosstalk included in timing closure, not analysed after it
EM checked on signal nets as well as power
Dynamic IR analysed with realistic, localised activity
measuredBy: Crosstalk-induced delay against the timing budget
EM violations at signoff
Dynamic IR against budget with realistic activity

purpose: Extract the chip power model the package co-verification needs — per domain, per mode, with realistic switching — and hand it over as a versioned artifact.

SIPI-03 cannot analyse the die, package and board as one power delivery network without a model of the die's current draw. Producing that model is a small activity with an outsized dependency: without it the co-verification cannot start, and the co-verification gates mask release.

steps.text: Power model requirement definition with SIPI
CPM extraction per domain and operating mode
Switching scenario selection for the extraction
Model validation against internal IR analysis

PD-11.flowNote: Step 3 determines whether the model is useful. A CPM extracted under average activity understates the transient the package has to supply; extracting under the worst realistic burst is what makes SIPI-04's answer meaningful.
consumes: Placed and routed database from PD-05 or PD-06
Switching activity from DV-04 and SYN-06
produces: Chip power model per domain and mode

rel.text: Floorplan and PDN specification. The power model is the PDN's behaviour expressed for external consumers.
Bump map, RDL and package interface files. The model is part of what the package side needs alongside the physical interface.

risks: Model extracted under average activity. The package has to supply the transient, and an averaged model hides exactly the event that matters.
Delivered late. Co-verification is on the critical path to mask release, and it cannot start without this model.
Model not validated. A CPM that disagrees with the die's own IR analysis is wrong in one of the two places, and nobody knows which.
Single model for all modes. Different DVFS points and workloads draw very differently, and one model cannot represent them.
No version control. The package team analysing against a stale model produces conclusions about a die that no longer exists.
exit: Model extracted under realistic worst-case switching
Validated against the die's own IR analysis
Delivered versioned, on the date SIPI needs it
measuredBy: Model delivery against the SIPI need date
Validation agreement with internal IR
Modes modelled against modes the product uses

purpose: Reorder and route the scan chains physically — shorter routes, less congestion — without destroying the chain-to-block mapping diagnosis depends on.

Scan chains as stitched by synthesis follow logical order and route terribly. Physical reordering fixes the routing and can scramble the relationship between chain position and physical location, which is exactly what failure diagnosis uses. Both constraints are real.

steps.text: Scan chain physical analysis and routing cost
DFT-aware routing and shielding of test paths

PD-12.flowNote: Step 6 is not optional. Reordering rewrites the netlist's scan connectivity, and a chain broken by the reorder makes everything behind it untestable — a failure that would otherwise be discovered at ATE bring-up.

rel.text: Interim physical DRC / LVS clean. Scan routing is routing, and it closes with everything else.
Final-turn routed database. The chains in the final database are the ones ATPG patterns were generated against.

risks: Reordering breaking diagnosis. Failure analysis relies on mapping a failing bit to a physical location, and a scrambled chain removes that.
Chains not verified after reorder. A break makes everything behind it untestable, and ATE bring-up is a costly place to find that.
Patterns generated before the final reorder. Any chain change after DFT-07 invalidates the pattern set and costs weeks of regeneration.
Test clock skew ignored. Scan shift reaches every flop, and skew on the shift clock produces shift failures that look like design bugs.
Chain imbalance after reorder. Physical reordering can lengthen one chain and shorten another, and shift time follows the longest.
entry: Physical DFT plan agreed in DFT-09
exit: Chains verified after every reorder
Diagnosis mapping preserved or explicitly traded
Chain order frozen before ATPG generates patterns
measuredBy: Routing resource saved by reordering
Chain integrity after reorder
Chain order changes after pattern generation

purpose: Run the final turn on the FFN and close it completely — timing, power, DRC, LVS — with no functional change admitted and no next turn to fall back on.

Everything the stage has done is preparation for this. Fifty-five man-months over eleven weeks, on a frozen netlist, closing every corner and every mode to signoff standard. The discipline that matters is refusing functional change: an ECO that alters behaviour restarts verification, and there is no schedule for that.

steps.text: FFN intake and delta assessment against N2
Final timing closure across all corners and modes

PD-13.flowNote: Step 3 runs across the whole turn and is a gate rather than a task. Every change request during the final turn has to be classified — timing ECO, functional change, or bug fix — and only the first is admitted without escalation.
consumes: FFN and handoff package from SYN-09 and SYN-12
Turn 2 database and risk from PD-06
produces: Final placed, clocked and routed database
Final power and IR convergence results
Final timing closure across corners and modes

rel.text: Final-turn routed database on the FFN, per block and top. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what signoff and tapeout consume.
MCMM timing closure reports. The final turn's closure report is the one Design Freeze is granted against.

risks: Functional change admitted during the final turn. It restarts verification and equivalence, and no schedule allows for that at this point.
Closure gap larger than turn 2 predicted. If the prediction was optimistic, the discovery comes with no remaining turns and only concessions available.
ECO volume degrading the database. Thousands of ECOs on a final database produce a physical result worse than a clean re-run, but a re-run costs weeks.
Remaining violations dispositioned informally. Every violation that survives to signoff must be a named, accepted waiver rather than an oversight.
Database frozen before LVS is clean. A handoff that fails LVS at SO-03 sends everything back with no time to spare.

roles.d: Owns the final turn and the freeze
Final closure across corners and modes

entry: FFN released by SYN-09 against frozen RTL
Turn 2 closure risk understood from PD-06
exit: Closed at every corner and mode to signoff standard
No functional change admitted, or each one escalated and recorded
Database frozen LVS-clean and accepted by signoff
measuredBy: Functional changes admitted during the final turn
Closure achieved against the turn-2 prediction
Violations dispositioned as waivers against oversights

purpose: Run the ECO machinery — flow, spare cells, metal-only strategy, impact tracking — that every turn depends on and that the final turn depends on absolutely.

ECOs are how a closed design absorbs change without a full re-run. The infrastructure matters more than any individual ECO: a spare cell strategy decided at floorplan time determines whether a late fix is metal-only or needs a base layer change, and that distinction is worth several weeks and a mask set.

steps.text: Spare cell and metal-only ECO strategy

PD-14.flowNote: Step 5 is decided early and matters late. Spare cells distributed through the floorplan cost area now and make a metal-only fix possible at tapeout; without them, a late functional fix needs base layers and a full mask set.
consumes: Change requests from RTL-10, DV-12 and timing closure
Placed and routed databases from each turn

rel.text: ECO log and change control record. This activity is the deliverable, and the log is what makes a late database traceable to the design that was verified.
Final-turn routed database. The final database is the FFN plus its ECO history, and the two are inseparable.

risks: No spare cell strategy. A late functional fix then requires base layers and a full mask set rather than a metal-only change.
ECOs applied without impact tracking. A database with untracked changes cannot be reconciled against the netlist that was verified.
ECO volume unbounded. Beyond some number, the physical result degrades enough that a clean re-run would be better — and nobody notices the crossing point.
Functional and timing ECOs not distinguished. They have completely different verification consequences, and conflating them lets functional change in unnoticed.
Spare cells consumed early. Using them for convenience during turn 1 leaves none for the fix that actually needs them at tapeout.

roles.d: Owns the flow, the strategy and the log

entry: Spare cell placement decided in PD-02
Change control process running in RTL-10
exit: Metal-only fix path available at tapeout

Functional and timing ECOs distinguished in the log

purpose: Finish the die as a manufacturable object — seal ring, metal fill, dummy, alignment marks, identification — and verify that none of it broke what was closed.

Chip finishing is mechanical and it is not free. Metal fill changes coupling capacitance and therefore timing; the seal ring consumes die edge; and dummy fill interacts with the analog matching that AMS-12 spent weeks building. Every one has to be applied and then re-verified.

steps.text: Seal ring and die edge implementation
Fill impact on timing and extraction
Alignment marks, logos and die identification
Finishing verification against the closed database

PD-15.flowNote: Step 3 is why finishing is not a formality. Fill adds capacitance to every net near it, and a design closed before fill and taped out after it has been signed off against a database that no longer exists.

Seal ring and frame rules from PDK-02
Fill and density rules from the DRM
Analog macro fill exclusions from AMS-12

rel.text: Final-turn routed database. The database handed to tapeout is the finished one, and the finishing is part of it.
Interim physical DRC / LVS clean. Density and fill rules are DRC rules, and finishing is where they are met.

risks: Timing signed off before fill. The taped-out database has fill and the signed-off one did not, which is a signoff against a different design.
Fill applied over analog matching structures. It disturbs the parasitics AMS-12 tuned, and the damage is invisible until silicon characterisation.
Seal ring area not reserved. Discovered late, it forces the die edge inward and moves the bump map.
Die identification omitted. Traceability at yield analysis and field return depends on being able to identify the die, and it cannot be added later.
Finishing treated as a checkbox. Each step changes the physical database, and each needs verification against what was closed.
