purpose: Close the blocks independently and assemble them into a top level that meets timing across their boundaries — the hierarchical discipline a die this size requires.

A design of this size cannot be closed flat: runtime and capacity make it impossible. Hierarchical closure lets blocks converge in parallel, at the cost of interface budgets that have to be right. A block that closes internally and misses its boundary budget has not helped.

steps.text: Block closure criteria and handoff definition
Inter-block timing budget and interface closure
Block abstract and timing model generation
Hierarchical timing correlation, block model against flat

PD-16.flowNote: Step 7 is the check that keeps hierarchy honest. A block's timing model is an abstraction, and if it disagrees with a flat analysis of the same block then the top level has been closed against a fiction.

rel.text: Signoff-ready database handoff. This activity is the deliverable — the assembled top level signoff and tapeout actually consume.
Final-turn routed database on the FFN, per block and top. The per-block half of the deliverable comes from here.

risks: Block models disagreeing with flat analysis. The top level is then closed against an abstraction that does not represent the block.
Interface budgets set late. Blocks close internally and fail at their boundaries, and the fix requires reopening blocks that were declared done.
Feedthroughs not planned. Signals crossing a block have to be routed through it, and a block closed without feedthrough provision blocks the top level.
Blocks closed to different criteria. Without an enforced standard, each block closes to what its owner considered sufficient, and the top level inherits the weakest.
Top-level assembly left to the end. Assembly finds interface problems, and finding them after the final turn leaves no time to fix them.

purpose: Rehearse the entire signoff flow on the turn 2 database — decks, runtimes, capacity, violation triage — so the final turn is not the first time it runs at full chip.

Signoff is a large, slow, deck-heavy flow, and the first run always finds problems that have nothing to do with the design. Finding them on turn 2 costs a week of a database nobody is waiting for; finding them on the final turn costs a week of the tapeout schedule.

steps.text: Signoff flow assembly and deck integration

Flow issue resolution and rehearsal findings

produces: Assembled signoff flow with integrated decks

rel.text: Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. The rehearsal is what makes the real campaign's schedule credible.

risks: Dry run skipped for schedule. The flow's first full-chip run then happens on the critical path, and every problem it finds costs tapeout days.
Runtime not measured. A signoff campaign planned without knowing its runtime is planned against a guess.
Dry run on an unrepresentative database. Turn 2 has to be close enough in size and structure that the runtimes and violation counts mean something.
Triage tooling built during the real campaign. Thousands of violations arrive at once, and sorting them by hand is how a week disappears.
Findings not fixed before the final turn. A rehearsal that identifies problems and does not resolve them has only produced a list.

purpose: Prove the final database meets timing at every corner and every mode, in the signoff tool, and dispose of every remaining violation as a fix or a signed waiver.

This is the largest activity in the stage and the one Design Freeze most depends on. It differs from PD-09 in that it is judgement rather than optimisation: the signoff tool, the foundry-agreed derates and the full corner set, with no ECO loop to fall back on.

rel.text: STA signoff reports across all corners and modes, with waiver list. This activity is the deliverable, and the waiver list is the part that carries risk into silicon.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. Timing signoff is the largest single input to the freeze decision.

risks: Corners deferred to fit the schedule. The deferred corner is the one that fails, and it fails in silicon where there is no fix.
Waivers granted without root cause. A waived violation with no understood cause is a silicon risk being accepted blind.
Test modes not signed off. Scan shift and at-speed timing failures produce parts that work functionally and fail at ATE.
Signoff and implementation disagreeing late. If SO-12 has not correlated the two, the first signoff run can show a design weeks from closure.
ECO loop reopening after signoff starts. Each ECO invalidates the analysis it was based on, and uncontrolled iteration never converges.

purpose: Run full-chip physical verification — DRC, LVS, antenna, density — to clean, on the database that will become masks.

Physical verification is binary and unforgiving: the foundry will not accept a database with violations it has not waived. On a die this size the runs take days, the violation counts start in the tens of thousands, and the last hundred are the ones that need a human.

steps.text: Full-chip DRC setup and hierarchical run strategy
Full-chip DRC execution and violation triage
Physical verification closure and waiver preparation

SO-03.flowNote: Step 4 is where the hardest problems hide. An LVS mismatch on a full chip can take days to localise, and the causes are usually elsewhere — a macro abstract that disagrees with its layout, or an ECO applied to one view and not the other.
consumes: Final database from PD-13 and PD-16
Macro layouts and abstracts from AMS-12 and AMS-15
produces: Physical verification clean reports and waiver candidates

rel.text: Clean DRC / LVS / antenna / density reports. This activity is the deliverable, and it is a precondition for mask release rather than an opinion.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. A design with open physical violations cannot be frozen.

risks: LVS mismatch traced late. Full-chip mismatches take days to localise, and they are frequently caused by macro views rather than by the design.
Runs started too late. Each full-chip run takes days, and the iteration count is what sets the schedule rather than any single run.
Antenna fixes needing space that is gone. Diodes and layer jumps need room, and a fully routed design has none.
Waivers assumed acceptable. Foundry waivers are granted case by case, and a design that assumes one will be granted may not tape out.
Verification on a database that then changes. Any ECO after a clean run invalidates it, and re-running costs days.

roles.d: Owns DRC, LVS and antenna closure
Abstract and layout consistency for LVS

entry: Decks validated and versioned in PDK-10
exit: DRC, LVS, antenna and density all clean or formally waived
LVS mismatches resolved, not waived
No database change after the last clean run
measuredBy: Violations remaining at freeze
Full-chip run iterations required
LVS mismatches resolved against waived

purpose: Sign off electromigration and IR drop — static and dynamic, with real switching — because a design that meets timing and fails EM will not survive its warranty.

EM and IR are reliability and performance at once. IR drop consumes timing margin the STA assumed; EM limits how long the part will work. Both are analysed on the final database with real activity, and both can send routing back for changes that reopen timing.

steps.text: EM/IR setup and activity scenario definition
Static IR drop analysis and closure
Dynamic IR analysis under realistic switching
Electromigration analysis on power and signal

SO-04.flowNote: Step 5 closes a loop that is often left open. IR drop lowers the local supply and slows the logic, and unless that is back-annotated into timing the STA has been run at a voltage the die does not actually see.
consumes: Switching activity from DV-04 and SYN-06
Chip power model and co-analysis from SIPI-04
produces: Dynamic IR results under real switching
EM analysis on power and signal nets

rel.text: EM/IR and SI/PI signoff reports. The EM and IR half of the deliverable; SO-05 supplies the SI/PI half.
STA signoff reports. IR-aware timing is timing, and the two signoffs have to be reconciled rather than reported separately.

risks: IR not back-annotated into timing. The design is then signed off at a supply voltage it never sees, and the margin was never real.
Dynamic IR analysed with uniform activity. Real switching is bursty and local, and uniform assumptions understate the worst case.
Package effects excluded. Die-only IR is optimistic; the number that matters includes the package inductance SIPI-04 models.
Signal EM overlooked. High-toggle nets on advanced nodes carry real EM exposure, and checking only power misses them.
EM fixes reopening timing. Widening wires changes delay, and a fix applied after timing signoff invalidates it.

roles.d: Owns EM and IR analysis and closure

entry: Realistic switching activity available from DV-04
Package co-analysis results available from SIPI-04
exit: IR back-annotated into timing signoff
Dynamic IR analysed with realistic localised activity
EM checked on signal nets as well as power
measuredBy: IR drop against budget with realistic activity
Timing margin consumed by IR
EM violations at freeze

purpose: Sign off signal integrity — crosstalk delay, noise, glitch — on the final database, and confirm the numbers the timing signoff assumed.

Crosstalk is timing. Coupling between adjacent nets changes delay in both directions and can inject glitches that propagate as functional failures. The analysis is separate from STA and its results feed straight back into it, which makes the two inseparable at signoff.

steps.text: SI signoff setup and coupling extraction
Crosstalk delay analysis and timing impact

SO-05.flowNote: Step 4 is where the analysis becomes actionable. A global crosstalk number tells nobody what to fix; a victim-aggressor list on the critical paths tells routing exactly which nets to space or shield.
consumes: Final database and extraction from PD-13
Noise rules and thresholds from PDK-02
produces: SI signoff setup and coupling extraction
Crosstalk delay analysis and timing impact

rel.text: EM/IR and SI/PI signoff reports. The signal integrity half of the deliverable.
STA signoff reports. Crosstalk delay is part of the timing number, not a separate finding.

risks: Crosstalk reported and not reconciled with timing. Two separate reports means the design is signed off against timing that excludes coupling.
Glitch analysis omitted. Noise on a static net can propagate as a functional failure that no timing analysis would show.
Analysis on a subset of nets. Coupling is a property of adjacency, and the critical net set is not the same as the coupled net set.
Fixes applied after timing signoff. Spacing and shielding change delay, and a late fix invalidates the timing it was meant to protect.
Thresholds set by tool default. Noise thresholds are a library and technology property, and defaults are either optimistic or unnecessarily punitive.
entry: Final database and extraction available from PD-13
exit: Crosstalk delay included in the timing signoff numbers
Glitch analysis run, not only delay analysis
Noise thresholds set from library data, not defaults
measuredBy: Crosstalk delay against the timing budget
Glitch violations at freeze
Nets analysed against nets coupled

purpose: Review the chip-package-system co-verification result as a signoff item in its own right, rather than assuming the die-only analysis covers it.

SIPI analysed the die, package and board as one electrical system. This activity brings that result into the signoff record and reconciles it against the die-only numbers — because where they disagree, the system-level answer is the one silicon will produce.

steps.text: SIPI result intake and scope confirmation
Channel compliance review against the interface budgets

SO-06.flowNote: Step 2 is the reconciliation that matters. Die-only IR analysis excludes package inductance, and the difference between the two numbers is margin the design either has or does not — a discrepancy that has to be resolved before mask release rather than explained afterwards.
consumes: Channel budgets from ARCH-04 and AMS-03

rel.text: EM/IR and SI/PI signoff reports. The system-level results belong in the same report as the die-only ones, reconciled rather than filed separately.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. Co-verification signoff is a freeze precondition, since mask release follows it.

risks: Co-verification treated as a package deliverable. It constrains the die's signoff, and excluding it from the signoff record means freezing without it.
Discrepancies explained rather than resolved. Where die-only and system-level disagree, one is wrong, and the difference is real margin.
Channel compliance reviewed against internal assumptions. The interface specification's mask is what compliance means, and internal budgets can be more generous.
Review scheduled after Design Freeze. The freeze is what gates mask release, and a co-verification finding afterwards has nowhere to go.
Power-aware timing not reviewed. STA at nominal voltage and IR analysis showing droop are two views of the same design, and only the reconciliation is the truth.

roles.d: Owns the review and its disposition
IR reconciliation between die and system

entry: Die-only IR results available from SO-04
exit: Die-only and system-level results reconciled, not merely compared
Channel compliance reviewed against the specification mask
Review completed before Design Freeze, not after
measuredBy: Discrepancies resolved against identified
Channel margin against the compliance mask
Review completion against the freeze date

purpose: Verify the reliability requirements the product will be qualified against — ESD paths, latch-up structures, soft error rate — on the final database rather than in the qualification lab.

Qualification failures are the most expensive kind: they arrive after silicon, after packaging and after months of stress testing. Every one of these checks has a design-time equivalent, and running them here converts a possible respin into a layout fix.

steps.text: Reliability requirement collection and rule setup
ESD path verification through the full chip
Latch-up structure and guard ring verification
Soft error rate and FIT estimation

SO-07.flowNote: Step 2 traces the discharge path through the actual layout rather than confirming the strategy. A clamp that exists and a path that reaches it are different claims, and only the full-chip trace establishes the second.
consumes: ESD strategy and clamps from PDK-07
Soft error requirements from the qualification plan
produces: Soft error rate and FIT estimate

rel.text: Reliability reports — ESD, latch-up, FIT. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what MP-03 will be measured against.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. Reliability findings are part of the risk the freeze decision accepts.

risks: ESD verified as a strategy rather than a path. A clamp with no complete discharge path to it protects nothing, and only a full-chip trace finds the gap.
Latch-up checked only at the IO ring. Internal structures near power domain boundaries can latch up too, and they are rarely checked.
Soft error rate not estimated. FIT is a product requirement in many markets, and estimating it after qualification leaves no mitigation options.
Reliability waivers granted without lifetime analysis. A waiver with no quantified impact cannot be defended when qualification fails.
Analysis on a database that then changes. Late ECOs can break an ESD path, and nobody re-runs the check.

roles.d: Owns ESD, latch-up and FIT verification

exit: ESD paths traced through the full chip, not assumed from strategy
Latch-up checked internally as well as at the ring
FIT estimated against the product requirement
measuredBy: ESD paths verified against IO count
Latch-up violations at freeze
FIT estimate against requirement

purpose: Check the design against manufacturability — lithography hotspots, CMP density, DFM recommended rules — so the foundry can print it at yield.

A DRC-clean design can still be difficult to manufacture. Litho hotspots print differently from what was drawn, and CMP density variation produces thickness variation that moves timing. Both are checked with foundry-supplied models and both are cheaper to fix here than to yield-learn in production.

steps.text: DFM deck setup and model version confirmation

SO-08.flowNote: Step 4 quantifies what PDK-02 decided. Recommended-rule compliance is a score rather than a pass, and it correlates with yield — a design that scored 60% on the rules it chose to ignore is a design whose yield learning curve starts lower.
consumes: DFM decks and litho models from the foundry
produces: DFM deck setup and model versions
Hotspot fixes and DFM closure report

rel.text: DFM and lithography hotspot report. This activity is the deliverable, and its compliance score is a yield predictor.
Clean DRC / LVS / antenna / density reports. DFM fixes are layout changes and close alongside physical verification.

risks: DFM checked after routing is frozen. Hotspot fixes are layout changes, and a frozen database has no room for them.
Recommended rules ignored without scoring. The yield cost of ignoring them is real and unmeasured unless someone scores compliance.
Litho models outdated. Foundry models improve through the node's life, and an old model finds the wrong hotspots.
CMP variation not linked to timing. Thickness variation changes resistance and capacitance, and the timing impact is rarely fed back.
Fixes applied without re-verification. A DFM fix is a layout change, and it can create DRC or timing problems of its own.

roles.d: Owns hotspot analysis and DFM closure
Compliance score against the yield model

entry: DFM decks and current litho models available
exit: Hotspots fixed or accepted with a yield impact estimate
Compliance scored rather than assumed
Fixes re-verified against DRC and timing
measuredBy: Hotspots remaining at freeze
Recommended rule compliance score
Yield impact of accepted hotspots

purpose: Prove for the last time that the database being taped out is the design that was verified — final formal equivalence and netlist-to-layout consistency.

Between the FFN and the tapeout database sit hundreds of ECOs, a scan reorder, fill and finishing. Each was individually correct; the question is whether the composition still implements the RTL that DV signed off. This is the last check that answers it.

steps.text: Final equivalence setup against the FFN and the RTL
ECO reconciliation against the change log

SO-09.flowNote: Step 3 pairs the formal result with the ECO log from PD-14. Equivalence proves the netlists match; reconciliation proves that every difference between them was an ECO somebody approved rather than a change nobody noticed.
consumes: Final database and netlist from PD-13
produces: RTL to final netlist equivalence results

rel.text: Final formal equivalence report. This activity is the deliverable, and it is the last evidence that verification's conclusions still apply.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. Freezing a database that has not been proved equivalent freezes an unverified design.

risks: Equivalence run against the FFN rather than the RTL. That proves the ECOs preserved the netlist and not that the netlist implements the verified design.
ECO log not reconciled. A difference that no ECO explains is an unapproved change, and it is exactly what this check exists to find.
Non-equivalences waived under tapeout pressure. Each waiver is a region where the silicon may not do what verification proved.
Run before the last ECO. Any change after the equivalence run invalidates it, and re-running takes days nobody has.
Layout consistency assumed from LVS. LVS compares layout to netlist; that the netlist is the right one is a separate claim.

roles.d: Owns the final check and its report
Confirms the RTL reference is the verified one

exit: Equivalence proved against the verified RTL, not only the FFN
Every netlist difference traced to an approved ECO
Run performed after the last database change
measuredBy: Non-equivalences at the final check
Netlist differences traced to approved ECOs
Database changes after the equivalence run

purpose: Run the waiver review board — every violation that survives signoff, examined, owned and either fixed or accepted — and assemble the Design Freeze package.

Every large design tapes out with waivers. What distinguishes a controlled tapeout from a hopeful one is whether each waiver was understood, quantified and signed, or simply ran out of time. This board is where that distinction is made, and its package is what the Go / No-Go decision reads.

steps.text: Waiver intake and classification across all signoff domains
Root cause and risk quantification per waiver
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package assembly

SO-10.flowNote: Step 3 has a duration outside the program's control. Foundry waivers are reviewed on the foundry's schedule, and a design that assumes approval and does not receive it cannot release masks — which makes early submission worth more than a complete submission.
consumes: Reliability and DFM waivers from SO-07 and SO-08
produces: Root cause and risk quantification per waiver
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package

rel.text: Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what the tapeout decision is taken on.
STA signoff reports with waiver list. The timing waiver list is dispositioned here rather than inside the STA activity.

risks: Waivers accumulated rather than reviewed. A register nobody dispositioned is a set of accepted risks nobody accepted.
Foundry waivers submitted late. Their review is on the foundry's schedule, and an unapproved waiver blocks mask release.
Risk quantified qualitatively. "Low risk" is not a basis for a tapeout decision; a stated failure mode and probability is.
Board without authority. A review that cannot refuse a waiver is a review that approves everything.
Residual risk not summarised. The Go / No-Go decision needs one statement of what is being accepted, not a register of two hundred entries.

roles.d: Chairs the board and owns the package
Carries the residual risk into the Go / No-Go

entry: Foundry waiver process understood from TECH-06
Board membership named with authority to refuse
exit: Every waiver has a root cause, a quantified risk and a signature
Foundry waivers submitted and answered before freeze
Residual risk summarised in one statement for the gate
measuredBy: Waivers dispositioned against raised
Foundry waivers answered before freeze
Waivers with a quantified risk

purpose: Run gate-level simulation with the final SDF — the last dynamic check that the design behaves correctly with real timing on the database being taped out.

Static timing analysis proves paths meet constraints; it does not prove the design works. Simulating with final timing catches what STA structurally cannot — race conditions, reset behaviour under real delays, and any place where the constraints described a design different from the one built.

steps.text: Final SDF generation and simulation setup
Test mode simulation with final timing

SO-11.flowNote: Step 3 is the check most likely to find something. Reset behaviour depends on relative delays across the die, and a sequence that works with estimated timing can fail with the real numbers — a failure that would otherwise appear at first power-on.
consumes: Final database and SDF from PD-13 and PD-09
Test patterns and modes from DFT-08

rel.text: Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. Dynamic evidence on the final database belongs in the freeze package alongside the static analysis.
STA signoff reports. A gate-level failure with clean STA means the constraints described a different design, which is a timing finding.

risks: Skipped because STA is clean. They answer different questions, and the failures gate-level simulation finds are invisible to static analysis.
Run on an earlier database. A simulation against pre-final timing says nothing about the database being taped out.
Reset simulation omitted. Reset ordering under real delays is a common silicon failure and one of the cheapest to catch here.
X failures forced away. Initialising signals to make the simulation run hides exactly the uninitialised state that will fail at power-on.
Runtime prohibiting meaningful scenarios. Full-timing simulation is slow, and a scenario set trimmed to fit may exclude the case that matters.

roles.d: Owns the runs and the report
Accepts the dynamic evidence into the package

entry: Final database and SDF available from PD-13 and PD-09
exit: Simulated against the final SDF, not an earlier one
Reset and initialisation simulated with real delays
X failures fixed rather than forced
measuredBy: Scenarios simulated with final timing
Failures found that STA could not show
X issues fixed against forced

purpose: Correlate the signoff flow against the foundry's own decks and the implementation tool, so that a number produced here means the same thing everywhere it is read.

Three parties analyse this design: the implementation tool, the signoff tool and the foundry. If they disagree, the design can be closed in one and rejected by another. Establishing the correlation early is what lets physical design close with the right margin instead of re-closing after signoff reports.

steps.text: Correlation methodology and reference case selection

SO-12.flowNote: Step 5 is the output physical design actually uses. Knowing that signoff reads 40 ps more pessimistic than implementation on long paths lets PD-09 close with that margin built in, rather than closing to zero and discovering the gap at SO-02.
consumes: Foundry decks and derates from PDK-11

rel.text: STA signoff reports. Correlation is what makes the signoff numbers comparable to the ones physical design closed against.
Signoff summary and Design Freeze package. A stated correlation is part of what makes the signoff result defensible to the foundry.

risks: Correlation established after signoff starts. The gap is then discovered on the final database, when closing it means re-opening closure.
Correlation on unrepresentative paths. Tool differences concentrate on long, heavily coupled paths, and correlating on short clean ones shows agreement that does not generalise.
Extraction differences overlooked. Parasitic differences between flows can exceed timing tool differences and are less often checked.
Margin guidance not adopted. Correlation that physical design does not close against has produced information nobody used.
Foundry decks assumed identical to internal ones. Derates and corner definitions can differ in detail, and the foundry's version is the one that decides acceptance.

roles.d: Reference case analysis in both flows

entry: Foundry decks and derates available from PDK-11
exit: Correlation established on representative, difficult paths
Margin guidance published and adopted by physical design
Foundry deck differences understood, not assumed away
measuredBy: Correlation gap on representative paths
Margin guidance adopted in closure
Surprises at first signoff run

purpose: Assemble the final GDSII or OASIS database from the closed design — every block, every macro, every layer — and verify that the layer map the foundry will read matches the one the design was built with.

This is a mechanical activity with no tolerance for error. A layer misassigned in the stream-out produces masks that are wrong in a way no verification would have caught, because the design was correct and the translation was not.

steps.text: Closure database intake and provenance check
GDSII / OASIS stream out from the closed database
Macro and hard IP GDS merge
Layer map verification against the foundry definition

TO-01.flowNote: Step 4 is checked against the foundry's layer map rather than the internal one. The two are usually identical and occasionally are not, and the difference is only visible at the mask shop — by which point the masks exist.
consumes: Frozen signoff database from PD-13 and PD-16
Foundry layer map and stream-out rules

rel.text: Released GDSII / OASIS database with checksum record. This activity is the deliverable, and the checksum is what makes every later reference unambiguous.
Tapeout checklist with sign-off matrix. Database assembly and layer verification are checklist entries in their own right.

risks: Layer map mismatch. A misassigned layer produces masks that are wrong in a way no design verification would have found.
Macro GDS from the wrong version. An abstract that matched and a layout that did not is discovered at LVS, or worse, not at all.
Stream-out from an unfrozen database. The design has to stop moving before it is streamed, or the streamed version is not the signed-off one.
No checksum. Without one, the question "is this the database we signed off" has no answer.
Assembly compressed to hours. Stream-out on a die this size takes real time, and rushing it is how a merge error is missed.

roles.d: Confirms the database is the frozen one
Stream-out flow and layer map configuration

entry: Foundry layer map and format confirmed
exit: Layer map verified against the foundry's definition, not the internal one
Every macro GDS traced to its released version
Database checksummed and recorded
measuredBy: Layer map discrepancies found
Macro versions traced to release
Stream-out reruns required

purpose: Re-run full-chip physical verification on the released database — not on the one signoff checked, but on the exact bytes going to the mask shop.

Between the signoff run and the released database sit stream-out, macro merge and possibly a late fix. Each is a chance to introduce something. This re-run is short, expensive in compute and non-negotiable: it is the only check that the thing being released is the thing that was verified.

steps.text: Verification setup on the released database
Checksum confirmation against the released database

TO-02.flowNote: Step 5 sounds pedantic and prevents the worst class of error. Verifying one database and releasing another has happened on real programs, and the only defence is confirming the checksum of what was verified against the checksum of what was sent.
produces: Verification results on the released database

rel.text: Released GDSII / OASIS database with checksum record. The release is only complete when the released bytes have been verified.
Tapeout checklist with sign-off matrix. Verification on the released database is one of the checklist's non-waivable entries.

risks: Skipped because signoff was clean. Signoff checked a different database, and the difference between them is exactly what this run exists to catch.
Run on the signoff database rather than the released one. That repeats the earlier check and proves nothing new.
Compute capacity unavailable. A full-chip run takes days and needs to be scheduled, not requested.
New violations discovered with no time to fix. Which is why SO-03 has to close cleanly rather than nearly.
Checksums not compared. Verifying one file and releasing another is a documented failure mode with a trivial defence.

roles.d: Owns the re-run and its results

entry: Decks versioned and matching the submission
exit: Verification run on the exact released database
Checksums confirmed identical between verified and released
No violations outstanding that were not already waived
measuredBy: New violations found on the released database
Checksum agreement
Run completion before the Go / No-Go

purpose: Walk the tapeout checklist — every domain, every entry, evidence attached, owner signed — so the Go / No-Go decision is taken on facts rather than on confidence.

The checklist is the program's collected memory of what has to be true before masks are cut. Its value is entirely in the evidence: an entry ticked because the owner believes it is true is worth nothing, and the difference between a checklist and a ritual is whether anyone reads the attachments.
TO-03.flowNote: Step 3 runs in parallel because it is where the time goes. Chasing an owner who has not signed, or an entry whose evidence does not exist, is the real work — the checklist itself takes an afternoon.
consumes: Signoff results from SO-02 through SO-11

rel.text: Tapeout checklist with sign-off matrix. This activity is the deliverable, and the sign-off matrix is what makes accountability explicit.
Go / No-Go decision minutes. The decision reads the checklist; entries without evidence are decisions being taken blind.

risks: Entries ticked without evidence. A checklist of assertions is a ritual, and it produces confidence rather than information.
Sign-off by proxy. An entry signed by someone other than the accountable owner has moved the signature without moving the accountability.
Checklist assembled at tapeout. It should be maintained across the program; assembling it in the last week means discovering gaps with no time to close them.
Domains missing from the checklist. Test, package and reliability entries are easy to omit from a design-centred checklist and expensive to miss.
Gaps escalated too late. An unsigned entry three days before the Go / No-Go is a decision the meeting cannot take.

roles.d: Owns the checklist and the sign-off matrix
Sign their own entries with evidence

entry: Checklist template maintained across the program
exit: Every entry carries evidence, not an assertion
Signatures from accountable owners, not proxies
Gaps escalated with time to close them
measuredBy: Entries with attached evidence
Signatures from accountable owners
Gaps open at the Go / No-Go

purpose: Take every open issue the program is carrying — bugs, waivers, unclosed items — and turn it into an accepted risk with a name against it.

No large program tapes out with nothing open. The question is whether what remains was assessed and accepted, or simply ran out of time. This activity converts a list of loose ends into a set of decisions, each with an owner, a consequence and a mitigation.

steps.text: Open item consolidation across design, verification and test

TO-04.flowNote: Step 3 is what gives the Go / No-Go meeting something to decide. An item with a mitigation — a test screen, a software workaround, a bin split — is a different decision from one without, and identifying which is which is this activity's contribution.
consumes: Open bug list and risk statement from DV-12
Package and assembly open items from PKGD-11
produces: Risk acceptance record with named owners

rel.text: Open issue and risk acceptance record. This activity is the deliverable, and named ownership is what distinguishes acceptance from omission.
Go / No-Go decision minutes. The decision is largely a decision about this list.

risks: Items carried without assessment. An open issue nobody classified is a risk being accepted without anyone accepting it.
Risk stated qualitatively. "Low risk" gives the decision room nothing; a failure mode, a probability and an affected population gives it a decision.
Mitigations not identified. Many silicon risks can be screened at test or worked around in software, and the option is worth knowing before the gate.
Test and package items excluded. Risk consolidation that covers only design misses the categories that most often cause a late problem.
Acceptance without an owner. An accepted risk with no name against it has nobody watching for it at bring-up.

roles.d: Owns consolidation and the acceptance record
Screening and mitigation options at test
Product impact of each accepted risk

entry: Bug and waiver lists available from DV-12 and SO-10
Test and package open items collected
exit: Every open item classified with a stated consequence
Mitigation options identified where they exist
Each accepted risk has a named owner
measuredBy: Items with a quantified consequence
Accepted risks with a named owner
Mitigations identified against items carried

purpose: Hold the Go / No-Go decision — the moment the program commits several million dollars of masks and a quarter of schedule to the design as it stands.

Half a week of activity and one man-month, preceded by three weeks of preparation. That ratio is correct: a gate argued in the room rather than before it is a gate whose outcome depends on who attended. The meeting exists to take a decision, record its conditions and name who owns them.

steps.text: Decision pack presentation — checklist, risks, readiness

TO-05.flowNote: Step 2 captures dissent deliberately. The objection nobody minuted is the one that resurfaces at first silicon with nothing to point at, and recording it costs a line.

rel.text: Go / No-Go decision minutes. This activity is the deliverable, and the conditions attached are as important as the decision itself.
FEOL MTO release package. Mask data is not released before this decision, whatever the schedule pressure.

risks: Decision taken because the date arrived. A gate that cannot say no is not a gate, and the organisation learns that quickly.
Conditions accepted verbally. A Go granted "subject to" something unrecorded is an unconditional Go.
Wrong people in the room. The decision needs someone who can say no and someone who owns the consequence, and both have to attend.
Dissent unrecorded. It is the cheapest insurance available and it is routinely omitted.
Material presented for the first time in the room. A pack circulated on the day produces a decision based on whoever speaks most confidently.

roles.d: Chairs the decision and owns the outcome
Presents the pack and records the minutes

entry: Checklist complete with signatures from TO-03
Risk acceptance record available from TO-04
exit: Decision recorded with conditions and their owners
Dissent captured in the minutes
Conditions assigned before mask data is released
measuredBy: Conditions attached and assigned
Dissent recorded
Days between pack circulation and decision

purpose: Prepare and release the front-end layer data to the mask shop — the first of the two mask tape-outs, and the one that starts the fab clock.

FEOL goes first because it is the longest lead item and the least likely to change. Releasing it now starts mask writing while the back-end layers are still absorbing late fixes, which is the entire reason the two releases are separated.

steps.text: FEOL layer selection and data preparation
Mask data preparation handoff — fracture, OPC scope
Submission to the foundry and acceptance confirmation

TO-06.flowNote: Step 1's layer selection has to be exact. A layer released with FEOL that later needs a fix cannot be fixed in the BEOL window, and a layer held back that the mask shop needed delays the whole set.
consumes: Foundry submission format and MDP requirements
Mask order and slot from TECH-05

rel.text: FEOL MTO release package and mask order confirmation. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what starts the mask and fab clock.
Released GDSII / OASIS database. The FEOL release is a subset of it, and the two must be traceable to the same checksum.

risks: Layer split wrong. A layer released as FEOL that later needs a fix cannot use the BEOL window, and the fix costs a new mask.
Released before the Go / No-Go. Schedule pressure makes this tempting and it removes the gate's authority entirely.
MDP requirements misunderstood. Fracture and OPC expectations differ per foundry, and a non-compliant submission is rejected.
Submission not acknowledged. A release nobody confirmed received is a release that may not have started the clock.
Traceability lost between database and submission. The submitted layers have to be provably from the checksummed database.

exit: Layer split matches the FEOL/BEOL plan exactly

Released layers traceable to the database checksum

purpose: Confirm the FEOL mask order and get a mask shop schedule the program can plan wafer start against.

One man-month of administration that fixes a date the whole downstream schedule hangs on. Mask writing takes weeks, and knowing when the FEOL set will be ready is what tells FAB-02 when wafers can start.

steps.text: Mask order confirmation and purchase authorisation
Delivery date communication to the program

TO-07.flowNote: Step 3 sounds trivial and is where schedules break. A mask completion date known only to the person who confirmed it is a date the rest of the program plans without.
consumes: Capacity and slot commitment from TECH-05
produces: Mask shop schedule with completion date
Delivery date communication to the program

rel.text: FEOL MTO release package and mask order confirmation. The order confirmation half of the release record.
Full mask set completion record. FEOL completion is the first half of the set.

risks: Order placed without confirmed pricing. Mask cost is a large line item and an unconfirmed order produces an invoice nobody budgeted.
Mask shop schedule assumed. Mask writing capacity is shared, and the completion date is the shop's to give rather than the program's to assume.
Completion date not communicated. Wafer start planning depends on it, and a date held by one person is a date the program does not have.
No escalation path. Mask shop delays happen, and knowing who to call is worth arranging before it is needed.
Order and submission mismatched. The order has to name the exact layer set that was submitted.

purpose: Use the four weeks between the two mask releases to make metal-layer fixes — the last window in which a design change is possible without a new front-end mask set.

This window is the reason the releases are split. FEOL masks are being cut and cannot change; BEOL is still open, and any fix implementable in metal can still be made. It is a genuine and finite opportunity, and it closes on a date.

steps.text: Fix window scope and admission rules
Equivalence and consistency check per fix
Window close and BEOL database freeze

TO-08.flowNote: Step 1 has to be strict. Every late fix carries risk, and a window with no admission rules fills with changes that individually look safe and collectively make the BEOL database something nobody has verified as a whole.
consumes: Late findings from bring-up preparation, verification and signoff
Spare cell and metal-only strategy from PD-14
produces: Fix window scope and admission rules

rel.text: BEOL ECO log covering the fix window. This activity is the deliverable, and the log is what makes the BEOL database traceable.
BEOL MTO release package. The database released to BEOL is the FEOL database plus this window's fixes.

risks: Window used as general contingency. Fixes admitted without rules accumulate into a database that differs from the verified one in ways nobody assessed as a whole.
Fix requiring base layers. If PD-14's spare cell strategy was not put in place, the fix cannot be made in metal and the window is useless.
Verification per fix but not in combination. Individually correct changes can interact, and the combined database needs a check of its own.
Window extended. BEOL mask release has a date; extending the window pushes the whole mask set and with it wafer start.
Equivalence skipped for speed. A metal ECO can change function, and the only detector is an equivalence run.

roles.d: Equivalence per fix and at window close

entry: Admission rules agreed before the window opens

purpose: Re-verify the metal stack after the fix window — DRC, LVS, antenna, density on the changed layers — before the back-end data is released.

The BEOL database is not the one that was signed off. It carries the fix window's changes, and every one of them touched routing. This re-verification is what makes the BEOL release as trustworthy as the FEOL one, and it has to fit inside the window's tail.

steps.text: Re-verification scope on the changed layers
DRC and antenna verification on the metal stack
Timing impact confirmation for the applied fixes

TO-09.flowNote: Step 1 decides between a targeted re-run and a full one. Targeted is faster and risks missing an interaction; full is safe and may not fit the window. The scope decision has to be made on what the fixes actually touched.

rel.text: BEOL MTO release package. The release is only defensible if the changed layers were re-verified.
BEOL ECO log. The log and the re-verification results are read together — what changed, and what was checked afterwards.

risks: Scope too narrow. A targeted re-run that misses an interaction between two fixes releases a violation into the mask set.
Timing not re-confirmed. Metal ECOs change delay, and a fix that breaks timing has replaced one problem with another.
Re-verification not fitting the window. Full-chip runs take days, and a window planned without them cannot accommodate them.
LVS skipped because the change was metal-only. Metal changes connectivity, which is exactly what LVS checks.
Results arriving after the release. Verifying after submission is verifying something already committed to masks.

purpose: Prepare and release the back-end layer data — the second mask tape-out, and the moment the design is fully committed to silicon.

BEOL release is the real tapeout. After it nothing about the design can change without a new mask set, and the milestone the program has been working toward for eighty weeks is this submission being accepted.

steps.text: BEOL layer data preparation from the re-verified database
Submission to the foundry and acceptance confirmation

TO-10.flowNote: The layer set here has to be exactly the complement of what TO-06 released. A layer released twice or not at all produces a mask set that is either wrong or incomplete, and the mask shop will not necessarily notice.

rel.text: BEOL MTO release package and mask order confirmation. This activity is the deliverable, and the milestone the stage carries — Tapeout.
BEOL ECO log. The released database is the FEOL one plus the logged fixes, and the two travel together.

risks: Layer set not complementary to FEOL. A layer released twice or omitted produces an incomplete or contradictory mask set.
Released before re-verification completes. The fix window's changes are then committed unchecked.
Submission rejected on format. BEOL layers have their own OPC and fracture requirements, and a rejection costs days against a running FEOL clock.
No acceptance confirmation. An unconfirmed release may not have started the second mask clock.
Traceability broken. The BEOL database differs from the checksummed original, and the difference has to be exactly the ECO log.

exit: Layer set exactly complementary to the FEOL release
Submission acknowledged in writing
Database difference from the original traced to the ECO log

Release date against plan

purpose: Confirm the BEOL order and track the mask set to completion, so that FAB-05 knows when back-end layers will be available and the line does not stall mid-lot.
The BEOL masks are needed several weeks into wafer processing, not at wafer start. Tracking them to completion is what confirms that the parallel schedule the FEOL/BEOL split assumed actually holds.
TO-11.flowNote: Step 2 tracks the whole set rather than the second half. A mask set is only usable when every layer is complete, and the last layer to finish is the one that decides.

rel.text: Full mask set completion record. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what confirms the split schedule held.
BEOL MTO release package and mask order confirmation. The order half of the BEOL release record.

risks: BEOL masks late against the wafer schedule. Wafers reach the metallisation steps and stop, which is worse than starting late.
Completion tracked per layer rather than per set. The set is usable when the last layer is done, and per-layer optimism hides that.
Availability not communicated to fabrication. The line plans against the date, and a date nobody passed on is a date the line does not have.
Order mismatched to submission. The order has to name exactly the layers submitted, and BEOL sets are large.
No contingency for a mask defect. Masks fail inspection sometimes, and a remake takes weeks.

roles.d: Communicates availability into the fab plan

entry: BEOL data submitted and accepted in TO-10

Wafer processing plan available from FAB-04
exit: Order confirmed against the submitted layer set

purpose: Get the front-end mask set written, inspected and qualified — seven weeks of the mask shop's calendar that the program can watch but not accelerate.

EUV mask sets at this node are slow and expensive to produce, and a single mask failing inspection means a remake measured in weeks. The program's role is oversight rather than execution: confirm the data was accepted, review inspection results and escalate when a layer slips.

steps.text: Mask data acceptance and mask data preparation
Mask defect disposition and remake decisions
Mask qualification and release to the line

FAB-01.flowNote: Step 5 is where a schedule is saved or lost. A mask defect can sometimes be repaired, sometimes waived as non-printing, and sometimes requires a remake — and the three outcomes differ by weeks.
consumes: Mask order and schedule from TO-07
Mask cost and remake terms from TECH-04
produces: Qualified mask set released to the line

rel.text: FEOL and BEOL mask sets with qualification reports. The front-end half of the deliverable.
Wafer-out forecast versus actual log. Mask completion is the first date the wafer-out forecast is built on.

risks: Mask defect requiring a remake. Weeks of schedule, and the program has no way to accelerate the replacement.
Inspection criteria not understood. Whether a defect is printing depends on layer and position, and the disposition needs design input the foundry does not have.
Critical layers not prioritised. Mask shops write in a sequence, and the layers on the critical path can sometimes be pulled forward if anyone asks.
Data preparation rejected late. MDP problems surface days after submission and consume the schedule silently.
No visibility into progress. A seven-week activity with no status reporting means the first news is either completion or a delay.

exit: Every mask inspected and dispositioned, not only written

purpose: Start wafers the moment the front-end masks are qualified — lot definition, starting material, split strategy — because every day of delay here is a day at the far end of the program.

A single week of activity that gates the remaining eleven. The decisions it carries are small and consequential: how many wafers, what splits, which lots are hot, and whether any material is held back for a second attempt.

steps.text: Wafer start authorisation and lot definition
Starting material and lot split decision

FAB-02.flowNote: Step 2 decides the split strategy — whether all wafers run the same process conditions or some are deliberately skewed. Splits cost wafers and buy information about process sensitivity that no simulation can provide.

Capacity and hot-lot terms from TECH-05
Wafer quantity plan from the engineering lot requirement
Split strategy from TECH-07 node risk

rel.text: Processed engineering-lot wafers. The lot definition here determines what comes out at the end.
Wafer-out forecast versus actual log. Wafer start is the point from which the forecast is measured.

risks: Start delayed after masks are ready. Every day is a day at the far end of a schedule with no recovery mechanism.
Wafer quantity too small. Bring-up, characterisation, qualification and customer samples all draw from this lot, and running short means a second lot and a quarter.
No process splits. A single condition gives one data point; splits reveal process sensitivity while there is still time to act on it.
Hot-lot status not invoked. The priority negotiated in TECH-05 has to be requested at start, not assumed.
Starting material not specified. Substrate type and specification affect device behaviour, and defaulting is how an unexpected variable enters.
entry: Capacity and hot-lot terms confirmed in TECH-05
Wafer quantity agreed against downstream needs
exit: Wafers started within days of mask qualification
Quantity sufficient for bring-up, qual and samples
Hot-lot priority invoked where it was negotiated

purpose: Write and qualify the back-end mask set while front-end processing runs — the parallelism the FEOL/BEOL split was designed to create.

This activity is the payoff of the two-stage release. BEOL masks are written during the weeks the wafers spend in front-end processing, so the fix window cost the program nothing in schedule as long as these masks are ready when the lots reach metallisation.

steps.text: BEOL mask data acceptance and preparation
Release to the line ahead of metallisation

FAB-03.flowNote: Step 5's date is the one that matters. The masks do not need to exist at wafer start; they need to exist before the lots reach the first metal layer, and that is several weeks of margin the split created deliberately.
produces: Qualified BEOL masks released to the line

rel.text: FEOL and BEOL mask sets with qualification reports. The back-end half of the deliverable.
Wafer-out forecast versus actual log. A BEOL mask delay stops lots mid-process, which the forecast has to reflect.

risks: Masks late against metallisation. Lots stop mid-process, which wastes fab capacity and is harder to recover from than a late start.
Parallelism assumed rather than tracked. The split only pays off if the BEOL schedule is actively compared against the front-end progress.
Defect disposition slower on BEOL layers. There are more of them, and a per-layer process that worked for FEOL can bottleneck here.
Metallisation start estimate stale. The masks are needed against a moving date, and planning against the original estimate is planning against fiction.
No priority on the first metal layers. They are needed first and can often be written first if anyone asks.
entry: BEOL data submitted and accepted in TO-10
exit: Masks qualified before lots reach metallisation
Progress tracked against the front-end schedule, not in isolation
First metal layers prioritised in the writing sequence

purpose: Watch the wafers through front-end processing — transistor formation, contacts, local interconnect — and respond when the line reports something unexpected.

Eight weeks in which the program does almost nothing and cannot afford to do nothing. The lots are the foundry's to run; what belongs to the program is understanding the inline data, recognising an excursion early and deciding what to do about it.

steps.text: Lot release and front-end entry confirmation
Inline monitoring at front-end critical steps
Front-end exit and handoff to back end

FAB-04.flowNote: Step 5 needs a standing decision framework. When a lot goes out of control limits the choices are scrap, rework, continue at risk or split — and making that decision in the moment, without a framework, tends to produce whichever answer is least disruptive rather than best.
produces: Inline monitoring findings at critical steps

rel.text: Processed engineering-lot wafers. Front-end processing is where the transistors are actually made.
Inline, PCM and WAT data package. Front-end inline data is the earliest indication of how the lot is running.

risks: Excursion response improvised. Without a framework the decision defaults to whatever is least disruptive rather than what is best for the lot.
Inline data not reviewed by the program. The foundry monitors its process; only the design team can say whether a deviation matters for this device.
Hot-lot priority lost mid-flow. Priority granted at start can quietly lapse, and nobody notices until the cycle time slips.
Scrap decision taken too late. A lot continuing through eight weeks of processing after a fatal excursion wastes capacity that a second lot needed.
No second lot in reserve. If the first lot is lost, having no material started means restarting the whole cycle.

roles.d: Inline data interpretation for this device

entry: Inline monitoring plan running from FAB-06
exit: Every excursion dispositioned against a framework, not improvised
Inline data reviewed by the design team, not only the foundry
Hot-lot priority maintained through the flow

Excursions dispositioned within the framework
Wafers surviving front-end processing

purpose: Complete the wafers through back-end-of-line processing — metallisation, vias, top metal, passivation — and finish the lot.

The back end is where the design's routing becomes physical. It is also where the BEOL masks are consumed, which makes it the point at which the FEOL/BEOL split either paid off invisibly or produces a stall that everyone notices.

steps.text: Back-end entry and mask availability confirmation

FAB-05.flowNote: Step 1 is a confirmation with real consequences. If FAB-03 has not delivered qualified masks by this point the lots wait in the line, and waiting mid-process is more expensive than waiting at the start.

rel.text: Processed engineering-lot wafers. This activity is where the wafers are finished — the deliverable the whole stage exists to produce.
Inline, PCM and WAT data package. Back-end inline data completes the process record for the lot.

risks: BEOL masks not ready at back-end entry. Lots stall mid-process, consuming fab capacity and adding cycle time nobody planned.
Metallisation defects detected late. Back-end defects affect yield directly, and inline detection is what allows a response.
Passivation and top metal treated as routine. They affect bump attachment and package assembly, and problems here surface at ASSY-03.
Lot completion not confirmed against quantity. Wafers lost during processing reduce the number available downstream, and the count has to be checked rather than assumed.
Process changes between split lots not tracked. If splits were run, which wafer had which condition has to be traceable to the end.

roles.d: Defect response in the back end

entry: BEOL masks qualified and released by FAB-03
exit: Wafers completed without a mask-driven stall

Wafers completed against started

purpose: Watch the inline metrology and defect inspection data across the whole run, so an excursion is caught while the lot can still be saved rather than at final test.

The foundry monitors its process against its own control limits; the program needs to know whether a deviation matters for this device. A defect density excursion on a layer the design uses heavily is a different event from one on a layer it barely touches, and only the design team can tell the difference.

steps.text: Monitoring plan and critical step selection

FAB-06.flowNote: Step 1 chooses where to look. Monitoring every step equally wastes attention; selecting the layers and dimensions this design is most sensitive to — minimum-pitch metal, critical gate dimensions, via layers — is what makes the monitoring informative.
consumes: Design sensitivity analysis from TECH-03 and SO-08
produces: Monitoring plan with critical step selection

rel.text: Inline, PCM and WAT data package. The inline half of the deliverable, and the earliest signal the program gets.
Wafer acceptance disposition record. Inline findings inform the acceptance decision rather than being separate from it.

risks: Monitoring every step equally. Attention spread evenly finds nothing; the design's sensitivities decide where to look.
Data reviewed only by the foundry. Process control answers whether the line is in control, not whether this device is affected.
Excursions detected after the affected step. Once the lot has moved on, the response options narrow sharply.
Defects classified but not attributed. Knowing the count without the source gives no basis for a corrective action.
Monitoring stopping at front-end exit. Back-end defects affect yield as much and are often less well monitored.

purpose: Read the e-test and PCM data — device parameters measured on structures in the scribe line — and compare them against what the models predicted.

PCM data arrives before packaged parts and answers process questions weeks earlier than the lab can. Threshold voltages, resistances, capacitances and ring oscillator frequencies measured on real silicon are the first hard evidence of whether the design's assumptions about the process were right.

steps.text: PCM structure and parameter list confirmation
Parameter comparison against target and model

FAB-07.flowNote: Step 4 is where the value is. A threshold voltage 30 mV from target changes timing across the whole design, and knowing that before parts arrive lets bring-up be planned around it rather than surprised by it.

Model predictions from PDK-03 and TECH-03
produces: Parameter comparison against model and target

rel.text: Inline, PCM and WAT data package. The PCM half of the deliverable, and the earliest device-level data available.
Wafer acceptance disposition record. Parameter deviations are part of what acceptance is decided on.

risks: PCM data not reviewed until parts arrive. It answers process questions weeks earlier and costs nothing extra to read.
Comparison against target only. The design was built against models; comparing against the model is what predicts silicon behaviour.
Variability ignored. Across-wafer parameter spread predicts the bin distribution, and the mean alone does not.
Split lots analysed together. If splits were run, aggregating them averages away exactly the information the splits were for.
No link to the test chip results. TC-07 correlated models against silicon; this data either confirms that correlation or contradicts it.

purpose: Run wafer acceptance testing and decide whether the lot is accepted — the formal gate between the fab and everything downstream.

WAT is the contractual boundary. Parameters within specification mean the foundry delivered what was agreed; parameters outside mean a conversation about disposition, rework or credit. Either way the decision has to be taken deliberately rather than by default.

steps.text: Acceptance criteria confirmation with the foundry

FAB-08.flowNote: Step 4 can accept a lot that is out of specification. On an engineering lot the priority is usually silicon in the lab rather than perfect silicon, and accepting a marginal lot with the deviation documented is often the right call — but it must be a call.

rel.text: Wafer acceptance disposition record. This activity is the deliverable, and the record is what a later yield discussion refers back to.
Processed engineering-lot wafers. Wafers are not released downstream until this decision is taken.

risks: Acceptance by default. A lot released without a decision has been accepted by nobody, and the deviation is discovered later with no record.
Criteria not agreed in advance. Negotiating acceptance criteria after the data exists favours whoever is more motivated.
Marginal lot rejected on principle. On an engineering lot, silicon in the lab is usually worth more than a lot within every limit.
Deviations not documented. A parameter out of specification affects bring-up interpretation, and the bring-up team has to know.
Disposition delayed. Every day the lot sits undispositioned is a day of bring-up not happening.

Assembly, test, bring-up and qualification all schedule against wafer-out. The forecast will move — fab schedules do — and the program's exposure is not the movement but the surprise. Four man-months across eighteen weeks buys a date everyone can plan against and early warning when it changes.

steps.text: WIP tracking setup and reporting cadence

Hot-lot priority lapsing. Priority is maintained by attention, and a lot that quietly loses it takes standard cycle time.
Deviations not escalated. A slip identified and not raised becomes a slip everyone discovers at the same time, too late to replan.
Forecast presented without confidence. A date with no stated uncertainty invites downstream teams to plan to the day.
Tracking limited to the fab. Wafer-out is not the same as parts available; sort, logistics and assembly all sit between.

purpose: Choose the package architecture — interposer type, substrate construction, layer count, body size — and commit to it, because everything from bump pitch to assembly capacity follows.

This decision has the same character as the monolithic-versus-chiplet call in ARCH-02: it looks like an engineering choice and it is a supply chain commitment. A 2.5D silicon interposer is a different supplier, a different capacity queue and a different cost structure from an organic bridge, and switching later is not practical.

purpose: Negotiate the bump map with physical design — pitch, count, power-to-signal ratio, position — until both the die and the package can build what the other needs.

The bump field is where two design teams share one constraint. The die wants bumps where its logic is; the package wants them where its escape routing can reach; and the power delivery requirement takes most of the field regardless. Convergence takes iteration, and the iteration has to finish before PD-04 freezes.

steps.text: Bump pitch and field definition against the architecture
Power-to-signal ratio derivation from the power envelope
Escape feasibility check against the substrate

PKGD-02.flowNote: Step 4 is the check that usually forces the iteration. A bump assignment that works on the die can require escape routing the substrate cannot provide at its layer count, and finding that early is what keeps the map from being redone after freeze.

rel.text: Bump map and interposer / RDL database. The bump map half of the deliverable; PKGD-03 supplies the interposer routing.

risks: Bump map converged on the die side only. A map that cannot escape on the substrate has to be redone, and by then the die may be placed around it.

Pitch chosen from the previous program. Pitch depends on the interposer technology and the assembly process, both of which may have changed.
Signal assignment ignoring channel quality. Which bump a high-speed signal uses affects its escape path and its crosstalk exposure.
Iteration continuing past the freeze date. PD-04 and the substrate order both depend on this closing on time.

purpose: Route the interposer and its redistribution layers — the silicon layer that carries the die-to-HBM channels and everything else the substrate cannot.

On a 2.5D part the interposer carries the highest-density and highest-performance connections in the package. HBM channels alone run to thousands of nets at fine pitch, and their routing quality decides whether the memory interface trains at speed.

risks: HBM channel lengths unmatched. Skew across a wide parallel interface eats the training margin, and the failure appears at bring-up as a memory that will not train at speed.

Interposer power distribution underprovisioned. Current for two HBM stacks and the die passes through the interposer, and its resistance is part of the IR budget.
Manufacturability checked late. Interposer rules differ from die rules, and a design that violates them is a supplier rejection rather than a warning.
Routing started before the bump map converges. Every bump change is an interposer rework, and the rework is expensive at this density.

Package routing is where high-speed channels are made or ruined. A via with a long stub, a trace crossing a plane split, or a differential pair routed without its partner all cost margin that the PHY then has to make up. SIPI-07 will measure the result; this activity is what determines it.

The package sits between the die's instantaneous current demand and the board's slower supply. Its planes, vias and decoupling determine the impedance in the mid-frequency band where neither the die's on-chip decap nor the board's bulk capacitors help. Designing it is here; proving it works is co-verification.

A package at this power dissipates hundreds of watts through a stack of materials with different expansion coefficients. The thermal path decides the achievable power envelope; the mechanical behaviour decides whether the assembly survives reflow. Both are simulated here and measured on real vehicles in PTV.

Material properties assumed. Substrate and underfill properties vary by supplier and lot, and simulation is only as good as the inputs.

A TTV is a die that only makes heat, in the pattern the real die will make it. Uniform heaters measure an average the product will never experience; heaters matched to the compute cluster distribution measure the hotspot that decides the achievable power envelope.
