Simulation comparison skipped. Without correlation the model stays unvalidated, and the next package has to be measured from scratch.
Co-planarity ignored. Ball flatness determines whether the package mounts to the board reliably, and it is a separate property from warpage.
Too few units to see condition effects. Warpage varies unit to unit, and distinguishing a condition effect from noise needs population.
Results not linked to assembly conditions. Knowing the warpage without knowing which condition produced it gives no basis for a window.
exit: Warpage measured across the full reflow profile
Simulation correlated against measurement
Results attributed to assembly conditions
measuredBy: Peak warpage against the limit
Simulation error against measurement
Condition effects distinguishable from noise

purpose: Evaluate chip-package interaction — the stress the package puts into the die's low-k dielectric stack, and whether the bumps and back-end metal survive it.

CPI is the failure mode that makes 2.5D packaging risky at advanced nodes. Ultra-low-k dielectrics are mechanically weak, the package expands differently from the silicon, and the resulting stress concentrates exactly where the bumps meet the top metal. It cracks or it does not, and simulation alone is not enough to know.

steps.text: CPI stress evaluation plan and structure selection
Cross-section and failure analysis on affected units

PTV-08.flowNote: Step 5 is destructive and necessary. Electrical and acoustic methods say something is wrong; only cross-sectioning shows what failed and where, and the design implication depends entirely on which layer cracked.
consumes: Die stack and ULK information from TECH-03
produces: CPI evaluation plan and structure selection

rel.text: CPI stress assessment report — ULK, bump and BEOL integrity. This activity is the deliverable, and it is the most consequential result the vehicle programme produces.
Package validation complete record. CPI is usually the risk the gate most depends on.

risks: CPI evaluated by simulation alone. Material behaviour at these dimensions is not predictable to the accuracy the decision needs.
Insufficient thermal cycles. CPI failures accumulate; a short cycle count shows nothing and reassures wrongly.
Cross-sectioning skipped. Detection without localisation gives no design implication, and the implication is the output that matters.
Only nominal units stressed. The DOE's edge conditions are where CPI is most likely, and testing only the centre misses it.
Findings arriving after package design freezes. A CPI problem needs an underfill, bump or design change, none of which are available after PKGD-11.
entry: Die stack information available from TECH-03
Thermal cycling and FA capability available
exit: Stress applied to a cycle count that would reveal accumulation
Failures cross-sectioned and localised, not only detected
Findings delivered before the package design freeze
measuredBy: Thermal cycles survived against the qualification requirement
Failures localised against detected
Weeks between findings and package design freeze

purpose: Characterise the package's thermal performance — junction-to-case and junction-to-ambient resistance, TIM behaviour, hotspot mapping — and correlate it against the simulation.

The thermal path decides the achievable power envelope, and the product is sold on that envelope. Measuring it on a TTV that reproduces the real power distribution is what turns a simulated Rjc into a number the datasheet can carry.

steps.text: Thermal measurement setup and sensor calibration
Hotspot mapping across the heater zones
TIM performance and bond line study
Correlation against the PKGD-07 thermal model

PTV-09.flowNote: Step 4 measures the interface nobody can simulate reliably. TIM performance depends on bond line thickness, pressure and pump-out over time, and the datasheet value is a starting point rather than an answer.
produces: TIM performance and bond line results

rel.text: Thermal characterisation report with model correlation. This activity is the deliverable, and the correlation is what makes the model reusable.
Frozen assembly process window definition. TIM bond line is an assembly parameter, and its thermal effect is measured here.

risks: TIM performance taken from the datasheet. Bond line thickness and pressure are assembly parameters, and the achieved performance differs from the specification.
Hotspot not measured. The average junction temperature is not what limits the part; the hottest zone is.
Simulation not correlated. The model then remains unvalidated, and every future thermal question needs another vehicle.
Transient response ignored. An accelerator's power is bursty, and the transient behaviour determines whether the package can absorb a workload spike.
Measured at a single ambient condition. Rja depends on airflow and ambient, and one condition does not characterise the range the product will see.

roles.d: TIM options and bond line study

entry: Assembled TTV units available from PTV-06
Sensors calibrated per the PTV-03 approach
exit: TIM performance measured as assembled, not as specified
Hotspot mapped rather than averaged
Thermal model correlated and updated
measuredBy: Measured Rjc against simulation
Hotspot temperature against the envelope requirement
TIM performance as assembled against specification

purpose: Stress the vehicles through board-level reliability — temperature cycling, drop, bend — because the package has to survive being mounted in a system, not only being assembled.

Board-level reliability is where the package meets the customer's manufacturing process. Solder joints crack under thermal cycling, boards flex during handling, and a package that passes component qualification and fails board-level testing is a package the customer cannot use.

steps.text: Board-level test plan and coupon board design
Coupon board fabrication and vehicle mounting
Failure mode analysis and characteristic life

PTV-10.flowNote: Step 3 runs to failure rather than to a pass criterion. Characteristic life — the cycle count at which a defined fraction fails — is what a customer needs to assess the package in their system, and a pass at a fixed cycle count does not provide it.
produces: Board-level test plan and coupon boards
Failure mode analysis and characteristic life

rel.text: Board-level reliability data on vehicles. This activity is the deliverable, and characteristic life is what customers will ask for.
Package validation complete record. Board-level survival is part of what "validated" has to mean.

risks: Testing to a pass criterion rather than to failure. A pass tells the customer nothing about margin; characteristic life does.
Coupon board unrepresentative. Board thickness and pad design affect solder joint stress, and a test board unlike the customer's predicts poorly.
Started too late to finish. Temperature cycling to failure takes months, and it is the longest test in the vehicle programme.
Failure modes not analysed. Knowing units failed at a cycle count without knowing how gives no route to improvement.
Only one mounting condition. Different customers mount differently, and the package's sensitivity to that is worth knowing.
entry: Board-level standards and customer requirements known
exit: Testing run to failure, with characteristic life established
Coupon boards representative of customer mounting
Failure modes identified, not only counted
measuredBy: Characteristic life against the requirement
Failure modes identified against failures observed
Test completion against the wafer-out gate

purpose: Measure assembly yield electrically through the daisy chains, localise what failed, and turn that into process learning before the product is assembled.

Assembly yield on a 2.5D package with hundreds of thousands of interconnects is not guaranteed. The daisy chains make it measurable, and the segmentation makes it attributable — which is what lets the OSAT fix a process problem rather than accept a yield number.

steps.text: Continuity test setup and measurement plan
Assembly yield learning and process feedback

PTV-11.flowNote: Step 5 is why the DOE was run. Yield varying with bond force or reflow profile identifies the parameter that matters, and that is the parameter the process window in PTV-12 will be built around.
consumes: Yield expectations from the cost model
produces: Assembly yield learning and process feedback

rel.text: Built vehicle lots with assembly travelers. The travelers' condition data is what makes this analysis possible.
Frozen assembly process window definition. Yield against condition is the window's most direct evidence.

risks: Yield measured without localisation. A number with no location gives the OSAT nothing to act on.
Marginal interconnects passing continuity. A high-resistance joint conducts and will fail in the field; Kelvin measurement is what distinguishes it.
Condition correlation not performed. The DOE's whole purpose is to link yield to parameters, and skipping the analysis wastes the build.
Feedback arriving after the process freezes. Learning that cannot change the process window is learning with no consequence.
Sample size too small for yield estimation. Assembly yield is a rate, and estimating it needs enough units for the rate to be meaningful.
entry: Assembled daisy-chain units available from PTV-06
exit: Failures localised to interconnect level and position
Marginal joints identified by resistance, not only by continuity
Feedback delivered before the process window freezes
measuredBy: Assembly yield against the cost model assumption
Failures localised against detected
Yield variation explained by DOE conditions

purpose: Freeze the assembly process window, feed the findings back into package design, and declare package validation complete — the gate product wafer-out has to clear.

This is the activity the whole stage exists for. It converts a large body of measurement into two things: a process window ASSY will run to, and a statement that the package has been validated. Product wafers must not come out before it is issued, because the alternative is learning about the package on real dies.

steps.text: Result consolidation across all vehicle characterisation
Risk retirement assessment against the coverage matrix
Package design feedback and change requests
Assembly process window definition and freeze
Residual risk statement for unretired items

PTV-12.flowNote: Step 2 is the honest accounting. Some risks in the matrix will not have been retired — a vehicle failed, a measurement was inconclusive — and the declaration has to say which, rather than declaring completion because the date arrived.
produces: Risk retirement assessment against the matrix
Package design feedback and change requests

rel.text: Frozen assembly process window definition. The window ASSY will build the product to, derived from evidence rather than from the OSAT's standard recipe.
Package validation complete record — gate for product wafer-out. This activity carries the stage's milestone and the gate.

risks: Completion declared because the date arrived. The gate exists to be capable of holding wafer-out, and a declaration that cannot say no is not a gate.
Unretired risks not stated. A validation record that implies full coverage when some risks remain open misleads exactly the decision it informs.
Feedback arriving after PKGD-11. Package design changes are not available after the freeze, so vehicle findings have to land before it.
Process window frozen too wide. A window that accommodates every observed condition is not a window; the boundaries have to exclude what produced failures.
Window not transferred to the OSAT as a specification. A window that exists in a report and not in the assembly instructions will not be followed.

roles.d: Owns consolidation, the window and the declaration

entry: Characterisation complete from PTV-07 through PTV-11
exit: Every matrix risk marked retired or explicitly not retired
Process window frozen with boundaries that exclude observed failures
Window transferred to the OSAT as a specification, not a report
measuredBy: Risks retired against the coverage matrix
Weeks of margin against the wafer-out gate
Process window adopted by the OSAT

purpose: Get a chip power model that represents the die's current demand honestly — per domain, per mode, under the switching the product actually produces.

Everything in this stage depends on this model. A CPM extracted under averaged activity understates the transient the package must supply, and every downstream conclusion inherits that error without any indication that it did.

steps.text: Model requirement definition with physical design
Switching scenario selection from real workloads
Model validation against die-level IR analysis

SIPI-01.flowNote: Step 2 decides everything the stage can conclude. The worst realistic transient — a workload burst arriving after an idle period — is what the package has to absorb, and a model built on steady-state activity cannot represent it.
consumes: Placed and routed database from PD-05 and PD-06
Chip power model extraction from PD-11
Switching activity from DV-04 and SYN-06
Model format requirements from the analysis tools

rel.text: Chip power model (CPM/CPS) release per domain and mode. This activity is the deliverable, and everything else in the stage consumes it.
PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. The model is the die-side input to every co-simulation.

risks: Model built on averaged activity. The transient is what the package must supply, and averaging removes exactly the event of interest.
Single model for all modes. DVFS points and workloads draw very differently, and one model represents none of them well.
Not validated against die-level IR. A CPM that disagrees with the die's own analysis is wrong somewhere, and nobody knows where.
Delivered late. The stage cannot start without it, and the stage gates mask release.
Version drift. Analysis run against a stale model produces conclusions about a die that has since changed.
exit: Model built on the worst realistic transient, not an average
Separate models per domain and mode
Validated against die-level IR before release
measuredBy: Modes modelled against modes the product uses
Validation agreement against die-level IR
Model delivery against the stage start

purpose: Extract electrical models of the package and the board — 3D field solution, S-parameters, RLC networks — so the system can be analysed as one circuit rather than three assumptions.

Each of the three parties has been designing against a model of the other two. Extraction replaces those assumptions with a solved answer: what the interposer, substrate and board actually do electrically, at the frequencies the design cares about.

steps.text: Extraction scope and frequency range definition

SIPI-02.flowNote: Step 1's frequency range decides the extraction cost and its usefulness. PDN analysis needs DC to the switching harmonics; channel analysis needs far higher. Extracting once for both is efficient and extracting for the wrong range wastes the effort entirely.
consumes: Bump and ball assignment from PKGD-02 and PD-04

rel.text: Extracted package and board electrical models. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what turns three design intents into one analysable circuit.
Channel compliance report per interface. Channel simulation runs on these models rather than on idealised transmission lines.

risks: Frequency range too narrow. A model extracted for PDN analysis cannot support channel simulation, and re-extraction is expensive.
Extraction on an unfinished design. Package routing changes invalidate the model, and re-extraction is measured in weeks.
Board model omitted. The board is part of the PDN and part of the channel, and excluding it makes the analysis die-and-package only.
Models not validated. A 3D extraction has convergence and meshing choices, and an unvalidated result can be confidently wrong.
Socket and connector effects ignored. The bring-up platform includes them, and channel margin measured at bring-up will reflect them.
entry: Interposer and substrate designs stable from PKGD-03 and PKGD-04
exit: Frequency range covers both PDN and channel needs
Board and socket included, not only die and package
Models validated rather than assumed correct
measuredBy: Frequency coverage against analysis needs
Model validation error
Re-extractions required after design change

purpose: Simulate the die, package and board as one power delivery network and check its impedance against target across the frequency range that matters.

The three levels each cover a different band: on-die decap handles the highest frequencies, package decoupling the middle, board bulk capacitance the lowest. Analysed separately each looks adequate; analysed together the gaps between them appear, and those gaps are where the supply actually sags.

steps.text: DC resistance and static drop analysis

SIPI-03.flowNote: Step 5 finds what separate analyses cannot. Anti-resonances form between the package's inductance and the die's capacitance, at frequencies neither level would identify alone, and they are where impedance peaks far above target.
consumes: Package and board models from SIPI-02
produces: DC resistance and static drop results

rel.text: PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. The impedance half of the deliverable; SIPI-04 supplies the dynamic IR half.
Decap budget and placement specification. The impedance profile is what the decap budget is designed to flatten.

risks: Levels analysed separately. Each looks adequate in isolation and the transitions between them are where the impedance peaks.
Anti-resonances missed. They occur at frequencies no single level would examine and can exceed target by a large factor.
Impedance target derived from a rule of thumb. The target follows from the current step and the allowable ripple, and a generic value is either wasteful or inadequate.
DC analysis only. Static drop is the easy half; the frequency-dependent behaviour is where the problems are.
Findings without recommendations. An impedance plot that exceeds target tells the team there is a problem, not which level to fix.
entry: Chip power model released by SIPI-01
Package and board models extracted in SIPI-02
exit: Impedance analysed across the full frequency range as one network
Anti-resonances identified and addressed
Findings carry recommendations naming which level to change
measuredBy: Impedance against target across frequency
Anti-resonance peaks identified
Recommendations adopted by the responsible level

purpose: Analyse dynamic voltage droop with the package's inductance included, under the switching profiles the product actually produces — the number the die-only analysis is optimistic about.

Die-only dynamic IR excludes the package's series inductance, which is the dominant impedance at the frequencies a workload burst excites. The difference between the two numbers is real margin, and it is the reason this stage exists rather than trusting SO-04.

steps.text: Transient scenario selection from the workload profiles
Combined transient simulation with package inductance
Droop magnitude and duration analysis per domain
Dynamic IR findings and margin assessment

SIPI-04.flowNote: Step 4 is the comparison the program most needs. Where die-only analysis says 4.1% and the co-analysis says 5.0% against a 5% budget, the design has no margin — and the two numbers have to be reconciled before SO-04 signs off on the optimistic one.
consumes: Die-only IR results from PD-03 and SO-04
produces: Droop magnitude and duration per domain

rel.text: PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. The dynamic IR half of the deliverable, and the number signoff should be using.
Power-aware STA correlation report. Droop is what gets back-annotated into timing in SIPI-09.

risks: Package inductance excluded. It dominates at the frequencies a burst excites, and excluding it produces a comfortable and wrong answer.
Transient scenario too gentle. The worst case is a burst after idle, and a scenario built from steady-state activity never reaches it.
Droop duration ignored. A deep short droop and a shallow long one have different timing consequences, and only the magnitude is usually reported.
Die-only comparison not made. Without it nobody knows whether SO-04's number is optimistic, and the two signoffs disagree silently.
Findings arriving after timing signoff. Droop consumes timing margin, and a late finding invalidates closure.

roles.d: Owns dynamic analysis and margin assessment

entry: Chip power model and PDN model available
Die-only IR results available from PD-03
exit: Package inductance included in every result
Die-only and co-analysis numbers reconciled
Findings delivered before timing signoff closes
measuredBy: Droop against budget with package inductance
Gap between die-only and co-analysis results
Timing margin consumed by droop

purpose: Allocate the decoupling budget across die, package and board — how much capacitance, of what type, mounted where — so the three levels cover the frequency range between them rather than overlapping.

Decoupling is a system-level allocation that is usually made three times independently. On-die capacitance is expensive in area, package capacitors are limited by mounting positions, and board bulk is cheap and slow. Optimising them together is what covers the band; optimising them separately leaves the middle uncovered.

steps.text: Frequency band allocation across the three levels
On-die decap requirement and area cost
Package capacitor selection and mounting position
Combined impedance verification with the allocation
Decap specification and handoff to each level

SIPI-05.flowNote: Step 2 carries a real cost. On-die decoupling consumes die area that could have been logic, and the trade between area and package capacitors is a system decision rather than a physical design one.
consumes: On-die decap capability and area cost from PD-03
produces: On-die decap requirement with area cost

rel.text: Decap budget and placement specification across die, package and board. This activity is the deliverable, and it is the only place the three levels are allocated together.
PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. The allocation is verified against the impedance target it was designed to meet.

risks: Each level decoupled independently. The bands overlap in places and leave gaps in others, and the gaps are where the impedance peaks.
Package capacitors placed where there is room. Mounting position determines loop inductance, and a capacitor far from the current draw contributes little.
On-die decap area not costed. It is die area, and treating it as free produces a design that traded logic for decoupling without anyone deciding to.
Allocation not verified. A budget that has not been re-simulated against the impedance target is a proposal rather than a solution.
Specification not handed to each level. A system allocation that stays in a report is not implemented by anyone.
entry: Mounting and area constraints known from each level
exit: Bands allocated so the three levels cover the range without gaps
Package capacitors placed for loop inductance
Allocation verified against the impedance target before handoff
measuredBy: Impedance gaps between levels
On-die decap area against the budget
Specification adopted by each level

purpose: Analyse simultaneous switching noise at the IO ring — the supply disturbance many outputs switching together inject into their own reference.

SSN is a local problem with system consequences. When a wide interface switches together, the current through the shared return path moves the reference the receivers are measuring against, and the resulting noise appears as jitter and reduced eye margin on the very interface that caused it.

steps.text: SSN analysis scope — which interfaces switch together
IO ring power and ground network modelling
Ground bounce and reference shift analysis

SIPI-06.flowNote: Step 5 usually points back at the bump map. The most effective SSN mitigation is more or better-placed power and ground bumps for that interface, which is a PKGD-02 decision — and one that has to be made before the map freezes.
consumes: Package and board models from SIPI-02
Bump and ball assignment from PKGD-02
On-die IO power distribution from PD-03
produces: IO ring power and ground models
Ground bounce and reference shift analysis

rel.text: Channel compliance report per interface. SSN degrades the eye of the interface that causes it, so it belongs in the same compliance assessment.
PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. SSN is a local PDN problem and is reported alongside the global one.

risks: SSN analysed per pin rather than per interface. The problem is simultaneity, and a single-pin analysis cannot see it.
Reference shift not included in the eye budget. Ground bounce moves the receiver's threshold, and excluding it overstates the margin.
Mitigation identified after bump map freeze. The most effective remedy is bump assignment, and it is unavailable after PKGD-02 closes.
Worst-case switching pattern not simulated. All outputs switching the same direction simultaneously is the worst case and is rarely the default pattern.
IO ring modelled as ideal. The ring's own power distribution is what carries the return current, and idealising it removes the effect being analysed.

roles.d: IO driver characteristics and reference behaviour

exit: Worst-case simultaneous switching simulated per interface
Reference shift included in the interface eye budget
Mitigations identified before the bump map freezes
measuredBy: Ground bounce against the reference budget
Eye margin consumed by SSN
Mitigations available before bump map freeze

purpose: Simulate the high-speed channels end to end with extracted package models — insertion loss, crosstalk, return path, reflections — rather than against the idealised channel the PHY was designed to.

Every PHY closes its margin against an assumed channel. This activity produces the real one: interposer, substrate, board, socket, connectors and all their discontinuities. Where the real channel is worse than assumed, the margin the PHY reported never existed.

steps.text: End-to-end channel assembly from extracted models
Insertion loss and return loss analysis
Crosstalk analysis — near and far end
Channel characterisation against the PHY assumption

SIPI-07.flowNote: Step 6 is the reconciliation that matters. The PHY in AMS-03 closed against a channel budget; this activity says what the channel actually is, and any gap between them is margin the interface does not have.
consumes: Package and board models from SIPI-02
Channel budgets from AMS-03 and ARCH-04

rel.text: Channel compliance report per interface, with margins. This activity is the deliverable, and the margin is stated against the real channel.
Extracted package and board electrical models. Channel simulation is the primary consumer of the extraction.

risks: Channel simulated on nominal models only. Manufacturing variation moves impedance and loss, and the compliance margin has to survive it.
PHY assumption not reconciled. The PHY closed against a budget; if the real channel is worse, the interface has no margin and nobody has noticed.
Crosstalk analysed only at the near end. Far-end crosstalk on a long dense channel can dominate, and it behaves differently.
Socket and connector excluded. The bring-up platform includes them, and margin measured at bring-up will reflect them.
Findings after the package design freeze. Channel improvements are routing changes, and they are unavailable after PKGD-11.
entry: Package and board models extracted in SIPI-02
Package SI routing complete in PKGD-05
exit: Channels simulated end to end including socket and connectors
Real channel reconciled against the PHY's assumed budget
Findings delivered before the package design freeze
measuredBy: Channel loss against the PHY's assumed budget
Crosstalk against the interface allowance
Discontinuities identified and addressed

purpose: Close the eye, jitter and BER budget per interface — combining channel loss, crosstalk, SSN, PHY equalisation and jitter into one number that either meets the compliance mask or does not.

This is where all the electrical work resolves into a pass or a fail. Every contribution — the channel from SIPI-07, the noise from SIPI-06, the PLL jitter from AMS-02 and the PHY's own equalisation — lands in a single budget, and the interface either has margin or it is shipping on hope.

steps.text: Budget structure and contribution allocation per interface
Jitter budget assembly — random, deterministic, correlated
BER estimation and margin against the mask
Sensitivity to channel and process variation

SIPI-08.flowNote: Step 2 is where interfaces are usually lost. Jitter contributions from the PLL, the PHY, the channel and the SSN do not add linearly, and a budget that sums them naively either over-designs or, more often, over-promises.
consumes: PHY equalisation and BER capability from AMS-03

rel.text: Eye, jitter and BER budget closure record. This activity is the deliverable — the statement that each interface will work.
Channel compliance report per interface. Compliance is a budget conclusion rather than a channel property alone.

risks: Jitter contributions summed naively. Random and deterministic components combine differently, and getting it wrong produces a budget that is confidently wrong.
Equalisation assumed at its maximum. A PHY closing only with full equalisation has no adaptation range left for a worse-than-nominal channel.
Variation sensitivity ignored. The budget has to hold across manufacturing spread, not only at nominal.
SSN excluded from the budget. It is a real contribution and it degrades the interface that generates it.
Interface failing the mask with no route to fix. Late findings leave only channel changes, PHY changes or a rate reduction, and all three are expensive.

roles.d: Owns the budget and its closure

entry: PHY and PLL contributions available from AMS-02 and AMS-03
exit: Every interface closed against its compliance mask with stated margin
Jitter combined correctly rather than summed
Budget holds across variation, not only at nominal
measuredBy: Eye margin against the compliance mask
Equalisation range remaining at closure
Budget margin under variation

purpose: Back-annotate the voltage droop into static timing analysis — because a design signed off at nominal voltage was signed off at a voltage the die does not see.

Timing and power are analysed by different teams with different tools, and the connection between them is usually a margin someone assumed. This activity replaces the assumption: the droop map from SIPI-04 applied to the timing analysis, so that closure reflects the supply the logic actually has.

steps.text: Droop map generation per region and mode
Margin impact assessment per timing path group
Reconciliation with the SO-02 signoff margin

SIPI-09.flowNote: Step 5 is the reconciliation. If timing signoff already carries a flat voltage margin and this analysis shows the droop is worse in some regions and better in others, the flat margin was both too generous and insufficient — and the recommendation is regional rather than global.
consumes: Timing analysis from PD-09 and SO-02
Region and instance mapping from PD-02
produces: Droop map per region and mode

rel.text: Power-aware STA correlation report. This activity is the deliverable, and it connects two signoffs that otherwise run independently.
PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. The timing consequence is what makes the IR number actionable.

risks: Flat voltage margin used instead. Droop is regional, and a flat margin is simultaneously wasteful where droop is low and inadequate where it is high.
Analysis run after timing closure. Findings then require reopening closure, which is expensive at this point in the schedule.
Droop map too coarse. Region granularity determines whether the analysis can distinguish a hot spot from an average.
Reconciliation skipped. Two signoffs with different voltage assumptions produce a design that satisfies neither cleanly.
Recommendations global rather than regional. The remedy is usually local — more decoupling or a PDN change in one region — and a global response over-corrects.
exit: Droop applied regionally rather than as a flat margin
Reconciled with the SO-02 signoff assumption
Recommendations targeted at the regions that need them
measuredBy: Timing margin change from droop back-annotation
Regional variation in droop impact
Agreement with the signoff voltage assumption

purpose: Couple the electrical and thermal analyses — because leakage rises with temperature, temperature rises with power, and the two feed each other until they settle somewhere the isolated analyses did not predict.

Electro-thermal coupling matters at this power density. A hotspot raises local leakage, which raises local power, which raises the hotspot. Analysing power at a fixed temperature and temperature at a fixed power finds an equilibrium that is optimistic in exactly the region that matters.

steps.text: Thermal model integration with the package model

SIPI-10.flowNote: Step 4 iterates to convergence, and whether it converges is itself information. A design where the leakage-temperature loop does not settle is a design with a thermal runaway risk, which is a different and more serious finding than a high temperature.

rel.text: PDN impedance and dynamic IR co-simulation report. Temperature affects both resistance and leakage, and the coupled result is the honest one.
Power-aware STA correlation report. Temperature affects timing as well as voltage, and both belong in the same correlation.

risks: Analyses run at fixed temperature and fixed power. The equilibrium the coupled analysis finds is worse, and it is the one that occurs.
Leakage-temperature model too coarse. The feedback is exponential, and a linear approximation understates the hotspot.
Non-convergence dismissed as a numerical issue. It can indicate a real thermal runaway risk and deserves investigation rather than a damping factor.
Package thermal model unvalidated. If PTV-09 has not correlated it, the coupled analysis inherits an unknown error.
Gradient ignored in favour of peak temperature. Gradients drive mechanical stress and timing variation across the die, and the peak alone does not capture them.

roles.d: Electrical side of the coupled analysis

entry: Package thermal model available from PKGD-07
Chip power model available from SIPI-01
exit: Coupled analysis converged, or non-convergence investigated
Compared against the isolated analyses to quantify the difference
Gradients assessed alongside peak temperature
measuredBy: Temperature difference between coupled and isolated analysis
Convergence of the coupled iteration
Gradient magnitude across the die

purpose: Hold the co-verification signoff — every result reviewed against named exit criteria, dispositioned, and signed — because mask release depends on it.

This is the gate the stage exists to reach. Without a signoff with criteria, co-verification is a collection of analyses that each conclude something and together conclude nothing. The disposition here is what SO-06 reviews and what makes the MTO gate at week 78 meaningful.

steps.text: Exit criteria confirmation across all analyses
Open item disposition with die, package and board owners
Signoff review with design and package teams

SIPI-11.flowNote: Step 3 is a three-party disposition. Every open item belongs to the die, the package or the board, and closing it requires the owner in the room — which is why co-verification signoff is a joint review rather than a report circulated for comment.
consumes: Exit criteria defined at stage start
Package design freeze schedule from PKGD-11

rel.text: Chip-package-system co-verification signoff — tapeout gate. This activity is the deliverable, and it carries the stage's milestone.
Eye, jitter and BER budget closure record. An interface that has not closed its budget is an open item at this gate.

risks: Signoff without exit criteria. The analyses each conclude something and together conclude nothing that can be signed.
Open items dispositioned without their owners. An item closed by the analysis team rather than by the die, package or board owner has not actually been closed.
Signoff after the package design freeze. Findings then have nowhere to go, and the freeze was taken without them.
Residual risk not stated. Some margin will be thin; saying which and how thin is what lets the tapeout decision be informed.
Declared to meet the date. The gate exists to be able to hold mask release, and one that cannot is not a gate.

roles.d: Chairs the signoff and owns the declaration
Carries the result into SO-06 and the freeze

entry: Analyses complete from SIPI-03 through SIPI-10
Die, package and board owners available to disposition
exit: Every analysis assessed against a named exit criterion
Open items dispositioned by their owners, not by the analysis team
Signoff complete before the package design freeze and the MTO gate
measuredBy: Analyses assessed against exit criteria
Open items closed by their owners
Signoff date against the package freeze and MTO gate

purpose: Sort the wafers and pick the known-good die that will go into packages — because on a 2.5D part a bad die does not fail alone, it takes an interposer, two HBM stacks and an assembly with it.

Known-good-die screening is what makes multi-die packaging economically viable. The coverage achieved at sort determines how many assembled units fail for reasons that were detectable on the wafer, and each of those is a package's worth of material lost.

steps.text: Wafer receipt and sort setup on the probe station
Wafer sort execution against the KGD criteria
Die release to assembly with traceability

ASSY-01.flowNote: Step 3 is where the economics live. A marginal die is cheap to scrap and expensive to assemble; the criteria for rejecting one have to be set against the assembled unit's cost rather than against the die's.
consumes: Accepted wafers from FAB-08 and FAB-10
produces: Die released to assembly with traceability

rel.text: Assembled units. Everything assembled starts from a die this activity selected.
Assembly yield report and failure pareto. Assembly failures traceable to die quality belong against the sort coverage that let them through.

risks: KGD coverage below what the package economics need. Every escaped die costs an assembled unit, and the coverage target follows from that cost rather than from a test convention.
Marginal criteria set against die cost. On a 2.5D part the assembled unit is worth many times the die, and the reject threshold should reflect that.
Traceability lost between wafer and package. An assembly failure that cannot be traced back to a die and its wafer position cannot be attributed.
Sort program not ready. The probe card and program come from TEST, and a delay there stops assembly rather than delaying test.
Sorting only for function. Parametric marginality — leakage, Vmin — predicts field failure and is worth screening even when the die functions.

roles.d: Owns sort criteria and die disposition
Sort program and probe card execution
Wafer map analysis and marginal criteria
KGD criteria against assembled unit cost

entry: Sort program and probe card ready from TEST-03 and TEST-05
KGD criteria agreed with the OSAT
exit: Coverage sufficient for the assembled unit's economics
Marginal criteria set against package cost, not die cost
Every released die traceable to wafer and position
measuredBy: KGD coverage achieved
Assembly failures attributable to escaped die
Die traceability to wafer position

purpose: Procure and inspect the HBM stacks — bought components that go into the package alongside the program's own die, and that fail in ways the program does not control.

HBM is a purchased part with its own supply constraints and its own quality distribution. Incoming inspection matters because an HBM stack that fails after assembly costs the whole unit, and the supplier's outgoing quality is not the program's to verify after the fact.

steps.text: Stack qualification and release to assembly

ASSY-02.flowNote: Step 3 costs almost nothing and catches a class of problem inspection cannot. Supplier test data shows the distribution the delivered lot came from, and a lot at the edge of specification is worth knowing about before it is bonded in.
consumes: HBM purchase orders from MP-10 and procurement
HBM specification and requirements from ARCH-03

rel.text: Assembled units. HBM is part of every assembled unit, and its quality is part of the unit's.
Package-level inspection and test data. Incoming HBM data belongs with the assembly's own inspection record.

risks: HBM supply constrained. It is a scarce component with long lead times, and a shortage stops assembly regardless of how many die are ready.
Incoming inspection skipped. A marginal stack bonded into a unit costs the whole unit, and the fault is only visible afterwards.
Supplier data not reviewed. The distribution the lot came from predicts its behaviour, and the data is provided at no cost.
Lot traceability not maintained. An HBM-related failure that cannot be traced to a supplier lot cannot be escalated usefully.
Specification mismatch discovered at assembly. Stack height, bump pitch and thermal characteristics all have to match the package design.
exit: Every lot inspected and its supplier data reviewed
Stacks confirmed against the package specification
Lot traceability maintained into assembly
measuredBy: Stacks rejected at incoming inspection
Supply delivered against the assembly schedule
HBM-attributed failures after assembly

purpose: Bond the die and HBM stacks to the interposer — micro-bump preparation and thermo-compression bonding — inside the process window the vehicles established.

This is the step the whole PTV programme existed to de-risk. Bond force, temperature and time were characterised on vehicles; here they are applied to real die, and the process window is either followed or the vehicle work was wasted.

steps.text: Process setup to the frozen window
Bond parameter monitoring during the run
Thermo-compression bonding of die and stacks

ASSY-03.flowNote: Step 3 records what actually happened. The frozen window says what the parameters should be; monitoring says what they were, and a unit that failed can only be attributed if its actual bond conditions were captured.
produces: Process setup to the frozen window

rel.text: Assembly travelers and process data. This activity is where the traveler starts and where the actual bond conditions are recorded.
Assembled units. Bonding is the step that makes a set of components into a package.

risks: Running outside the frozen window. The PTV programme established boundaries; operating outside them discards the evidence it produced.
Bond parameters not recorded per unit. A failed unit cannot be attributed to its conditions, and the yield analysis loses its most useful variable.
Bump preparation inconsistent. Flux and surface condition affect joint formation, and variability here shows up as scattered yield.
Post-bond inspection sampled too thinly. Bonding defects are localised, and a sample that misses them lets them through to underfill where they are unfixable.
Process drift across the run. Long runs drift, and without monitoring the drift is only visible in the yield trend afterwards.
exit: Every unit bonded inside the frozen window
Actual bond parameters recorded per unit
Post-bond inspection coverage sufficient to catch localised defects
measuredBy: Units bonded within the window
Bond parameter capture rate
Post-bond defects found against escaped

purpose: Attach the interposer to the substrate and underfill and mold the assembly — the steps that make it mechanically robust and that lock in whatever went before.

Underfill is irreversible. Once it has flowed and cured, a bonding defect underneath is permanent and invisible to everything except acoustic imaging. The step's quality — void-free flow, complete fillet, correct cure — determines whether the mechanical stress the package will see is distributed or concentrated.
ASSY-04.flowNote: Step 3 is the last chance to catch a bonding problem. Acoustic imaging before cure can still identify a void or an incomplete fill; after cure the unit is what it is, and the defect surfaces during thermal cycling months later.

rel.text: Assembled units. After molding the unit is mechanically complete.
Package-level inspection and test data. Void and fillet inspection results are part of the unit's quality record.

risks: Underfill voids. They concentrate stress and are the mechanism behind delayed CPI failures, and they are invisible after cure without acoustic imaging.
Incomplete fillet. The fillet distributes stress at the die edge, and an incomplete one puts that stress into the die corner instead.
Cure profile deviation. Under-cured underfill has different mechanical properties, and the difference appears as reliability rather than as a visible defect.
Warpage during cure exceeding the window. The vehicle programme measured it; running outside that window reintroduces the risk that was retired.
Inspection only after molding. Once molded the assembly cannot be examined usefully, and the inspection has to happen before.
entry: Substrates delivered against the PKGD-09 order
exit: Void and fillet inspected before cure, not after
Cure profile within the frozen window
Warpage during the process inside the validated range
measuredBy: Void rate at inspection
Fillet completeness
Cure profile deviation from the window

purpose: Finish the package — TIM, lid and ball attach — and produce units that can be mounted, cooled and tested.

These are the last steps and they determine two things the product is judged on: the thermal interface that decides the achievable power envelope, and the ball array that decides whether the package mounts reliably. Both were characterised on vehicles and both are executed here.
ASSY-05.flowNote: Step 1 sets the thermal performance the product will actually have. Bond line thickness under the lid is a process parameter, and the difference between the characterised value and the achieved one is watts of headroom.
consumes: Ball attach process from the frozen window

rel.text: Assembled units — bring-up, qualification and sample lots. This activity is where a unit becomes a finished package.
Package-level inspection and test data. Dimensional and flatness data belongs with the unit's record.

risks: TIM bond line thicker than characterised. Thermal resistance rises, and the power envelope the product was sold on shrinks.
Lid flatness out of specification. The cooling solution then contacts unevenly, which produces hotspots the thermal design did not predict.
Ball co-planarity outside the mounting window. The package does not mount reliably, and the customer discovers it during their assembly.
Dimensional drift from the specification. The package has to fit sockets, heatsinks and board footprints that were designed to the drawing.
Final inspection sampled rather than complete. On an engineering build every unit is precious, and a defect shipped to bring-up costs lab days.

roles.d: Lid, TIM and ball attach execution
TIM bond line and thermal implications

exit: TIM bond line within the characterised range
Lid flatness and ball co-planarity inside specification
Every unit inspected, not a sample
measuredBy: TIM bond line against the characterised value
Flatness and co-planarity yield
Dimensional conformance

purpose: Inspect the assemblies without taking them apart — X-ray for joints, acoustic imaging for delamination and voids, metrology for warpage — because most assembly defects are invisible from outside.

A 2.5D package hides everything that matters. The joints are under the die, the underfill is under the interposer, and the only way to see any of it non-destructively is through imaging. What this activity catches is what does not reach bring-up as an unexplained failure.

steps.text: X-ray inspection of joints and voids

ASSY-06.flowNote: Step 1's sampling strategy is a real decision on a small build. Full inspection is affordable at engineering-lot quantities and not at production volume, and starting with full coverage is what tells you what sampling would have missed.
consumes: Assemblies at each process stage from ASSY-03 to ASSY-05
Inspection criteria from PTV vehicle results
X-ray and CSAM capability at the OSAT

rel.text: Package-level inspection and test data. This activity is the deliverable — the non-destructive record of what is inside each unit.
Assembly yield report and failure pareto. Inspection findings are the physical evidence behind the yield numbers.

risks: Sampling too thin on an engineering build. Full inspection is affordable at these quantities, and a defect reaching bring-up costs far more than the inspection would have.
Defects classified inconsistently. Without a scheme the same feature is a defect on Monday and acceptable on Tuesday, and the yield data becomes noise.
Inspection only at the end. Defects are cheapest to catch at the step that created them, and end-of-line inspection cannot attribute them.
Warpage limits not applied. The vehicle programme set them; a unit outside them is a reliability risk regardless of whether it functions.
Findings not fed back to process. Inspection that produces a pass/fail and no process signal wastes most of its value.
entry: Assemblies available at each process stage
Inspection criteria derived from PTV results
Imaging capability available at the OSAT
exit: Inspection at each process step, not only at the end
Defects classified against a consistent scheme
Findings fed back to the process that created them
measuredBy: Coverage of inspection against build quantity
Defects caught at the creating step
Classification consistency

purpose: Analyse the assembly yield, build the failure pareto, find the root causes with the OSAT and tune the process inside the window the vehicles defined.

First-build assembly yield on a 2.5D part is rarely what the cost model assumed. This activity turns the gap into a set of attributed causes and process adjustments — and compares the result against what the vehicle programme predicted, which is how the vehicle work gets validated in turn.

steps.text: Yield data collection across process steps
Failure pareto by mode and process step
Comparison against the PTV yield prediction
Root cause analysis with the OSAT
Process tuning inside the frozen window

ASSY-07.flowNote: Step 6 stays inside the window deliberately. Tuning beyond the validated boundaries would abandon the evidence the vehicle programme produced, and a yield improvement bought that way carries an unquantified reliability risk.
consumes: Yield data from every assembly step

rel.text: Assembly yield report and failure pareto. This activity is the deliverable, and the pareto is what the OSAT acts on.
Assembly travelers and process data. Yield attribution depends on the traveler data, and the analysis feeds back into what travelers should capture.

risks: Yield reported without attribution. A number tells the program it has a problem; a pareto by process step tells the OSAT what to change.
Tuning outside the validated window. It may improve yield and it discards the reliability evidence the vehicles produced.
Vehicle prediction not compared. The comparison is what validates or invalidates the whole PTV programme, and it is cheap to make.
Root cause pursued without the OSAT. Process knowledge sits with the assembler, and analysis without them produces hypotheses rather than causes.
Corrective actions untracked. An agreed action that nobody follows up is an action that did not happen.

roles.d: Owns yield analysis and the pareto
Failure classification and corrective action tracking
Yield against the cost model assumption

entry: Assembly running with data collection in place
Vehicle yield prediction available from PTV-11
exit: Failures attributed to process steps, not only counted
Tuning kept inside the validated window
Yield compared against the vehicle prediction
measuredBy: Assembly yield against the cost model
Failures attributed to a process step
Corrective actions completed

purpose: Test the assembled packages electrically for opens, shorts and marginal joints before they go anywhere — the cheapest possible screen on the most expensive units the program has.

A package-level continuity test costs minutes and catches assembly failures that would otherwise consume lab days at bring-up. On units this expensive, screening before shipping is not optional economics.
ASSY-08.flowNote: Step 3 separates working from reliably working. A joint that conducts with elevated resistance passes a continuity test and fails in the field, and screening for it here is far cheaper than a field return.
produces: Open and short results per unit

rel.text: Package-level inspection and test data. The electrical half of the deliverable, alongside the imaging from ASSY-06.
Assembled units. A unit that fails continuity is not released to bring-up, however scarce units are.

risks: Screening skipped because units are scarce. A failed unit consumed at bring-up costs more lab time than the whole screen would have.
Continuity only, no resistance. Marginal joints conduct and fail later, and only a resistance measurement distinguishes them.
Criteria not derived from vehicle data. PTV-11 measured what good and marginal look like, and the criteria should come from there.
Failures not fed to yield analysis. An electrical failure is yield data and belongs in the pareto.
Test fixture damaging units. On packages this expensive the fixture itself has to be qualified.

roles.d: Owns the screen and its criteria

exit: Every unit screened before release
Marginal joints identified by resistance, not only continuity
Failures fed into the yield pareto
measuredBy: Units screened against units built
Marginal units identified
Fixture-induced damage

purpose: Allocate the finished units — bring-up, qualification, customer samples — and build to that allocation, because the first build never has enough for everyone.

Three groups need units simultaneously and all of them are on the critical path of something. Bring-up needs them to start debugging, qualification needs them to start a months-long stress campaign, and customers were promised samples. The allocation is a program decision, not an assembly one.

steps.text: Allocation requirement collection from each consumer

ASSY-09.flowNote: Step 3 is a program decision escalated deliberately. Qualification starting late delays mass production; bring-up starting late delays everything; and customer samples are often contractual. Resolving that trade below the program level puts it in the wrong hands.
consumes: Build quantity from the assembly run

rel.text: Unit allocation record across bring-up, qual and customers. This activity is the deliverable, and it settles a contention that would otherwise be settled by whoever asks loudest.
Assembled units — bring-up, qualification and sample lots. The units as allocated lots rather than as an undifferentiated build.

risks: Allocation decided by whoever asks first. The three consumers have different downstream consequences, and the trade belongs to the program.
Qualification starved. Reliability stress runs for months; starting it late moves mass production directly.
Customer samples cut. They are frequently contractual, and missing them has commercial consequences the program may not see.
Build quantity below the sum of needs. Which is normal, and it means the shortfall has to be decided rather than discovered.
Traceability lost per allocation. A qualification failure has to be traceable to its lot and its assembly conditions.

roles.d: Owns the allocation and its contention

entry: Units screened and released from ASSY-08
Requirements collected from all three consumers
exit: Allocation decided at program level, not by request order
Qualification quantity sufficient to start its campaign
Every allocated unit traceable to its lot and conditions
measuredBy: Units allocated against requested per consumer
Qualification start date against the plan
Traceability maintained per allocation

purpose: Decide what the silicon will be validated on — how many platforms, in what configuration, at what quantity — before anyone draws a schematic.

The board is the only way to touch the silicon, and its capability bounds everything bring-up and characterisation can do. A platform that cannot reach a rail, cannot socket a part, or cannot be temperature-soaked closes off measurements that the qualification plan assumes are available.

steps.text: Validation requirement collection from bring-up, characterisation and qual
Platform topology options — socketed, soldered, mezzanine
Topology selection with its trade-offs recorded

EVB-01.flowNote: Step 3 is where a schedule can be bought. An existing platform that carries 70% of the requirement, adapted, beats a new design by a quarter — and the assessment costs a week.
consumes: Bring-up requirements from BU-02 through BU-08 planning

rel.text: Validation platform specification. This activity is the deliverable, and everything the board team builds derives from it.
Fabricated and assembled boards. The quantity and revision plan decides how many boards exist and when.

risks: Requirements collected from bring-up only. Characterisation and qualification also live on this platform, and their needs — soak capability, instrumented rails — differ.
Socket versus solder decided late. It changes the board, the mechanical design and the unit consumption, and reversing it costs a board revision.
Quantity underestimated. Boards are the constraint on parallel debug, and a second fabrication run costs two months.
Reuse not assessed. An adaptable existing platform is the cheapest schedule available and it is often never looked for.
Specification written after design started. The board then documents what was built rather than bounding what should be.

roles.d: Owns the requirement and the specification

entry: Package pin map stable enough to plan against
exit: Requirements collected from all three consumers, not just bring-up
Socket-versus-solder decided and its consequences accepted
Quantity plan sized against parallel debug needs
measuredBy: Requirements traceable into the specification
Reuse opportunities identified
Board quantity against parallel debug demand

purpose: Design the EVB schematic — power tree, host interface, socket, clocking, debug headers — and its bill of materials.

The schematic is where the platform's capability is fixed. A rail without a sense point cannot be measured, a debug header omitted cannot be added, and a component with a 40-week lead time turns a board schedule into a procurement schedule.

steps.text: BOM construction and component sourcing check
Schematic review and release to layout

EVB-02.flowNote: Step 7 runs alongside deliberately. Component lead times are discovered during sourcing, and a part found to be 40 weeks out while the schematic is still editable can be substituted; found after layout it cannot.
produces: Bill of materials with sourcing status

rel.text: EVB schematics, BOM and layout database. The schematic half of the deliverable.
Validation platform specification. Schematic decisions feed back into what the specification can promise.

risks: Rails without sense points. A rail that cannot be measured cannot be characterised, and the omission is only discovered during bring-up.
Long-lead components found after layout. The substitution then costs a board revision instead of a schematic edit.
Debug headers designed for the debugger nobody uses. The tooling has to be agreed with validation rather than assumed.
Pin map changing after schematic release. The package pin map has to be frozen for the schematic to be worth reviewing.
Power tree sized without the real power envelope. A VRM sized to an early estimate cannot supply the silicon's actual transients.
entry: Package pin map frozen from PKGD-04
Power rail requirements available from PD-08
exit: Every rail instrumented with a sense point
BOM sourced with lead times confirmed against the schedule
Schematic reviewed by validation, not only by hardware
measuredBy: Rails with sense points against total rails
Long-lead components identified before layout
Review findings against post-fabrication rework

purpose: Lay out the PCB with signal and power integrity simulated on the critical channels, because a validation board carrying PCIe Gen6 or CXL is itself a high-speed design.

The board is in series with every interface measurement bring-up will make. A channel with a marginal board contribution produces link failures that look like silicon problems, and separating the two costs weeks of debug time that the simulation would have avoided.

steps.text: SI simulation on the critical channels
PI simulation on the board PDN
DRC, review and release to fabrication

EVB-03.flowNote: Steps 3 and 5 run against the routing rather than after it. A channel simulated after the board is routed produces a report; simulated during, it produces a routing change.
consumes: Released schematic and BOM from EVB-02
produces: SI simulation results on critical channels
PI simulation on the board PDN
DRC-clean layout database released to fabrication

rel.text: EVB schematics, BOM and layout database. The layout half of the deliverable — what fabrication is built from.
Fabricated and assembled boards. Fabrication takes the released layout database directly.

risks: Board channel contribution not budgeted. The SIPI channel budget covers package and board together, and a board that consumes more than its share leaves the silicon nothing.
SI simulated after routing. The result is a report rather than a design change, and fixing it costs a revision.
Board PDN inadequate for the transient. The silicon's di/dt is on the package model; a board PDN sized without it droops.
Stack-up chosen for cost before impedance. Controlled impedance on the high-speed layers is not negotiable, and a cheaper stack-up that misses it is not cheaper.
Mechanical constraints applied last. The cooling solution and socket need space, and finding that out after routing costs a revision.
entry: Channel and PDN budgets from SIPI-04 and SIPI-06
exit: Board channel contribution inside its share of the SIPI budget
SI and PI simulated during routing, not after
Mechanical and thermal constraints met without a revision
measuredBy: Board channel loss against its budget share
Simulation findings resolved in layout
DRC and DFM clean at release

purpose: Get the boards fabricated, assembled and inspected — an eight-week vendor cycle that is mostly waiting and entirely on the critical path to bring-up.

This is procurement work with an engineering tail. The board has to arrive before silicon does, its quantity has to match the parallel-debug plan, and every board that arrives faulty is a debug station that does not exist.

steps.text: Fabrication vendor selection and data release

EVB-04.flowNote: Step 5 catches assembly problems on one board before they are replicated across the whole run. It costs a day and it is routinely skipped in the interest of speed, which is how twenty identically-wrong boards get built.
produces: Vendor selection and released fabrication data

rel.text: Fabricated and assembled boards, rev A/B with quantity plan. This activity is the deliverable.
EVB schematics, BOM and layout database. Fabrication findings — DFM issues, substitutions — feed back into the database.

risks: Long-lead components blocking assembly. The board is fabricated and waiting on one part, which is the most common way this activity slips.
First article skipped. An assembly error is then replicated across the entire run and discovered at bring-up.
Quantity cut for cost. Boards are the constraint on parallel debug, and the saving is repaid in serialised lab time.
Boards arriving after silicon. Silicon waiting on a board is the worst schedule outcome the program can produce.
Controlled impedance not verified. The stack-up was designed for it; the fabricated board has to be coupon-tested to confirm it.

roles.d: Quantity and schedule against silicon arrival

entry: Components ordered against confirmed lead times
exit: Boards delivered before silicon arrives
First article inspected before the run completes
Controlled impedance verified by coupon
measuredBy: Board delivery against silicon arrival
Boards accepted against boards built
First article findings caught before the run

purpose: Design and bring up the power delivery, VRM and telemetry on the platform — the rails the silicon runs on and the instrumentation that measures them.

Characterisation is mostly a power measurement. Shmoo needs rails that can be swept, power validation needs rails that can be measured accurately, and both need protection that trips before an expensive part is destroyed rather than after.

steps.text: Power tree requirement from the die and package
Transient response design against the SIPI budget
Power bring-up and validation on the board

EVB-05.flowNote: Step 5 is what protects the units. A sequencing error or an overcurrent event on a first-silicon part costs a package worth many thousands, and the protection has to be validated before a real part is ever inserted.

rel.text: EVB schematics, BOM and layout database. The power subsystem design is part of the schematic package.
Board bring-up report and known issues. Power bring-up results are the first part of the board's own bring-up record.

risks: Rails not sweepable across the shmoo range. Characterisation then cannot reach the corners the qualification plan requires.
Protection untested before a real part goes in. A sequencing fault destroys a first-silicon unit, and there are very few of them.
Telemetry accuracy insufficient. Power measurements at the resolution characterisation needs demand real instrumentation, not a rough monitor.
Transient response inadequate. The die's di/dt is known from SIPI; a VRM that cannot follow it produces droop that looks like a silicon failure.
Sequencing not matching the silicon's requirement. The power-up order comes from the design, and getting it wrong is a common first-board fault.
exit: Rails sweepable across the full shmoo range
Protection validated before any real part is inserted
Telemetry accurate enough for characterisation
measuredBy: Rail sweep range against the shmoo requirement
Protection trip validated before first insertion
Telemetry accuracy against characterisation need

purpose: Build the debug access — JTAG and trace pods, interposers, probe points — because silicon debug is bounded by what can be observed.

When first silicon does something unexpected, the difference between a day and a month is whether the state that explains it can be read out. The DFT infrastructure provides the internal access; this activity provides the physical path to it.

steps.text: Debug requirements from validation and DFT
JTAG and trace pod interface design
Logic analyser and scope access design

EVB-06.flowNote: Step 6 validates the debug path before it is needed. A trace pod that does not work is discovered during the crisis it was meant to resolve, which is the worst possible moment.
consumes: Debug and trace architecture from DFT-08
Silicon debug requirements from BU-09 planning
Debug tooling from the DFT flow

rel.text: Debug and trace access documentation. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what the bring-up team reads at 2am.
EVB schematics, BOM and layout database. Debug headers and access points are schematic and layout content.

risks: Debug access designed without DFT. The internal observability comes from DFT-08, and the board access has to match what it exposes.
Trace bandwidth insufficient. Trace is only useful if it can keep up with the events being traced, and the bandwidth is a board design parameter.
Probe points unreachable once the cooling solution is mounted. The thermal solution and the probe access compete for the same physical space.
Debug path unvalidated before silicon. It is then debugged during the emergency it exists to resolve.
Software tooling not integrated. A hardware debug path with no software to drive it is not a debug path.

roles.d: Probe access against the thermal solution

entry: DFT debug architecture available from DFT-08
exit: Debug access matching what DFT actually exposes
Trace bandwidth sufficient for the events being traced
Debug path validated before silicon, not during a crisis
measuredBy: Debug access coverage against DFT observability
Trace bandwidth against event rate
Debug path validated before silicon arrival

purpose: Bring the board itself up — with dummy parts or a socketed loopback — so that when silicon arrives, every failure is the silicon's.

This is the single highest-leverage activity in the stage. A board debugged before first silicon means bring-up starts on a known-good platform; a board debugged alongside first silicon means every anomaly has two possible causes and each takes days to separate.

steps.text: Bring-up plan and dummy part fitting
Power tree bring-up and rail verification

EVB-07.flowNote: The whole activity is scheduled to complete before silicon arrives. Every hour spent here is an hour not spent, at ten times the cost, debugging a board while first silicon waits on the bench.
produces: Bring-up plan and fitted dummy parts
Interface loopback and signal validation results
Board bring-up report and known issues

rel.text: Board bring-up report and known issues. This activity is the deliverable, and the known-issues list is what stops board faults being mistaken for silicon faults.
Fabricated and assembled boards. A board is not released to silicon bring-up until it has passed this.

risks: Board bring-up deferred until silicon arrives. Every anomaly then has two candidate causes, and separating them costs days each.
Known issues not documented. The bring-up team then rediscovers each board quirk independently, once per engineer.
Dummy parts not representative. A loopback that does not load the rails or exercise the channels validates less than it appears to.
Only one board brought up. Board-to-board variation is real, and a fleet where only one is characterised is a fleet with unknown members.
Thermal fit checked after silicon insertion. A cooling solution that does not fit is discovered with an irreplaceable part underneath it.

roles.d: Known-issue capture for the bring-up team

exit: Board bring-up complete before silicon arrives

Every board in the fleet brought up, not just one

Boards brought up against boards built

purpose: Design and validate the cooling for the lab platform — which is not the product's thermal solution, but has to remove the same power.

A part that thermally throttles during characterisation produces data about the cooling rather than about the silicon. The lab solution can be oversized and ugly in ways the product's cannot, and it should be, because measurement validity depends on it.

steps.text: Thermal requirement from the package envelope

EVB-08.flowNote: Step 5 is what makes qualification-adjacent measurement possible. Characterisation needs the part held at a temperature, not merely kept cool, and a solution that only cools cannot produce a hot-corner shmoo.

rel.text: Validation platform specification. Thermal capability is part of what the platform can promise.
Board bring-up report and known issues. Thermal validation results belong in the platform's own record.

risks: Cooling sized to the product's solution rather than to the lab's need. The lab platform can be oversized, and measurement validity is worth more than realism.
No temperature control, only cooling. Characterisation needs the part held at a set point, including a hot one.
Throttling during characterisation. The data then describes the cooling rather than the silicon, and it is often not noticed.
Mounting competing with probe access. The debug points and the heatsink want the same space, and the conflict has to be resolved in layout.
Thermal validated only at nominal power. The interesting measurements are at maximum power, which is where the solution is stressed.
exit: No throttling at maximum power during characterisation
Temperature held at set point, including the hot corner
Mounting compatible with debug probe access
measuredBy: Throttling events during characterisation
Temperature set-point range achieved
Probe access retained with cooling mounted

purpose: Reserve the instruments and build the lab racks — because characterisation needs equipment that is expensive, shared and booked months ahead.

A high-speed oscilloscope or a BERT is a capital item with a queue in front of it. Discovering during bring-up that the scope with the right bandwidth is committed elsewhere for six weeks does not delay the measurement by six weeks — it delays everything downstream of it.

steps.text: Instrument requirement from the characterisation plan

EVB-09.flowNote: Step 3 decides whether characterisation is manual or automatic. A shmoo run by hand takes days per corner; the same shmoo automated runs overnight, and the automation is written here rather than improvised during bring-up.
consumes: Bring-up plan from BU-02 through BU-08
produces: Lab setup and instrument reservation plan

rel.text: Lab setup and instrument reservation plan. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what stops bring-up queueing for a scope.
Board bring-up report and known issues. The lab setup is the context every bring-up measurement is made in.

risks: Instruments booked too late. High-bandwidth equipment is shared and queued, and a six-week wait delays everything downstream.
Automation deferred to bring-up. It is then written under time pressure by people who should be debugging silicon.
Racks not calibrated. Measurements from an uncalibrated setup are unusable for characterisation and often not questioned.
Lab power or space insufficient. A rack that cannot be powered is a rack that does not exist, and facilities lead times are long.
Instrument bandwidth below the signal rate. A scope that cannot resolve the edge produces a plausible and wrong measurement.

purpose: Provide the minimum host-side software needed to power on and talk to the part — boot, register access, enumeration, logging — without taking on the product's software stack.

SW/FW is outside this program's scope, but silicon cannot be brought up without something on the other end of the link. The boundary matters: this activity delivers exactly enough to reach first register read and no more, and where that line sits should be agreed rather than discovered.

steps.text: Handoff boundary definition with the firmware team
Host enablement validation on the platform

EVB-10.flowNote: Step 1 is the activity's most valuable hour. Without an explicit boundary, hardware validation writes software the firmware team is also writing, and each assumes the other is doing it.

rel.text: Board bring-up report and known issues. Host enablement is validated as part of the platform and reported with it.
Debug and trace access documentation. The diagnostic tooling is how debug access is actually used.

risks: Boundary with firmware left implicit. Either the work is duplicated or nobody does it, and both are discovered at power-on.
Register map drifting from the RTL. A diagnostic tool built against a stale map reads the wrong addresses and reports plausible nonsense.
Scope creeping into the product stack. Minimal enablement becomes a driver project, and the validation team stops validating.
Logging insufficient for post-mortem. A failure that cannot be reconstructed from the log has to be reproduced, which on first silicon may not be possible.
Enablement unvalidated before silicon. Software bugs then present as silicon bugs during the most expensive week of the program.

roles.d: Scope discipline against the product stack

purpose: Decide what will be tested, where, and to what defect level — the plan every other activity in the stage implements.

Test is where quality is bought and where cost per unit is set, and the two trade directly. The plan is the document where that trade is made explicitly: a DPPM target implies coverage, coverage implies content, content implies test time, and test time is money on every unit ever shipped.

steps.text: Coverage requirement from the specification and DFT
Test flow architecture — sort, final, characterisation
DPPM target derivation from the coverage

TEST-01.flowNote: Step 5 is the one that closes the loop. Coverage without a DPPM target is an engineering preference; a DPPM target derived from the coverage is a commitment the customer can be given.
consumes: Product specification and quality target from DEF-04
DFT coverage from DFT-03 and DFT-05
Quality and reliability requirement from MP-01

rel.text: Test plan and test coverage matrix. This activity is the deliverable, and every other TEST activity implements part of it.
Test time and test cost model. The flow architecture and insertion strategy set the cost model's structure.

risks: Coverage chosen without a DPPM target. There is then no way to say whether the test is sufficient, only whether it is thorough.
Test time not budgeted at plan time. Content accumulates and the cost per unit is discovered at production readiness when it is expensive to change.
Burn-in decided late. It is a capital and cycle-time commitment, and reversing it after qualification planning is expensive.
Sort and final coverage overlapping without intent. Testing the same thing twice costs money on every unit and often happens by accretion.
DFT coverage assumed rather than measured. The plan then promises a DPPM the actual pattern set cannot deliver.

roles.d: Owns the plan and the coverage matrix
Test cost against the product cost target

exit: DPPM target derived from actual coverage, not asserted
Test time budgeted before content is written
Sort and final coverage split deliberately
measuredBy: Coverage against the DPPM target

Overlap between sort and final content

purpose: Choose the ATE platform and book the tester time — a capital and capacity decision that has to be made long before there is anything to test.

Tester capacity is a shared, scheduled resource. Program development time, characterisation time and production capacity are all booked against the same pool, and a program that has not committed its slots competes with programs that have.

steps.text: Tester requirement from the test plan
ATE platform evaluation against the requirement
Tester time booking and capacity commitment

TEST-02.flowNote: Step 6 is why this runs early. Development, characterisation and production all draw on the same testers, and slots that are not booked are taken.
