Pin count and interface rates from PKGD-04
Available ATE platforms and their capability
produces: Tester time bookings across development, characterisation and production

rel.text: Test time and test cost model. The platform's cost per hour is the model's rate.
Wafer sort and final test programs. Programs are written for a specific platform and its instrument set.

risks: Tester time not booked ahead. Capacity is shared, and a program without commitments waits behind programs with them.
Instrument options short of the interface rate. High-speed content cannot be run, and the shortfall is discovered when the program is written.
Pin count insufficient for parallel sites. Multi-site conversion later becomes impossible, and test cost stays where it started.
Platform chosen on capital cost alone. Cost per tested unit depends on throughput as much as on the tester's price.
Development capacity not separated from production. Program debug then competes with the ramp it is meant to enable.

purpose: Design, fabricate and qualify the probe card — the physical interface between the tester and the wafer, and the longest lead time in the stage.

Nothing can be sorted without it, and sort gates assembly. Twenty weeks of design and fabrication sit in front of the first wafer, which means the card has to be committed against a bump map that is frozen far earlier than most people expect.

steps.text: Probe card requirement and bump map extraction

TEST-03.flowNote: Step 4's eight weeks are pure vendor lead time and cannot be compressed. Step 1's bump map therefore has to be frozen roughly five months before sort, which is well before most people believe the design is stable.
consumes: Bump map from PD-15 and PKGD-03
Test plan and sort content from TEST-01
ATE platform and interface from TEST-02
produces: Probe card requirement and bump map

rel.text: Qualified probe card and load board. The probe card half of the deliverable.
Wafer sort and final test programs. A sort program cannot be debugged on silicon without a qualified card.

risks: Bump map changing after card release. Eight weeks of fabrication are lost, and sort — and therefore assembly — moves by that much.
Contact resistance out of specification. Marginal contact produces failures that look like silicon defects and corrupts the whole sort yield.
Planarity insufficient across the touchdown area. Some probes contact and some do not, and the pattern is subtle enough to be missed.
No spare card. A damaged card with a ten-week replacement stops sort entirely, and cards are damaged routinely.
Touchdown life below the wafer volume. Card degradation then appears as a yield trend that gets chased as a process problem.

purpose: Design, build and bring up the load board and socket — the package-level equivalent of the probe card, and what every final-test and characterisation measurement passes through.

The load board carries the tester's signals to the package at full rate and delivers its power at full current. It is a high-speed board design in its own right, and its own contribution to a measurement has to be small enough that what is measured is the silicon.

steps.text: Load board requirement and socket selection
Load board design with signal integrity
Socket contact and insertion life analysis
Power delivery design on the load board

TEST-04.flowNote: Step 5 is routinely underestimated. A high-power part draws current through the socket, and a load board whose power delivery droops produces failures at speed that are indistinguishable from silicon marginality.
consumes: Package pin map and ball map from PKGD-04
Test plan and final content from TEST-01
produces: Load board requirement and socket selection
Load board released to final test

rel.text: Qualified probe card and load board. The load board half of the deliverable.
Wafer sort and final test programs. The final test program is debugged on this hardware.

risks: Load board power delivery droop. It produces at-speed failures that look exactly like silicon marginality and consume weeks of debug.
Socket insertion life below the test volume. Contact degrades, yield trends downward, and the cause is looked for in the process.
Board channel loss consuming the measurement margin. The interface test then fails on the board rather than on the part.
Socket selected before the package is dimensioned. A socket that does not fit the finished package is discovered very late.
No correlation fixture. ATE and bench results then cannot be reconciled, and both are distrusted.

roles.d: Channel and power delivery on the board

exit: Power delivery adequate at maximum test current

purpose: Write the wafer sort test program — the screen that decides which die are worth assembling into a package.

On a 2.5D part, sort is the most economically consequential test in the flow. Everything it lets through carries an interposer, two HBM stacks and an assembly with it, so its coverage is measured against package cost rather than against die cost.

steps.text: Sort flow and test list definition
Parametric and process monitor test development
Program integration and debug on the tester

TEST-05.flowNote: Step 7 is where the program's economics are set. Limits too tight throw away good die; too loose and packages are built on bad ones. The guard bands should come from measurement uncertainty and package cost, not from convention.
consumes: Test plan and coverage matrix from TEST-01

rel.text: Wafer sort and final test programs, release-tagged. The sort half of the deliverable.
Test plan and test coverage matrix. What the program actually achieves updates what the plan claimed.

risks: Guard bands set by convention. On a part where an escape costs an assembled package, the limits should be derived from that cost.
Coverage below what the package economics need. Assembly yield then absorbs the difference, at many times the price.
Program debugged only in simulation. Tester behaviour differs from the model, and the difference is found on the first wafer.
Wafer map output not matching the assembly requirement. KGD selection depends on the map format, and a mismatch stops assembly.
Test time growing without check. Sort time multiplies across every wafer ever run, and content accretes silently.

roles.d: Wafer map format and KGD criteria

exit: Guard bands derived from package cost and measurement uncertainty
Coverage sufficient for the assembly economics
Wafer map format agreed with assembly

Sort test time against budget

purpose: Write the final test program that runs on the assembled package — at speed, at temperature, across every interface the product ships with.

Final test is the last screen before a customer sees the part. It exercises what sort could not: the assembled interfaces, the HBM stacks, the full power envelope, and the at-speed behaviour of a part that is now mechanically complete.

steps.text: Final test limits and guard bands

TEST-06.flowNote: Step 6 is where the 2.5D part differs most from a monolithic one. The HBM interfaces exist only after assembly, they cannot be tested at sort, and they are the most likely thing to be wrong about an assembled unit.
produces: Final test limits and guard bands

rel.text: Wafer sort and final test programs, release-tagged. The final-test half of the deliverable.
Test time and test cost model. Final test time is the larger half of the per-unit test cost.

risks: HBM interface content insufficient. The interfaces only exist after assembly, and a marginal one shipped is a field failure.
At-speed content not run at temperature. Timing marginality appears at the hot corner, and testing only at room temperature misses it.
Binning content added late. Grading is how the product line is built, and retrofitting it changes the flow and its cost.
Test time not tracked against the cost model. Final test dominates per-unit test cost and grows quietly.
Program debugged without real assembled units. The first units are precious, and the program has to be ready when they exist.
exit: HBM interfaces exercised at their operating rate
At-speed content run across the temperature range
Test time inside the cost model's allowance
measuredBy: Final test coverage against the DPPM target

Escapes found at system level

purpose: Build the characterisation content — shmoos, corners, parametric sweeps, datasheet parameter measurement — that turns silicon into a specified product.

Production test asks whether a part passes. Characterisation asks what the part actually does, across voltage, frequency and temperature, over a statistically meaningful sample. Every number in the datasheet comes from here, and so do the guard bands production test uses.

steps.text: Characterisation requirement from qualification and marketing

TEST-07.flowNote: Step 5 decides whether the results mean anything. A datasheet number from three units is an anecdote; the sample size follows from the distribution being characterised and the confidence the specification claims.
consumes: Load board and correlation fixture from TEST-04

rel.text: Characterisation test suite. This activity is the deliverable, and every datasheet number traces to it.
Test time and test cost model. Characterisation guard bands set how much production test time is spent on margin.

risks: Sample size too small for the claim. A datasheet parameter from a handful of units is a number without confidence behind it.
Corners not spanning the qualification range. Qualification then stresses conditions characterisation never measured.
Sweeps not automated. Manual shmoo consumes engineer-weeks per corner, and the corners get quietly reduced.
Datasheet parameters not traceable to a measurement. A customer question about a number then has no answer.
Analysis pipeline built after the data. Data is collected in a format nobody can analyse, and the campaign is re-run.
exit: Sample size supporting the datasheet's confidence claim
Corners spanning the qualification range
Every datasheet number traceable to a measurement
measuredBy: Sample size against the confidence claim
Corner coverage against qualification range
Datasheet parameters with traceable measurements

purpose: Port the DFT patterns to the tester's format and debug them there — the step between a pattern that simulates and a pattern that runs.

ATPG produces patterns against an idealised model. The tester has finite memory, real timing resolution, protocol constraints and a specific pin electronics behaviour. Every one of those turns a pattern that passes in simulation into one that fails on hardware, and finding out which is the work.

steps.text: Pattern translation to the tester format
Pattern simulation against the tester model
Pattern debug on silicon or emulation

TEST-08.flowNote: Step 3 is a hard constraint, not an optimisation. Tester pattern memory is finite, and a pattern set that exceeds it simply cannot be loaded — which is discovered at translation, not at ATPG.
consumes: ATE platform and memory depth from TEST-02

rel.text: ATE-ready pattern set with debug log. This activity is the deliverable.
Wafer sort and final test programs. Both programs run these patterns as their structural content.

risks: Pattern volume exceeding tester memory. The set cannot be loaded at all, and reduction after ATPG loses coverage.
Timing not mappable to the tester's resolution. At-speed patterns then run at the wrong speed, silently.
Patterns not simulated against the tester model. Failures are then debugged on silicon at tester rates rather than in simulation.
Pattern set not versioned. A yield excursion cannot be correlated to a pattern change nobody recorded.
Debug deferred until first silicon. Pattern problems and silicon problems then arrive together and cannot be separated.
entry: ATE platform and memory depth known from TEST-02
exit: Pattern set fitting tester memory without coverage loss
Timing mapped within the tester's resolution
Patterns simulated against the tester model before silicon
measuredBy: Coverage retained after volume reduction
Patterns passing tester-model simulation
Pattern failures found on silicon that simulation missed

purpose: Reduce test time and test cost per unit — an activity that starts early, because content is far cheaper to not write than to remove.

Test time is paid on every unit for the product's whole life. A second saved at final test on a million units is real money, and the savings available at plan time are much larger than the ones available after the program is written and qualified.
TEST-09.flowNote: Step 4's reordering is often the largest single win and costs nothing. Running the tests that fail most first means failing parts leave the tester early, and the average test time drops without any coverage change.
consumes: Test plan and flow from TEST-01
Tester cost per hour from TEST-02

rel.text: Test time and test cost model. This activity is the deliverable.
Test plan and test coverage matrix. Reduction decisions change what the plan promises, and the matrix has to follow.

risks: Optimisation started after qualification. Any content change then requires re-qualification, which is why this starts early.
Coverage traded away silently. Time reduction that loses coverage has to be an explicit decision against the DPPM target.
Reordering not done. It is free and it is the largest single lever, and it is routinely overlooked.
Multi-site assumed without pin count. The tester configuration from TEST-02 has to support it, and retrofitting it does not work.
Cost model without a yield assumption. Cost per good unit depends on yield, and a model without it understates the cost.
entry: Test plan and flow available from TEST-01
Content estimates or early programs available
exit: Optimisation done before qualification freezes the content
Coverage trades made explicitly against the DPPM target
Cost model including a yield assumption
measuredBy: Test time against the plan's budget
Cost per good unit against target
Coverage retained after reduction

purpose: Correlate ATE, bench and system results so that a part passing on the tester behaves the same way in a customer's system.

Three measurement environments produce three numbers for the same parameter, and they never agree exactly. What matters is whether the disagreement is understood: an unexplained gap between tester and system is either an escape path or an over-screen, and both are expensive.
TEST-10.flowNote: Step 5 is what makes correlation repeatable. A retained set of golden units re-measured after any change is how tester drift, load board degradation and program regressions are caught before they become yield excursions.
consumes: Load board and correlation fixture from TEST-04

rel.text: Characterisation test suite. Correlation validates that characterisation numbers hold outside the tester.
Wafer sort and final test programs. Guard-band adjustments from correlation go back into the programs.

risks: Discrepancy accepted without root cause. The gap is either an escape or an over-screen, and 'they just differ' resolves neither.
Correlation on too few units. Two units that agree prove very little about the population.
No golden units retained. Drift in the tester, the load board or the program then has nothing to be measured against.
System correlation skipped. ATE-to-bench is the easy half; ATE-to-system is the one the customer experiences.
Guard bands not updated. The correlation produced the information and nothing acted on it.
entry: Final test program running from TEST-06
Bench and system results available from bring-up
exit: Every material discrepancy root-caused, not accepted
Golden units retained and re-measurable
Guard bands updated from what correlation found
measuredBy: Discrepancies root-caused against found
Correlation sample size
Guard-band changes traced to correlation findings

purpose: Build the test data infrastructure — STDF collection, parsing, a yield database and the analysis on top of it — so that test results become information rather than files.

Every yield decision the program makes for the rest of its life is made from this data. Without a pipeline, the data exists as per-lot files nobody can query, and questions that should take an hour take a week or go unasked.

steps.text: Data requirement from yield, quality and characterisation
Traceability keys — lot, wafer, unit, assembly

TEST-11.flowNote: Step 3 is the piece that is hardest to add later. A unit's test result is only useful if it can be joined to its wafer position, its assembly lot and its bring-up history, and those keys have to be carried from the beginning.

Traceability scheme from ASSY-01 and ASSY-09

rel.text: Test data infrastructure and yield database. This activity is the deliverable.
Test plan and test coverage matrix. What the data shows about actual failure modes updates the plan's assumptions.

risks: Traceability keys added retroactively. Historical data then cannot be joined, and the most valuable early lots become unanalysable.
Pipeline built after the first lots run. The first silicon's data is the most informative the program will ever have, and it is the data most often lost.
Retention policy absent. Field returns arrive years later, and the test record for that unit has to still exist.
Dashboards without an alerting layer. A yield excursion is noticed at the weekly review rather than the same day.
Schema not covering characterisation. Characterisation data has a different shape, and a sort-only schema forces it into a separate silo.

exit: Traceability keys carried from the first lot

Retention policy covering the field-return horizon

Traceability join completeness

purpose: Receive the first units, check them and mount them — a short activity whose only job is to make sure the most valuable objects the program has ever produced are not damaged before they are powered.

There are very few first-silicon units and each represents the whole program's schedule. A unit destroyed by a mounting error or an unnoticed shipping defect is not replaceable inside any useful timeframe.

steps.text: Unit tracking register and allocation record
Pre-power checklist against the board's known issues

BU-01.flowNote: Step 4 is the reason board bring-up happened first. The checklist is only meaningful because EVB-07 already established which board behaviours are normal and which are faults.

Failure analysis reports. A unit's history starts here, and an FA needs to know how it was handled.

risks: Handling damage on an irreplaceable unit. ESD or mechanical damage at mounting costs a unit the program cannot replace.
Mounting onto an unvalidated board. A board fault then destroys the part, and EVB-07 exists to prevent exactly this.
No unit tracking. Every subsequent result has to be attributable to a specific unit and its history.
Incoming inspection skipped in the rush. Shipping damage is real and is much cheaper to find before power than after.
All units mounted at once. A systematic board or handling fault then takes the whole fleet rather than one unit.

purpose: Apply power for the first time — sequenced, current-limited and instrumented — and establish that the part is alive.

First power-on is the moment the whole design becomes physical. It is also the moment a shorted rail or a sequencing error can destroy a unit in milliseconds, which is why it is done with limits, with measurement, and with the ability to stop.

steps.text: Power sequencing verification against the specification
First power application with current limits
Anomaly triage on the first application
Health check and go/no-go for the next step

BU-02.flowNote: Step 2's current limits are what turn a fatal event into a diagnostic one. A rail that draws far more than expected trips the limit and the part survives to be investigated; without the limit it is destroyed and the information goes with it.
consumes: Power subsystem and protection from EVB-05

rel.text: Bring-up report with per-milestone health status. Power-on is the first milestone and its result sets the program's tone.

risks: Power applied without current limits. A short then destroys the unit instead of revealing itself.
Sequencing not verified against the specification. A wrong power-up order damages the part and the fault is the platform's, not the silicon's.
Rail currents not profiled. The first real power data is available at exactly this moment and is easy to not capture.
Multiple units powered before the first is understood. A systematic fault then takes several units instead of one.
Anomalies pushed past to reach the next milestone. Something unexplained at power-on rarely stays harmless.

purpose: Validate reset, clocking and PLL lock — the infrastructure everything else depends on, and the layer where a fault masquerades as a fault somewhere else.

A PLL that locks unreliably or a reset domain released in the wrong order produces symptoms all over the chip: boot failures, interface training failures, sporadic functional errors. Clearing this layer first means the failures found later are real.

steps.text: PLL lock across the frequency range
Reset sequence and domain release verification

BU-03.flowNote: Step 5's jitter measurement is easy to skip because the part appears to work without it. It matters because interface training margin depends on clock quality, and a jitter problem found here explains a class of failures that would otherwise be chased in the SerDes.
produces: PLL lock results across the range
Reset sequence and domain release verification

rel.text: Bring-up report with per-milestone health status. Clocking and reset form the second milestone.
Characterisation data set. PLL lock range and jitter are datasheet-relevant measurements.

risks: PLL lock validated only at nominal. The lock range matters because shmoo and characterisation will operate outside nominal.
Reset domain release order not verified. The resulting failures appear anywhere on the chip and are attributed to the wrong block.
Jitter unmeasured. Interface training margin depends on it, and a jitter problem is then debugged inside the SerDes.
Clock tree assumed correct because the part boots. A misconfigured divider is compatible with booting and incompatible with performance.
Clock quality measured through the board without accounting for it. The board contributes jitter and its contribution has to be separated.
entry: Units powered and healthy from BU-02
exit: PLL lock verified across the full operating range
Reset domain release order confirmed against the architecture
Jitter measured with the board's contribution separated

Jitter against the interface budget
Reset-related failures found later

purpose: Boot the part — ROM, firmware load, register access, first functional response — and confirm that the design does what it was written to do.

First boot is the milestone that turns a powered die into a working processor. It is also the point at which the design, the firmware, the board and the host software are all exercised together for the first time, which is why it is the milestone most likely to expose an integration assumption nobody wrote down.

steps.text: Boot ROM and initialisation sequence execution
Register access and device identity read
First bring-up report and status broadcast

BU-04.flowNote: Step 4's first successful register read is the moment the program knows the silicon is fundamentally sound. Everything before it is infrastructure and everything after it is degrees of correctness.
consumes: Boot ROM and firmware from the firmware team

rel.text: Bring-up report with per-milestone health status. First boot is the report's central milestone and where it starts being published widely.
Errata list with workarounds. Boot-time deviations are the earliest errata the program records.

risks: Boot failure with no state visible. Without debug access the failure is a symptom with no information, and debug access comes from EVB-06.
Firmware and hardware assumptions differing. The handoff is where two teams' expectations meet, and nobody wrote them down.
Register map drift. The tool reads addresses the silicon does not implement and reports plausible garbage.
Smoke test too shallow. A part that boots and does nothing else has passed a milestone without demonstrating much.
Status not broadcast. First boot is the news the whole program is waiting for, and silence is read as failure.

roles.d: Boot ROM, firmware load and handoff

entry: Clocking and reset validated in BU-03
exit: Successful register read and device identity confirmed
Boot-time deviations captured as errata candidates
Status broadcast to the program
measuredBy: Time from power-on to first register read
Boot failures with usable state captured
Smoke test coverage at first boot

purpose: Bring up the interfaces — PCIe/CXL link training, HBM training, die-to-die — which on this part is the largest single body of bring-up work and the most likely to produce a respin decision.

Interfaces are where design, package, board and protocol all meet. Training failures are notoriously hard to attribute because every layer can cause them, and the margin measurements taken here are what tell the program whether the part is comfortable or on the edge.
BU-05.flowNote: Step 3 is not optional even when training succeeds. A link that trains with no margin trains today and fails at temperature or on a different host, and only the eye measurement distinguishes the two.
consumes: SIPI channel budget and predictions from SIPI-04 and SIPI-05
Debug and trace access from EVB-06

rel.text: Interface compliance results with training margins. This activity is the deliverable, and the margins are what say whether the part is comfortable.
Bring-up report with per-milestone health status. Interface training is the milestone that decides whether the product works as designed.

risks: Training success accepted without margin measurement. A zero-margin link works on the bench and fails in the field.
Failures not attributable across layers. Design, package, board and protocol can all cause the same symptom, and the SIPI predictions are what separate them.
HBM training treated as a vendor problem. The interface is the program's, and its training parameters have to be understood locally.
Interoperability tested against one host. Customers use many, and a link that only works with the lab's host is not compliant.
Compliance run deferred. Formal compliance is a gate for certification and takes lab time that has to be booked.

roles.d: Margin attribution against the channel budget

entry: SIPI predictions available from SIPI-04 and SIPI-05
exit: Every interface's margin measured, not only its training result
Failures attributed to a layer against the SIPI prediction
Interoperability confirmed on more than the lab's host
measuredBy: Training margin against the SIPI prediction
Interfaces trained against interfaces designed
Interoperability across host platforms

purpose: Validate the memory subsystem — controller, address map, bandwidth, latency, ECC — because on an AI accelerator the memory system is most of the performance.

HBM training establishes that the links work; this establishes that the memory system delivers. Bandwidth and latency against the architecture model is the measurement the product's performance claims rest on, and it is where architectural assumptions meet a real memory controller.
BU-06.flowNote: Step 3 has to be done deliberately by injecting errors. ECC that has never corrected anything is ECC that has never been shown to work, and a broken correction path is silent until it matters.

rel.text: Characterisation data set. Memory bandwidth, latency and efficiency are core characterisation results.
Interface compliance results with training margins. Sustained memory operation is what proves the trained interfaces hold.

risks: ECC never exercised. A correction path that has never corrected an injected error has not been validated.
Bandwidth measured without the model to compare against. A number without a target says nothing about whether the design met its intent.
Refresh behaviour at temperature not checked. HBM refresh scales with temperature and the effect on bandwidth is real.
Address map validated only at the boundaries. Aliasing errors sit in the middle of the map and pass boundary tests.
Efficiency ignored in favour of peak. Peak bandwidth is a datasheet number; achieved efficiency is what workloads see.
entry: Architecture memory model available from ARCH-04
exit: ECC validated by injected errors, not by absence of failures
Bandwidth and latency compared against the architecture model
Efficiency characterised, not only peak
measuredBy: Achieved bandwidth against the model
Latency against the architectural target
ECC correction verified by injection

purpose: Shmoo the part across voltage, frequency and temperature — the measurement that establishes how much margin the design actually has.

Every operating condition the product will be specified at comes out of this. The shmoo shows where the part stops working, and the distance between that boundary and the nominal operating point is the margin the datasheet, the guard bands and the qualification plan all depend on.
BU-07.flowNote: Step 5 is what separates a characteristic from an anecdote. One unit's shmoo is that unit; the fleet's spread is what the population looks like, and the specification has to be set against the population.
consumes: Booted and interface-trained units from BU-04 and BU-05

rel.text: Characterisation data set — V/F/T shmoo and power measurements. This activity is the deliverable.
Bring-up report with per-milestone health status. Margin is the strongest single indicator of whether the silicon is healthy.

risks: Shmoo on a single unit. The result describes that unit and is used as if it described the population.
Room temperature only. The hot and cold corners are where the margin is smallest and where qualification will operate.
Manual sweeps. The corner count then gets reduced to fit the available engineer time, silently.
Thermal throttling inside the sweep. The shmoo then maps the cooling solution rather than the silicon.
Margin measured but not fed into guard bands. The data exists and production test still uses convention.

roles.d: Failure mode interpretation at the boundaries

entry: Units functional from BU-04 and BU-05
exit: Shmoo across a fleet, not a single unit
Temperature corners included, not only room
No throttling inside the measured region
measuredBy: Margin at the worst corner
Units in the shmoo sample
Corners measured against planned

purpose: Measure real performance against the architecture model — the check on whether the product does what it was sold as doing.

The whole program was justified by a performance projection. This is where that projection meets a physical part running real workloads, and any gap has to be attributed: to the model, to the design, to the memory system, or to the software driving it.
BU-08.flowNote: Step 6 is where the program learns something durable. A gap attributed to the model improves the next program's projections; a gap attributed to the design becomes an errata or a respin input; an unattributed gap teaches nothing.
consumes: Functional units from BU-04 through BU-06

rel.text: Characterisation data set. Performance and efficiency measurements are part of the product's characterisation.
Bring-up report with per-milestone health status. Performance against target is the milestone the business cares about most.

risks: Performance measured on unrepresentative workloads. A benchmark that is not what customers run produces a number that does not predict their experience.
Gap reported without attribution. Nobody can act on it, and the next program repeats the modelling error.
Software limiting the measurement. An immature stack understates the silicon, and the difference has to be established rather than assumed.
Efficiency ignored. Performance per watt is the metric this product class is bought on, and raw throughput alone misleads.
Measured at a single operating point. Real deployment spans conditions, and performance at nominal is not the whole picture.
exit: Every material gap attributed to a cause
Efficiency measured alongside throughput
Software's contribution to the measurement established
measuredBy: Performance against the architecture projection
Efficiency against the target
Gaps attributed against gaps found

purpose: Debug what is wrong — reproduce it, isolate it, extract the internal state, find the root cause, and get failure analysis where physical evidence is needed.

This is the activity the whole DFT and debug infrastructure investment exists to serve. It runs alongside every other bring-up activity because anomalies arrive from all of them, and its throughput largely determines how long bring-up takes.

steps.text: Internal state extraction via DFT and trace

BU-09.flowNote: Step 3 is the highest-leverage step in the activity. An anomaly reproduced in simulation can be examined with full visibility and unlimited retries, which is an environment no amount of silicon debug can match.
consumes: DFT and trace access from DFT-08 and EVB-06
Simulation and emulation environments from DV-08 and DV-11
Design database and RTL from RTL-09

rel.text: Failure analysis reports. This activity is the deliverable, and physical FA is its most conclusive form.
Errata list with workarounds. Every root cause found here becomes an errata entry or a fix.

risks: Symptoms treated instead of causes. A workaround without a root cause hides a mechanism that resurfaces in the field.
No path back to simulation. Debug then happens only on silicon, with limited visibility and long turnaround per hypothesis.
Design team engaged late. The people who wrote the logic can often recognise a symptom in minutes, and validation debugs alone for days first.
Units consumed by destructive FA too readily. Physical analysis destroys the unit, and there are very few.
Findings not captured. The same anomaly is then debugged twice by different engineers.
entry: DFT and trace access working from EVB-06
exit: Root cause established rather than symptom suppressed
Anomalies reproduced in simulation where possible
Findings captured so they are debugged once
BU-09.dependsNote: Anomalies arrive from every bring-up activity; the dependencies listed are the ones that supply the debug capability rather than the problems.
measuredBy: Anomalies root-caused against opened
Median time from anomaly to root cause
Anomalies reproduced outside silicon

purpose: Turn what is wrong into a documented errata list with workarounds — the honest account of the silicon's behaviour that customers and the next revision both need.

Every part ships with errata. What distinguishes a well-run program is that its errata are known, characterised, worked around and disclosed, rather than discovered by a customer. This activity is where debug findings become a product document.
BU-10.flowNote: Step 4's validation is the part that gets skipped. A workaround that has been described but never run is a hypothesis, and shipping it as a mitigation is how a known issue becomes a field failure anyway.

rel.text: Errata list with workarounds. This activity is the deliverable, and it is what ships alongside the product.
Respin versus metal-fix decision record. Which errata are tolerable with a workaround is the decision's main input.

risks: Workarounds documented but never validated. The mitigation then fails in the field and the errata gave false comfort.
Severity assessed by engineering alone. Customer impact depends on use models, and the assessment needs that perspective.
Errata suppressed for commercial reasons. Undisclosed known issues discovered by a customer damage far more than the disclosure would have.
Errata list not versioned against silicon revision. Which errata apply to which stepping becomes ambiguous the moment a second stepping exists.
Documentation deferred to the end. The context is freshest at root cause, and reconstructing it months later loses detail.
exit: Every workaround validated on silicon, not only described
Severity assessed with customer use models in view
Errata versioned against silicon revision
measuredBy: Workarounds validated against documented
Errata found by customers after release
Time from root cause to documented errata

purpose: Decide whether the silicon needs a respin, a metal fix, or nothing — the single most consequential decision the program makes after tapeout.

A full-mask respin costs a mask set and roughly a quarter of schedule. A metal fix costs far less but can only reach defects in the routing layers. Shipping as-is with workarounds costs nothing now and possibly a great deal later. The decision has to weigh all three against evidence rather than optimism.
BU-11.flowNote: Step 2 is bounded by physics rather than by will. A metal fix can only change routing layers, and whether the required change fits inside them is a question with a factual answer that has to be established before the decision is framed.
consumes: Errata list and severity from BU-10
Mask and fab cost from TECH-08

rel.text: Respin versus metal-fix decision record. This activity is the deliverable, and the record is what the program is held to.
Errata list with workarounds. Errata not fixed by the decision become permanent, documented behaviour.

risks: Decision made on schedule pressure alone. Shipping a part with a real defect to protect a date routinely costs more than the delay would have.
Metal-fix feasibility assumed. It is a physical question about which layers the fix touches, and it is often answered optimistically.
Margin data not weighed. A part with adequate function and no margin fails in the field, and the shmoo already said so.
Decision unrecorded. Six months later nobody can reconstruct what was known and what was accepted.
Customer input excluded. Whether an errata is tolerable depends on what customers do with the part.

roles.d: Owns the decision and its record

entry: Errata list and severities available from BU-10
Margin and performance data from BU-07 and BU-08
exit: Metal-fix feasibility established physically, not assumed
Margin evidence weighed alongside functional defects
Decision recorded with what was known at the time
measuredBy: Decision made against the planned date
Feasibility claims that held
Defects found later that the decision did not consider

purpose: Get samples to customers with everything they need to use them — screened units, documentation, errata, and a channel to report back.

Customer samples start the evaluation cycle that decides design wins, and they start it months before mass production. What ships with the unit determines whether the customer's first week is productive or spent rediscovering issues the program already knows about.

steps.text: Unit selection and screening for samples

BU-12.flowNote: Step 5 is the one that pays back most. A customer who finds something and has an obvious route to report it gives the program early field data; one who does not gives it a design loss with no explanation.
produces: Shipped samples with support in place

rel.text: Customer sample release package. This activity is the deliverable — units plus everything needed to use them.
Errata list with workarounds. The errata pack that ships with samples is the errata list's first external use.

risks: Samples shipped without errata. The customer spends their first week rediscovering known issues and loses confidence in the part.
Units not screened before shipping. A marginal sample creates a customer-visible failure that the program cannot investigate remotely.
Documentation lagging the silicon. A datasheet describing behaviour the sample does not have generates support load and doubt.
No feedback channel. Customer findings then arrive as rumour or not at all, and the program loses its earliest field data.
Samples shipped before the respin decision. If a respin follows, customers are evaluating a stepping that will not ship.
exit: Errata pack shipping with every sample
Units screened before shipment
Feedback channel established and staffed
measuredBy: Samples shipped against commitment
Customer issues that were already documented
Feedback received through the channel

purpose: Define what qualification means for this product — which standards apply, which stresses run, on how many units, and against what acceptance criteria.

Qualification is the evidence that the part survives its intended life. The plan is where that evidence is designed: too little and a customer's own qualification finds what yours did not, too much and months of chamber time are spent on stresses nobody required.

steps.text: Standard selection — JEDEC, AEC and customer applicability
Stress matrix and sample size definition

MP-01.flowNote: Step 4 is why this activity runs first. HTOL occupies a chamber for a thousand hours, and chambers are shared; a booking made late pushes the whole qualification campaign and therefore mass production.
consumes: Product requirements and quality target from DEF-04
Application and use conditions from DEF-03

rel.text: Qualification plan and JEDEC-compliant qualification report. The plan half of the deliverable; the report follows from executing it.
Production readiness review sign-off. The plan defines what evidence the readiness review will be asked to accept.

risks: Chamber capacity booked late. Stress duration is fixed and capacity is shared, so a late booking moves mass production directly.
Sample sizes below the confidence the claim needs. A reliability claim from too few units does not support the specification.
Customer requirements collected after the plan. A customer-specific stress discovered later restarts a months-long campaign.
Three lots not planned. Standards generally require multiple production lots, and a single-lot qualification is not accepted.
Use conditions assumed rather than specified. The acceleration factors depend on them, and wrong conditions make the whole campaign non-representative.
entry: Product use conditions defined in DEF-03
exit: Chamber capacity booked against the full stress duration
Sample sizes supporting the reliability claim
Customer-specific requirements included before release
measuredBy: Chamber capacity secured against the plan
Sample size against the confidence claim
Customer requirements captured before execution

purpose: Run the reliability stresses — HTOL, high-temperature storage, temperature cycling, uHAST, THB — that demonstrate the silicon survives its specified life.

This is eighteen weeks of mostly waiting, and it is the longest fixed-duration item between first silicon and mass production. HTOL alone is a thousand hours; it cannot be shortened, only started earlier or run in parallel.

steps.text: Stress chamber loading and campaign start

MP-02.flowNote: Step 5's interim readouts are what turn a pass/fail campaign into a learning one. A parameter drifting at 500 hours predicts a failure at 1000 that would otherwise arrive as a surprise at the end of a four-month run.

rel.text: Reliability and package qualification data packages. The silicon-reliability half of the deliverable.
Qualification plan and JEDEC-compliant qualification report. These are the results the report is written from.

risks: Campaign started late. The duration is fixed, so every week of delay is a week of mass production delay, one for one.
No pre-stress characterisation. Drift cannot be measured without a baseline, and a failure cannot be distinguished from a part that was always marginal.
Interim readouts skipped. Failures then arrive only at the end, with no time left to respond before the ramp.
Stress failures not analysed. A failure without a mechanism cannot be judged as systematic or as a one-off, and the distinction decides the ramp.
Units insufficient for the full matrix. A stress dropped for lack of units is a gap in the qualification the customer will find.
exit: Pre-stress baseline recorded for every unit
Interim readouts taken at the planned intervals
Every stress failure analysed to a mechanism
measuredBy: Campaign start against plan
Failures per stress against the acceptance criterion
Failures analysed to a mechanism

purpose: Qualify the part's ESD and latch-up robustness — HBM and CDM discharge, and latch-up immunity — the handling-survival properties every downstream user depends on.

ESD failures happen in assembly lines, in labs and in the field, and they are almost never traced back to the part that could not take them. The classification levels are what tell a customer's manufacturing engineer how to handle the device.

steps.text: ESD and latch-up test plan and pin classification

MP-03.flowNote: Step 4 matters more than step 2 on a package this size. CDM stress scales with package capacitance, and a large 2.5D package charges to a far higher energy than a small one — the CDM level is usually the binding constraint.
consumes: ESD protection design from AMS-09 and PD-11

rel.text: Reliability and package qualification data packages. ESD and latch-up classification are part of the qualification package.
Datasheet and product documentation set. ESD classification is a datasheet parameter every handler reads.

risks: CDM underestimated for the package size. A large package stores far more charge, and the CDM level is usually the binding one.
ESD failures not analysed. Which pin and which protection element failed is what makes the result actionable for a fix.
Latch-up tested only at room temperature. Latch-up susceptibility increases with temperature, and the hot corner is the real test.
Classification below what customer assembly requires. A part that cannot survive a customer's line is a part they cannot buy.
Pin classification incomplete. Untested pin combinations are unqualified pins, and there is no assumption to fall back on.
exit: CDM evaluated against the package's actual capacitance
Latch-up tested at the hot corner
Classification meeting customer assembly requirements
measuredBy: ESD classification achieved against target
Latch-up immunity at maximum temperature
Pin combinations tested against total

purpose: Qualify the package — moisture sensitivity, board-level reliability, drop and bend — which on a 2.5D structure is where the reliability risk actually concentrates.

The silicon's reliability is a well-understood function of process and use conditions. The package's is not: a large interposer on an organic substrate with two HBM stacks has thermal expansion mismatches on every interface, and this is where they are proven or found out.

steps.text: Board-level reliability — temperature cycling on board
Warpage and co-planarity tracked through stress

MP-04.flowNote: Step 3 is what turns this campaign into a predictive model rather than a single data point. Correlating measured joint life against the model means the next package variant can be assessed without repeating twelve weeks of testing.

rel.text: Reliability and package qualification data packages. The package half of the deliverable.
Qualification plan and JEDEC-compliant qualification report. Package qualification is a required section of the report.

risks: MSL classification worse than the assembly process needs. A high moisture sensitivity forces bake-and-handle procedures on every customer line.
Board-level reliability short of the application requirement. The joints, not the die, then set the product's life.
PTV results not compared. The vehicles predicted this behaviour, and the comparison validates or invalidates the whole vehicle programme.
Warpage measured only before stress. The interesting change is what stress does to it, and that requires measurement through the campaign.
Failures attributed to the package without analysis. A CPI failure and a solder joint failure need different fixes and look similar from outside.
entry: PTV reliability data available from PTV-10
exit: MSL classification compatible with customer assembly
Board-level life meeting the application requirement
Results compared against the PTV prediction
measuredBy: MSL level achieved
Board-level cycles to failure against requirement
Correlation between measured and modelled joint life

purpose: Run yield learning continuously through the ramp — pareto, defect analysis, corrective action, and a yield model checked against the cost target.

Yield is the difference between a product that makes money and one that does not, and first-ramp yield is never where the cost model assumed. This activity runs for the whole stage because yield learning is a rate, not an event: what matters is how fast the pareto's top item is removed and replaced by the next.

steps.text: Yield data pipeline and baseline establishment
Failure pareto by bin and failure mode
Yield model against the cost target

MP-05.flowNote: Step 5 is the split that decides who acts. Die yield, assembly yield and test yield have different owners and different fixes, and a combined number tells none of them what to do.
produces: Failure pareto by bin and mode

rel.text: Yield model versus cost target report. This activity is the deliverable, and the model is what the business plan is checked against.
Production readiness review sign-off. Yield at the readiness review is one of its principal acceptance criteria.

risks: Yield reported as one number. Die, assembly and test yield have different owners, and a combined figure directs nobody.
Spatial signatures not analysed. Edge, centre and radial patterns each point at a different process cause and are visible only on the wafer map.
Corrective actions not verified. An action taken without confirming the pareto moved is an action that may have done nothing.
Excursions detected at the weekly review. By then a week of material is affected, and detection has to be automatic.
Yield model not checked against the cost target. The gap between achieved and assumed yield is the product's margin, and it can go unnoticed for months.

roles.d: Owns yield learning and the pareto
Yield model against the business case

entry: Test data infrastructure running from TEST-11
Fab and assembly yield data flowing
exit: Yield split by die, assembly and test
Corrective actions verified against the pareto
Yield model reconciled with the cost target
measuredBy: Yield against the cost model assumption
Pareto top-item removal rate
Time from excursion to detection

purpose: Release the production test program — frozen, guard-band-validated, qualified and version-controlled — for every unit the product will ever ship.

After this release, a change to test content requires re-qualification. That makes the release a genuine freeze, and it makes the guard-band validation that precedes it the last chance to be sure the limits neither throw away good parts nor let bad ones through.

steps.text: Production flow validation on volume lots

MP-06.flowNote: Step 3 quantifies both directions of error. Escapes cost the customer's trust and over-kill costs yield, and a limit set without measuring both is optimising one at the other's expense without knowing it.
consumes: Sort and final programs from TEST-05 and TEST-06
Characterisation data from TEST-07 and BU-07
produces: Production flow validation on volume lots

rel.text: Production test program release. This activity is the deliverable, and after it the content is frozen.
Production readiness review sign-off. A released and qualified test program is a precondition for the review.

risks: Guard bands not validated against characterisation. Limits then rest on convention rather than on what the silicon actually does.
Over-kill unmeasured. Good parts are discarded on every lot and the loss is attributed to yield rather than to the limits.
Flow validated on one lot. Lot-to-lot variation is the thing the flow has to tolerate, and one lot cannot show it.
Porting across the tester fleet without correlation. Tester-to-tester differences then present as yield differences by machine.
Released without version control. A yield excursion cannot be correlated with a program change nobody can identify.

roles.d: Owns the release and its guard bands

entry: Programs debugged from TEST-05 and TEST-06
Volume lots available for flow validation
exit: Guard bands derived from characterisation, not convention
Both escape and over-kill quantified
Flow validated across multiple lots and testers
measuredBy: Escape rate against the DPPM target
Over-kill rate at the released limits
Tester-to-tester yield spread after porting

purpose: Convert production test to multi-site and cut test time — the change that makes the cost per unit sustainable at volume.

Single-site testing is fine for a hundred units and ruinous for a million. Multi-site conversion multiplies throughput per tester and divides the capital needed for the ramp, and it is a real engineering exercise because parallel sites interfere with each other in ways single-site testing never reveals.

steps.text: Multi-site feasibility on the production hardware
Multi-site load board and probe card conversion
Test time reduction on the released content

MP-07.flowNote: Step 5 is what makes the conversion trustworthy. Sites differ — in contact, in power delivery, in noise coupling — and a systematic site bias shows up as a yield difference that gets chased as a process problem for weeks.
consumes: Tester pin count and configuration from TEST-02
Load board and probe card designs from TEST-03 and TEST-04
produces: Test time reduction on released content

rel.text: Production test program release. The multi-site flow is a controlled revision of the released program.
Ramp plan and supply commitment. Throughput per tester is what the capacity commitment is built from.

risks: Site-to-site bias undetected. It appears as a yield difference and is investigated as a process problem for weeks.
Pin count insufficient for the site count. The tester configuration from TEST-02 bounds this, and it cannot be changed now.
Parallel power delivery inadequate. Four parts drawing full current through one load board droop in ways one part does not.
Conversion done after the ramp starts. Capital is then committed at single-site throughput and cannot be recovered.
Time reduction changing coverage. Any content change after MP-06 requires re-qualification, which is expensive at this point.

roles.d: Load board and probe card conversion

entry: Tester configuration supporting the site count
Test time analysis available from TEST-09
exit: Site-to-site bias measured and within tolerance
Parallel power delivery adequate at full current
Conversion complete before capital is committed to the ramp
measuredBy: Throughput multiple achieved against site count
Site-to-site yield spread
Cost per tested unit after conversion

purpose: Validate the design across process corners using split lots — material deliberately fabricated at the edges of the process window.

Production silicon spans the process distribution, and the units bring-up characterised came from one lot near its centre. Split lots produce the fast and slow corners on purpose, which is the only way to know whether the design's margin survives the population it will actually be built from.
MP-08.flowNote: Step 6 closes a loop opened right back at signoff. The design was timed against corner models; measuring real corner silicon says whether those models were pessimistic, accurate, or — the dangerous case — optimistic.

rel.text: Yield model versus cost target report. Corner yield is what the model has to predict across the real distribution.
Qualification plan and JEDEC-compliant qualification report. Corner validation is part of demonstrating the design is production-worthy.

risks: Corner models optimistic against real silicon. The design was signed off against those models, and a gap here means the margin does not exist.
Split lots not actually at the corners. Material that drifted back toward centre proves nothing about the edges.
Cpk not computed. Capability against the specification is what predicts production yield, and a pass/fail result does not.
Corner characterisation skipped for schedule. The population's edges are then only seen in production, as an unexplained yield tail.
Process window recommendation not fed back to the fab. The data exists and the process keeps running at its original centre point.
entry: Split lot material available from FAB-06
exit: Split material verified to be at the intended corners
Cpk computed against the specification
Model-to-silicon correlation established at both corners
measuredBy: Corner spread achieved against intended
Cpk against the specification
Model-to-silicon gap at the corners

purpose: Hold the production readiness review — the cross-functional gate where every function states whether it is ready — and stand up change control for everything that follows.

This is the program's last formal decision point. After it, the product is in production and every change goes through customer notification. The review's value is that it forces each function to say ready or not ready on the record, which is a different act from being asked in a meeting whether there are any concerns.

steps.text: Gap closure and conditional item tracking

MP-09.flowNote: Step 4's conditional items are where a review either works or becomes theatre. A conditional pass with an owner, a date and a consequence is a real mechanism; a conditional pass without them is an unconditional pass with a note attached.
consumes: Qualification results from MP-02, MP-03 and MP-04
produces: Gap closure and conditional item tracking
Signed-off readiness and established PCN process

rel.text: Production readiness review sign-off. This activity is the deliverable — the record of who declared ready and on what evidence.
Mass Production release record. The formal statement that the product is in production, with its conditions.

risks: Review held without evidence. Function-by-function assurances are not the same as qualification data, and a review that accepts them is not a gate.
Conditional items without owners or dates. The condition is then never closed and the pass was unconditional in practice.
Change control not established. Post-production changes then reach customers without notification, which is a contractual failure.
Dissent not recorded. A function that said not-ready and was overruled is the program's most valuable record if something goes wrong.
Document baseline not frozen. Which datasheet, which errata, which test program was released becomes ambiguous immediately.

roles.d: Owns the review and its record

entry: Qualification results available from MP-02 through MP-04
exit: Every conditional item with an owner, a date and a consequence
Change control and PCN process established before release
Dissenting positions recorded, not resolved off the record
MP-09.dependsNote: The review is the convergence point for the whole stage — it consumes the output of nearly every other MP activity.
measuredBy: Readiness criteria met against total
Conditional items closed by their date
Post-release issues that the review had evidence for

purpose: Commit the supply chain and the ramp — wafers, substrates, HBM, assembly and test capacity — against a demand forecast, with the lead times and second sources that make the commitment real.

A ramp is a chain of commitments made months before the volume they serve. Substrates have long lead times, HBM is allocated across the industry, and assembly capacity is booked. Any one of them short stops the ramp, and none of them can be fixed quickly.

steps.text: Wafer, substrate and HBM supply commitment
Supply chain risk and second-source plan

MP-10.flowNote: Step 8 runs last but covers everything before it. Each commitment made in steps 2 and 4 is a single point of failure, and the plan has to say what happens if any one of them fails — before it does.
consumes: Demand forecast from DEF-05 and product marketing
Substrate and interposer supply from PKGD-09
produces: Wafer, substrate and HBM supply commitments
Supply chain risk and second-source plan

rel.text: Ramp plan and supply commitment. This activity is the deliverable.
Yield model versus cost target report. Cost per unit at volume is where the yield model meets the actual supply cost.

risks: HBM allocation insufficient. It is allocated across the industry and a shortfall stops the ramp regardless of everything else.
Substrate lead time underestimated. Advanced substrates are long-lead and capacity-constrained, and the buffer has to reflect that.
Ramp planned against an optimistic yield. Volume commitments then require more wafer starts than were booked.
No second source anywhere in the chain. Every single-source node is a single point of failure for the whole product.
Capacity committed before the readiness review. A conditional readiness outcome then meets an unconditional supply commitment.

roles.d: Owns the ramp and supply commitments

exit: Every long-lead item committed with buffer
Ramp built on the achieved yield, not the assumed one
Single-source nodes identified with a contingency
measuredBy: Long-lead items committed against required
Ramp achieved against plan
Single-source nodes with a contingency

purpose: Obtain the compliance and certification the product cannot ship without — interface compliance, EMC and safety, and materials declarations.

These are gates rather than engineering activities: without a PCIe or CXL compliance listing, without EMC certification, without RoHS and REACH declarations, the product cannot be sold in most markets regardless of how well it works.

steps.text: PCIe/CXL compliance testing at a plugfest
Materials compliance — RoHS, REACH, conflict minerals

MP-11.flowNote: Step 2 depends on an event calendar the program does not control. Plugfests happen on fixed dates a few times a year, and missing one costs a quarter rather than a week.
consumes: Materials declarations from the supply chain

rel.text: Compliance certificates. This activity is the deliverable, and without it the product cannot ship.
Datasheet and product documentation set. Compliance statements and classifications are part of the product documentation.

risks: Plugfest date missed. They occur a few times a year on fixed dates, and missing one delays the listing by a quarter.
Materials declarations not collected from suppliers. Every component in the package needs one, and collecting them takes months.
Compliance failure discovered at the plugfest. Pre-compliance testing exists precisely so that formal testing is a confirmation.
Export classification left late. A high-performance accelerator may be controlled, and the classification determines which markets exist.
Certification scope assessed for one region. Requirements differ by market, and a missing certification closes a region entirely.
entry: Package construction and materials known from PKGD-11
exit: Compliance listing obtained, not just tested
Materials declarations collected for every component
Export classification completed before shipment
measuredBy: Certifications obtained against required
Plugfest attendance against schedule
Markets open at launch

purpose: Release the product documentation — datasheet, user guide, errata, application notes — the artefacts a customer actually receives alongside the silicon.

The documentation is the product as far as most customers experience it. A datasheet parameter that cannot be traced to a measurement, a programming model that omits a required sequence, or an errata list that lags the silicon each cost far more support effort than the writing would have.
MP-12.flowNote: Step 3 is what makes the datasheet defensible. Every number should point at a measurement, its conditions and its sample size, so that a customer's question about a parameter has an answer rather than a search.
consumes: Characterisation data from TEST-07 and BU-07
Programming model from RTL-06 and ARCH-06
produces: User guide and programming model documentation

rel.text: Datasheet and product documentation set. This activity is the deliverable.
Mass Production release record. A released documentation set is part of what the release record attests to.

risks: Datasheet parameters without traceable measurements. A customer question then has no answer, and the number cannot be defended.
Errata lagging the silicon. The most useful document ships out of date, which is worse than shipping it late.
Programming model incomplete. Required initialisation sequences omitted from the guide become support cases, one per customer.
Documentation written from specifications rather than measurements. It then describes the intended product rather than the one shipping.
No revision control on released documents. Which datasheet revision a customer holds becomes unknowable.
entry: Characterisation data available from TEST-07 and BU-07
exit: Every datasheet parameter traceable to a measurement
